title: 09-6: Vector Meets Raster: Cropping, Masking and Extracting Values
section: What you will and will not learn today
text:
What you will and will not learn today

The planDirections


Weather, soil, satellite images and elevation come as rasters (grids of cells, lecture 09-2). Your units of analysis, such as fields, counties and farms, are usually vector features (lecture 09-1). Most research that uses both needs one step: putting the raster’s values onto the vector features. An AI assistant can write that step in one line. What it cannot do is:

know whether the raster covers all of your features
decide which cells count as “in” a polygon when a cell is only partly inside
know what the raster’s values mean: their units, and which day each layer is
tell whether the numbers it returns are right

So today is about:

The concept: cropping, masking and extracting values, and which cells count for a polygon
Reading code: the patterns these lines follow
Asking AI: what to say about the raster and the features
Checking: rows returned, cells per feature, features with no value, and maps




Ask your AI assistant to install the sf, terra, tidyterra, tidyverse and here packages if you have not already. terra is the package for rasters; tidyterra lets ggplot draw them.
This lecture assumes lecture 09-1 (vector basics) and lecture 09-2 (raster basics): what a cell, a layer and a CRS (coordinate reference system) are.
The data files used on these slides sit in the same folder as the slides, so a path here is just the file name. In your own project, paths are built with here::here() (lecture 03-1).

title: 09-6: Vector Meets Raster: Cropping, Masking and Extracting Values
section: The data on these slides
text:
The data on these slides

Two layersA map



ne_ppt_2012aug.tif: daily precipitation from PRISM (a US weather dataset), in millimetres, one layer per day from 1 to 5 August 2012, cells about 3.5 km wide, NAD83 longitude and latitude
ne_counties.gpkg: the 93 counties of Nebraska, in the same CRS

The slides mostly use the total over the five days, one layer made by adding the five (sum(ppt)).











The question the slides answer: how much rain fell in each county over those five days?

title: 09-6: Vector Meets Raster: Cropping, Masking and Extracting Values
section: Three operations
text:
Three operations









Operation
What it does
Shape of the result
Typical reason




Crop
Cuts the raster to the rectangle around the vector features
a smaller raster
a smaller file, a map of just your area


Mask
Sets every cell outside the polygons to missing (NA)
a raster of the same size
a map that shows only your area; leaving outside cells out of a calculation


Extract
Reads the raster’s values at the vector features
a table, one row per feature or per cell
putting weather, soil or crop data onto your fields or counties



Extracting is the one your analysis depends on. Cropping and masking are usually steps before it, or for maps.



Note


Cropping a raster is like st_crop() for vector layers in lecture 09-4: it cuts to a rectangle, not to the outline. Masking is what cuts to the outline.

title: 09-6: Vector Meets Raster: Cropping, Masking and Extracting Values
section: Extracting: points get one cell, polygons get many
text:
Extracting: points get one cell, polygons get many

PointsPolygons: which cells countCells used by each ruleWhy it matters


Each point lies in exactly one cell, so it gets that cell’s value: one value per point and layer. Five layers give five values per point.


A polygon covers many cells, some only partly. There are three rules for which cells count, and they give different answers:



















Rule
Cells used
terra::extract() option




1. The cell’s centre (black dot) is inside
14
the default


2. Any part of the cell is inside
26
touches = TRUE


3. Every touched cell, weighted by the share of it inside (shown by how dark the cell is)
26, with weights
exact = TRUE (returns a fraction column)





The rule decides the answer when the cells near the edge differ from those in the middle and when the polygon covers few cells. With 3.5 km cells, a Nebraska county covers between 40 and 941 cell centres, and the rule changes county averages very little. With cells five times wider (about 18 km), 19 counties cover only 1 or 2 cell centres, and the default and weighted averages differ by up to 5.5 mm for the same county (silent failures, later).
The weighted rule is the most accurate; the default is the fastest. What matters is that you choose, knowing the cell size relative to your polygons.

title: 09-6: Vector Meets Raster: Cropping, Masking and Extracting Values
section: Cropping and masking
text:
Cropping and masking

The patternA real example



new_raster <- raster_function(raster, vector_layer)









Part
What it is
Required?




raster_function
crop or mask, from terra
Yes


raster
The raster to cut, always first
Yes


vector_layer
The features that decide which cells stay; an sf layer works, or a terra vector made with vect()
Yes



The two are usually chained, crop first to make the raster small, then mask: mask(crop(ppt, counties), counties).



ppt_ne <- mask(crop(ppt_total, vect(counties)), vect(counties))










The cells outside Nebraska are now missing (NA), drawn transparent. vect() turns the sf layer into a terra vector, which some terra functions require.

title: 09-6: Vector Meets Raster: Cropping, Masking and Extracting Values
section: Extracting values
text:
Extracting values

The patternVariations you will seeA real example: pointsA real example: polygons



values_table <- terra::extract(raster, vector_layer, fun = summary, exact = TRUE_or_FALSE)









Part
What it is
Required?




values_table <-
A table (not a layer): column ID, then one column per raster layer
Needed to keep the result


raster
The raster to read, always first
Yes


vector_layer
Points or polygons, always second
Yes


fun =
For polygons: summarise each polygon’s cells (mean, sum, …) into one row per polygon
No; without it, one row per cell


exact = TRUE
For polygons: add the share of each cell inside (rule 3)
No; default is rule 1


na.rm = TRUE
Ignore missing cells when summarising
No



ID is the row number of the feature in the vector layer: ID == 3 is the third county. It is not the county’s own ID.



terra::extract(ppt, counties, fun = mean, na.rm = TRUE, ID = FALSE): no ID column; the rows are in the vector layer’s order
terra::extract(ppt, counties, bind = TRUE): the values added to the vector layer directly, as a terra vector
exactextractr::exact_extract(ppt, counties, "mean"): another package, often written by AI; it always uses rule 3 (weighted by share), and returns a plain table in the layer’s order
terra::zonal(ppt, vect(counties), fun = "mean"): a summary per polygon; the same as extract() with fun



Precipitation at each well, all five days:

ppt_wells <- terra::extract(ppt, vect(wells))
head(ppt_wells, 3)

  ID ppt_2012_08_01 ppt_2012_08_02 ppt_2012_08_03 ppt_2012_08_04 ppt_2012_08_05
1  1          3.438         15.859              0          8.652              0
2  2          8.752         14.504              0          0.413              0
3  3         12.323         26.124              0          0.049              0


One row per well (1000 rows for 1000 wells), one column per day. Putting it back on the wells is a column bind, since the rows are in the same order: bind_cols(wells, select(ppt_wells, -ID)).


Average five-day total in each county, rule 3:

ex <- terra::extract(ppt_total, vect(counties), exact = TRUE)
head(ex, 3)

  ID ppt_total  fraction
1  1    20.734 0.2410224
2  1    20.515 0.2716368
3  1    20.718 0.2704296


One row per cell per county, with fraction the share of the cell inside the county. Summarised to one row per county, weighting by fraction:

county_ppt <- ex |>
  group_by(ID) |>
  summarise(ppt_mm = sum(ppt_total * fraction) / sum(fraction)) |>
  mutate(countyfp = counties$countyfp[ID])
nrow(county_ppt)

[1] 93


counties$countyfp[ID] turns each row number back into the county’s own ID, so the table can be merged onto the counties by key column (Chapter 3).

title: 09-6: Vector Meets Raster: Cropping, Masking and Extracting Values
section: Conditions for extracting values
text:
Conditions for extracting values

The conditionsCRS: two functions, two behaviours



The raster and the vector are in the same CRS. A mismatch does not give a clear error: crop() reports a different problem, and extract() transforms with a warning.
The raster covers every feature, fully. A feature outside the raster gets no value; one partly outside gets a value from the part that is covered.
The cell-counting rule suits the cell size. When cells are large relative to your polygons, the rule changes the answer.
Missing cells are handled on purpose. A mean over cells that include NA is NA unless told to ignore them.
You know what the values are: their units, and which layer is which day (lecture 09-2).
Rows are matched back by position. ID is a row number, so the vector layer must not be re-sorted between extracting and merging back.



The counties transformed to UTM zone 14N (metres), the raster left in longitude and latitude:

counties_utm <- st_transform(counties, 26914)
crop(ppt_total, vect(counties_utm))

Error: [crop] extents do not overlap


crop() stops, but its message says the extents do not overlap, not that the CRSs differ: the numbers in metres and the numbers in degrees describe different places. extract() behaves differently:

x <- terra::extract(ppt_total, vect(counties_utm), fun = mean)

Warning: [extract] transforming vector data to the CRS of the raster


It transforms the counties for you and warns, and the result is correct. Do not depend on either behaviour: transform the vector to the raster’s CRS yourself (rasters lose detail when transformed, vectors do not), and ask for the CRS check.

title: 09-6: Vector Meets Raster: Cropping, Masking and Extracting Values
section: Silent failures
text:
Silent failures

Edge cells on a coarse rasterA raster that does not cover the areaMissing cellsRows matched back by position


The same county averages from the coarse raster (cells about 18 km), by the default rule and by the weighted rule:









Each dot is a county; on the grey line, the two rules agree. 27 counties differ by more than 1 mm, up to 5.5 mm. No error either way. With the 3.5 km cells of the original raster, the two rules give nearly the same numbers; with large cells, they do not.


Suppose the raster you were given stopped at 100 degrees west, the eastern part of Nebraska only:









Extracting county averages gives a value for every county that touches the raster:

26 counties entirely west of it get NA, which a count of missing values finds
9 counties straddling the edge get an average of their eastern part only, with no NA and no warning

The second group is the silent one. The check is whether each county lies entirely inside the raster’s rectangle: here 58 of 93 do.


A mean over cells that include NA is NA:

mean(c(10, 12, NA))

[1] NA

mean(c(10, 12, NA), na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 11


So a county with one missing cell gets NA from fun = mean, and with na.rm = TRUE it gets the mean of its other cells. The second is usually what you want, but then a county entirely of missing cells gets NaN (not a number), and one mostly of missing cells gets a mean of a few cells. Ask for the number of non-missing cells per feature.


extract() returns rows in the order of the vector layer at the moment it ran. If the layer is sorted, filtered or joined before the values are bound back by position, each value lands on the wrong feature, with no error. The fix is the one in the polygon example: turn ID into the feature’s own ID column straight away, and merge by that column.

title: 09-6: Vector Meets Raster: Cropping, Masking and Extracting Values
section: Working with AI on your own research
text:
Working with AI on your own research
The same way of working as on the slide of this name in lecture 02-1: you ask, the AI writes into your .qmd with one plain-English sentence above each chunk, you render, and you judge the HTML. For an extraction, judging the HTML means putting the map of the results next to the map of the raster: the same pattern should appear in both. Every request for code ends with the closing instructions of lecture 03-1, under Recommended requests.

title: 09-6: Vector Meets Raster: Cropping, Masking and Extracting Values
section: Look at both before you ask
text:
Look at both before you ask

What to find outWhat to write down


From the raster (lecture 09-2): its CRS, cell size, extent (the rectangle it covers), number of layers and what each one is, the units of its values, and how it marks missing cells. From the vector layer (lecture 09-1): its CRS, number of features, and ID column. Then one map of the two together.


From those, before any extraction:

Does the raster’s rectangle contain every feature? If not, which features are partly or wholly outside?
How many cells does the smallest polygon cover? If only a few, the cell-counting rule matters: ask for the weighted rule.
What should the result look like: one row per feature, one column per layer, values within the raster’s own range (a county average cannot be above the raster’s largest cell).

For the precipitation and counties: the raster’s rectangle covers Nebraska, apart from at most a few hundred metres at the eastern edge (the raster stops at -95.312 degrees, the counties at -95.308); the smallest county covers 40 cell centres, so the rule matters little; the result should have 93 rows, and values between 0 and the raster’s largest five-day total, 83.2 mm.

title: 09-6: Vector Meets Raster: Cropping, Masking and Extracting Values
section: What to put in your request
text:
What to put in your request
The AI knows terra::extract(). Your request supplies what it cannot know:

The files: the raster and the vector layer, where they are, and their CRSs
What the raster holds: units, what each layer is (which day, which variable), how missing cells are marked
What one row of the result is, and the ID column of the features
How to summarise each polygon’s cells: mean, sum, maximum, and the cell-counting rule (weighted by share, unless you have a reason)
What to do with missing cells
Checks: rows, cells per feature, features with no value, whether each feature lies inside the raster, the range of results, a map
The closing instructions

title: 09-6: Vector Meets Raster: Cropping, Masking and Extracting Values
section: A weak request and a strong one
text:
A weak request and a strong one

WeakStrongWhat came backThe checks it printed


Get the average precipitation for each county from the PRISM file.
The AI has to guess the files, which layer, how to treat edge cells and missing cells, and how to put the numbers back on the counties. It will usually write terra::extract(..., fun = mean) and bind the result by position.


In my R project, data/ppt.tif is a raster of daily precipitation in mm,
one layer per day (5 layers), NAD83 longitude and latitude, with cells
about 3.5 km wide. data/counties.gpkg has 93 counties, ID column
countyfp, in the same CRS. I want one row per county with the average
over the county of the total precipitation of the 5 days, weighting each
cell by the share of it inside the county, in a table called county_ppt
with countyfp and ppt_mm. Ignore missing cells.

Then check: the CRS of both, the number of rows (I expect 93), the
number of counties with no value (I expect 0), the number of counties not
entirely inside the raster's rectangle (I expect 1, Richardson, whose
eastern tip passes the raster's edge by a few hundred metres), the
smallest number of cells touched by a county (I expect more than 40),
and the range of ppt_mm (between 0 and the raster's largest 5-day
total). Draw a map of the counties filled by ppt_mm.

Put the code in my Quarto document analysis/weather.qmd, under the
heading "County precipitation", as R code chunks. Above each chunk,
write one plain-English sentence saying what it does and why. Build
every path with here::here(); no setwd(), no absolute paths. Print each
check on its own line as "name of check: expected X, got Y". Render the
document to HTML.


In the rendered HTML, a sentence, then the chunk it describes.
Read the raster and the counties, and add the five days into one layer of totals.

ppt <- rast(here::here("data", "ppt.tif"))
counties <- st_read(here::here("data", "counties.gpkg"), quiet = TRUE)
ppt_total <- sum(ppt)
names(ppt_total) <- "ppt_total"

For each county, read every cell it touches with the share of the cell inside, and average weighting by that share.

county_ppt <- terra::extract(ppt_total, vect(counties), exact = TRUE) |>
  filter(!is.na(ppt_total)) |>
  group_by(ID) |>
  summarise(ppt_mm = sum(ppt_total * fraction) / sum(fraction), n_cells = n()) |>
  mutate(countyfp = counties$countyfp[ID])



Print the checks.

inside <- relate(vect(counties), vect(ext(ppt_total), crs = crs(ppt_total)), "within")[, 1]
cat(
  paste("CRS match: expected TRUE, got", st_crs(counties) == st_crs(crs(ppt_total))),
  paste("rows: expected 93, got", nrow(county_ppt)),
  paste("counties with no value: expected 0, got", n_counties - nrow(county_ppt)),
  paste("counties not inside the raster: expected 1 (Richardson), got", sum(!inside),
        paste0("(", paste(counties$name[!inside], collapse = ", "), ")")),
  paste("fewest cells touched by a county: expected more than 40, got", min(county_ppt$n_cells)),
  paste("ppt_mm range: expected 0 to", round(global(ppt_total, "max", na.rm = TRUE)[1, 1], 1),
        "got", round(min(county_ppt$ppt_mm), 1), "to", round(max(county_ppt$ppt_mm), 1)),
  sep = "\n"
)

CRS match: expected TRUE, got TRUE
rows: expected 93, got 93
counties with no value: expected 0, got 0
counties not inside the raster: expected 1 (Richardson), got 1 (Richardson)
fewest cells touched by a county: expected more than 40, got 56
ppt_mm range: expected 0 to 83.2 got 0 to 41.3


Every line matches, including the one you expected to show a county outside the raster: Richardson’s eastern edge, on the Missouri River, reaches about 354 m past the raster’s last column. You knew that from looking at the extent before asking, and a sliver that small cannot move a county average. On another raster, the same check is the one that catches a county left half covered.
The fewest-cells line counts every cell the county touches (56); the 40 on the “Look at both before you ask” slide counted only the cells whose centre is inside.
The AI tested “inside the rectangle” with terra::relate(). The sf version, st_within(counties, st_as_sfc(st_bbox(ppt_total))), reports 13 counties outside instead, because in longitude and latitude sf draws the rectangle’s edges as the shortest paths over the globe, which curve away from the lines of latitude. If a check gives a surprising count, ask the AI why before acting on it.

text:
Checks: what to ask for, and why

The map from the strong request, next to the raster it came from:


Code the AI wrote
counties_ppt <- left_join(counties, select(county_ppt, countyfp, ppt_mm), by = "countyfp")
ggplot(counties_ppt) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = ppt_mm), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "mm") +
  theme_void()









The wetter counties sit where the raster map on “The data on these slides” shows heavier rain, and the scale runs over the same values. A result whose pattern does not match the raster’s is the sign of values bound back to the wrong features.

title: 09-6: Vector Meets Raster: Cropping, Masking and Extracting Values
section: Checks that come from knowing the data
text:
Checks that come from knowing the data
The checks above apply to any extraction. What you know about the data gives stronger ones.

A value you can look up. A weather station’s own record for one county and one day should be close to the county’s value for that day.
A believable range. A county average of five days of summer rain in Nebraska above about 100 mm would be extraordinary. A result of 500 mm points to the wrong units (some files store tenths of a millimetre) or a missing-value code such as -9999 read as a value (lecture 09-2).
Totals that must agree. For a raster of counts or amounts (people, tonnes) rather than rates, the sum over all features should equal the raster’s sum over the same area.

For three counties of my choice, <county names>, print the number of
cells used, their smallest and largest value, and the county's result,
so I can check the result lies between them.

Put the code in my Quarto document analysis/analysis.qmd, under the
heading "Checks", as R code chunks. Above each chunk, write one
plain-English sentence saying what it does and why. Build every path
with here::here(); no setwd(), no absolute paths. Print each check on
its own line as "name of check: expected X, got Y". Render the document
to HTML.

title: 09-6: Vector Meets Raster: Cropping, Masking and Extracting Values
section: Your turn: read the AI’s code
text:
Your turn: read the AI’s code
A student asked an AI to “add mean precipitation to my county table”, and got this:

ppt <- rast("ppt.tif")
counties <- st_read("counties.gpkg") |> arrange(name)
vals <- terra::extract(ppt, st_transform(counties, 32614), fun = mean)
counties_ppt <- bind_cols(st_read("counties.gpkg"), vals)


QuestionsAnswers


A. What does each line do?
B. Which line puts values on the wrong counties, and why is there no error?
C. What does line 3 do with the CRS, and what would crop() have done in its place?
D. What happens to a county with one missing cell?


A. Reads the raster; reads the counties and sorts them by name; extracts the mean of each layer for each county, after transforming the counties to UTM zone 14N; binds the values onto a fresh copy of the counties, which is in the file’s order.
B. Line 4. The values are in alphabetical order (line 2 sorted the counties) but are bound to the counties in the file’s order. Both have the same number of rows, so bind_cols() has nothing to complain about.
C. It transforms the counties away from the raster’s CRS; extract() transforms them back with a warning, so the values are right. crop() would stop with “extents do not overlap”.
D. Without na.rm = TRUE, its mean is NA.

title: 09-6: Vector Meets Raster: Cropping, Masking and Extracting Values
section: Requests you can copy
text:
Requests you can copy
Copy one, then replace every <...> with what you found by looking at the files. Every request for code ends with the closing instructions.

Closing instructionsLook at a raster and a layerValues at pointsSummaries over polygonsCrop and mask for a mapExplain code


The lines that end every request for code. Replace the two blanks; leave “expected X, got Y” as it is, because it tells the AI how to print each check:
Put the code in my Quarto document <path to your .qmd>, under the
heading "<heading>", as R code chunks. Above each chunk, write one
plain-English sentence saying what it does and why. Build every path
with here::here(); no setwd(), no absolute paths. Print each check on
its own line as "name of check: expected X, got Y". Render the document
to HTML.
A chat assistant cannot render: paste its chunks into your .qmd and render it yourself. An agent in your editor or terminal can do every step.


In my R project, <path to the raster> is a raster and <path to the
vector layer> is a vector layer. For the raster, print its CRS, cell
size, extent, number of layers, layer names, and smallest and largest
value. For the layer, print its CRS, number of features and bounding
box. Then print whether every feature lies entirely inside the raster's
rectangle, and draw one map with the raster and the features' outlines
on top.

Put the code in my Quarto document <path to your .qmd>, under the
heading "<heading>", as R code chunks. Above each chunk, write one
plain-English sentence saying what it does and why. Build every path
with here::here(); no setwd(), no absolute paths. Print each check on
its own line as "name of check: expected X, got Y". Render the document
to HTML.


In my R project, <path to the raster> holds <what the values are, with
units>, one layer per <what each layer is>, in EPSG <code>. <path to the
point layer> has <number> points, ID column <the column that identifies
each point>. Add the raster's value at each point, one column per layer,
to the point layer, in a layer called <name>. Transform the points to
the raster's CRS first.

Then check: the number of rows before and after (I expect them equal),
the number of points with a missing value (I expect <number>), the range
of each new column, and draw a map of the points coloured by <layer>.

Put the code in my Quarto document <path to your .qmd>, under the
heading "<heading>", as R code chunks. Above each chunk, write one
plain-English sentence saying what it does and why. Build every path
with here::here(); no setwd(), no absolute paths. Print each check on
its own line as "name of check: expected X, got Y". Render the document
to HTML.


In my R project, <path to the raster> holds <what the values are, with
units>, in EPSG <code>. <path to the polygon layer> has <number>
polygons, ID column <the column that identifies each polygon>. I want one
row per polygon with the <mean, sum, or other summary> of <which
layers>, weighting each cell by the share of it inside the polygon, and
<ignoring or keeping> missing cells, in a table with the polygon's ID
column. Match rows back by the ID column, not by position.

Then check: the number of rows (I expect <number>), the number of
polygons with no value, the number not entirely inside the raster's
rectangle, the smallest number of cells in a polygon, and the range of
the results. Draw a map of the polygons filled by the result next to a
map of the raster.

title: 09-4: Two Vector Layers: Relations, Subsetting, Buffers and Clipping
section: What you will and will not learn today
text:
What you will and will not learn today

The planDirections


Lecture 09-1 (vector basics) handled one layer at a time. Research questions usually involve two: which counties lie over an aquifer, which wells are within 2 km of a river, how much of a railroad runs through a county. An AI assistant can write the code for each of these in one line. What it cannot do is:

know which spatial relation your question means: “over the aquifer” can mean “any part over it” or “entirely over it”
know what distance in what units you mean
see whether the result is the set of places you had in mind

Those are your job. So today is about:

The concept: what a spatial relation is, and the three things you can do with one (test, keep, cut), plus buffers
Reading code: the patterns these lines follow
Asking AI: how to say which relation and which distance you mean
Checking: counts and maps whose right answer you know before the code runs




Ask your AI assistant to install the sf, tidyverse and here packages if you have not already.
This lecture assumes lecture 09-1 (vector basics): what a layer, a feature and a CRS (coordinate reference system) are, and the four checks for a single layer.
The data files used on these slides sit in the same folder as the slides, so a path here is just the file name. In your own project, paths are built with here::here() (lecture 03-1).

title: 09-4: Two Vector Layers: Relations, Subsetting, Buffers and Clipping
section: A spatial relation is a yes-or-no test between two features
text:
A spatial relation is a yes-or-no test between two features

The ideaFive shapes and a squareWhich tests each shape passes


A spatial relation (also called a topological relation) is a question about where two features sit relative to each other, with a yes or no answer: do they share any point? Is one entirely inside the other? Are they within 1 km of each other?
The same pair of shapes can pass one test and fail another. That is the whole difficulty: an everyday phrase such as “the counties over the aquifer” does not say which test it means.











Shape 1 is inside the square, 2 crosses its edge, 3 shares part of its edge from outside, 4 is outside but close, 5 is far away.







shape
intersects
within
touches
within 1 unit




1
yes
yes
no
yes


2
yes
no
no
yes


3
yes

yes

no

no

Test
Means
sf function




intersects
the two share at least one point, including a shared edge
st_intersects()


within
the first is entirely inside the second
st_within()


touches
they share edge points but no area
st_touches()


within a distance
some part of one is no farther than the distance from the other
st_is_within_distance()



Notice shape 3: it passes “intersects” without overlapping the square at all, because sharing an edge counts as sharing a point.

title: 09-4: Two Vector Layers: Relations, Subsetting, Buffers and Clipping
section: Three things you do with a relation, and one new shape
text:
Three things you do with a relation, and one new shape
Every operation in this lecture uses a relation in one of three ways, or makes a buffer first:









Operation
What you get
Shapes changed?
Example question




Test
for each feature of A, which features of B pass
no
how many railroads cross each county?


Keep (spatial subsetting)
the features of A that pass, whole
no
which counties lie over the aquifer?


Cut (clipping)
only the parts of A’s shapes that lie inside B
yes
how many km of railroad lie inside the county?


Buffer
a new polygon covering everything within a distance of a feature
new shape
which wells are within 2 km of the river?






Note


Keeping and cutting are easy to confuse. Keeping a railroad that crosses a county keeps the whole railroad, including the part outside. Only cutting gives you the part inside.



The next lecture, 09-5, uses relations to join two layers: bring B’s columns onto A’s rows. This lecture covers everything that comes before that.

title: 09-4: Two Vector Layers: Relations, Subsetting, Buffers and Clipping
section: Testing a relation
text:
Testing a relation

The patternEvery relation follows the patternReading the result



result <- st_relation(layer_a, layer_b, options)









Part
What it is
Required?




st_relation
The test: st_intersects, st_within, …
Yes


layer_a
The layer you ask about: one answer per feature of A
Yes


layer_b
The layer you test against
Yes


options
dist = for distance tests; sparse = FALSE for a table of TRUE and FALSE
Only dist for distance tests



The order matters. st_within(a, b) asks “is each A inside a B?”; st_within(b, a) asks the opposite question.










Function
Passes when
Extra input




st_intersects(a, b)
any shared point



st_within(a, b)
a entirely inside b



st_contains(a, b)
b entirely inside a (the reverse of within)



st_touches(a, b)
shared edge, no shared area



st_is_within_distance(a, b, dist)
no farther apart than dist
dist, required


st_nearest_feature(a, b)
for each a, the single closest b




st_nearest_feature() is different from the others: it always returns exactly one feature of B for each feature of A, however far away that feature is.


The result has one entry per feature of A, listing which features of B passed, by row number:

st_intersects(shapes, square)

Sparse geometry binary predicate list of length 5, where the predicate
was `intersects'
 1: 1
 2: 1
 3: 1
 4: (empty)
 5: (empty)


Shapes 1 to 3 pass (row 1 of square); 4 and 5 list nothing, shown as (empty). AI-written code usually turns this into a count per feature with lengths():

lengths(st_intersects(shapes, square))

[1] 1 1 1 0 0


A count of 0 means “no match” and a count above 1 means “several matches”. Those two numbers are the start of most checks in this lecture.

title: 09-4: Two Vector Layers: Relations, Subsetting, Buffers and Clipping
section: Keeping the features that pass
text:
Keeping the features that pass

The patternVariations you will seeA real example



kept <- st_filter(layer_a, layer_b, .predicate = st_relation)









Part
What it is
Required?




kept <-
The new layer: the features of A that passed, each whole
Needed to keep the result


layer_a
The layer you keep features from
Yes


layer_b
The layer you test against
Yes


.predicate =
The relation
No; the default is intersects



Nothing about layer_b is added to the result. Only which rows of A survive changes.


The same operation, written three ways:

st_filter(counties, aquifer, .predicate = st_within)
counties[aquifer, , op = st_within]: square brackets, as when choosing rows by number, with a layer in place of the numbers
filter(counties, lengths(st_within(counties, aquifer)) > 0): test, count, keep counts above zero

A fourth keeps every row and adds a column saying whether it passed (a flag):

counties <- mutate(counties, over_aquifer = lengths(st_intersects(counties, aquifer)) > 0)



The High Plains aquifer (an underground water reservoir) lies under most of Nebraska. Keep the counties that lie over it:

over <- st_filter(counties, aquifer)
nrow(over)

[1] 84











84 of the 93 counties, in orange; the aquifer’s outline in blue. No .predicate was given, so this is “intersects”: any part of the county over the aquifer.

title: 09-4: Two Vector Layers: Relations, Subsetting, Buffers and Clipping
section: Cutting shapes, and making buffers
text:
Cutting shapes, and making buffers

The patternst_crop() cuts to a rectangleA real example: railroads in Lancaster County


These functions return new shapes, not a selection of old ones:

new_layer <- st_cutting_function(layer_a, layer_b_or_distance)









Function
Returns
Second input




st_intersection(a, b)
the parts of A inside B, with B’s columns attached
a layer


st_difference(a, b)
the parts of A outside B
a layer


st_crop(a, b)
the parts of A inside the rectangle around B (its bounding box)
a layer or a box


st_buffer(a, dist)
a polygon around each feature of A, dist wide
a distance, in the units of the CRS


st_union(a)
all of A’s shapes merged into one
none





st_crop() is fast, which is why AI code uses it, but it cuts to the bounding box (the smallest rectangle around B), not to B’s outline:









The aquifer’s rectangle covers almost all of Nebraska, so cropping kept 91 of the 93 counties, most of them unchanged. For the parts inside the aquifer itself, the function is st_intersection().



rail_lan <- st_filter(railroads, lancaster)                       # keep: whole segments
rail_cut <- st_intersection(rail_lan, st_geometry(lancaster))     # cut: parts inside
units::set_units(c(kept = sum(st_length(rail_lan)), cut = sum(st_length(rail_cut))), km)

Units: [km]
    kept      cut 
294.5544 282.1574 


Keeping gives 294.6 km of railroad, because every segment that crosses the county line is kept whole. Cutting gives 282.2 km, the length actually inside the county. st_geometry(lancaster) passes only the county’s shape, so no county columns are attached.

title: 09-4: Two Vector Layers: Relations, Subsetting, Buffers and Clipping
section: Conditions for combining two layers
text:
Conditions for combining two layers

The conditionsWith and without an error



Both layers have the right CRS, and the same one. Lecture 09-1 covers this; it matters even more now, because every relation compares the coordinates of two layers.
The relation is the one your question means. “Over”, “in”, “near” and “along” each need translating into a test.
Distances are in the units you meant. A buffer or a distance test uses the units of the CRS.
The shapes are valid. A polygon whose boundary crosses itself gives wrong answers.
You know whether you want whole features or parts. Keeping and cutting give different lengths and areas.




If the two layers have different CRSs, sf stops with an error (lecture 09-1). Good: you know.
Everything else fails silently: you get a layer, a count or an area with no error, and it is wrong. The next slide shows each one.

title: 09-4: Two Vector Layers: Relations, Subsetting, Buffers and Clipping
section: Silent failures
text:
Silent failures

Neighbours “intersect”Intersects is not withinA distance in the wrong unitsAn invalid shape


Which counties intersect Lancaster County?

nrow(st_filter(counties, lancaster))

[1] 9

nrow(st_filter(counties, lancaster, .predicate = st_touches))

[1] 8


9 counties: Lancaster itself, and its 8 neighbours, which share only a boundary line with it. Counties in a state share boundaries, so “intersects” between two layers of neighbouring polygons picks up every neighbour. If you meant “overlap by some area”, that is not what you got, and nothing warns you.



nrow(st_filter(counties, aquifer))                          # any part over it

[1] 84

nrow(st_filter(counties, aquifer, .predicate = st_within))  # entirely over it

[1] 54


84 against 54: 30 counties differ between “over the aquifer” read one way and read the other. Neither number is wrong; one of them does not answer your question. The AI picks intersects unless told, because it is the default.


A 10 km buffer around Lancaster County, written as dist = 10000, in three CRSs:

area_km2 <- function(x) round(as.numeric(units::set_units(st_area(x), km^2)))
c(
  longitude_latitude = area_km2(st_buffer(lancaster, 10000)),
  utm_metres = area_km2(st_buffer(st_transform(lancaster, 26914), 10000)),
  state_plane_feet = area_km2(st_buffer(st_transform(lancaster, 26852), 10000))
)

longitude_latitude         utm_metres   state_plane_feet 
              4479               4423               2804 


The county alone is 2189 km². In longitude and latitude, sf reads the distance as metres. In UTM zone 14N (EPSG 26914), the units are metres too. In the Nebraska state plane CRS in US feet (EPSG 26852), 10,000 is 10,000 feet, about 3 km, so the buffer is much smaller. No error in any of the three.


A polygon whose boundary crosses itself (a “bow tie”) is invalid. sf still computes with it:

bowtie <- st_polygon(list(rbind(c(0, 0), c(2, 2), c(2, 0), c(0, 2), c(0, 0))))
st_is_valid(bowtie)

[1] FALSE

st_area(bowtie)

[1] 0


Two triangles of area 1 each, and an area of 0. Files drawn by hand or converted between formats sometimes contain such shapes. st_is_valid() finds them and st_make_valid() repairs most of them; the check is to count invalid shapes before combining layers.

title: 09-4: Two Vector Layers: Relations, Subsetting, Buffers and Clipping
section: Working with AI on your own research
text:
Working with AI on your own research
The same way of working as on the slide of this name in lecture 02-1: you ask, the AI writes into your .qmd with one plain-English sentence above each chunk, you render, and you judge the HTML. With spatial data the last step matters more than usual: a map in the HTML shows at a glance whether the features kept are the ones you meant, which no chat reply can. Every request for code ends with the closing instructions of lecture 03-1, under Recommended requests.

title: 09-4: Two Vector Layers: Relations, Subsetting, Buffers and Clipping
section: Look at both layers before you ask
text:
Look at both layers before you ask

WhyWhat the map tells youWrite the expectation down


You cannot say which features you expect to keep without seeing where the two layers lie relative to each other. Ask for the four checks of lecture 09-1 on each layer, and one more thing: a map of the two layers drawn together.











From this map, before any code: the aquifer covers most of the state but not the east, and its outline is not a rectangle, so cropping to it would not do.


From the map, a student might write: “Roughly 80 to 90 counties have some part over the aquifer; roughly 50 to 60 are entirely over it; the counties in the far east have no part over it.” Rough is fine. The point is to have something to compare against before the AI’s number arrives.

title: 09-4: Two Vector Layers: Relations, Subsetting, Buffers and Clipping
section: What to put in your request
text:
What to put in your request
The AI knows every function. Your request supplies what it cannot know:

The layers: file names, where they are, and their CRSs (from looking)
Which layer you ask about (A) and which you test against (B)
The relation in plain words: “any part over”, “entirely inside”, “within 2 km of”, “shares a boundary with”
Whole features or parts: keep whole counties, or cut the railroads at the county line
Distances with units, and that they must be computed in a CRS in metres
Checks: counts you expect, features with no match, a map of the result over the other layer
The closing instructions

title: 09-4: Two Vector Layers: Relations, Subsetting, Buffers and Clipping
section: A weak request and a strong one
text:
A weak request and a strong one

WeakStrongWhat came back


Find the counties over the aquifer.
The AI has to guess the files, their CRSs, and the meaning of “over”. It will usually write st_intersects(), the default, which includes every county with a sliver over the aquifer, and print nothing that tells you so.


In my R project, data/counties.gpkg (93 counties) and data/aquifer.gpkg
(the aquifer outline) are both in EPSG 4269. I want the counties that lie
ENTIRELY over the aquifer, kept whole, in a layer called counties_over.
I expect between 50 and 60.

Then check: the CRS of both layers, the number of counties kept, the
number of invalid shapes in each layer (I expect 0), and draw a map of
all counties with the kept ones filled and the aquifer outline on top.

Put the code in my Quarto document analysis/aquifer.qmd, under the
heading "Counties over the aquifer", as R code chunks. Above each chunk,
write one plain-English sentence saying what it does and why. Build every
path with here::here(); no setwd(), no absolute paths. Print each check
on its own line as "name of check: expected X, got Y". Render the
document to HTML.


In the rendered HTML, a sentence, then the chunk it describes.
Read the two layers.

counties <- st_read(here::here("data", "counties.gpkg"), quiet = TRUE)
aquifer  <- st_read(here::here("data", "aquifer.gpkg"), quiet = TRUE)

Keep the counties that lie entirely inside the aquifer outline.

counties_over <- st_filter(counties, aquifer, .predicate = st_within)

Print the checks.


CRS of counties: expected EPSG 4269, got EPSG 4269
CRS of aquifer: expected EPSG 4269, got EPSG 4269
counties kept: expected 50 to 60, got 54
invalid shapes in counties: expected 0, got 0
invalid shapes in aquifer: expected 0, got 0


Every line matches. The map, which the HTML also shows, is the one on the “Keeping the features that pass” slide with fewer counties filled.

title: 09-4: Two Vector Layers: Relations, Subsetting, Buffers and Clipping
section: Checks: what to ask for, and why
text:
Checks: what to ask for, and why

The checksTotals that must be preservedReading the HTML


The four checks of lecture 09-1 (CRS, number of features, bounding box, a map) still apply to each layer. Combining two layers adds these:










Ask the AI to print
Catches
What only you can supply




1
features before and after keeping
the wrong relation (too many or too few kept)
a rough count from the map


2
features with no match, and with more than one
points or shapes in the wrong place, neighbours picked up by a shared edge
how many should match


3
invalid shapes in each layer
wrong areas and failed tests from broken polygons
(0 is always right)


4
a map of the result over the other layer
anything the counts did not show
what the place looks like


5
a total that must be preserved
parts lost or counted twice when cutting
the total, from another source





Cutting is the step where length or area can quietly go missing or be counted twice. A total that should not change is the check:

Cut the aquifer at county lines: the pieces should add up to the area of the aquifer inside Nebraska
Cut railroads at county lines: the pieces should add up to the length of railroad in the state
Keep whole features: the kept total can be larger than the total inside the area, because whole features stick out



The aquifer cut at county boundaries, with its total checked:


Code the AI wrote
pieces <- st_intersection(counties, st_union(aquifer))
in_state <- st_intersection(st_union(aquifer), st_union(counties))
km2 <- function(x) round(sum(as.numeric(units::set_units(st_area(x), km^2))))
cat(
  paste("pieces: expected", nrow(st_filter(counties, aquifer)), "(one per county over the aquifer), got", nrow(pieces)),
  paste("area of pieces: expected", km2(in_state), "km2, got", km2(pieces)),
  paste("invalid pieces: expected 0, got", sum(!st_is_valid(pieces))),
  sep = "\n"
)


pieces: expected 84 (one per county over the aquifer), got 84
area of pieces: expected 167219 km2, got 167219
invalid pieces: expected 0, got 0


All three pass: one piece per county that intersects the aquifer, and the pieces add up to the aquifer’s area inside the state. st_union(aquifer) merges the aquifer’s two polygons first, so a county touching both polygons gives one piece, not two, and no area is cut twice.

title: 09-4: Two Vector Layers: Relations, Subsetting, Buffers and Clipping
section: Checks that come from knowing the place
text:
Checks that come from knowing the place
The checks above apply to any two layers. Checks from what you know about this place are stronger, and no AI will think of them.

A feature you knowA share that should be large


You know Lancaster County (Lincoln) is not over the High Plains aquifer and Hall County (Grand Island) is. Ask for those two by name: if either comes out wrong, so does the rest.


A feature can pass “intersects” with a sliver. For a study, that sliver may not count. Example: the Iowa counties that intersect watershed 07060004 (a hydrologic unit, the area draining to one river), and the share of each county’s area that lies inside the watershed:
Using the layers ia_counties and watersheds, both in EPSG 4269, keep
the counties that intersect watershed 07060004, and for each, compute
the share of its area inside the watershed, in a CRS in metres. Print
the shares, smallest first, with the county codes.

Put the code in my Quarto document analysis/analysis.qmd, under the
heading "Checks", as R code chunks. Above each chunk, write one
plain-English sentence saying what it does and why. Build every path
with here::here(); no setwd(), no absolute paths. Print each check on
its own line as "name of check: expected X, got Y". Render the document
to HTML.
The AI’s code, and what it printed:


Code the AI wrote
ws <- filter(watersheds, HUC_CODE == "07060004") |> st_transform(26915)
ia_kept <- st_filter(st_transform(ia_counties, 26915), ws)
inside <- st_intersection(ia_kept, st_geometry(ws))
share <- tibble(
  countyfp = inside$countyfp,
  share = round(as.numeric(st_area(inside)) / as.numeric(st_area(ia_kept[match(inside$countyfp, ia_kept$countyfp), ])), 3)
) |> arrange(share)
share


# A tibble: 8 × 2
  countyfp share
  <chr>    <dbl>
1 005      0.002
2 061      0.019
3 055      0.089
4 037      0.241
5 191      0.293
6 089      0.504
7 065      0.687
8 043      0.717


8 counties intersect the watershed, but 2 of them have less than 5% of their area inside it. Whether those belong in a study of the watershed is a decision for you; the list is what lets you make it, and defend it.

title: 09-4: Two Vector Layers: Relations, Subsetting, Buffers and Clipping
section: Your turn: read the AI’s code
text:
Your turn: read the AI’s code
A student asked an AI to “find how many km of railroad run within 5 km of Lincoln”, and got this:

lincoln <- st_point(c(-96.70, 40.81)) |> st_sfc(crs = 4269)
lincoln <- st_transform(lincoln, 26852)
zone <- st_buffer(lincoln, 5000)
rail <- st_filter(st_transform(railroads, 26852), zone)
sum(st_length(rail))


QuestionsAnswers


A. What does each line do?
B. EPSG 26852 is NAD83 / Nebraska in US feet. How wide is the zone really?
C. Which line keeps whole segments when the question asks for the length inside the zone?
D. Rewrite the request so the AI could not make these mistakes.


A. Makes a point for Lincoln in longitude and latitude; transforms it to the state plane CRS; draws a zone around it; keeps railroad segments that intersect the zone; adds up their lengths.
B. 5,000 feet, about 1.5 km, not 5 km. No error, because 5,000 is a valid distance in feet.
C. Line 4. st_filter() keeps every segment that touches the zone, whole. st_intersection() would cut them at the edge of the zone.
D. Say “within 5 km”, ask for the buffer to be made in a CRS in metres and for its radius to be printed in km, ask for the railroads to be cut at the zone’s edge, and ask for a map of the zone with the cut railroads.

title: 09-4: Two Vector Layers: Relations, Subsetting, Buffers and Clipping
section: Requests you can copy

What you must understand, and what the AI can write







You need to understand
The AI can write




Which relation your question means: intersects, within, touches, within a distance
st_intersects(), st_within(), st_filter(.predicate = )

title: 09-2: Raster Data
section: What you will and will not learn today
text:
What you will and will not learn today

The planDirections


Weather, elevation, soil and satellite images come as raster data: a grid of cells, each with a value. An AI assistant can read any raster format and compute anything on it. What it cannot do is:

know what the numbers in the cells mean: their units, their scale, which value means “no data”
know where the grid should be
tell whether a value it computed is believable

Those are your job. So today is about:

The concept: what a raster is, and what has to be true before its values can be used
Reading code: recognising what a line of raster code does
Asking AI: what to put in your request
Checking: what to print for every raster, and why




Ask your AI assistant to install the terra and tidyterra packages if you have not already. terra reads and computes on rasters; tidyterra lets ggplot2 draw them.
The data files used on these slides sit in the same folder as the slides, so a path here is just the file name. In your own project, paths are built with here::here() (lecture 03-1).

title: 09-2: Raster Data
section: A raster is a grid of cells
text:
A raster is a grid of cells

The ideaA whole rasterClose up


A raster covers a rectangle with a grid of equal cells. Each cell holds one value. What describes the grid:







Term
What it is




Extent
The rectangle the grid covers: lowest and highest x, lowest and highest y


Resolution
The width and height of one cell, in the units of the CRS


Rows and columns
How many cells down and across


CRS
What the x and y numbers mean, as in lecture 09-1


Layers
A raster can hold several grids on the same cells, for example one per day. Each layer has a name.



A cell with no value (outside the area measured, or a failed reading) holds NA, R’s missing value, if the file says which value means “no data”.


Daily precipitation in millimetres on 1 August 2012, from PRISM (a US weather dataset), for the rectangle around Nebraska. Cells outside Nebraska hold no data.











The 8-by-8 block of cells in the north-west corner of the state, with the value of each cell written in it:









Each square is one cell, about 4 km across, and the number in it is the whole of what the raster knows about that square.

title: 09-2: Raster Data
section: What a raster file does and does not say
text:
What a raster file does and does not say

Stored, and not always storedVector or raster









Always in the file
Sometimes in the file, sometimes only in the documentation




The numbers in the cells
Which value means “no data” (often -9999)


The extent, resolution, rows, columns
The units (millimetres or inches, degrees C or F)


The number of layers
The scale: values stored as whole numbers, such as hundredths of a millimetre, to save space


Usually the CRS
What each layer is (which date), beyond a name



Whatever is not in the file, only you can tell the AI, from the documentation of the data.











Vector (lecture 09-1)
Raster




Stores
separate features, each with a shape
one value per cell of a grid


One row or cell is
a county, a well
a 4 km square


Typical data
boundaries, locations, roads
weather, elevation, satellite images


R package
sf
terra



Both need a CRS, and both must share a CRS with any layer they are combined with.

The same reader opens all of them:








Extension

title: 09-2: Raster Data
section: Doing things with a raster
text:
Doing things with a raster

The patternOne real exampleVariations you will see


Most raster functions take the raster first and return a new raster:

result <- raster_function(raster, other_inputs)









Function
What it does
Default that matters




raster1 + raster2, raster * 10, log(raster)
Arithmetic, cell by cell. Rasters must share extent and resolution.



raster[[2]] or raster[["name"]]
One layer



global(raster, "mean")
One number per layer, over all cells
Without na.rm = TRUE, a single NA makes the result NA


classify(raster, cbind(-9999, NA))
Replaces values, here -9999 by NA



aggregate(raster, fact = 5)
Coarser cells: each 5-by-5 block becomes one cell
Averages the block (fun = "mean")


resample(raster, template)
Moves values onto another grid
Interpolates between cells (method = "bilinear")


project(raster, "EPSG:5070")
Moves the raster into another CRS
Recomputes every cell value


crop(), mask(), extract()
Combine a raster with vector data
Lecture 09-6





The total over the five days, cell by cell, and its largest value:

ppt_total <- sum(ppt_days)
global(ppt_total, "max", na.rm = TRUE)

       max
sum 83.239


sum() over the layers of one raster adds them cell by cell, giving a raster with one layer.



terra::rast(...): the package name in front
rast(here::here("data", "ppt.tif")): the path built by another function
ppt_days$ppt_2012_08_01: one layer by name, like a column of a table
ggplot() + geom_spatraster(data = raster): a map of a raster, from tidyterra (lecture 09-3)

title: 09-2: Raster Data
section: Conditions for raster values to be right
text:
Conditions for raster values to be right

The conditionsWith and without an error



The no-data value is declared, so cells without data are NA, not a number such as -9999.
The units and scale are known, so a stored 7381 is read as 73.81 millimetres.
The grid is where the place is: the CRS and extent are right.
Each layer is what you think: the right date, the right variable.
Every operation’s default fits the kind of value: averaging works for amounts such as rainfall, not for codes such as 1 = corn, 2 = soybean.
A raster combined with vector data shares its CRS. Transform the vector layer to the raster’s CRS, not the other way: projecting a raster recomputes its values.



Raster operations stop with an error when two rasters do not share extent and resolution, or a file does not exist. Conditions 1 to 5 failing gives numbers with no error: the silent failures on the next slide are three of them.

title: 09-2: Raster Data
section: Silent failures: cell values misread
text:
Silent failures: cell values misread

An undeclared no-data valueValues in a scaleAveraging codes


ne_ppt_raw.tif holds the same 1 August 2012 precipitation, stored the way some data providers store it: -9999 in the cells outside Nebraska, and no line in the file saying that -9999 means “no data”.

raw <- rast("ne_ppt_raw.tif")
raw

class       : SpatRaster 
size        : 73, 210, 1  (nrow, ncol, nlyr)
resolution  : 0.04166667, 0.04166667  (x, y)
extent      : -104.0625, -95.3125, 39.97917, 43.02083  (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax)
coord. ref. : lon/lat NAD83 (EPSG:4269) 
source      : ne_ppt_raw.tif 
name        :   ppt 
min value   : -9999 
max value   :  7381 


The average over the cells:

global(raw, "mean")

         mean
ppt -1547.469


An average daily precipitation of -1547 millimetres, impossible, and no error. 2,580 cells hold -9999 and were averaged with the rest. The printout above shows it: min value: -9999.


The largest value in the same file is 7381. 7,381 millimetres in a day is impossible: the file stores hundredths of a millimetre as whole numbers. Only the documentation says so. Both fixes together, declare -9999 as no data, then divide by 100:

fixed <- classify(raw, cbind(-9999, NA)) / 100
global(fixed, c("min", "max", "mean"), na.rm = TRUE)

    min   max     mean
ppt   0 73.81 1.627232


Now the values run from 0 to 73.8 millimetres, and the average is 1.63 millimetres, the same as the file that declares its no-data value and units.


A small land-cover raster where 1 means corn and 2 means soybean, made coarser by aggregate(), which averages by default:

landcover <- rast(nrows = 4, ncols = 4, xmin = 0, xmax = 4, ymin = 0, ymax = 4,
                  vals = c(1, 1, 2, 2, 1, 2, 2, 2, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 1, 1))
values(aggregate(landcover, fact = 2))

     lyr.1
[1,]  1.25
[2,]  2.00
[3,]  1.50
[4,]  1.25


Values of 1.25 and 1.5 are neither corn nor soybean, and nothing warns you. For codes, the right rule is the most common value in each block, fun = "modal":

values(aggregate(landcover, fact = 2, fun = "modal"))

     lyr.1
[1,]     1
[2,]     2
[3,]     1
[4,]     1


resample() has the same problem when codes are stored as plain numbers: its default, "bilinear", interpolates between neighbouring cells. Tell it method = "near". (If the raster is declared categorical, terra uses "near" itself; aggregate() averages either way.) project(), which moves a raster to another CRS, has the same default and needs the same instruction.

title: 09-2: Raster Data
section: Working with AI on your own research
text:
Working with AI on your own research
The way of working from lecture 02-1, “Working with AI on your own research”, applies unchanged:

You ask. Your request says what you want, what you know about the data, and which checks to print.
The AI writes into a Quarto document (.qmd). Code goes into code chunks, with one plain-English sentence above each chunk saying what it does and why.
You render the .qmd to HTML.
You read the HTML and decide whether the work is right: the sentences, the code, and the check results side by side.

A raster’s printout, its value ranges and a quick map are checks you judge by eye. In the HTML they sit next to the code that produced them, and the document records which no-data value and scale you told the AI to use, and why.



Note


Every request that asks for code ends with the same few lines, the closing instructions; the full text is under Recommended requests near the end.

title: 09-2: Raster Data
section: Look before you ask
text:
Look before you ask

Read the documentationPrint the raster before computing anything


Raster data almost always comes with documentation: a README, a metadata page, a .txt or .xml file next to the data. Find in it:

The variable and its units: precipitation in millimetres, temperature in degrees C
The scale: are values stored as they are, or multiplied (by 10, 100, 10,000) to make whole numbers?
The no-data value: often -9999, sometimes 0 or 255
The CRS
What each layer is: which date, which band of a satellite image



The printout of rast() reads only the file’s description and, if the file stores them, its smallest and largest values, so it is quick even for a large file. If the printout has no min value line, ask for the range before anything else.

rast("ne_ppt_raw.tif")

class       : SpatRaster 
size        : 73, 210, 1  (nrow, ncol, nlyr)
resolution  : 0.04166667, 0.04166667  (x, y)
extent      : -104.0625, -95.3125, 39.97917, 43.02083  (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax)
coord. ref. : lon/lat NAD83 (EPSG:4269) 
source      : ne_ppt_raw.tif 
name        :   ppt 
min value   : -9999 
max value   :  7381 


From this alone: one layer, longitude and latitude around Nebraska, values from -9999 to 7381. Compare that with the documentation before asking for any calculation.

title: 09-2: Raster Data
section: What to put in your request
text:
What to put in your request
The AI knows every terra function. Your request supplies what it cannot know:

The file: name, format, where it is in your project
What the values mean: the variable, its units, its scale
The no-data value
The CRS, and what each layer is
What you want back: which layers, which units, which calculation, and for codes, that values must not be averaged
Ask for checks: next section
The closing instructions





Using an agent in your editor or terminal?


An agent such as Claude Code can open the raster and print it for itself. It still cannot know a scale or a no-data value that is only in the documentation. Write those down before it runs.

title: 09-2: Raster Data
section: A weak request and a strong one
text:
A weak request and a strong one

WeakStrongWhat came back


Load the precipitation raster and give me the average rainfall.
A typical reply:

ppt <- rast("ppt.tif")
global(ppt, "mean", na.rm = TRUE)

On a file like ne_ppt_raw.tif this prints -1547, with no error: the -9999 cells and the hundredths are both taken at face value.


An example for a precipitation file like the one on the “Silent failures” slide:
In my R project, data/ppt_raw.tif is a GeoTIFF of daily precipitation
on 1 August 2012 around Nebraska, one layer. Its documentation says:
values are hundredths of a millimetre stored as whole numbers, -9999
means no data, and the CRS is NAD83 longitude and latitude (EPSG 4269).

Read it, mark -9999 as missing, and convert the values to millimetres,
in a raster called ppt. Then print the average precipitation over the
cells with data.

Check: the CRS (I expect EPSG 4269), the extent (I expect longitude
between -104 and -95 and latitude between 40 and 43), the smallest and
largest value after conversion (I expect 0 and something below 150 mm),
and the number of missing cells. Draw a quick map of the raster.

Put the code in my Quarto document analysis/weather.qmd, under the
heading "Read the precipitation", as R code chunks. Above each chunk,
write one plain-English sentence saying what it does and why. Build
every path with here::here(); no setwd(), no absolute paths. Print each
check on its own line as "name of check: expected X, got Y". Render the
document to HTML.


In the rendered HTML, a sentence, then the chunk it describes.
Read the raster, mark -9999 as missing, and convert hundredths of a millimetre to millimetres.

ppt <- rast(here::here("data", "ppt_raw.tif"))
ppt <- classify(ppt, cbind(-9999, NA)) / 100

Print the checks against what was expected, then the average.

rng <- global(ppt, c("min", "max"), na.rm = TRUE)
cat("CRS: expected EPSG 4269, got EPSG", crs(ppt, describe = TRUE)$code, "\n")
cat("longitude: expected -104 to -95, got", round(xmin(ppt), 1), "to", round(xmax(ppt), 1), "\n")
cat("latitude: expected 40 to 43, got", round(ymin(ppt), 1), "to", round(ymax(ppt), 1), "\n")
cat("smallest value: expected 0, got", rng$min, "\n")
cat("largest value: expected below 150, got", rng$max, "\n")
cat("missing cells: expected some (the rectangle reaches outside Nebraska), got", global(ppt, "isNA")[1, 1], "of", ncell(ppt), "\n")
global(ppt, "mean", na.rm = TRUE)

crs(ppt, describe = TRUE)$code pulls the EPSG code out of the CRS description. The output is in the next section.

title: 09-2: Raster Data
section: What to check for every raster
text:
What to check for every raster

One sentence at the end of your request:
Print the CRS, the extent, the resolution, the name, smallest and
largest value of each layer, and the number of missing cells, and draw
a quick map of each layer.
Better, with what you expect:
I expect EPSG <code>, longitude between <west> and <east> and latitude
between <south> and <north>, layers named <names>, and values between
<lowest> and <highest> <units>. Print each check on its own line as
"name of check: expected X, got Y".


What the checking code on the previous slide printed, run on ne_ppt_raw.tif:


CRS: expected EPSG 4269, got EPSG 4269 


longitude: expected -104 to -95, got -104.1 to -95.3 


latitude: expected 40 to 43, got 40 to 43 


smallest value: expected 0, got 0 


largest value: expected below 150, got 73.81

        mean
ppt 1.627232

title: 09-2: Raster Data
section: Checks that come from knowing the data
text:
Checks that come from knowing the data
The checks above apply to any raster. Checks from what you know about this variable are stronger:

Precipitation is never negative, and a daily total above a few hundred millimetres would be a record.
Five different days should not have identical values. A file in which two layers are the same is a file with a mistake in it.

Using the raster ppt_days with five daily layers, print the smallest value
of each layer (I expect 0 or more), and for each pair of consecutive
days, whether the two layers are identical (I expect not).

Put the code in my Quarto document analysis/weather.qmd, under the
heading "Check against the data", as R code chunks. Above each chunk,
write one plain-English sentence saying what it does and why. Build
every path with here::here(); no setwd(), no absolute paths. Print each
check on its own line as "name of check: expected X, got Y". Render the
document to HTML.
The AI’s code, and what it printed:


Code the AI wrote
mins <- global(ppt_days, "min", na.rm = TRUE)$min
cat("smallest value per day: expected 0 or more, got", round(mins, 2), "\n")


smallest value per day: expected 0 or more, got 0 0 0 0 0 


Code the AI wrote
for (i in 1:(nlyr(ppt_days) - 1)) {
  same <- all(values(ppt_days[[i]]) == values(ppt_days[[i + 1]]), na.rm = TRUE)
  cat(names(ppt_days)[i], "and", names(ppt_days)[i + 1], "identical: expected FALSE, got", same, "\n")
}


ppt_2012_08_01 and ppt_2012_08_02 identical: expected FALSE, got FALSE 
ppt_2012_08_02 and ppt_2012_08_03 identical: expected FALSE, got FALSE 
ppt_2012_08_03 and ppt_2012_08_04 identical: expected FALSE, got FALSE 
ppt_2012_08_04 and ppt_2012_08_05 identical: expected FALSE, got FALSE 


All pass. When a check like this fails, the code is usually not the problem: the file is. Stop, and ask whoever produced it.

title: 09-2: Raster Data
section: Your turn: read the AI’s code
text:
Your turn: read the AI’s code
A student has a land-cover raster, where 1 means corn, 2 soybean and 3 pasture, stored as plain numbers, and a weather raster on a different grid. They asked an AI to “put the land cover on the weather grid”, and got this:

landcover <- rast(here::here("data", "landcover.tif"))
weather <- rast(here::here("data", "weather.tif"))
landcover_on_weather <- resample(landcover, weather)


QuestionsAnswers


A. What does each line do?
B. Which line gives a wrong result without an error, and what will the result contain?
C. Which check would catch it?
D. What should the request have said?


A. Reads the land-cover raster; reads the weather raster; moves the land-cover values onto the weather grid.
B. Line 3. Without a method, resample() interpolates between neighbouring cells ("bilinear"). Codes are not amounts, so the result holds values between the codes. On the 4-by-4 land-cover raster from the “Silent failures” slide, moved to a shifted 3-by-3 grid, it gives values such as 1.09, 1.21, 1.3: neither corn nor soybean.
C. The list of distinct values before and after. Before: 1, 2 and 3. After: many values that are not whole numbers. The smallest and largest value would not catch it, because every interpolated value lies between them.
D. That the values are codes that must not be averaged or interpolated, so that each new cell takes the value of the nearest old cell (method = "near"), and to print the distinct values before and after.

title: 09-2: Raster Data
section: Requests you can copy

Requests you can copy

Closing instructionsLook at a rasterRead a rasterChange the gridSave and read backExplain code

title: 08-3: Tables in Your Paper
section: What you will and will not learn today
text:
What you will and will not learn today

The planDirections


Lecture 08-1 was about designing a table for a message. This lecture is about getting that table to the reader: into a paper, a thesis chapter or a report, without ever typing a number by hand. It is short.

The concept: why a table in a paper should come from code, and why it must be checked where the reader sees it
Reading code: the same table pattern as 08-1, written in the gt package, and the code that saves a table to a file
Asking AI: what to say about where the table is going
Checking: that the numbers in the saved file are the numbers in your analysis




Ask your AI assistant to install the gt, flextable and officer packages if you have not already.
The data is the same as in 08-1: countrypops, which comes with gt.

title: 08-3: Tables in Your Paper
section: The table in your paper comes from code
text:
The table in your paper comes from code

What is neededWhy


Every number in a table in your paper should be written there by code, from your data, the same code that wrote the table in your HTML. Never copy numbers from the HTML or the Console into Word by hand.
It is done when you can change something upstream (the data, a definition, a model), render again, and every table in the paper changes with it, with no typing.



Copying makes errors, and nobody checks a number that “came from R”. A transposed digit or a row pasted one line off gives no warning.
Analyses change. An advisor asks for one more year of data or a different definition. With copied numbers, every table has to be retyped, and every retyping is another chance for an error.
The record. With code, the .qmd and its HTML say exactly where each number in the paper came from (lecture 02-1, “Working with AI on your own research”).

title: 08-3: Tables in Your Paper
section: Where the reader sees the table
text:
Where the reader sees the table
The table has to look right where the reader sees it, not only in your HTML. Which package and which way of saving depend on the destination:








Destination
What works
Notes




Your HTML report (.qmd rendered to HTML)
gt or flextable, printed in a chunk
What you have been doing


A Word document
flextable, saved with save_as_docx(); or gt, saved with gtsave()
Both make a real Word table that a coauthor can edit


A .qmd rendered to Word
either package, printed in a chunk
Check the result: not every part survives (see “Checking the saved table”)


A PDF through LaTeX
gt (gtsave() to .tex), or modelsummary(output = "latex")
Common in economics journals



flextable was built for Word and PowerPoint first; gt for HTML first. Both do the jobs in 08-1’s table “Common steps”. If your paper is in Word, flextable is the safer default; for an HTML report, either is fine. Use the one your coauthors and your AI already work with, and check the result.

title: 08-3: Tables in Your Paper
section: The pattern, in gt
text:
The pattern, in gt
gt follows the same two-stage pattern as flextable (lecture 08-1, “The pattern every table shares”): build the display table with data code, then turn it into a table and change one part at a time.

The patternOne real exampleThe finished table



display_table |>
  gt() |>
  step_function(columns = ..., setting = value) |>
  step_function(columns = ..., setting = value)

Function names in gt begin with what they act on, which helps you read them:








Beginning
What the function acts on
Examples




cols_
columns: headers, alignment, width
cols_label(), cols_align()


fmt_

fmt_number(), fmt_percent(), fmt_integer()


tab_

tab_header(), tab_source_note(), tab_spanner()


opt_
the whole table
opt_stylize()



Where a step applies is written columns = and rows =.


The finished table from 08-1, written in gt. A sentence, then the chunk, as in the HTML:
Turn the display table into a finished table: plain headers with units, whole numbers, a title, and notes on the source and on how growth was computed.


Code the AI wrote
pop_gt <- pop_table |>

    pop_2020 = "Population, 2020 (thousands)",
    growth = "Growth, 2000 to 2020 (%)"

title: 08-3: Tables in Your Paper
section: A gt default that surprises
text:
A gt default that surprises
fmt_percent() shows a number as a percentage, and by default it multiplies by 100 first, because it expects a share such as 0.35. The growth column already holds percentages (77 for Papua New Guinea):


Code the AI wrote
pop_table |>
  head(3) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(country_name = "Country", region = "Region",
             pop_2020 = "Population, 2020 (thousands)", growth = "Growth, 2000 to 2020") |>
  fmt_number(columns = pop_2020, decimals = 0) |>
  fmt_percent(columns = growth, decimals = 0)








Country
Region
Population, 2020 (thousands)
Growth, 2000 to 2020




Papua New Guinea
Melanesia
9,750
7,700%


Vanuatu
Melanesia
312
6,227%


Solomon Islands
Melanesia
691
