No error, and the table looks finished. Papua New Guinea’s population did not grow by thousands of percent.

The fix: fmt_percent(..., scale_values = FALSE), or keep the column as a share (0.77) and let fmt_percent() multiply.
The check: one value you computed by hand. You know Papua New Guinea’s growth is 77% (2020 population divided by 2000 population, minus 1); the table must say 77%.

title: 08-3: Tables in Your Paper
section: How saving code is written
text:
How saving code is written
Saving a finished table follows the same pattern as saving data (lecture 03-1, “How writing code is written”): a function, the table, and a path.

The patternSave, then read back










Package
Shortest call
The file it makes




flextable
save_as_docx(table, path = "table.docx")
Word; save_as_pptx(), save_as_html(), save_as_image() for others


gt
gtsave(table, "table.docx")
Word; the extension chooses the format, such as .html, .tex, .rtf


modelsummary
modelsummary(models, output = "flextable") \|> save_as_docx(path = "table.docx")
Word, through flextable. (output = "table.docx" also works, but needs the pandoc R package installed.)



As with data, a file that already exists at the path is replaced without asking, and in your project the path is built with here::here(), for example here::here("tables", "population.docx").


The only way to know what the file holds is to read it back. For a Word file, the officer package lists the text of every cell:


Code the AI wrote
word_file <- file.path(tempdir(), "population.docx")
gtsave(pop_gt, word_file)

cells <- officer::docx_summary(officer::read_docx(word_file))
png_cell <- which(cells$text == "Papua New Guinea")
png_row <- cells$row_id[png_cell]
png_cells <- cells[cells$content_type == "table cell" & cells$row_id == png_row, ]
png_values <- png_cells$text[order(png_cells$cell_id)]

cat(paste0("growth of Papua New Guinea in the Word file: expected ", png_growth,
           ", got ", tail(png_values, 1)), "\n")


growth of Papua New Guinea in the Word file: expected 77, got 77 


On these slides the file goes to a temporary folder (tempdir()), so that rendering the slides leaves no files behind. In your project it goes to a folder such as tables/.

title: 08-3: Tables in Your Paper
section: Checking the saved table
text:
Checking the saved table

What to checkA title that went missing


Open the saved file in the program the reader will use, and check:

One number, against the HTML. Pick a cell and compare. The read-back on the previous slide prints it for you.
The title and notes are there. Not every part of a table survives every route into Word.
It fits the page. A table that fits a wide HTML page can run off a Word page.
Change something upstream and render again. The file should change with it, with no typing.



When these slides were made, a .qmd rendered to Word that printed a flextable with a title set by set_caption() produced a Word table without the title, and no warning. The same table saved with save_as_docx() kept it, and a gt title set with tab_header() survived both routes.
If the title is missing, ask the AI to set it with the chunk options #| label: tbl-<name> and #| tbl-cap: "<title>" instead, which Word keeps (tested: without a label starting tbl-, the caption was dropped too).
Package versions change, so do not memorise which route loses what. Open the Word file and look: that is the check that does not go out of date.

title: 08-3: Tables in Your Paper
section: What to put in the request
text:
What to put in the request
Everything from 08-1’s “What to put in a table request” (the data, the message, the reader, the layout, what each computed number means, the checks, the table standard), plus what only you know about where the table is going:

The destination: an HTML report, a Word document, a PDF through LaTeX
The package, if your coauthors or your document already use one
The path of the file to save, inside your project
The check in the destination: read the saved file back and print one value you know, next to the value in the HTML




Tip


Ask for the table to be printed in the HTML and saved to the file, from the same code. Then the HTML is the record, and the file is what goes into the paper.

title: 08-3: Tables in Your Paper
section: Requests you can copy
text:
Requests you can copy
Copy one, then replace every <...> with what you know. Every table request ends with the table standard and then the closing instructions.

Closing instructionsThe table standardSave a table for a paperExplain code


The lines that end every request for code. Replace the two blanks; leave “expected X, got Y” as it is, because it tells the AI how to print each check:
Put the code in my Quarto document <path to your .qmd>, under the
heading "<heading>", as R code chunks. Above each chunk, write one
plain-English sentence saying what it does and why. Build every path
with here::here(); no setwd(), no absolute paths. Print each check on
its own line as "name of check: expected X, got Y". Render the document
to HTML.
A chat assistant cannot render: paste its chunks into your .qmd and render it yourself. An agent in your editor or terminal can do every step.


The same block as in lecture 08-1. Paste it into every table request, just before the closing instructions:
Every table must meet this standard:
1. Column headers and row labels in plain words with units, such as
   "Corn yield (bushels per acre)", never a column name such as
   corn_yield.
2. Categories in words, such as "Irrigated", never a code such as 1.
3. Numbers rounded to what the message needs, with the same number of
   decimals down each column.
4. Thousands separators in large numbers, except in years.
5. Percentages shown as percentages.
6. Numbers right-aligned so that the digits line up; text left-aligned.
7. Text no smaller than the document's body text.
8. Fits the page width where it will appear, without scrolling.
9. Rows in an order that serves the message (by value, or in time
   order), not alphabetical unless the reader will search a long table.
10. A title that says what the numbers are.
11. A note giving the source of the data.
12. A note saying how any computed column was computed.
13. The number of observations behind each value, when it varies.
14. Nothing the message does not need: no extra columns, no row
    numbers, no heavy borders, no colours that only decorate.
For regression tables, also:
15. One column per model, with headers or a title saying what each
    model explains.
16. Standard errors in parentheses below each estimate, with their kind
    stated in a note.
17. Significance stars left out, or defined in a note and used the same
    way in every table.
18. The number of observations for every model.


The table made under the heading "<heading>" goes into <the
destination, such as a Word document>. Using <gt or flextable>, print
it in the HTML and also save it as <path for the new file, such as
tables/name.docx>, from the same code. Then read the saved file back
and check <one value> (I computed <the value> myself), and check that
the title and every note are in the file.

Put the code in my Quarto document <path to your .qmd>, under the
heading "<heading>", as R code chunks. Above each chunk, write one
plain-English sentence saying what it does and why. Build every path
with here::here(); no setwd(), no absolute paths. Print each check on
its own line as "name of check: expected X, got Y". Render the document
to HTML.
Then open the file yourself, in the program the reader will use.


For code you did not write, or code you are not sure about:
Explain this R code to me. For each line, write one plain-English
sentence. Then list:
1. any number format that changes the values, such as multiplying by
   100, and whether the column already holds that unit
2. any file the code writes, and whether it could replace a file that
   already exists

<paste the code here>

title: 08-3: Tables in Your Paper
section: What you must understand, and what the AI can write
text:
What you must understand, and what the AI can write







You need to understand
The AI can write




Why no number in a paper is typed by hand
The code that saves the table


Where the reader will see the table
gtsave(), save_as_docx(), output =


What unit each column holds, so that a format does not change it
fmt_number(), fmt_percent() and the rest


One value you can compute yourself
The read-back check



Every table in a paper: made by the same code as the table in your HTML, saved to a file in your project, read back with a check, and opened in the program the reader will use.

title: 08-1: Communicating with Tables
section: What you will and will not learn today
text:
What you will and will not learn today

The planDirections


An AI assistant can turn any data into a table in seconds, and it knows every option of every table package. What it cannot do is:

know what the table is supposed to tell the reader
know who the reader is
decide which numbers the reader must compare
tell whether the numbers in the table are the ones you meant

Those are your job. So today is about:

The concept: what a table is for, and the design choices that decide whether it tells the reader anything
Reading code: recognising what a line of table code does, without memorising it
Asking AI: what to put in a table request, including a standard every finished table must meet
Checking: how to tell that the numbers in the table are right

This deck shows the code of the flextable package. Lecture 08-3 shows the same pattern in the gt package, and 08-2 covers regression tables.



Ask your AI assistant to install the flextable and gt packages if you have not already. Installing is a one-time step per computer.
The data on these slides is countrypops, which comes with the gt package, so there is no file to download.

title: 08-1: Communicating with Tables
section: A table or a figure?
text:
A table or a figure?
Both exist to tell a reader something. They are good at different things:








Choose
When the reader needs to
Example




A figure
see a pattern: a trend, a gap, a shape
yields rising over twenty years


A table
read exact values, or look up the one row they care about
each county’s yield, so a farmer can find their own


A table
compare a few numbers that a figure would not make clearer
the average yield in three states



If the reader will only take away a pattern, a figure usually does it faster. If the reader will quote a number, or look one up, use a table.

title: 08-1: Communicating with Tables
section: One sentence and one reader
text:
One sentence and one reader

What you needWhy the AI cannot do this


Before any table, write down two things:

The message: the one sentence the reader should take away. For example: “From 2000 to 2020, Papua New Guinea, Vanuatu and the Solomon Islands, all in Melanesia, grew fastest, and Tonga and the Federated States of Micronesia barely grew.”
The reader: who will see the table and what they already know. For example: students in a development course who know the Pacific but have not seen these numbers.

Every design decision on the following slides is judged against that sentence and that reader.


Ask an AI for “a table of this data” and it shows every column of the data, in the order they are stored, with every decimal. That is a table of the data, not of a message. Nothing in it tells the reader where to look.
The AI can only design for a message if you give it one.

title: 08-1: Communicating with Tables
section: The data on these slides
text:
The data on these slides
pacific holds the population of 13 Pacific countries in 2000 and 2020. One row is one country in one year, so it has 26 rows:

head(pacific, 4)

# A tibble: 4 × 4
  country_name region       year population
  <chr>        <chr>       <int>      <int>
1 Australia    Australasia  2000   19028802
2 Australia    Australasia  2020   25655289
3 Fiji         Melanesia    2000     832509
4 Fiji         Melanesia    2020     920422


Every table on the following slides is built from this data.




Three names used in this deck



Table: data in R, as in every lecture of this course. pacific is a table.
Finished table: what the reader sees in your HTML or your paper.
Display table: the table in R that holds exactly the rows and columns of the finished table, in order, before any styling.

title: 08-1: Communicating with Tables
section: Rows, columns, and what the reader compares
text:
Rows, columns, and what the reader compares
The numbers the reader must compare should sit next to each other, ideally in one column, where the eye runs straight down.

One row per country and yearOne row per countryThe rule


The data as it is stored. To see how much Australia grew, the reader has to find two rows and subtract:


CountryRegionYearPopulationAustraliaAustralasia200019,028,802AustraliaAustralasia202025,655,289Federated States of MicronesiaMicronesia2000111,709Federated States of MicronesiaMicronesia2020112,106FijiMelanesia2000832,509FijiMelanesia2020920,422


(The first 6 of 26 rows.)


The years side by side, and the comparison the message is about, the growth, computed and put in its own column. The reader runs down one column to compare countries:


Population (thousands)CountryRegion20002020Growth (%)AustraliaAustralasia19,02925,65535FijiMelanesia83392011Federated States of MicronesiaMicronesia1121120KiribatiMicronesia8912642New CaledoniaMelanesia21327228New ZealandAustralasia3,8585,09032





What the reader compares goes down a column.
What the reader looks up (the country, the state, the year) goes in the first column.
A number the reader would have to compute in their head (a difference, a growth rate, a share) goes in the table as its own column.

Deciding this is deciding the display table. That happens before any styling (see “How table code is written”).

title: 08-1: Communicating with Tables
section: Order the rows for the message
text:
Order the rows for the message

AlphabeticalBy growth




CountryRegionGrowth, 2000 to 2020 (%)AustraliaAustralasia35Federated States of MicronesiaMicronesia0FijiMelanesia11French PolynesiaPolynesia20KiribatiMicronesia42New CaledoniaMelanesia28New ZealandAustralasia32Papua New GuineaMelanesia77SamoaPolynesia17Solomon IslandsMelanesia61TongaPolynesia3TuvaluPolynesia15VanuatuMelanesia62


Which countries grew fastest? The reader has to read all 13 numbers to find out.




CountryRegionGrowth, 2000 to 2020 (%)Papua New GuineaMelanesia77VanuatuMelanesia62Solomon IslandsMelanesia61KiribatiMicronesia42AustraliaAustralasia35New ZealandAustralasia32New CaledoniaMelanesia28French PolynesiaPolynesia20SamoaPolynesia17TuvaluPolynesia15FijiMelanesia11TongaPolynesia3Federated States of MicronesiaMicronesia0


The message is in the first three and last two rows: three Melanesian countries at the top, Tonga and the Federated States of Micronesia at the bottom.
Grouping is another order: rows under a heading per region, countries ordered by growth inside each. It serves a message about the regions.
Alphabetical order serves a reader who will look up one row, in a long table: a county list that farmers search for their own county. For a message about which rows are largest or smallest, order by the value. For years, use time order.

title: 08-1: Communicating with Tables
section: Round to what the message needs, and align
text:
Round to what the message needs, and align

Too many digitsRounded and right-alignedThe rule


The growth rates as R computes them, centred in their column:


country_namegrowthPapua New Guinea76.9991705Australia34.8234587Federated States of Micronesia0.3553877


Seven decimals claim a precision no population estimate has, and centring puts the digits in different places on each line.




CountryGrowth, 2000 to 2020 (%)Papua New Guinea77Australia35Federated States of Micronesia0


Whole percentages are enough to say “fastest” and “barely”. With the same number of decimals in every row and the numbers right-aligned, the ones digits line up, so the size of a number is visible at a glance.



Round to the digits the message needs. A difference the message talks about must still be visible after rounding.
The same number of decimals all the way down a column.
Numbers right-aligned, text left-aligned.
Big numbers in a unit the reader can read: “thousands” or “millions” in the header, or thousands separators (19,028,802).

title: 08-1: Communicating with Tables
section: Say what the numbers are
text:
Say what the numbers are
A reader who sees a number must know what it is without reading your code.

Headers in plain words, with units: “Growth, 2000 to 2020 (%)”, never growth; “Population (thousands)”, never pop_2020.
A title that says what the table shows: which units (countries), which numbers, which years.
Notes under the table for what does not fit in a header: the source of the data, how a computed column was computed, and how many observations are behind each number when that varies.

A header such as “Growth” can mean several things. The section “A table must be correct before it can communicate” shows two of them giving different numbers from the same data, and how a note prevents the confusion.

title: 08-1: Communicating with Tables
section: The pattern every table shares
text:
The pattern every table shares
Table code always has two stages. First, ordinary data code builds the display table. Then a table function turns it into a finished table, and a chain of steps changes one part of it at a time.

The patternCommon stepsVariations you will see





Important


The steps change how numbers are shown (rounding, units, percent signs); which rows appear, their order, and the values are decided in the display table. A formatting step can still show a value wrongly (lecture 08-3 shows one that multiplies by 100), so check one shown value against the data.




display_table |>
  table_function() |>
  step_function(where, setting = value) |>
  step_function(where, setting = value)









Part
What it is
Required?




display_table
The rows and columns the reader will see, built with ordinary data code (pivot_wider(), mutate(), arrange(), select())
Yes


table_function()
Turns the display table into a finished table: flextable() or gt()
Yes


step_function(...)
Changes one part: headers, number format, title, notes, alignment
No; each part has a default


where
Which columns or rows the step applies to. Leave it out and the step applies everywhere
No


\|>
Passes the result on to the next step






The same jobs, in the two packages you will see most:








Job
flextable
gt




Rename headers
set_header_labels(growth = "Growth (%)")
cols_label(growth = "Growth (%)")


Round numbers
colformat_double(j = "growth", digits = 0)
fmt_number(columns = growth, decimals = 0)


A header over several columns
add_header_row(values = ..., colwidths = ...)
tab_spanner(label = ..., columns = ...)


Title
set_caption("...")
tab_header(title = "...")


Notes under the table
add_footer_lines("...")
tab_source_note("...")


Alignment
align(j = ..., align = "right")
cols_align(align = "right", columns = ...)


Column widths
autofit()
cols_width(...)


Fit the page width
fit_to_width(max_width = 6) (inches)
cols_width(...), shorter headers


Rows under group headings
as_grouped_data(), or merge_v() to merge repeated cells
gt(groupname_col = "region")


A ready-made look
theme_booktabs()
opt_stylize()



Where a step applies is written j = (columns) and i = (rows) in flextable, and columns = and rows = in gt.



flextable::flextable(...): the package name, then ::, then the function, without loading the whole package.
The display table built in the same chain, straight into the table function: pacific |> pivot_wider(...) |> flextable().
The finished table stored under a name first (pop_ft <- ...) and printed on a later line.
modelsummary(...) for regression tables, which builds the display table for you (lecture 08-2).

title: 08-1: Communicating with Tables
section: One real example

title: 08-1: Communicating with Tables
section: The table standard
text:
The table standard
Every table you hand in must meet this standard, whatever its message. Each item has a yes or no answer.








Item




1

title: 08-1: Communicating with Tables
section: The numbers must be the ones you meant
text:
The numbers must be the ones you meant

Two meanings of “growth”The checkChecks for any table


Ask an AI for “population growth by region” and either of these can come back. Both run without an error:


Code the AI wrote
pacific_wide |>
  group_by(region) |>
  summarise(
    countries = n(),
    mean_of_countries = mean(growth),
    from_totals = 100 * (sum(pop_2020) / sum(pop_2000) - 1)
  )


# A tibble: 4 × 4
  region      countries mean_of_countries from_totals
  <chr>           <int>             <dbl>       <dbl>
1 Australasia         2              33.4        34.3
2 Melanesia           5              47.7        66.5
3 Micronesia          2              21.4        19.0
4 Polynesia           4              13.6        15.7



mean_of_countries: the average of the countries’ growth rates. Vanuatu, which had 192 thousand people in 2000, counts as much as Papua New Guinea, which had 5,508 thousand.
from_totals: the growth of the region’s total population.

For Melanesia, 48% against 66%. Neither is wrong; they answer different questions. A table headed “Growth (%)” does not say which one the reader is looking at.


Decide which one the message needs before you ask, and compute one value yourself from numbers you can see. Melanesia’s total population was 7,176,088 in 2000 and 11,945,398 in 2020, so the growth of the total is 66.5%. Then ask the AI to print the check:


Code the AI wrote
growth_table <- pacific_wide |>
  group_by(region) |>
  summarise(growth = mean(growth))

cat("Melanesia growth: expected 66.5, got",
    round(growth_table$growth[growth_table$region == "Melanesia"], 1), "\n")


Melanesia growth: expected 66.5, got 47.7 


The check fails: this code computed the average of the countries. Ask the AI to compute growth from the regional totals, and write in a note which one the table shows.



Rows: the number of rows is the number of things the reader should see (here, 13 countries or 4 regions).
One value, computed by hand: pick one cell and compute it yourself from the data.
Counts behind each value: when a cell is an average, print how many observations it averages. A region with 2 countries and one with 5 look the same in a table of averages.
Totals: if the counts should add up to the number of rows in the data, check that they do.

title: 08-1: Communicating with Tables
section: The checklist
text:
The checklist
Apply it to any table, yours or the AI’s, by looking at it in the rendered HTML. Each question has a yes or no answer.

Can someone who has not seen the data state the message within a few seconds?
Are the numbers the reader must compare next to each other, ideally down one column?
Is every number one the message needs?
Does every header say what its numbers are, with units?
Does it meet every item of the table standard?
Did one value, computed by hand, match?

A “no” to any question is something to fix.

title: 08-1: Communicating with Tables
section: Your turn: judge a table
text:
Your turn: judge a table
The message is meant to be: “From 2000 to 2020, Melanesia’s total population grew fastest of the four regions.”


regioncountriesmean_of_countriespop_total_2020Australasia233.386330,745,489Melanesia547.672111,945,398Micronesia221.3635238,569Polynesia413.6393633,172



QuestionsAnswers


A. Apply questions 1 to 5 of the checklist. Which answers are “no”?
B. Does the table show the number the message is about?
C. List the changes you would ask for, most important first.


A. Question 1 is close to “yes” only because the table is small: Melanesia has the largest number, but the reader must first work out which column to read. Question 3 is “no”: pop_total_2020 is not needed for the message. Question 4 is “no”: raw column names, and nothing says which kind of growth mean_of_countries is. Question 5 is “no”: four decimals, no title, no notes. Question 6 fails: Melanesia’s total population grew by 66.5%, and the table says 47.7.
B. No. It shows the average of the countries’ growth rates, not the growth of each region’s total population. Melanesia comes first either way (66% for its total, against 34%, 19%, 16% for Australasia, Micronesia, Polynesia), but a reader who quotes “48%” for Melanesia’s population growth would be wrong.
C. Compute growth from each region’s total population; order the regions by it; plain-word headers with units; whole percentages; drop pop_total_2020; a title; a note saying how growth was computed, how many countries each region has, and where the data comes from.

title: 08-1: Communicating with Tables
section: Working with AI on your own research
text:
Working with AI on your own research
Tables follow the same way of working as everything else (lecture 02-1, “Working with AI on your own research”): you ask, the AI writes into a Quarto document (.qmd) with one plain-English sentence above each chunk, you render it to HTML, and you judge the HTML.
For tables, judging the HTML matters even more:

The reader sees the finished table, not the data behind it. The HTML shows exactly what they will see.
The table sits next to the sentence that says what it shows, so you can check that the two agree.
The checks (rows, one value computed by hand) print right under the table.

Every table request ends with the table standard and then the closing instructions. Both are under Recommended requests.

title: 08-1: Communicating with Tables
section: What to put in a table request
text:
What to put in a table request
The AI already knows every table package. Your request supplies what it cannot know:

The data: which table or file, what one row is, and which columns the table uses, with their units
The message: the one sentence the reader should take away
The reader: who will see it, and what they already know
The layout: what one row of the table is, which columns, and the order of the rows
What each computed number means: “growth of the regional total”, not just “growth”
The checks: the number of rows, and one value you computed yourself
The table standard, then the closing instructions





Using an agent in your editor or terminal?


An agent such as Claude Code can open the data and look for itself. It still cannot know your message, your reader, or which meaning of a number you intend. Write those down before it runs.

title: 08-1: Communicating with Tables

text:
A weak request and a strong one

WeakStrongWhat came back


Make a table of the Pacific population data.
The AI has to guess which columns, which rows, which order and which message. What comes back is the “Before” table on “Before and after”: every column, raw names, seven decimals.

(2000 and 2020), with the columns country_name, region, year and

not seen these numbers.

Code the AI wrote

title: 08-1: Communicating with Tables
section: Requests you can copy
text:
Requests you can copy
Copy one, then replace every <...> with what you know: the message, the reader, the layout, what you found in the data. Every table request ends with the table standard and then the closing instructions.

Closing instructionsThe table standardMake a table for a messageAsk for layoutsImprove a tableCheck a table against the dataExplain code


The lines that end every request for code. Replace the two blanks; leave “expected X, got Y” as it is, because it tells the AI how to print each check:
Put the code in my Quarto document <path to your .qmd>, under the
heading "<heading>", as R code chunks. Above each chunk, write one
plain-English sentence saying what it does and why. Build every path
with here::here(); no setwd(), no absolute paths. Print each check on
its own line as "name of check: expected X, got Y". Render the document
to HTML.
A chat assistant cannot render: paste its chunks into your .qmd and render it yourself. An agent in your editor or terminal can do every step.


Paste this into every table request, just before the closing instructions:
Every table must meet this standard:
1. Column headers and row labels in plain words with units, such as
   "Corn yield (bushels per acre)", never a column name such as
   corn_yield.
2. Categories in words, such as "Irrigated", never a code such as 1.
3. Numbers rounded to what the message needs, with the same number of
   decimals down each column.
4. Thousands separators in large numbers, except in years.
5. Percentages shown as percentages.
6. Numbers right-aligned so that the digits line up; text left-aligned.
7. Text no smaller than the document's body text.
8. Fits the page width where it will appear, without scrolling.
9. Rows in an order that serves the message (by value, or in time
   order), not alphabetical unless the reader will search a long table.
10. A title that says what the numbers are.
11. A note giving the source of the data.
12. A note saying how any computed column was computed.
13. The number of observations behind each value, when it varies.
14. Nothing the message does not need: no extra columns, no row
    numbers, no heavy borders, no colours that only decorate.
For regression tables, also:
15. One column per model, with headers or a title saying what each
    model explains.
16. Standard errors in parentheses below each estimate, with their kind
    stated in a note.
17. Significance stars left out, or defined in a note and used the same
    way in every table.
18. The number of observations for every model.
Keep your own copy of this block, and add to it each time you find something the AI keeps getting wrong.

The table uses the columns <columns>, which mean <what they mean> and

section: What you must understand, and what the AI can write

What you must understand, and what the AI can write







You need to understand
The AI can write

title: 06-2: Version Control: Keeping a History of Your Project
section: What you will and will not learn today
text:
What you will and will not learn today

The planDirections


An AI assistant can run every git command there is, and get each one right. What it cannot do is:

decide which of your changes belong together
know why you made them
know which files must never leave your computer
know whether it is safe to send your work to GitHub, where others can see it

Those four are your job. So today is about:

The concept: what version control is for, and what each of its steps does (stage, commit, push, pull, branch, merge, pull request)
Reading code: recognising what a git command will do, and reading what git prints
Asking AI: what to tell the AI, and what it must not do on its own
Checking: what to look at before you let the AI commit or push

You will not learn to type git commands from memory.



Getting a repository onto your computer (cloning) is in lecture 02-0. This lecture is about what to do with one.
To follow along on your own project you need git, a free GitHub account, and a few one-time settings. The Before class section of exercise 6-2 lists them, each with a check whose answer you know (for example, git config --global pull.rebase prints false). Do it before class; an AI assistant can help.
The git output on these slides comes from a small practice repository that is built in a temporary folder each time the slides are made. Every output is real. Where the code that produced an output is shown, put() writes a file into that repository and git() runs one git command in it; both are small functions written for these slides.

title: 06-2: Version Control: Keeping a History of Your Project
section: What version control is for
text:
What version control is for

The folder you already haveWhat you want to answerWhy a synced folder is not this


analysis.qmd
analysis_v2.qmd
analysis_v2_new.qmd
analysis_final.qmd
analysis_final_USE_THIS.qmd

You do not know what is different between any two of them.
You do not know why any of them exists.
You do not know which one produced the numbers in your paper.
You cannot go back to a moment you did not think to save.

You have the files. What is missing is a record of what changed, when, and why.



“What did I change last Tuesday, and why?”
“Put the whole project back the way it was before I started the revision.”
“Which version of the code produced the table in the submitted paper?”
“My coauthor changed the cleaning step this week. Which lines?”
“The AI edited six files. What exactly did it change?”

Version control is a record of a project’s history that answers these. Git is the program that keeps that record, on your computer. GitHub is a website that keeps a copy of it, so others can see and add to it.


Dropbox, Google Drive and OneDrive keep old copies of each file. That is not the same:

A change spans files. Renaming a column changes three steps at once, for one reason. Git records that as one change. A synced folder records three unrelated file times.
Nothing records why. There is no place for the reason, and the reason is what you need later.
You cannot go back to a moment. You restore files one at a time and hope you found them all.

Keep a git repository on your computer’s own disk, not inside a synced folder; sync programs and git can each change files the other is using. For a copy elsewhere, use GitHub.

title: 06-2: Version Control: Keeping a History of Your Project
section: Repository and commit
text:
Repository and commit

A repositoryA commitWhat a commit is not


A repository is your project folder plus its full history. Making a folder a repository adds one hidden folder, .git, where git keeps the history. Every other file stays an ordinary file you edit as usual.

One repository per research project, at the project root, next to the .Rproj file.
The history is on your disk. Git needs no internet connection; GitHub is optional.



A commit is a stored copy of the whole project at one moment, with a message saying why. The history is the list of commits, each one pointing back to the one before it.

main is the name of the line of commits; HEAD marks the one you are on (more on both under Branch and merge).

Complete: going back to a commit gives you the whole project as it was, not one old file among new ones.
Permanent: it stays in the history. Only the few commands under “Commands that can lose work” can remove it from a branch, and even then git keeps it for a while.
It carries a reason: the message.




Not saving a file. You save without thinking. You commit on purpose, when you have finished something that makes sense on its own, a few times a day.
Not a backup. A backup protects against losing your computer. A commit protects against losing track of what changed and why. Have both; GitHub gives you a copy of the history.
Not only the changes. A commit stores the whole project. The list of changed lines you see for a commit (git calls it a diff) is worked out by comparing it with the commit before.

title: 06-2: Version Control: Keeping a History of Your Project
section: Stage, then commit
text:
Stage, then commit


Your project folder: the files as you see and edit them, with every change you have made. Git’s messages call this the working directory; that is not the same as R’s working directory from 03-1.
Staging (git’s word: add): choosing which of those changes go into the next commit.
Committing: storing the staged changes as one commit, with a message.





Why the middle step exists


A morning’s work often holds several unrelated changes: a fix to the cleaning step, a half-finished figure, a line you added to find a bug. Staging lets you commit the fix alone, with its own message, and leave the rest for later. Without it, every commit would be “everything I touched since the last one”.

title: 06-2: Version Control: Keeping a History of Your Project
section: What goes into one commit
text:
What goes into one commit
This is your decision, not the AI’s: it cannot know which changes belong together or why you made them.

One changeThe message



One thing. You can describe it in one line without the word “and”.
Complete. The project still renders afterwards, so every commit in the history is a state you could go back to.
Small enough to read. A diff of 900 lines will not be read, by you or anyone.

When to commit:

When you would be annoyed to lose the last hour.
Before anything risky: a large rewrite, a step that overwrites files, and before you let an AI edit your project. Afterwards, the diff shows exactly what it changed, and you can undo any of it.



Drop fields with zero yield before averaging

NASS writes 0 for counties with no harvested acres. Including them
pulled the average irrigated yield down by 4 bu/ac.

First line: what the commit does, in under about 50 characters, written as an instruction (“Drop fields…”, not “dropped” or “changes”).
Then a blank line and a few sentences, if the reason is not obvious. Say why. What changed is already in the diff; why is only in your head, and you will forget it.




Important


A message such as update, fix or changes tells a reader nothing. AI assistants write messages like “Update files” unless told the reason. Give it the reason.

title: 06-2: Version Control: Keeping a History of Your Project
section: What stays out of the repository
text:
What stays out of the repository
Also your decision. Everything committed is kept for good, and anyone with a copy of the repository has all of it.

In, out, and it depends.gitignoreA key that was committed











What
Why




In
.qmd and .R files, README.md, .gitignore, renv.lock, the .Rproj file
Written by you, small, text


Never
Passwords and API keys (often in a file called .Renviron), data under a data use agreement, data that identifies people
Permanent once committed, visible to anyone with a copy


Usually out
Rendered HTML and its _files folders, data/processed/, results/
Your steps rebuild them (06-1)


Out
.Rhistory, .RData, .Rproj.user/, .DS_Store
Files RStudio and macOS write for themselves


Depends
data/raw/
In if small and you may share it; out if large (GitHub refuses files over 100 MB) or restricted





A text file at the project root listing what git should ignore. Each line is a file name or a pattern; * stands for any characters, and a name ending in / means a folder.
# files RStudio and macOS write
.Rhistory
.RData
.Rproj.user/
.DS_Store

# secrets
.Renviron

# rendered output, rebuilt by rendering
*.html
*_files/



Important


.gitignore only affects files git is not already tracking. A file committed once stays in the history even if you add it to .gitignore later. Write .gitignore before the first commit.





Deleting a password in a later commit does not remove it: the earlier commit still holds it, and anyone who copies the repository gets every commit.
If a key ever reaches GitHub, replace the key (make a new one, cancel the old one) at once. Do not try to erase it from the history.

title: 06-2: Version Control: Keeping a History of Your Project
section: Branch and merge
text:
Branch and merge

A branchWhen research needs oneMergingMerge conflict


A branch is a name that points at a commit and moves forward as you commit. Your main line of work is a branch called main. Making a new branch lets you work on a separate line of commits; main stays as it was.

Switching to a branch changes the files in your folder to match that branch. HEAD in the figure means “the branch you are on”.



A revision. The paper is submitted. Work on a branch called revision, and main stays exactly what you submitted.
An idea you doubt. Try it on a branch. If it does not work, delete the branch, and nothing of it is left in main.
An AI’s larger change. Let it work on a branch, read what it did, then decide whether to bring it into main.

For a project you work on alone, main and well-made commits are enough until one of these comes up.


Merging brings the commits of one branch into another. On main, merge revision, and its commits become part of main.

If the two branches changed different files, or different parts of a file, git combines them without asking. If both changed the same lines, git stops: that is a merge conflict, the next tab.




$ git merge units-in-labels
Auto-merging analysis/02-summary.qmd
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in analysis/02-summary.qmd
Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result.


Both branches changed the same line of analysis/02-summary.qmd, the label of the y-axis. Git wrote both versions into the file, between marker lines:


Draw yields of irrigated and non-irrigated fields.

```{r}
corn <- readRDS(here::here("data", "processed", "corn_clean.rds"))
ggplot2::ggplot(corn, ggplot2::aes(x = factor(Irrigated), y = Yield)) +
  ggplot2::geom_boxplot() +
  ggplot2::labs(
    title = "Corn yield by irrigation",
    x = "Irrigated",
<<<<<<< HEAD
    y = "Corn yield"
=======
    y = "Yield (bu/ac)"
>>>>>>> units-in-labels
  )
```



Between <<<<<<< and =======: the line on the branch you are on (HEAD, here main).
Between ======= and >>>>>>>: the line on the branch you are merging in.

Which label is right is a question about what your readers need, not about text, so git leaves it to you. The fix: edit the file to the version you want, delete the three marker lines, then stage and commit. An AI can do the editing; the choice is yours.

title: 06-2: Version Control: Keeping a History of Your Project
section: Push, pull, and GitHub
text:
Push, pull, and GitHub

A remoteTwo things that can stop a pullWhy pushA pull request


A remote is a copy of your repository somewhere else, usually on GitHub. By convention it is called origin.


Push: send your new commits to the remote.
Pull: get the commits others have pushed, and merge them into yours. A pull can stop with a merge conflict, for the same reason and with the same fix as on the previous slide.
Fetch: get them without merging, to look first.



If a pull stops and git says it needs to know how to reconcile divergent branches, the one-time setting git config --global pull.rebase false is missing. It tells git to merge on a pull (the default this lecture assumes), not to rewrite your commits.
When a pull has to merge, git opens a text editor for the merge message. git pull --no-edit accepts git’s standard message instead. Ask an AI agent for --no-edit: it cannot type into an editor, and would wait forever.



A copy off your computer, history included.
Your coauthors and advisor see the same history and add to it.
The paper. Many journals ask for the code. A repository can be private while you work and made public when you publish; making it public shows its entire history, so read the history first.



A pull request is a proposal, made on GitHub, to merge one branch into another. Its page shows every changed line, and people can comment on single lines before anyone presses Merge.

With a coauthor: they push a branch, open a pull request, you read and comment, and one of you merges.
With an AI: the AI works on a branch and opens a pull request; you read the diff on the page, as carefully as a coauthor’s, and merge only what you understand.
Alone: optional, but it gives you one page that lists everything a branch changed.

After a merge on GitHub, main on GitHub has a commit your computer does not. Pull to get it.

title: 06-2: Version Control: Keeping a History of Your Project
section: Going back
text:
Going back
Each commit has an identifier, a code git gives it, such as a3f9c21; git log --oneline lists them. Going back always names either a file or a commit:









You want
What git does
What is lost
When it is safe




A. Throw away the uncommitted changes to one file
git restore <file> puts the file back as it was at the last commit
Those uncommitted changes, for good: git never stored them
After reading git diff <file> and deciding you want none of it


B. Undo a change that is already committed
git revert <identifier> adds a new commit that reverses that commit
Nothing: both commits stay in the history
Always, even after a push, because it only adds


C. One file as it was at an earlier commit
git restore --source <identifier> <file> puts that version of the file in your folder, as an uncommitted change
Any uncommitted changes to that file
After reading git diff <file>; then commit it, with a message saying why




A and C can lose work, and only work you never committed. That is the strongest reason to commit often.
B is the way to undo anything already on GitHub: the history shows both the change and its undoing. If later commits changed the same lines, B stops with a conflict, with the same fix as for a merge.
Undoing by rewriting the history (reset, commit --amend, rebase) also exists. It is in the table “Commands that can lose work”, and it is never needed for the three cases above.

title: 06-2: Version Control: Keeping a History of Your Project
section: A working day
text:
A working day








Step
What it is for
Who decides




1. Pull
Start from the newest version, including your coauthors’ work
Routine


2. Work
Edit, render, read the HTML
You, or the AI


3. Look at what changed
Find the debugging line, the file you did not mean to touch
You


4. Stage and commit one change
One change, with a message saying why
You: what goes in, and the reason


5. Push
A copy on GitHub, for you and others
You: after checking what is in it




RStudio’s Git tab has a button for each step. A commit made by clicking, by typing a command, or by asking an AI is the same commit.

title: 06-2: Version Control: Keeping a History of Your Project
section: How git commands are written
text:
How git commands are written
An AI that works with git runs commands in a terminal and shows them to you. Every git command follows the same pattern.

The patternThe common verbsCommands that can lose workVariations you will see


git  verb  target  --option value








Part
What it is
Required?




git
The program
Yes


verb
What to do: status, add, commit, push, …
Yes, exactly one


target
Which files, branch or remote. Left out, it usually means “all” or “the current one”
Depends on the verb


--option value
Changes what the verb does: -m "message", --staged, --force
No



A real line that follows the pattern:
git add analysis/01-clean.qmd
Stage the changes in analysis/01-clean.qmd, and only that file.


The column that matters is the last one: what the command changes.








Command
What it does
What it changes




git status
Lists changed, staged and untracked files
Nothing


git diff
Shows changed lines (--staged: the staged ones)
Nothing


git log
Lists commits
Nothing


git add <files>
Stages changes
Only what is staged


git commit -m "<message>"
Makes a commit from what is staged
Adds to the history


git switch <branch>
Moves to a branch (-c: makes a new one)
The files in your folder


git merge <branch>
Brings another branch’s commits into this one
Adds to the history; can stop with a conflict


git push
Sends new commits to the remote
The copy on GitHub


git pull
Gets new commits from the remote and merges them
The history and your files


git restore <file>
Puts a file back as it was at the last commit
Throws away uncommitted changes to it, for good


git revert <identifier>
Adds a commit that reverses an earlier one
Adds to the history





These are the commands to stop and read before they run:







Command
What it does




git restore <file>, git checkout -- <file>
Throws away uncommitted changes to a file


git reset --hard
Throws away all uncommitted changes


git push --force
Replaces the history on GitHub with yours, deleting commits others pushed


git commit --amend, git rebase
Rewrites commits that may already be on GitHub


git clean -fd
Deletes every untracked file



Committed work can almost always be recovered. Uncommitted work, once thrown away, cannot.



git add . or git add -A: stage every change in the folder, including files you did not mean to commit.
git commit -am "<message>": stage every change to tracked files and commit, in one command.
gh repo create, gh pr create: commands of gh, GitHub’s own program, for things that happen on GitHub (make a repository, open a pull request).
git -C <folder> status: run the command in another folder.
git add . && git commit -m "...": && runs the second command only if the first succeeded.

title: 06-2: Version Control: Keeping a History of Your Project
section: Reading what git prints
text:
Reading what git prints
The practice repository, after the figure title in the summary step was changed and two new files appeared:

git statusgit diffgit log




$ git status
On branch main
Changes not staged for commit:
  (use "git add <file>..." to update what will be committed)
  (use "git restore <file>..." to discard changes in working directory)
    modified:   analysis/02-summary.qmd

Untracked files:
  (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed)
    .Renviron
    analysis/03-regression.qmd

no changes added to commit (use "git add" and/or "git commit -a")



First line: the branch you are on.
“Changes not staged for commit”: tracked files that changed. “modified” means edited.
“Untracked files”: files git has never stored. .Renviron is here because there is no .gitignore yet, so git add . would commit the key in it.





$ git diff
diff --git a/analysis/02-summary.qmd b/analysis/02-summary.qmd
index d8cc48b..bc72b0c 100644
--- a/analysis/02-summary.qmd
+++ b/analysis/02-summary.qmd
@@ -5,7 +5,7 @@ corn <- readRDS(here::here("data", "processed", "corn_clean.rds"))
 ggplot2::ggplot(corn, ggplot2::aes(x = factor(Irrigated), y = Yield)) +
   ggplot2::geom_boxplot() +
   ggplot2::labs(
-    title = "Corn yield by irrigation",
+    title = "Corn yield by irrigation, 2008",
     x = "Irrigated",
     y = "Yield (bu/ac)"
   )



--- a/ and +++ b/: the file, before and after.
A line starting with - was removed; a line starting with + was added; other lines are shown for context.
Here, one line: the figure title gained its year.





$ git log --oneline --graph --decorate
*   1f43de3 (HEAD -> main) Keep the units in the y-axis label
|\  
| * b5a5559 (units-in-labels) Give the units in the y-axis label
* | 4e77786 Name the crop in the y-axis label
|/  
* 3686623 Start the project



One commit per line, newest first, each with the first 7 characters of its identifier (see Going back) and the first line of its message.
* marks a commit; the lines on the left show the two branches and where they were merged.
(HEAD -> main): the commit you are on, and the branch you are on.

title: 06-2: Version Control: Keeping a History of Your Project
section: Working with AI on your own research
text:
Working with AI on your own research
The way of working from lecture 02-1, “Working with AI on your own research” (the AI writes into a .qmd, you render and read the HTML) gains three habits once the project has a history:

Commit before the AI starts. Then every change it makes shows up in git diff, and any of it can be undone.
Read the diff after it finishes, as well as the HTML. The HTML shows what the code produced; the diff shows every line it touched, including in files you did not ask about.
Commit what you accept, with a message saying why, and only then push.




Note


Requests in this lecture ask the AI to run git, not to write R code into a .qmd, so they do not end with the closing instructions from 03-1. They end with the git safety instructions, under Recommended requests: show each command that changes anything before running it, and never run the commands that can lose work.

title: 06-2: Version Control: Keeping a History of Your Project
section: What to put in your request
text:
What to put in your request
The AI can see your files and run any command. What it cannot know:

Which changes belong together: name the files (or the change) for this commit.
Why you made them: give the reason, so the message can say it.
What must stay out: files with keys, restricted data, large files; or ask it to show you the list first.
Where it goes: which branch, and whether it may push at all.
What it must not do: the git safety instructions.





Using a chat assistant?


It cannot run anything. It gives you commands to paste into RStudio’s Terminal tab. Read each one against “How git commands are written” before you press Enter, and paste the output back if you are unsure what it means.

title: 06-2: Version Control: Keeping a History of Your Project
section: A weak request and a strong one
text:
A weak request and a strong one

WeakStrongWhat came back


Commit and push my changes.
A typical reply runs:
git add .
git commit -m "Update files"
git push
git add . stages every change, including .Renviron with its key and the unfinished 03-regression.qmd. The message says nothing. The push sends all of it to GitHub before you have looked.


In my project, I added the year, 2008, to the figure title in
analysis/02-summary.qmd, because the figure will be shown next to
figures for other years. Commit only that file, with a message that
says so. Do not stage anything else; .Renviron must never be
committed. Show me git status and git diff --staged before you
commit. Do not push.

Before you run any command that changes my files, my history or GitHub,
show me the command, say in one plain-English sentence what it does,
and wait for me to say yes. Never run git push --force, git reset
--hard, git rebase, git commit --amend or git clean. After each
command, show me what git printed.


The AI stages the one file and shows what is staged, before committing:


$ git add analysis/02-summary.qmd


$ git diff --staged
diff --git a/analysis/02-summary.qmd b/analysis/02-summary.qmd
index d8cc48b..bc72b0c 100644
--- a/analysis/02-summary.qmd
+++ b/analysis/02-summary.qmd
@@ -5,7 +5,7 @@ corn <- readRDS(here::here("data", "processed", "corn_clean.rds"))
 ggplot2::ggplot(corn, ggplot2::aes(x = factor(Irrigated), y = Yield)) +
   ggplot2::geom_boxplot() +
   ggplot2::labs(
-    title = "Corn yield by irrigation",
+    title = "Corn yield by irrigation, 2008",
     x = "Irrigated",
     y = "Yield (bu/ac)"
   )


$ git status --short
M  analysis/02-summary.qmd
?? .Renviron
?? analysis/03-regression.qmd


git status --short prints one line per file: M (letter in the first column) means staged, ?? means untracked. One file is staged, with the one line you meant to change; .Renviron and 03-regression.qmd are untracked and stay out. You say yes, and it commits:


$ git log --oneline --decorate -1
a86ecb2 (HEAD -> main) Add the year to the figure title

title: 06-2: Version Control: Keeping a History of Your Project
section: Checking: what to look at, and why
text:
Checking: what to look at, and why

The six checksAsking for themReading the result


Run them before every commit and push the AI makes. You know each right answer before you look:










Ask the AI to show
Why
What only you know




1
git status: the branch
A commit on the wrong branch goes to the wrong line of work
which branch this belongs on


2
git status: the staged files
git add . takes everything
which files you meant to change


3
git diff --staged
Every line that will be committed, including ones you did not ask for
what the change should be


4
the staged files, for keys, restricted data and large files
Once pushed, they are public to anyone with access, for good
which files are secret or restricted


5
the commit message
It is the only record of why
the reason


6
git remote -v, and the push command itself
Pushing to the wrong repository, or with --force
where the project lives





Before you commit, show me: the branch, the list of staged files,
and git diff --staged. I expect only <the files you changed> on branch
<branch name>, and no .Renviron or data files.

Before you run any command that changes my files, my history or GitHub,
show me the command, say in one plain-English sentence what it does,
and wait for me to say yes. Never run git push --force, git reset
--hard, git rebase, git commit --amend or git clean. After each
command, show me what git printed.


The weak request’s git add ., run on the practice repository, with the check printed:


Code that ran the check

invisible(git("add", ".", show = FALSE))

$ git diff --staged -- analysis/02-summary.qmd

+print(nrow(corn))  # debugging

Code that ran the check
invisible(git("reset", "-q", show = FALSE))


The branch is right; the other two checks fail. Three files are staged instead of one, and one of them is the key. The staged diff of 02-summary.qmd shows a second problem: the only line it adds is a debugging line, which nobody meant to commit. Nothing is committed yet, so nothing is lost: unstage (git restore --staged), add a .gitignore, and stage only what you meant.

title: 06-2: Version Control: Keeping a History of Your Project
section: What the AI may run on its own
text:
What the AI may run on its own
One question decides it: could this command lose work that git has not stored, or change something other people already have?

Read-only: no approval neededSay yes after reading the commandNever



status, diff, log, show: “what changed since Tuesday?”, “what is this conflict about?”
Drafting a commit message from the diff, or the lines of a .gitignore, as text for you to read




add and commit: once you have checked what is staged
switch, and making a branch: commit first if there are uncommitted changes
merge and pull: they change your files; commit first, so you can see what changed
revert: adds a commit that undoes another; safe even after a push
restore: only after reading git diff for that file, because it throws away its uncommitted changes
push: after the six checks
gh repo create and anything else that makes something on GitHub: check whether it is private




reset --hard, clean: throw away uncommitted work, in every file at once
push --force, rebase, commit --amend on pushed commits: rewrite history your coauthors already have

If an AI suggests one of these to “fix” an error, stop and ask it what the error means first. A refused push, for example, usually means someone else pushed first: the fix is git pull --no-edit, then push again.

title: 06-2: Version Control: Keeping a History of Your Project
section: Your turn: read the AI’s commands
text:
Your turn: read the AI’s commands
A student asked an AI to “save my work to GitHub, it says the push failed”, and it ran:
git add -A
git commit -m "update"
git push --force

QuestionsAnswers


A. In plain words, what does each command do?
B. Why did the first push probably fail?
C. Which command can delete someone else’s work, and whose?
D. What else might have gone into the commit without the student knowing?
E. Rewrite the request so the AI could not do this.


A. Stages every change in the folder; commits it with the message “update”; replaces the history on GitHub with the student’s own.
B. Someone (a coauthor, or the student from another computer, or a pull request merged on GitHub) pushed commits the student did not have. Git refuses a push that would drop them.
C. git push --force. It deletes from GitHub the commits the student did not have, which are someone else’s work.
D. Anything in the folder that is not in .gitignore: a .Renviron with a key, rendered HTML, data files, half-finished steps.
E. Say which files to commit and why, ask to see git status and git diff --staged first, say “if the push is refused, pull with git pull –no-edit and show me what came in; never use –force”, and end with the git safety instructions.

title: 06-2: Version Control: Keeping a History of Your Project

title: 06-2: Version Control: Keeping a History of Your Project
section: What you must understand, and what the AI can run
text:
What you must understand, and what the AI can run







You need to understand
The AI can run




What a commit is: the whole project, at one moment, with a reason
git commit

git add, and a first draft of the message

The .gitignore

git switch, git merge, the edit that resolves it

git push, git pull, gh pr create
