title: 05-1: Functions, Loops and Parallel Processing
section: What you will and will not learn today
text:
What you will and will not learn today

The planDirections


Research is full of repetition: the same steps for every county, every year, every field, every file, every simulated dataset. An AI assistant can write the code that repeats them. What it cannot do is:

know which steps you want repeated, and over which inputs
know what the correct result for one input looks like
notice that one of your inputs is not like the others
tell whether the repeated result is right

Those are your job. So today is about:

The concept: what a function, a loop and parallel processing are, and what has to be true for each to give the right answer
Reading code: recognising a function definition, a loop and a parallel loop when the AI writes one, without memorising them
Asking AI: what to put in your request
Checking: how to tell whether the repeated work was done right




Ask your AI assistant to install the tidyverse, future.apply and here packages if you have not already. Installing is a one-time step per computer (see the packages slide in Chapter 1).
The three small data files used on these slides, yields_2016.csv, yields_2017.csv and yields_2018.csv, sit in the same folder as the slides, so paths on the slides are bare file names. In your own project, paths are built with here::here() (lecture 03-1).

title: 05-1: Functions, Loops and Parallel Processing
section: What a function is
text:
What a function is

Inputs, steps, outputWhen one is worth writing


A function is a named set of steps. You give it inputs, it runs the steps on them, and it gives back one output. You have used many already: mean() takes a column of numbers (the input), adds them and divides by how many there are (the steps), and gives back the average (the output).
You can also define your own. A function written for your project has the same three parts:



Part
Example: convert Fahrenheit to Celsius




Inputs
a temperature in Fahrenheit


Steps
subtract 32, multiply by 5, divide by 9


Output
the temperature in Celsius



Once it is defined, you use it by its name, the same way you use mean().


Write a function when the same steps are repeated with different inputs. The sign is code you have copied and pasted with one value changed each time:

yield_2016 <- mean(read_csv("yields_2016.csv")$corn_yield)
yield_2017 <- mean(read_csv("yields_2017.csv")$corn_yield)
yield_2018 <- mean(read_csv("yields_2018.csv")$corn_yield)

Three copies of the same steps, with only the file name changing. Copies like these go wrong in a way R does not report: you fix a mistake in one copy and forget another, or change the file name in one copy but not the variable name. With a function, the steps are written once, and fixing them once fixes every use.
A function is not worth it for steps you run once. The payoff grows with the number of inputs and the number of steps.

title: 05-1: Functions, Loops and Parallel Processing
section: How a function definition is written
text:
How a function definition is written
Whatever the function does, its definition follows the same pattern. Recognise the pattern and you can read any function the AI writes.

The patternA real exampleCalling a functionVariations you will see



function_name <- function(input_1, input_2 = default) {
  step
  step
  output
}









Part
What it is
Required?




function_name <-
The name you will call it by. <- stores the function under that name.
Yes


function(...)
The word function, then the names of the inputs, separated by commas
Yes; there can be zero inputs, but the brackets stay


input_2 = default
An input with a default (a value used when you leave that input out)
No


{ ... }
The steps, between curly brackets
Yes


last line
The output. Whatever the last line produces is given back. return(output) says the same thing explicitly.
Yes





A real function that follows the pattern:

fahrenheit_to_celsius <- function(fahrenheit) {
  (fahrenheit - 32) * 5 / 9
}

fahrenheit_to_celsius(212)

[1] 100


Running the definition only stores the steps. Nothing is calculated until the function is called (used), as in the last line.


A call is the function name followed by the inputs in brackets. Inputs can be given in two ways:







Call
How R matches the inputs




revenue(200, 4)
By position: first value to the first input, second to the second


revenue(yield = 200, price = 4)
By name: order does not matter



Names are safer once there are two or more inputs. A call by position with the values in the wrong order still runs and gives a wrong number, with no error.
Objects created inside a function exist only while it runs; only the output comes back. A function that needs to keep something must return it.


AI-written functions often look different from the pattern while following it:

\(x) x^2: a short way to write function(x) x^2, common for one-line functions used once, inside a loop
return(result) as the last line: the same as writing result alone
A function defined inside another one’s brackets, with no name: it is used once, on the spot
stopifnot(is.numeric(fahrenheit)) as the first step: the function stops with an error when given an input of the wrong kind, instead of returning nonsense

title: 05-1: Functions, Loops and Parallel Processing
section: What has to be true for a function to be right
text:
What has to be true for a function to be right

The three conditionsTest on a known answerA value from outsideInputs you did not test



It gives the right answer on an input whose answer you already know. Water boils at 212 degrees Fahrenheit and 100 Celsius, and freezes at 32 and 0. A Fahrenheit-to-Celsius function that does not give those two is wrong, whatever else it does.
Everything it uses comes in as an input. A function that uses a value from outside its inputs gives different answers at different times, with no error.
It handles every kind of input it will be given, including missing values and inputs you did not test it on.



The AI writes the test; you supply the answers, because you know them before running anything:


Code the AI wrote
cat(
  paste("212 F in Celsius: expected 100, got", fahrenheit_to_celsius(212)),
  paste("32 F in Celsius: expected 0, got", fahrenheit_to_celsius(32)),
  sep = "\n"
)


212 F in Celsius: expected 100, got 100
32 F in Celsius: expected 0, got 0


Both pass. A test you cannot predict the answer to is not a test: the AI would be checking its own code against its own code.


This function uses price, which is not one of its inputs:

price <- 4
revenue <- function(yield) {
  yield * price
}
revenue(200)

[1] 800


It runs, and 800 is right while price is 4. Now some later code, written for something else, changes price:

price <- 5.5
revenue(200)

[1] 1100


The same call now gives 1100, with no error. The function quietly took whatever price happened to be. On someone else’s computer, where nothing called price exists, it stops with an error instead. The fix is to make price an input: revenue <- function(yield, price).


A function to average yields, tested on a column with no gaps:

average_yield <- function(yields) {
  mean(yields)
}
average_yield(c(150, 180, 210))

[1] 180

average_yield(c(150, NA, 210))

[1] NA


The first call gives 180, the known answer. The second gives NA (R’s mark for a missing value): one missing value made the whole answer missing. Whether that is right depends on the research question, and the AI cannot know. Tell it what should happen: skip missing values (mean(yields, na.rm = TRUE)), or stop with an error.

title: 05-1: Functions, Loops and Parallel Processing
section: What a loop is
text:
What a loop is

One result per inputDo you need a loop?


A loop runs the same steps once for each of several inputs. One run of the steps for one input is a repetition. Most loops in research have this layout:









Inputs
One repetition
Results
Combined




3 files
read the file, average the yields
3 averages
one table, 3 rows


12 fields
fit a yield curve to the field’s plots
12 fitted curves
one table, 12 rows


1,000 simulated datasets
estimate a regression
1,000 estimates
one column, 1,000 values



So before any code, you can say what the result of a correct loop looks like: one result per input, then combined. If there are 3 inputs and the combined table has 2 rows or 4, something went wrong.
The steps of one repetition are usually written as a function, and the loop calls that function once per input. That is why functions came first.


Many R functions already work on a whole column at once. Arithmetic does, so fahrenheit_to_celsius() does:

fahrenheit_to_celsius(c(32, 50, 212))

[1]   0  10 100


Three inputs, three outputs, no loop. A column of numbers given to a function as one input is called a vector (a sequence of values of one type). When each repetition is a calculation on one value, ask whether a loop is needed at all; the whole-column version is shorter and much faster:


Code the AI wrote
temps <- runif(1000000, 0, 100)

time_loop <- system.time(by_loop <- unlist(lapply(temps, fahrenheit_to_celsius)))["elapsed"]
time_once <- system.time(at_once <- fahrenheit_to_celsius(temps))["elapsed"]

cat(
  paste("same results: expected TRUE, got", all.equal(by_loop, at_once)),
  paste("seconds, one value at a time:", round(time_loop, 3)),
  paste("seconds, whole column at once:", round(time_once, 3)),
  sep = "\n"
)


same results: expected TRUE, got TRUE
seconds, one value at a time: 0.392
seconds, whole column at once: 0.002


Loops are for repetitions that take a whole table or file each: reading files, fitting a model per group, running a simulation.
The whole-column version holds every value in memory at once. When the table of every combination is too large for your computer’s memory, a loop over chunks is the way out.

title: 05-1: Functions, Loops and Parallel Processing
section: How looping code is written
text:
How looping code is written
R has several ways to write a loop. They differ in name and package, not in pattern.

The patternA real exampleEvery loop follows the patternThe for loopVariations you will see



results  <- lapply(inputs, function_name)
combined <- bind_rows(results)









Part
What it is
Required?




inputs
The things to loop over: file names, numbers, table names. Always the first input.
Yes


function_name
The steps for one input. Always the second input.
Yes


results <-
Stores the results, one per input, as a list (an R object that holds several results of any kind, in order)
Needed to keep them


bind_rows(results)
Combines the results into one table, one on top of the other
When each result is a table





A real example: three files in, three averages out, one table at the end.

files <- c("yields_2016.csv", "yields_2017.csv", "yields_2018.csv")

summarise_year <- function(file) {
  table <- read_csv(file, show_col_types = FALSE)
  tibble(file = file, counties = nrow(table), mean_yield = mean(table$corn_yield))
}

results <- lapply(files, summarise_year)
bind_rows(results)

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  file            counties mean_yield
  <chr>              <int>      <dbl>
1 yields_2016.csv       50       199.
2 yields_2017.csv       47       205.
3 yields_2018.csv       29       213.


tibble() builds a small table from named columns.










Shape of the call
Package
What comes back




lapply(inputs, f)
built into R
a list


sapply(inputs, f)
built into R
a vector when every result is one value


map(inputs, f)
purrr (tidyverse)
a list


map_dbl(inputs, f)
purrr
a vector of numbers


list_rbind(map(inputs, f))
purrr
one table


future_lapply(inputs, f)
future.apply
a list, computed in parallel (later in this deck)


future_map(inputs, f)
furrr
a list, computed in parallel



f stands for the function with the steps. Whatever the name, the inputs come first and the steps second.


The oldest form writes the repetition out in the open:

results <- vector("list", length(inputs))
for (i in seq_along(inputs)) {
  results[[i]] <- function_name(inputs[[i]])
}








Part
What it is




vector("list", length(inputs))
An empty list with one slot per input, made before the loop


for (i in seq_along(inputs))
i takes the values 1, 2, 3, … up to the number of inputs


results[[i]] <-
Stores this repetition’s result in slot i



It does the same job as lapply(). The extra parts are also extra places for a mistake: forget [[i]] and every repetition overwrites the last (see the next slide).



lapply(files, \(f) read_csv(f)): the steps written on the spot, as a function with no name
map(files, ~ read_csv(.x)): purrr’s older short form; .x is the current input
lapply(seq_len(nrow(table)), f): looping over row numbers, so each repetition uses one row of a table
expand.grid(price = c(3, 4, 5), rate = c(100, 200)) or tidyr::expand_grid(...): a table of every combination of two lists (here 6 rows), made so that a loop can go over its rows. This is how a loop covers several inputs at once.
bind_rows(results, .id = "name") or list_rbind(names_to = "name"): combine, and add a column saying which input each row came from

title: 05-1: Functions, Loops and Parallel Processing
section: What has to be true for a loop to be right
text:
What has to be true for a loop to be right

The four conditionsWhich year?A column with a different nameOnly the last result kept



The steps are right for one input. Test the function on one input, against an answer you know, before looping. A loop repeats a mistake as faithfully as it repeats correct steps, and one wrong result is easier to find than many.
Every input is the same kind of thing as the one you tested. Same columns, same names, same units. The loop assumes it; nothing checks it.
Each result records which input it came from. Once results are combined, a row that does not say where it came from cannot be traced back.
The results fit together. One result per input, with the same columns, so that combining them gives one row per input (or the sum of the rows of every part).

Conditions 2 to 4 fail without an error. The next tabs show each.


The yearly files have no year column; the year is only in the file name. A loop that drops the file name:

summarise_table <- function(file) {
  table <- read_csv(file, show_col_types = FALSE)
  tibble(counties = nrow(table), mean_yield = mean(table$corn_yield))
}
bind_rows(lapply(files, summarise_table))

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  counties mean_yield
     <int>      <dbl>
1       50       199.
2       47       205.
3       29       213.


Three rows, right numbers, and no way to tell which is 2016. If the files had been listed in a different order, the rows would be in a different order, and nothing would show it. The first version of this loop, on the pattern tab, kept file in each result; that one line is condition 3.


Suppose one year’s file calls the yield column Corn_yield instead of corn_yield. Combining the tables:

part_1 <- tibble(county_name = c("Adams", "Buffalo"), corn_yield = c(195, 210))
part_2 <- tibble(county_name = c("Clay", "Dawson"), Corn_yield = c(188, 201))
combined <- bind_rows(part_1, part_2)
combined

# A tibble: 4 × 3
  county_name corn_yield Corn_yield
  <chr>            <dbl>      <dbl>
1 Adams              195         NA
2 Buffalo            210         NA
3 Clay                NA        188
4 Dawson              NA        201


No error. bind_rows() matches columns by name, so the table now has two yield columns, each half missing. An average of corn_yield would quietly use half the data. Checks that catch it: the number of columns (expected 2, got 3), and missing values per column (expected 0, got 2 in corn_yield).


A for loop where the result is stored without [[i]]:

results <- vector("list", length(files))
for (i in seq_along(files)) {
  results <- summarise_year(files[[i]])
}
results

# A tibble: 1 × 3
  file            counties mean_yield
  <chr>              <int>      <dbl>
1 yields_2018.csv       29       213.


Each repetition replaced the one before, so only 2018 is left. It runs, and the one row it gives is correct, which is what makes it easy to miss. The check that catches it: the rows of the combined table, expected 3, got 1. Counting with length() would not catch it here: a one-row table with three columns has length 3.

title: 05-1: Functions, Loops and Parallel Processing
section: What parallel processing is
text:
What parallel processing is

Several repetitions at onceWhy some jobs speed up and others do notBefore reaching for it


A normal loop runs one repetition, then the next: sequentially. Your computer has several cores (processing units, each able to run one calculation at a time), and a sequential loop uses one of them.
Parallel processing starts several extra R sessions, called workers, each on its own core. The inputs are shared out among the workers, each worker runs its repetitions, and the results are collected back into one list, in the same order as the inputs. The computer that built these slides has 16 cores.
With 4 workers, 100 repetitions can at best take a quarter of the time. In practice it is less than that, for the reason on the next tab.


Parallel processing has a cost the sequential loop does not: starting the workers, sending each one the inputs and the function, and collecting the results. That cost is roughly fixed. So:

When each repetition is fast, that cost is larger than the time saved, and the parallel loop is slower.
When each repetition is slow (seconds, not microseconds), that cost is small next to the time saved.

Measured when these slides were built, with 4 workers:


Code the AI wrote
plan(multisession, workers = 4)

# fast: square a number, 1,000 times
fast_seq <- system.time(lapply(1:1000, \(x) x^2))["elapsed"]
fast_par <- system.time(future_lapply(1:1000, \(x) x^2))["elapsed"]

# slow: simulate 500,000 observations and fit a regression, 40 times
one_simulation <- function(i) {
  x <- rnorm(500000)
  y <- 1 + x + rnorm(500000)
  coef(lm(y ~ x))[["x"]]
}
slow_seq <- system.time(lapply(1:40, one_simulation))["elapsed"]
slow_par <- system.time(future_lapply(1:40, one_simulation, future.seed = TRUE))["elapsed"]

timings <- tibble(
  job = c("fast", "fast", "slow", "slow"),
  how = c("sequential", "parallel", "sequential", "parallel"),
  seconds = signif(c(fast_seq, fast_par, slow_seq, slow_par), 3)
)
timings


# A tibble: 4 × 3
  job   how        seconds
  <chr> <chr>        <dbl>
1 fast  sequential   0.001
2 fast  parallel     0.344
3 slow  sequential   2.82 
4 slow  parallel     0.944


The fast job took 0.344 seconds in parallel against 0.001 sequentially: slower. The slow job took 0.944 seconds in parallel against 2.82 sequentially. Numbers differ by computer; the direction does not.



If each repetition is a calculation on single values, a whole-column version (the “Do you need a loop?” tab under Loops) is usually a bigger gain than parallel processing, and has no setup cost.
If the whole loop takes a few seconds, parallel processing is not worth the extra things to check.
If it takes minutes or hours and the repetitions are independent (two slides on), it is.

title: 05-1: Functions, Loops and Parallel Processing
section: How parallel code is written
text:
How parallel code is written

The patternEvery parallel loop follows the patternOptions for plan()


A parallel loop is the sequential pattern with two changes: one line that starts the workers, and a parallel version of the looping function.

plan(multisession, workers = 4)
results <- future_lapply(inputs, function_name, future.seed = TRUE)









Part
What it is
Required?




plan(multisession, workers = 4)
Starts 4 workers. Every parallel loop after it uses them.
Yes, before the loop


future_lapply(inputs, function_name)
lapply() with the repetitions shared among the workers. Inputs first, steps second, as before.
Yes


future.seed = TRUE
Gives each repetition its own reproducible random numbers
Yes, if the steps use random numbers


plan(sequential)
Goes back to one repetition at a time and closes the workers
At the end, to free memory













Sequential
Parallel
Package




lapply(inputs, f)
future_lapply(inputs, f, future.seed = TRUE)
future.apply


map(inputs, f)
future_map(inputs, f, .options = furrr_options(seed = TRUE))
furrr


lapply(inputs, f)
mclapply(inputs, f, mc.cores = 4)
parallel (built into R); Mac and Linux only












Option
What it does




sequential
No workers: one repetition at a time, exactly like lapply()


multisession
Separate R sessions as workers. Works on every computer.


multicore
Faster to start, but only on Mac and Linux, and not in the RStudio Console. Elsewhere it runs one repetition at a time: correct, no faster, with only a one-time warning. future::nbrOfWorkers() printing 1 shows it.



parallel::detectCores() prints the number of cores. Leave one or two for the rest of the computer: workers = parallel::detectCores() - 1.

title: 05-1: Functions, Loops and Parallel Processing
section: What has to be true for parallel processing to be safe
text:
What has to be true for parallel processing to be safe
A parallel loop gives the same results as the sequential one only if each repetition is independent of the others. Three conditions follow from that.

No repetition uses another’s resultEach repetition returns its resultRandom numbers


Workers run at the same time, so a repetition cannot wait for another one’s result. This loop carries soil nitrogen from one year to the next:

applied <- c(150, 150, 0, 150)
soil_n <- numeric(4)
soil_n[1] <- 40
for (year in 2:4) {
  soil_n[year] <- 0.5 * soil_n[year - 1] + 0.2 * applied[year]
}
soil_n

[1] 40.0 50.0 25.0 42.5


Year 3 needs year 2’s answer, which needs year 1’s. It cannot be run in parallel. The sign to look for in code: the steps use [i - 1], or a result from an earlier repetition.


A repetition must hand its result back, not write it into something outside itself. Here each repetition adds to a running total with <<- (assign to a name outside the function):

plan(multisession, workers = 4)

total <- 0
invisible(lapply(1:10, \(i) total <<- total + i))
cat("sequential total: expected 55, got", total, "\n")

sequential total: expected 55, got 55 

total <- 0
invisible(future_lapply(1:10, \(i) total <<- total + i))
cat("parallel total: expected 55, got", total, "\n")

parallel total: expected 55, got 0 

plan(sequential)

The parallel loop gives 0, with no error: each worker changed its own copy of total, and the copies were thrown away. The safe form returns each result and combines them afterwards: sum(unlist(future_lapply(1:10, \(i) i))).
The same loop under plan(sequential) also gives 0, so comparing the two ways would not show the problem; counting the results would.


Simulations and resampling draw random numbers. Without future.seed = TRUE, future_lapply() warns UNRELIABLE VALUE (the workers’ random numbers may not be independent). With it, and with the same set.seed() before each run, the results are the same whatever the number of workers, which is what makes the next check possible:


Code the AI wrote
plan(sequential)
set.seed(1)
one_at_a_time <- future_lapply(1:5, one_simulation, future.seed = TRUE)

plan(multisession, workers = 4)
set.seed(1)
in_parallel <- future_lapply(1:5, one_simulation, future.seed = TRUE)
plan(sequential)

cat("parallel same as sequential: expected TRUE, got", identical(one_at_a_time, in_parallel), "\n")


parallel same as sequential: expected TRUE, got TRUE 


lapply() with set.seed(1) draws different numbers from future_lapply(), so compare future_lapply() with itself under plan(sequential), not with lapply().

title: 05-1: Functions, Loops and Parallel Processing
section: Working with AI on your own research
text:
Working with AI on your own research
Functions and loops follow the way of working with AI from lecture 02-1 (“Working with AI on your own research”), which is also how to work on your own research:

You ask. Your request says what you want, what you know about the data, and which checks to print.
The AI writes into a Quarto document (.qmd), with one plain-English sentence above each chunk saying what it does and why.
You render the .qmd to HTML.
You read the HTML and decide whether the work is right: the sentences, the code, and the check results side by side.




Note


Every request that asks for code ends with the same few lines telling the AI to work this way. This deck calls them the closing instructions; the full text is under Recommended requests near the end.

title: 05-1: Functions, Loops and Parallel Processing
section: Look at the inputs before you ask
text:
Look at the inputs before you ask

WhyListing and counting


A loop assumes every input is like the first. Before asking for one, find out:

how many inputs there are (so you know how many results to expect)
what one input looks like: its columns, their names, what one row is
whether the inputs say which one they are, or only their file names do
how many rows each has (so you know how many rows the combined table should have)



The AI can write this; you read the answers before asking for any loop:


Code the AI wrote
files <- list.files(".", pattern = "^yields_.*\\.csv$")
rows_per_file <- sapply(files, \(f) length(readLines(f)) - 1)
rows_per_file


yields_2016.csv yields_2017.csv yields_2018.csv 
             50              47              29 


Code the AI wrote
names(read_csv(files[1], show_col_types = FALSE))


[1] "county_name" "corn_yield" 


From this you learn: 3 files, 126 data rows in all, two columns, and no year column. A correct combined table has 126 rows and needs a year column taken from the file names. Write those down before you ask.

title: 05-1: Functions, Loops and Parallel Processing
section: What to put in your request
text:
What to put in your request
The AI already knows the functions. Your request supplies what it cannot know:

The inputs: what they are, where they are, how many, and how each one says which it is (a column, or only the file name)
The steps for one input, in words, and what one result should look like (one number, one row with named columns)
A known answer: an input whose result you can work out by hand, to test the function on before looping
How to combine, and what the combined result should look like: how many rows, which column says where each row came from
Whether to run in parallel, and only if the loop is slow and the repetitions are independent
Ask for checks: the test on the known answer, the number of results, the rows of the combined table (next section)
The closing instructions: which .qmd and heading the code goes under, a sentence above each chunk, paths built with here::here(), checks printed as expected and got, and render to HTML





Using an agent in your editor or terminal?


An agent such as Claude Code can open the files and count rows itself. Still write down what you expect (number of inputs, rows in the combined table, the answer for your known input) before it runs, so you have something to compare against.

title: 05-1: Functions, Loops and Parallel Processing
section: A weak request and a strong one
text:
A weak request and a strong one

WeakStrongWhat came backThe loop and its checks


Get the average corn yield for each year from my files.
The AI has to guess which files, where they are, what is in them, and what to return. A typical reply:

setwd("C:/Users/yourname/Documents/data")
results <- c()
for (f in list.files()) {
  d <- read.csv(f)
  results <- c(results, mean(d$corn_yield))
}
results

It runs on nobody’s computer as written. Fix the path, and it reads every file in the folder, yearly or not, and returns numbers with no year attached.


An example for the three yearly files:
In my R project, data/ holds three csv files, yields_2016.csv,
yields_2017.csv and yields_2018.csv: Nebraska corn yields by county,
one row per county, columns county_name and corn_yield (bu/acre). The
files have no year column; the year is only in the file name. They have
50, 47 and 29 rows.

Write a function that takes one file's path and returns a one-row table:
the year (from the file name), the number of counties and the mean
yield. Test it on a three-row table with yields 150, 180 and 210, whose
mean is 180. Then loop it over the three files with lapply() and combine
the results into one table called yearly.

Check: the test (expected 180), the number of results (expected 3), the
rows of yearly (expected 3), and the years in yearly (expected 2016,
2017, 2018).

Put the code in my Quarto document analysis/yearly.qmd, under the
heading "Average yield by year", as R code chunks. Above each chunk,
write one plain-English sentence saying what it does and why. Build
every path with here::here(); no setwd(), no absolute paths. Print each
check on its own line as "name of check: expected X, got Y". Render the
document to HTML.


What the AI’s answer looks like in the rendered HTML. Read each sentence and check that the code under it does what the sentence says. (On these slides, the files sit beside the deck, so the paths are bare file names instead of here::here("data", ...).)
The function takes one file’s path, reads it, and returns one row with the year taken from the file name.

summarise_file <- function(path) {
  table <- read_csv(path, show_col_types = FALSE)
  tibble(
    year = as.integer(gsub("\\D", "", basename(path))),
    counties = nrow(table),
    mean_yield = mean(table$corn_yield)
  )
}

Test the function on a small table whose mean is known to be 180, written to a temporary file.

test_path <- file.path(tempdir(), "yields_1999.csv")
write_csv(tibble(county_name = c("A", "B", "C"), corn_yield = c(150, 180, 210)), test_path)
test <- summarise_file(test_path)
cat("test mean: expected 180, got", test$mean_yield, "\n")

test mean: expected 180, got 180 




Loop the function over the three files and combine the results into one table.

paths <- c("yields_2016.csv", "yields_2017.csv", "yields_2018.csv")
results <- lapply(paths, summarise_file)
yearly <- bind_rows(results)

Print the checks on the number of results, the rows, and the years.

cat(
  paste("number of results: expected 3, got", length(results)),
  paste("rows in yearly: expected 3, got", nrow(yearly)),
  paste("years: expected 2016 2017 2018, got", paste(yearly$year, collapse = " ")),
  sep = "\n"
)

number of results: expected 3, got 3
rows in yearly: expected 3, got 3
years: expected 2016 2017 2018, got 2016 2017 2018

yearly

# A tibble: 3 × 3
   year counties mean_yield
  <int>    <int>      <dbl>
1  2016       50       199.
2  2017       47       205.
3  2018       29       213.


Every check passes. One thing to notice: gsub("\\D", "", ...) removes every character that is not a digit, so it works because the only digits in these file names are the year. A file called yields_2016_v2.csv would give the year 20162. Asking the AI “what would this line do with a file name that has other digits in it?” is how you find limits like that.

title: 05-1: Functions, Loops and Parallel Processing
section: Checking: what to ask for, and why
text:
Checking: what to ask for, and why

The checksAsking for themReading the HTML


The AI can write the checking code. It cannot decide which checks your loop needs, and it cannot know the right answers.










Ask the AI to print
Why
What only you can supply




1
the function’s result on an input with a known answer
A wrong step gives a wrong number every time, with no error
the input and its answer, worked out by hand


2
the number of results
One per input; fewer means some were lost or overwritten
the number of inputs


3
the rows and columns of the combined table
An extra column or missing rows means the inputs did not match
the expected rows (from counting each input) and columns


4
the values of the column saying where each row came from
Results that cannot be traced back to an input are no use
the list of inputs


5
the smallest and largest value per input
An input unlike the others shows up as one result out of line with the rest
what range is believable


6
for a parallel loop, the result of a small case run sequentially and in parallel, compared
Random numbers handled wrongly give different results. It does not catch a repetition that writes outside itself: under plan(sequential), future_lapply() loses those writes too. Checks 2 and 3 catch that one.
nothing; this one is always expected to be identical





One paragraph at the end of your request does it:
Test the function on <the known input>, whose answer is <the answer>.
After the loop, check the number of results (expected <number>), the
rows and columns of the combined table (expected <number> and <number>),
the values of <the column saying where each row came from>, and the
smallest and largest <column> for each input (believable: <lowest> to
<highest>).
Every number in it comes from looking at the inputs and working out the known answer before the AI writes anything. That part only you can do.


For the yearly files, the student expected 3 results, 126 rows when the three files are stacked into one table with a year column, and yields between 100 and 300 bushels per acre in every year. The AI’s check code, and what it printed:


Code the AI wrote
stacked <- bind_rows(lapply(paths, \(p) {
  read_csv(p, show_col_types = FALSE) |>
    mutate(year = as.integer(gsub("\\D", "", basename(p))))
}))

ranges <- stacked |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(lowest = min(corn_yield), highest = max(corn_yield))

cat(
  paste0("rows in stacked: expected ", sum(rows_per_file), ", got ", nrow(stacked)),
  paste("columns in stacked: expected 3, got", ncol(stacked)),
  paste("years: expected 2016 2017 2018, got", paste(unique(stacked$year), collapse = " ")),
  sep = "\n"
)


rows in stacked: expected 126, got 126
columns in stacked: expected 3, got 3
years: expected 2016 2017 2018, got 2016 2017 2018


Code the AI wrote
ranges


# A tibble: 3 × 3
   year lowest highest
  <int>  <dbl>   <dbl>
1  2016   149.    217 
2  2017   155.    228.
3  2018   171.    234.



Rows, columns and years match.
Every year’s yields lie between 100 and 300, and the three ranges are close to each other, as they should be for one state in three neighbouring years.

title: 05-1: Functions, Loops and Parallel Processing
section: Checks that come from knowing the data
text:
Checks that come from knowing the data
The checks above apply to any loop. The most useful ones come from what you know about these inputs, and no AI will think of them for you.
Nebraska has 93 counties, and each county appears at most once a year in a file of county yields. So in the stacked table:
Using the table stacked, check that no year has more than 93 rows and
that no county appears twice in the same year.

Put the code in my Quarto document analysis/yearly.qmd, under the
heading "Checks on the stacked table", as R code chunks. Above each
chunk, write one plain-English sentence saying what it does and why.
Build every path with here::here(); no setwd(), no absolute paths. Print
each check on its own line as "name of check: expected X, got Y". Render
the document to HTML.
The AI’s code, and what it printed:


Code the AI wrote
most_rows <- max(count(stacked, year)$n)
repeats <- stacked |> count(year, county_name) |> filter(n > 1) |> nrow()
cat(
  paste("most counties in one year: expected at most 93, got", most_rows),
  paste("counties listed twice in a year: expected 0, got", repeats),
  sep = "\n"
)


most counties in one year: expected at most 93, got 50
counties listed twice in a year: expected 0, got 0


Both pass. A file read twice by mistake, or two files for the same year, would fail the second check, and a row count alone would not tell you which.

title: 05-1: Functions, Loops and Parallel Processing
section: Your turn: read the AI’s code
text:
Your turn: read the AI’s code
A student asked an AI to “run my simulation 1,000 times in parallel and keep the estimates”, and got this:

library(future.apply)
plan(multisession, workers = 8)
estimates <- c()
future_lapply(1:1000, function(i) {
  x <- rnorm(500)
  y <- 2 + 0.5 * x + rnorm(500)
  estimates <<- c(estimates, coef(lm(y ~ x))[2])
})
mean(estimates)


QuestionsAnswers


A. What does each part do: line 2, line 3, the steps inside function(i), and the last line?
B. Is each repetition independent of the others? Which line breaks the rule that each repetition returns its result?
C. What will mean(estimates) give, and will R report an error?
D. What else is missing for a loop that uses random numbers?
E. Rewrite the request so the AI could not make these mistakes.


A. Line 2 starts 8 workers. Line 3 makes an empty vector. Each repetition simulates 500 observations with a true slope of 0.5, fits a regression and adds the estimated slope to estimates. The last line averages the estimates. The future_lapply() result itself is not stored, so it is printed and then lost.
B. The steps are independent: no repetition uses another’s result. But estimates <<- ... writes into a vector outside the function instead of returning the estimate.
C. Each worker changes its own copy of estimates, and the copies are thrown away, so estimates is still empty and mean(estimates) gives NA with a warning, not an error. Run sequentially with lapply(), the same code would have worked, which is why it looks right.
D. future.seed = TRUE, so that each repetition gets its own reproducible random numbers. Without it, future_lapply() warns UNRELIABLE VALUE.
E. Ask for a function that returns one estimate, looped with future_lapply(..., future.seed = TRUE), the estimates combined afterwards with unlist(), and checks: the number of estimates (expected 1,000), their average (expected close to the true slope, 0.5), and a run of 10 repetitions sequentially and in parallel, compared (expected identical).

title: 05-1: Functions, Loops and Parallel Processing
section: What you must understand, and what the AI can write
text:
What you must understand, and what the AI can write







You need to understand
The AI can write




Which steps repeat, and with which inputs
The function definition


What the correct result is for one input you can work out by hand
The test that compares against it


What every input looks like, and how each one says which it is
The code that reads them and adds that label


What one result per input, combined, should look like: rows, columns, labels
The loop and the combining step


Whether the repetitions are independent, and whether the loop is slow enough to be worth it
The parallel version, the count of its results, and the comparison with the sequential one



Every loop: look at the inputs and write down how many results and rows you expect. Test the function on an input whose answer you know. Ask the AI to write the loop and the checks into your .qmd, render it, and judge the HTML against what you wrote down. Run in parallel only a slow loop of independent repetitions, and only after a small case gives the same results both ways and the right number of results.

title: 04-1: Communicating with Figures
section: What you will and will not learn today
text:
What you will and will not learn today

The planDirections


An AI assistant can draw any figure in seconds. It knows every function and every option. What it cannot know is:

what the figure is supposed to tell the reader
who the reader is, and what they already know
which group or which year the message is about
whether the finished figure gets the message across

Those four are your job. So today is about:

The concept: a figure exists to convey one fact or idea, and every design choice is judged against it
Reading code: recognising which line of figure code does what, without memorising it
Asking AI: what to put in a figure request
Checking: how to judge whether a figure is correct and whether it conveys its message




Ask your AI assistant to install the tidyverse package if you have not already. It includes ggplot2, the package that draws every figure in this course.
The figures on these slides are drawn from one table, county_yield.csv. One row is one county in one year: corn yield and weeks of drought for 154 counties in Colorado, Kansas and Nebraska, 2000 to 2018.

title: 04-1: Communicating with Figures
section: One sentence and one reader
text:
One sentence and one reader

What you needWhy the AI cannot do this


Before you ask for any figure, write down two things:

The message: the one sentence the reader should take away. A finding, with a direction and if possible a size: “County-years with more than 10 weeks of extreme drought yielded about 22 bushels per acre less than county-years with none.”
The reader: who will look at the figure, and what they already know. A farm audience knows what a bushel per acre is; a general audience may not.

How to tell it is done: someone who sees only the figure, without your text, can say your sentence back to you.


The same table supports many sentences. Asked for “a figure of this data”, the AI has to choose a message without knowing yours, and it usually picks the figure that suits the types of the columns, not the point you want to make.
Every design decision in this lecture (type of figure, colour, order, axis range, title) is judged against your sentence. Without the sentence, there is nothing to judge against.

title: 04-1: Communicating with Figures
section: The message decides the figure
text:
The message decides the figure
Both figures are drawn from the same 1,956 rows. Each serves a different sentence.

Message AMessage B


“County-years with more than 10 weeks of extreme drought yielded about 22 bushels per acre less than county-years with none.”











“Extreme drought came in a few bad years, above all 2012 and 2013.”

title: 04-1: Communicating with Figures
section: The pattern every figure follows
text:
The pattern every figure follows
You will not write figure code from memory. You need to look at any figure code the AI writes and say which column is shown by what, because that is where a figure goes wrong. Every ggplot2 figure follows the same pattern.

The patternOne real exampleEvery mark follows the patternInside or outside aes()Variations you will see



ggplot(table, aes(x = column, y = column, colour = column)) +
  geom_mark() +
  optional_layer() +
  optional_layer()









Part
What it is
Required?




ggplot(table, ...)
The table the figure is drawn from, always the first input
Yes


aes(...)
Which column is shown by which visual property: position on the x axis, position on the y axis, colour, size (aes stands for aesthetics, ggplot’s word for visual properties)
Yes


geom_mark()
The kind of mark drawn: geom_point(), geom_line(), geom_col() and so on
Yes, at least one


+
Adds the next layer. It ends a line; a line never starts with it
Between layers


optional_layer()
Axis and legend titles (labs()), colours and axis ranges (scale_...()), small panels (facet_...()), text size and gridlines (theme())
No; each has a default



How to tell you can read it: for any figure code, you can fill in a table with one row per column of the data that is used, saying what it sets in the figure.


state_year has one row per state and year, with the average corn yield of the counties in the data.

ggplot(state_year, aes(x = year, y = corn_yield, colour = state_name)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = state_colours) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Average corn yield\n(bushels per acre)", colour = NULL)











Column
Shown by




year
position on the x axis


corn_yield
position on the y axis


state_name
colour, one line per state



The mark is lines. The two optional layers set the three colours and the axis and legend titles.


Marks differ in name, not in pattern. The visual properties each one needs inside aes():



Mark
In the code
Needs




Points
geom_point()
x, y


Lines
geom_line()
x, y


Bars whose length is a value in the table
geom_col()
x, y


Bars that count rows
geom_bar()
x


Histogram
geom_histogram()
x


Box plots
geom_boxplot()
x or y, usually both


Text
geom_text()
x, y, label



Any of them also accepts colour, fill (the colour inside a bar or box), size, shape (of points) and linetype inside aes().


The same word means two different things depending on where it is written:

Inside aes(): aes(colour = state_name) means “the colour depends on the column state_name”, and ggplot adds a legend.
Outside aes(): geom_line(colour = "grey40") means “every line is grey”. No column is involved, and there is no legend.

Writing a fixed colour inside aes() is a common slip. ggplot treats "blue" as a column whose value is the word “blue”, gives it the first default colour, and adds a legend for it:

ggplot(band_means, aes(band, corn_yield)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = "blue"), size = 4)








No error, and the points are not blue.


AI-written code often writes the same pattern differently. These change how the code looks, not what it draws:

aes(year, corn_yield): without x = and y =. The first two inputs are x and y.
ggplot(data = cy, mapping = aes(...)): the input names spelled out.
cy |> ggplot(aes(...)): the table passed in with |> instead of written first.
geom_point(aes(colour = state_name)): the aes() inside one mark instead of in ggplot(). It then applies to that mark only.
p <- ggplot(...) + geom_line() on one line, then p + labs(...) later: the figure is stored under a name and added to.

A + at the start of a line stops R with the error “Cannot use + with a single argument”. The fix is to move it to the end of the line above.

title: 04-1: Communicating with Figures
section: Five kinds of message
text:
Five kinds of message

The tableDistributionPart of a whole


The kind of sentence you wrote tells you the kind of figure to start from. The last column is the part of the code that names the figure type, so you can recognise it in what the AI writes.









Kind of message
A sentence from this data
A figure that suits it
In the code




A distribution
“Half of all county-years yielded between 164 and 195 bushels per acre.”
histogram
geom_histogram()


A relationship between two variables
“Yields fall as drought lasts longer.”
points, or averages per range
geom_point()


A comparison across groups
“Nebraska counties typically yield more than Kansas or Colorado counties.”
box plots, points, bars
geom_boxplot(), geom_col()


A change over time
“Extreme drought came in 2012 and 2013.”
line
geom_line()


A part of a whole
“Nebraska makes up 65% of the county-years.”
one bar split into parts
geom_col()



The next two slides take a comparison and a relationship and show how much the choice matters.


“Half of all county-years yielded between 164 and 195 bushels per acre.”









The shaded band is the middle half.


“Nebraska makes up 65% of the county-years.”

title: 04-1: Communicating with Figures
section: One message, three figures
text:
One message, three figures
Message: “Nebraska counties typically yield more corn than Kansas or Colorado counties.”

A. Overlapping histogramsB. Box plotsC. Bars of the averageWhich one?











Nebraska has the most rows, so its histogram covers the other two. The reader sees “Nebraska is big”, which is a fact about the data, not about yields.











The thick line in each box is the median (half the counties yield more, half less), and the box holds the middle half. Nebraska’s median is 184, against 174 for Kansas and 172 for Colorado, and the boxes show how much the states overlap.











The bars are correct, but they make the states look alike: Nebraska’s average (182) is only 8% above Colorado’s (168), so the difference is a sliver at the end of a long bar.


B serves this message. “Typically” is a statement about the middle of each state’s yields, and box plots put the middle and the spread side by side.

A hides the comparison under the difference in the number of rows.
C shows the averages but no spread, so the reader cannot tell whether the gap is large compared with the variation inside each state.

For another message, say “Colorado has the most variable yields”, B still works, while C would not show it at all.

title: 04-1: Communicating with Figures
section: Too many points
text:
Too many points
Message: “Yields fall when drought lasts longer.”

A. Every county-yearB. Box plots per drought range











73% of the county-years had no extreme drought, so most points sit on top of each other in one column at zero. The fall is there, but the eye cannot find it.











Grouping the drought weeks into ranges shows the drop at once. It also shows that the fall is not steady: the “2 to 5” group does better than the “0 to 2” group. Your sentence should not claim more than the figure shows; “yields are lowest after more than 10 weeks of drought” is what this figure supports.

title: 04-1: Communicating with Figures
section: When colour should carry information
text:
When colour should carry information

The ruleDecorationInformation


Use colour only for a variable the reader needs and that the position of the marks does not already show. How to tell: remove the colour in your head. If the reader loses nothing, the colour is decoration, and decoration makes the reader look for a meaning that is not there.











Each state already has its own place on the horizontal axis. The colours and the legend repeat the axis labels.











Three lines share one pair of axes. Colour is the only thing that says which line is which state.

title: 04-1: Communicating with Figures
section: Three kinds of colour scale
text:
Three kinds of colour scale

CategoriesAmountsAbove or below a midpoint


Groups with no order (states, crops) get clearly different hues, as in the line figure on the previous slide. Use as few as the message needs.


Amounts (weeks of drought, yield) get one hue, from light for small to dark for large, so “darker means more” reads without a legend.











A value above or below a meaningful middle (a change, a difference from normal) gets two hues that grow darker away from a neutral middle. Here, each county’s yield minus its own 2000 to 2018 average, averaged over the counties of each state:









Orange is below normal, purple above, and pale means close to normal. The neutral middle must sit at the value that means “no difference”, here zero.

title: 04-1: Communicating with Figures
section: Highlight the group the message is about
text:
Highlight the group the message is about

HighlightSame colour, same thing


Message: “Colorado’s 2002 drought lasted about twice as long as Kansas’s or Nebraska’s.”









In 2002: Colorado 15.3 weeks, Kansas 6.5, Nebraska 7.3. The other states stay in the figure, in grey, because the message is a comparison with them.


Every figure on this deck draws Colorado in orange, Kansas in blue and Nebraska in green, including the highlight, where Colorado keeps its orange. A reader who learns the colours on one figure can read the next one without the legend.
Left to its defaults, ggplot hands out colours to whichever groups are in each figure, in alphabetical order. A figure without Colorado gives Kansas the colour Colorado had in the figure before. Name the colours in your request: “Colorado #E69F00, Kansas #0072B2, Nebraska #009E73 in every figure”.

title: 04-1: Communicating with Figures
section: Colours every reader can tell apart
text:
Colours every reader can tell apart

ggplot’s defaultAs a red-green colour-blind reader sees itOkabe-Ito, as the same reader sees itHow many colours


A deliberately bad example. ggplot’s default colours for three groups put a red and a green of about the same lightness next to each other:











The same figure, with its colours converted to what a reader with red-green colour blindness sees (simulated with the colorspace package):









Colorado and Kansas now look nearly the same.


The Okabe-Ito palette is a set of eight colours chosen to stay distinct for colour-blind readers. The colours used for the states on this deck come from it:











A reader has to match each colour to the legend, and that gets unreliable well before a palette runs out. With more groups than you can give clearly different colours:

colour only the groups the message is about and grey the rest, or
draw one small panel per group (next section), or
combine the small groups into “Other”.

Check: would the message survive printing in black and white? If colour is the only thing separating two lines, label them directly too.

title: 04-1: Communicating with Figures
section: Order categories by value
text:
Order categories by value
The 12 counties with data in every year, all in Nebraska. Message: “Buffalo had the highest average yield.”

Alphabetical, names along the bottomBy value, names down the side











The names crowd together until they almost touch, and finding the highest county means comparing every point with every other.











Ordered by value, the ranking is the figure. With the names on the vertical axis they read horizontally and never overlap. Rotating the names by 45 or 90 degrees would also stop the overlap, but makes them harder to read.
Keep the natural order when the categories have one: years, months, drought ranges from none to most.

title: 04-1: Communicating with Figures
section: One panel or several
text:
One panel or several
Message: “Nebraska’s yields sit higher than the other two states’.”

Several small panelsWhen to use which











The overlapping histograms from “One message, three figures”, split into one panel per state. Stacked one above the other on the same horizontal axis, the shift of Nebraska’s yields to the right is visible.



One panel when the reader must compare values at the same point, for example three lines in the same year. Up to about three or four groups.
Several small panels when the groups overlap so much that one panel becomes a tangle, or there are too many groups to colour.
Panels must share the axis the comparison is made on. Here the horizontal axis (yield) is shared; the vertical axis (counts) differs on purpose, because Nebraska has far more rows and the message is about where the yields sit, not how many rows each state has. Say so when you ask, or the AI decides for you.

title: 04-1: Communicating with Figures
section: Axis ranges
text:
Axis ranges

Bars that do not start at zeroBars from zeroPoints and lines











A deliberately bad example. A bar’s length is read as its value. With the axis starting at 165, Nebraska’s bar is 5 times as tall as Colorado’s, although its average is only 8% higher.











Honest, and it shows the differences are small. If the message is about those small differences, bars are the wrong choice; use points, which need no zero.


For points and lines the reader reads position, not length, so the axis should cover the range where the variation that matters lies. The dot plot of county averages on the “Order categories by value” slide runs from about 183 to 197. Forced to start at zero, all 12 points would crowd into the right 7% of the panel’s width and the ranking would be hard to see.
The opposite mistake: an axis so narrow that a change too small to matter fills the whole figure. The range should match what the message calls large.

title: 04-1: Communicating with Figures
section: Titles, labels, and what to leave out
text:
Titles, labels, and what to leave out

A title that states the findingLabels on the linesRemove what the message does not need











A title such as “corn_yield by drought band” names the variables, which the axes already do. A title that states the finding tells the reader what to look for. In a report where the figure has a caption, the caption can carry the finding instead.


A legend makes the reader look away from the data, find the colour, read the name, and look back, once for every line. A label at the end of each line removes that trip. The “Highlight” figure in the colour section labels its lines directly; the before-and-after slide below does the same for three lines.
When there is only one group, there is nothing for a legend to explain. Remove it.


Look at each element and ask whether the message would suffer without it:

a legend that repeats the axis labels
colour that repeats position
heavy gridlines, a dark background, a box around the panel
numbers printed on every bar when the message is the ranking
a third dimension

What remains should be the data, the axes, and the words needed to read them.

title: 04-1: Communicating with Figures
section: The figure standard
text:
The figure standard
Every figure you hand in must meet this standard, whatever its message. Each item has a yes or no answer.

Plain-word labels. Axis titles and legend titles in plain words with units: “Corn yield (bushels per acre)”, never corn_yield. Category labels in words: “Irrigated”, not 1.
Readable text. Tick labels, axis titles and legend text no smaller than the document’s body text, at the size the figure appears in the HTML.
The legend where it costs least. In an empty corner of the plot, or above or below a wide figure, or removed when lines or points are labelled directly or there is only one group. Its order matches the order of the lines or bars.
Numbers formatted for reading. Thousands separators, no more decimals than the message needs, percentages shown as percentages.
No overlapping tick labels. For long category names, put the categories on the vertical axis.
The data is the darkest thing. Light or no gridlines, no heavy borders.
A shape that suits the content. Wide for a change over time, close to square for a relationship between two variables.
Colours every reader can tell apart. A palette readable by colour-blind readers, and no more colours than the message needs.

The copyable version, to add to every figure request, is in Recommended requests at the end of this deck.

title: 04-1: Communicating with Figures
section: Before and after
text:
Before and after
Message: “Extreme drought hit all three states in 2002, and again in 2012 and 2013.”

BeforeAfterWhat changed











A deliberately bad example: ggplot’s defaults, which is what comes back when a request says nothing about how the figure should look.




Code the AI wrote
last_points <- filter(state_year, year == max(year))

ggplot(state_year, aes(year, drought_weeks, colour = state_name)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(
    data = last_points, aes(label = state_name),
    direction = "y", hjust = 0, nudge_x = 0.4, size = 5.5, seed = 1
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = state_colours, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(2000, 2018, 2),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.12))
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Extreme drought hit all three states in 2002, and again in 2012 and 2013",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Weeks of extreme drought,\nMay to September"
  )





















Standard item
Before
After




1
Plain-word labels
drought_weeks, year, state_name
“Weeks of extreme drought, May to September”; no axis title for years, which need none


2
Readable text
far smaller than this slide’s text
the same size as this slide’s text


3
Legend
a legend to the right, which narrows the plot
removed; each line is labelled at its end


6
The data is darkest
grey background, white gridlines
no background, light gridlines


7
Shape
wide
wide, which suits a change over time


8
Colours
ggplot’s red, green and blue
the deck’s Okabe-Ito colours for each state



The title now states the finding. Items 4 and 5 needed no change here.

title: 04-1: Communicating with Figures
section: What must be true of the data
text:
What must be true of the data

The conditionsA year stored as a numberA year that is not thereThe check



One row per thing drawn. One row per point, per bar, or per point on a line. If the table has one row per county and the line is meant to show one value per state and year, the averaging must happen first.
The right type per column. A category the colour should separate (a year, an ID, a 0/1 code) must be stored as a category. Stored as a number, it gets a scale for amounts.
Nothing missing that the figure hides. A line joins whatever rows it is given, whether or not a year is missing between them.

None of these failures gives an error. The figure is drawn, and it is wrong.











The request was “colour the points by year” for three years. year is stored as a number, so ggplot drew a scale for an amount: a legend with shades for years that are not in the figure, and three shades of one blue that are hard to tell apart.











The data has no row for Hall County in 2014 or 2015. The line runs straight across both years, and nothing on the figure says they are missing.


Ask the AI to print, next to the figure in the HTML, the checks you can predict: here, one row per year.


Code the AI wrote
cat(
  paste0("rows for Hall County: expected ", n_distinct(cy$year), ", got ", nrow(hall)),
  paste("years with no row:", paste(setdiff(min(cy$year):max(cy$year), hall$year), collapse = ", ")),
  sep = "\n"
)


rows for Hall County: expected 19, got 17
years with no row: 2014, 2015


The check fails, and it names the missing years. A figure that should show them can break the line there (store the missing years as empty values) or say so in its caption. When a value is an average over several rows, print the number of rows behind each value as well: an average of very few rows can look like any other point.

title: 04-1: Communicating with Figures
section: The checklist
text:
The checklist
Apply it to any figure, yours or the AI’s, by looking at it in the rendered HTML, at the size a reader will see it. Each question has a yes or no answer.

Can someone who has not seen the data state the message within a few seconds?
Does every colour carry information? (No colour that only decorates.)
Would the message survive printing in black and white?
Is everything in the figure needed for the message?
Does it meet every item of the figure standard?
Does the table printed next to the figure have one row per thing drawn, with nothing missing that the figure hides?

A “no” to any question is something to fix or a reason to choose a different design.

title: 04-1: Communicating with Figures
section: Your turn: judge a figure
text:
Your turn: judge a figure
The message is meant to be: “Extreme drought came in a few bad years, above all 2012 and 2013.”


QuestionsAnswers


A. Apply questions 1 to 5 of the checklist. Which answers are “no”?
B. What does the colour show that the position of the bars does not?
C. List the changes you would ask for, in the order that matters most for the message.


A. Question 1 is close to “yes”: the tall bars are visible. Question 2 is “no”, question 4 is “no” (the colour and its legend), and question 5 is “no”: raw column names as axis titles, text far smaller than the slide’s, a grey background.
B. Nothing. The colour repeats the year, which the horizontal axis already shows, and its legend narrows the plot.
C. Remove the colour and the legend; put the finding in the title; plain-word axis title with units (“Weeks of extreme drought, May to September”); larger text; no grey background. Bars are a reasonable choice here, since the values are counts of weeks and start at zero; a line would also do.

title: 04-1: Communicating with Figures
section: Working with AI on your own research
text:
Working with AI on your own research
Figures follow the same way of working as everything else (lecture 03-1, “Working with AI on your own research”): you ask, the AI writes into a Quarto document, you render, and you judge the HTML.
For figures, judging the HTML matters even more:

A figure’s text size, shape and legend only exist at the size it is shown. The chat window shows it at a different size, or not at all.
The figure sits next to the sentence that says what it shows, so you can check that the two agree.
The table the figure is drawn from can be printed right next to it.

Every figure request ends with the figure standard and then the closing instructions. Both are under Recommended requests.

title: 04-1: Communicating with Figures
section: What to put in a figure request
text:
What to put in a figure request
The AI already knows how to draw any figure. Your request supplies what it cannot know:

The data: the file, what one row is, and which columns the figure uses, with their units
The message: the one sentence the reader should take away
The reader: who will see it, and what they already know
What matters: which group or which years the message is about, and colours that must stay fixed across figures
Alternatives, not one answer: two or three designs to choose from (next slide)
The figure standard, then the closing instructions





Using an agent in your editor or terminal?


An agent such as Claude Code can open the data and look for itself. It still cannot know your message or your reader. Write those down before it runs.

title: 04-1: Communicating with Figures
section: A weak request and a strong one
text:
A weak request and a strong one

WeakStrongWhat came back


Make a plot of my corn data.
The AI has to guess which columns, which message, which reader and which type of figure. Whatever it draws is a figure of the data, not of a message, and you have no sentence to judge it against.


In my R project, data/county_yield.csv has one row per county and year,
2000 to 2018, for Colorado, Kansas and Nebraska. drought_weeks is the
number of weeks from May to September the county spent in extreme
drought.

The message: extreme drought hit all three states in 2002, and again in
2012 and 2013. The reader: an extension audience who knows the states
but has not seen this data.

Average drought_weeks by state and year, and draw one line per state
over time. Colorado #E69F00, Kansas #0072B2, Nebraska #009E73. Print
the table the figure is drawn from, with the number of counties behind
each value.

[the figure standard, pasted here]

Put the code in my Quarto document analysis/figures.qmd, under the
heading "Drought by state", as R code chunks. Above each chunk, write one
plain-English sentence saying what it does and why. Build every path
with here::here(); no setwd(), no absolute paths. Print each check on
its own line as "name of check: expected X, got Y". Render the document
to HTML.


A version of what an AI returns, the code behind the “After” figure. You should be able to say which part does what:

last_points <- filter(state_year, year == max(year))

ggplot(state_year, aes(year, drought_weeks, colour = state_name)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(
    data = last_points, aes(label = state_name),
    direction = "y", hjust = 0, nudge_x = 0.4, size = 5.5, seed = 1
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = state_colours, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(2000, 2018, 2),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.12))
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Extreme drought hit all three states in 2002, and again in 2012 and 2013",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Weeks of extreme drought,\nMay to September"
  )


ggplot(...) with aes(...): which column goes on which axis, and which column sets the colour
geom_line(): draw lines; geom_text_repel(): the labels at the line ends
scale_colour_manual(): the fixed colours, and guide = "none" removes the legend
labs(): the title and the axis titles

title: 04-1: Communicating with Figures
section: Requests you can copy
text:
Requests you can copy
Copy one, then replace every <...> with what you know: the message, the reader, the group that matters, what you found in the data. Every figure request ends with the figure standard and then the closing instructions.

Closing instructionsThe figure standardAsk for designsImprove a figureCritique a figureCheck against the dataExplain code


The lines that end every request for code. Replace the two blanks; leave “expected X, got Y” as it is, because it tells the AI how to print each check:
Put the code in my Quarto document <path to your .qmd>, under the
heading "<heading>", as R code chunks. Above each chunk, write one
plain-English sentence saying what it does and why. Build every path
with here::here(); no setwd(), no absolute paths. Print each check on
its own line as "name of check: expected X, got Y". Render the document
to HTML.
A chat assistant cannot render: paste its chunks into your .qmd and render it yourself. An agent in your editor or terminal can do every step.


Paste this into every figure request, just before the closing instructions:
Every figure must meet this standard:
1. Axis titles, legend titles and category labels in plain words with
   units, such as "Corn yield (bushels per acre)", never a column name;
   categories in words, such as "Irrigated", never a code such as 1.
2. Tick labels, axis titles and legend text no smaller than the
   document's body text, at the size the figure appears in the HTML.
3. No legend when lines or points can be labelled directly or there is
   only one group. Otherwise, the legend inside an empty corner of the
   plot, or above or below a wide figure, in the same order as the lines
   or bars it describes.
4. Numbers formatted for reading: thousands separators, no more decimals
   than the message needs, percentages shown as percentages.
5. No overlapping tick labels; for long category names, put the
   categories on the vertical axis rather than rotating the text.
6. Light or no gridlines and no heavy borders, so the data is the
   darkest thing in the figure.
7. A shape that suits the content: wide for a change over time, close
   to square for a relationship between two variables.
8. Colours readable by colour-blind readers (such as the Okabe-Ito
   palette), and no more colours than the message needs.
Keep your own copy of this block, and add to it each time you find something the AI keeps getting wrong.


The central request: the AI makes alternatives cheaply, and choosing among them is your job.

is>. The figure uses the columns <columns>, which mean <what they mean>
and are measured in <units>.

title: 04-1: Communicating with Figures
section: What is yours, and what you can hand off
text:
What is yours, and what you can hand off







You need to decide or judge
The AI can write




The message, in one sentence, and who the reader is
The code for any type of figure


Which type of figure makes that message obvious, chosen from alternatives
Two or three alternatives, side by side


Whether colour carries information, and which group to highlight
The colour scales and the highlighting


The order, the panels, the axis ranges, the title that states the finding
