Every figure: write the message and the reader first. Ask for alternatives, choose one and write why. Append the figure standard and the closing instructions. Render, and judge the figure in the HTML with the checklist.

title: 03-2: The Core Operations of Data Wrangling
section: What you will and will not learn today
text:
What you will and will not learn today

The planDirections


Once a table is in R, almost every analysis starts by changing it: keeping some rows, keeping some columns, adding a column, summarising by group, sorting. This is called data wrangling. An AI assistant writes the code for all of it without effort. What it cannot do is:

know which rows and columns your question needs
know how the values in your table are written, and what a missing value means
know what one row of the result should be
tell whether the result is right

Those four are your job. So today is about:

The concept: the five operations, described in words, and what has to be true for each to do what you meant
Reading code: the pattern all wrangling code follows, so you can read a chain of steps the AI wrote
Asking AI: what to put in your request
Checking: how to tell whether the code did what you asked




You need the tidyverse package, installed in 03-1. It includes dplyr, the package whose functions appear on these slides.
The examples use corn_yields.csv from 03-1: corn yields for Nebraska counties in 2008, one row per county and irrigation status. On these slides the file sits in the same folder as the slides, so the code uses just its name.

title: 03-2: The Core Operations of Data Wrangling
section: Five operations, in words
text:
Five operations, in words
Almost every wrangling request is one of five operations, or several of them in a row. Say what you want in these words, and you have most of a request.











You want to
Example request in words
Rows after
Columns after




A
Keep rows that meet a condition
“keep only the irrigated rows”
fewer (or the same)
the same


B
Keep columns
“keep only the county name and the yield”
the same
fewer


C
Create a column from other columns
“add the yield in tonnes per hectare”
the same
one more


D
Summarise by group
“the average yield for irrigated and for non-irrigated rows”
one per group
the groups and the summaries


E
Sort
“sort from highest yield to lowest”
the same, reordered
the same



The last two columns are a first check you can make without reading any code: if “keep columns” changed the number of rows, something other than what you asked for happened.




What one row is


Every table has an answer to “what is one row?” In corn_yields.csv, one row is one county, in one year, with one irrigation status. Operations A, B, C and E leave that answer unchanged. Operation D changes it: after “average yield by irrigation status”, one row is one irrigation status. Before asking for a summary, say what one row of the result should be.

title: 03-2: The Core Operations of Data Wrangling
section: How wrangling code is written
text:
How wrangling code is written
Whichever operation you ask for, the code the AI writes follows the same pattern.

The patternEvery operation follows the patternConditionsVariations you will see



new_table <- table_name |>
  operation(what to do, written with column names) |>
  operation(what to do, written with column names)









Part
What it is
Required?




new_table <-
The name the result is stored under. Without it, the result is printed and then lost.
Needed to keep the result


table_name
The table you start from. It is never changed; the result is a new table.
Yes


|>
The pipe: “then”. It hands the table on its left to the operation on its right, as that operation’s first input.
Needed when there are several steps


operation(...)
A function that does one of the five operations
Yes


inside the ( )
What to do, written with column names as they are, without quotes: a condition, a formula, a list of columns
Yes



A real line that follows the pattern, with one step:

irrigated <- corn |>
  filter(Irrigated == 1)
nrow(irrigated)

[1] 74


74 of the 161 rows are irrigated.













Operation
Function you will see
Inside the ( )
Example




A
Keep rows
filter()
a condition
filter(Yield > 180)


B
Keep columns
select()
column names; a minus sign drops a column
select(County_name, Yield)


C
Create a column
mutate()
new_name = formula
mutate(yield_t_ha = Yield * 0.0628)


D
Summarise by group
group_by(), then summarise()
the grouping columns; then new_name = summary
group_by(Irrigated) |> summarise(avg = mean(Yield))


E
Sort
arrange()
columns; desc() for largest first
arrange(desc(Yield))



Others you will meet in AI-written code, each a variant of one of the five: rename() (change column names), distinct() (drop repeated rows), count() (number of rows per group, a short form of D), slice_max() (the rows with the largest values, A and E together), relocate() (move columns).


A condition is a statement that is true or false for each row; filter() keeps the rows where it is true. Conditions are written with these pieces:








Written
Means
Example




==
is equal to (two equals signs)
Irrigated == 1


!=
is not equal to
County_name != "BUFFALO"


>, >=, <, <=
greater than, at least, less than, at most
Yield >= 150


%in%
is one of
County_name %in% c("BUFFALO", "CUSTER")


&, or a comma
and: both must be true
Irrigated == 1 & Yield > 180


|
or: at least one must be true
Yield < 120 | Yield > 200


is.na()
is missing
is.na(Yield)


!
not
!is.na(Yield)



Text values go in quotes and must match exactly, capital letters included. Numbers go without quotes.


The same operations appear in other forms. They change how the code looks, not what it does:

%>% instead of |>. An older pipe from a package; for reading code, the two mean the same thing.
dplyr::filter(...): the package name, then ::, then the function, as in 03-1.
No pipe: filter(corn, Irrigated == 1). The table is the first input, which is exactly what the pipe supplies.
summarise(avg = mean(Yield), .by = Irrigated): the grouping written inside summarise() instead of in a group_by() before it.
Base R, without dplyr: corn[corn$Irrigated == 1, ] keeps rows, corn$yield_t_ha <- corn$Yield * 0.0628 creates a column, aggregate(Yield ~ Irrigated, data = corn, FUN = mean) summarises by group.

If you want all your code in one style, say so in your request (“use the tidyverse”).

title: 03-2: The Core Operations of Data Wrangling
section: Reading a chain of steps
text:
Reading a chain of steps
AI-written code usually strings several operations together with the pipe. Read it top to bottom, saying “then” at each |>:

top_irrigated <- corn |>
  filter(Irrigated == 1) |>
  mutate(yield_t_ha = Yield * 0.0628) |>
  select(County_name, Yield, yield_t_ha) |>
  arrange(desc(Yield))
head(top_irrigated, 3)

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  County_name Yield yield_t_ha
  <chr>       <dbl>      <dbl>
1 PHELPS        204       12.8
2 CUMING        202       12.7
3 WAYNE         200       12.6


“Take corn, then keep the irrigated rows, then add the yield in tonnes per hectare, then keep three columns, then sort from the highest yield down.” (A bushel of corn is 56 pounds, so 1 bushel per acre is 0.0628 tonnes per hectare.)




The order of the steps matters


Each step works on the result of the step above it, not on the original table. Two examples:

Moving select(County_name, Yield) to the top gives an error, because the Irrigated column is gone by the time filter() looks for it.
Keeping the rows with a yield above 180 and then averaging gives a different number from averaging and then keeping rows. The code runs either way, so read the order and check it matches what you meant.

title: 03-2: The Core Operations of Data Wrangling
section: What has to be true for each operation to work
text:
What has to be true for each operation to work

The conditionsValues written differentlyMissing values in a conditionMissing values in a summaryOne row per what?



The column names are right. A wrong column name gives an error, which is the good case.
The values are written the way the code assumes. A condition compares against values as they are stored: "BUFFALO" is not "Buffalo", and 1 is not "yes".
Missing values are handled the way you meant. Each operation treats missing values in its own way, and none of them tells you.
One row of the result is what you meant. Especially after summarising: one row per what?

If condition 1 fails, R stops with an error. If 2, 3 or 4 fails, R gives you a table and no error. This deck calls those the silent failures; the next tabs show one of each.



corn |>
  filter(County_name == "Buffalo") |>
  nrow()

[1] 0


No rows, and no error. The county names in this file are in capital letters, "BUFFALO", so nothing is equal to "Buffalo". The AI cannot know how your values are written unless it looks or you tell it.


A tiny table, written into the code, with one yield missing (NA, R’s mark for a missing value):

small <- tibble(
  county = c("A", "B", "C", "D"),
  yield  = c(150, 190, NA, 170)
)

Keep the rows above 160, and separately the rows at or below 160:

nrow(filter(small, yield > 160))

[1] 2

nrow(filter(small, yield <= 160))

[1] 1


2 + 1 = 3, not 4. County C is in neither: a condition on a missing value is neither true nor false, and filter() drops the row. Whether that is right depends on your question; the code never asks.


small$yield means the column yield of the table small.

mean(small$yield)

[1] NA

mean(small$yield, na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 170


Without instructions, the average of a column with a missing value is itself missing. With na.rm = TRUE (“remove missing values”), the average is over the 3 values that are there. The second looks fine, but it is an average of fewer values than you may think. If most of a group is missing, its average rests on a few rows, and the result does not say so.


Operation D is group_by() then summarise(). Swap summarise() for mutate() and the result looks similar but means something else:

by_status <- corn |>
  group_by(Irrigated) |>
  summarise(avg_yield = mean(Yield))
nrow(by_status)

[1] 2

with_avg <- corn |>
  group_by(Irrigated) |>
  mutate(avg_yield = mean(Yield))
nrow(with_avg)

[1] 161


summarise() gives one row per group. mutate() keeps all 161 rows and writes the group’s average on each one. Both are useful; they answer different requests. The number of rows tells you which one you got.
A second thing to watch: after group_by(), the table stays grouped until ungroup(), including after mutate() and, when there are two grouping columns, after summarise(). Every later step then works within each group, with no error. The printed table shows a # Groups: line when this is the case (summarise() also prints a message saying so; mutate() does not):

with_avg |>
  head(2)

# A tibble: 2 × 10
# Groups:   Irrigated [2]
   Year State FIPS  County_name State_name Commodity `Data item` Irrigated Yield
  <dbl> <dbl> <chr> <chr>       <chr>      <chr>     <chr>           <dbl> <dbl>
1  2008    31 31019 BUFFALO     NEBRASKA   CORN      CORN, GRAI…         0   173
2  2008    31 31019 BUFFALO     NEBRASKA   CORN      CORN, GRAI…         1   182
# ℹ 1 more variable: avg_yield <dbl>

title: 03-2: The Core Operations of Data Wrangling
section: Working with AI on your own research
text:
Working with AI on your own research
The same way of working as on the slide of this name in lecture 02-1: you ask, the AI writes into your .qmd with one plain-English sentence above each chunk, you render, and you judge the HTML. For wrangling, judging the HTML means reading the chain of steps: does each sentence say what you asked for, and does the code under it do what the sentence says? Every request for code ends with the closing instructions, under Recommended requests.

title: 03-2: The Core Operations of Data Wrangling
section: Look at the values before you ask
text:
Look at the values before you ask

WhyWhich values a column takesMissing values in each column


To write a condition, you need to know how the values are written. To ask for a summary, you need to know what the groups are and how many there are. To know what missing values will do, you need to know where they are. None of that is visible in the column names.


count() lists every value of a column and how many rows have it:

count(corn, Irrigated)

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  Irrigated     n
      <dbl> <int>
1         0    87
2         1    74


From this you learn: Irrigated is written as 0 and 1, not as “no” and “yes”, and a summary by irrigation status will have 2 rows, built from 87 and 74 rows.



colSums(is.na(corn))

       Year       State        FIPS County_name  State_name   Commodity 
          0           0           0           0           0           0 
  Data item   Irrigated       Yield 
          0           0           0 


No missing values anywhere in this file, so missing values cannot change any result here. In most real data this line is not all zeros, and then it tells you which columns need a decision.

title: 03-2: The Core Operations of Data Wrangling
section: What to put in your request
text:
What to put in your request
The AI already knows the functions. Your request supplies what it cannot know, most of it from looking at the values:

The table: its name, and what one row of it is
The operation, in words, with the exact column names and the values as they are written (Irrigated is 1 for irrigated, County_name is in capital letters)
Missing values: what to do with them in this step (leave them out, keep them, count them)
What you want back: the name of the new table, and what one row of it is
Ask for checks: the numbers you will compare against (see “Checking the result”)
The closing instructions: which .qmd and heading the code goes under, a sentence above each chunk, paths built with here::here(), checks printed as expected and got, and render to HTML

title: 03-2: The Core Operations of Data Wrangling
section: A weak request and a strong one
text:
A weak request and a strong one

WeakStrongWhat came back


Get the average corn yield by type.
The AI has to guess which table, which column means “type”, and whether you want one number per group or the average written on every row. If it guesses Commodity, which has one value in this file, it returns a single row: the code runs, and it answers a question you did not ask.


An example for the corn table:
In my table corn, one row is one county, in 2008, with one irrigation
status. Irrigated is 1 for irrigated and 0 for non-irrigated. There are
no missing values. Make a table called yield_by_status with one row per
irrigation status, holding the average Yield and the number of rows
behind each average, using the tidyverse.

Then check the number of rows of yield_by_status (I expect 2), and that
the numbers of rows behind the averages add up to the rows of corn (161).

Put the code in my Quarto document analysis/summary.qmd, under the
heading "Average yield by irrigation status", as R code chunks. Above
each chunk, write one plain-English sentence saying what it does and
why. Build every path with here::here(); no setwd(), no absolute paths.
Print each check on its own line as "name of check: expected X, got Y".
Render the document to HTML.


What the AI’s answer looks like in the rendered HTML: a sentence, then the chunk it describes, then what it printed.
Group the rows of corn by irrigation status, and for each group compute the average yield and count the rows.

yield_by_status <- corn |>
  group_by(Irrigated) |>
  summarise(avg_yield = mean(Yield), n_rows = n())
yield_by_status

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  Irrigated avg_yield n_rows
      <dbl>     <dbl>  <int>
1         0      158.     87
2         1      182.     74


Check that there is one row per irrigation status and that no row of corn was lost or counted twice.

cat("rows in yield_by_status: expected 2, got", nrow(yield_by_status), "\n")

rows in yield_by_status: expected 2, got 2 

cat("rows behind the averages: expected 161, got", sum(yield_by_status$n_rows), "\n")

rows behind the averages: expected 161, got 161 


Both checks pass. n() counts the rows in each group; it takes no input. Irrigated corn averaged 182 bushels per acre and non-irrigated corn 158.

title: 03-2: The Core Operations of Data Wrangling
section: Checking: what to ask for, and why
text:
Checking: what to ask for, and why

Checks for each operationAsking for themReading the HTML


The AI can write the checking code. It cannot know the right answers. These checks fit each operation:










Operation
Ask the AI to print
What only you can supply




A
Keep rows
the rows before and after; the values of the condition’s columns in the result; and, if missing values are possible, the rows kept plus the rows dropped
how many rows you expect, from counting values first


B
Keep columns
the column names of the result
which columns you need


C
Create a column
the smallest and largest value of the new column, its number of missing values, and one row you can work out by hand
a believable range, and the hand calculation


D
Summarise by group
the number of rows of the result; the number of rows, and of non-missing values, behind each summary; that those add up to the original rows; whether the result is still grouped
how many groups there are


E
Sort
the first and last rows
which row should come first





Tell the AI what you expect, so the HTML says which checks passed:
I expect <number> rows after keeping <the rows you want, in words>, and
only the values <values you expect> in <the column in the condition>.
Print each check on its own line as "name of check: expected X, got Y".
You can fill in those blanks only if you counted the values first (under “Look at the values before you ask”). That part only you can do.


A student asked for the irrigated rows with a yield above 180, and the yield in tonnes per hectare. From count() they knew there are 74 irrigated rows, so they expected at most that many. They also looked up one county in the file before asking, Phelps, with an irrigated yield of 204, and worked out 204 × 0.0628 = 12.81 tonnes per hectare by hand. The AI wrote the code; in the rendered HTML, you read each line:


Code the AI wrote
high <- corn |>
  filter(Irrigated == 1, Yield > 180) |>
  mutate(yield_t_ha = Yield * 0.0628)

cat(
  paste("rows: expected at most 74, got", nrow(high)),
  paste("values of Irrigated: expected 1, got", paste(unique(high$Irrigated), collapse = ", ")),
  paste("smallest Yield: expected above 180, got", min(high$Yield)),
  paste("yield_t_ha for PHELPS: expected 12.81, got", round(high$yield_t_ha[high$County_name == "PHELPS"], 2)),
  sep = "\n"
)


rows: expected at most 74, got 47
values of Irrigated: expected 1, got 1
smallest Yield: expected above 180, got 181
yield_t_ha for PHELPS: expected 12.81, got 12.81



The rows are fewer than 74, and only irrigated rows are left.
No yield at or below 180 got through.
The new column matches the value for Phelps worked out by hand before asking.

title: 03-2: The Core Operations of Data Wrangling
section: Checks that come from knowing the data
text:
Checks that come from knowing the data
The checks above apply to any table. The most useful checks come from what you know about this data.
In corn_yields.csv, two columns say the same thing in different ways: Irrigated is 1 or 0, and Data item is a description that contains the word IRRIGATED only for irrigated corn. If the file is right, the two always agree. So before trusting filter(Irrigated == 1), ask:
Using the table corn, count the rows for each combination of Irrigated
and whether Data item contains the word IRRIGATED. Print the counts as
one small table.

Put the code in my Quarto document analysis/summary.qmd, under the
heading "Do Irrigated and Data item agree?", as R code chunks. Above
each chunk, write one plain-English sentence saying what it does and
why. Build every path with here::here(); no setwd(), no absolute paths.
Print each check on its own line as "name of check: expected X, got Y".
Render the document to HTML.
The AI’s code, and what it printed:


Code the AI wrote
corn |>
  mutate(says_irrigated = grepl("IRRIGATED", `Data item`)) |>
  count(Irrigated, says_irrigated)


# A tibble: 2 × 3
  Irrigated says_irrigated     n
      <dbl> <lgl>          <int>
1         0 FALSE             87
2         1 TRUE              74


Only two combinations appear: 0 with FALSE and 1 with TRUE. The two columns agree on every row, so a condition on Irrigated selects what you think it selects. If a row showed 1 with FALSE, the file would contradict itself, and you would ask whoever produced it before using either column.

title: 03-2: The Core Operations of Data Wrangling
section: Your turn: read the AI’s code
text:
Your turn: read the AI’s code
A student asked an AI for “the average yield of irrigated counties, and the five counties with the highest yields”, and got this:

corn |>
  filter(Irrigated == 0) |>
  summarise(avg_yield = mean(Yield))

corn |>
  arrange(Yield) |>
  head(5)


QuestionsAnswers


A. Read each chain in words, saying “then” at each |>.
B. Which line gives the wrong average, without an error? How would you know, from what you looked at before asking?
C. The second chain has two problems. What are they?
D. Rewrite the request so the AI could not make these mistakes.


A. “Take corn, then keep the rows where Irrigated is 0, then compute the average yield.” “Take corn, then sort by yield, then show the first five rows.”
B. filter(Irrigated == 0) keeps the non-irrigated rows, so the average is 158.2, not 181.6. You know from count(corn, Irrigated) and the Data item check that 1 means irrigated.
C. arrange(Yield) sorts from the lowest yield up, so it shows the five lowest. And it starts again from all of corn, so non-irrigated rows are included; the request was about irrigated counties.
D. Say that Irrigated is 1 for irrigated, ask for the five irrigated rows with the highest yield, and ask it to print the values of Irrigated in the result and the first and last yields of the sorted table.

title: 03-2: The Core Operations of Data Wrangling
section: What you must understand, and what the AI can write
text:
What you must understand, and what the AI can write







You need to understand
The AI can write




Which of the five operations you want, in words, and in what order
filter(), select(), mutate(), group_by() and summarise(), arrange()


How the values in your table are written
The condition, with the right quotes and signs


Where the missing values are, and what each step should do with them
na.rm = TRUE, is.na() and so on


What one row of the result is
Whether to use summarise() or mutate()


How many rows and groups to expect
The checking code



Read a chain of steps top to bottom, saying “then” at each |>.
Every wrangling step: look at the values first and write down how many rows and groups you expect. Ask the AI to write the code and the checks into your .qmd. Render it, and judge the HTML against what you wrote down.

title: 02-4: Articles with Quarto
section: What you will and will not learn today
text:
What you will and will not learn today

The planDirections


A thesis chapter or a journal article can be written as a Quarto document: the text, the code that makes every figure and table, and the references, in one file that renders to Word, PDF or HTML. Every number and figure then comes from the data at each render, and the reference list is built from what you cite.
An AI assistant can set all of this up and write every line of it. What it cannot do is:

know which journal or committee the article is for, and the format and style they require
decide what each figure and table must show, and which claim in the text it supports
know whether a reference it writes down exists, and says what you cite it for

So today is about:

The concept: what an article needs that a report does not
Reading code: recognising how figures, tables, equations and citations are numbered and referred to
Asking AI: what to put in requests for an article, and what never to ask it to supply
Checking: the mistakes that render without an error, and how to find them




Lecture 02-1 (Quarto documents and rendering) comes first; this lecture assumes it.
Rendering to Word needs nothing extra. Rendering to PDF needs a LaTeX installation; if the PDF render fails, ask the AI how to install TinyTeX for Quarto (quarto install tinytex).

title: 02-4: Articles with Quarto
section: What an article needs that a report does not
text:
What an article needs that a report does not









Report (lecture 02-1)
Article




Reader
Advisor, coauthor: checks the work
Referee, journal reader: follows the argument


Code
Shown or folded
Hidden; the code stays in the .qmd


Figures and tables
Under the chunk that makes them
Numbered, with captions, and referred to by number (“Figure 2 shows”)


Claims from others’ work
Rare
Cited, with a reference list in the journal’s style


Format
HTML
What the journal asks for: usually Word or PDF



The last three rows are what this lecture is about. All three can go wrong without an error: a reference to a figure that does not resolve, a citation to a key that is not in your reference file, a reference that does not exist. The render finishes; only reading the output finds them.

title: 02-4: Articles with Quarto
section: The decisions that come before writing
text:
The decisions that come before writing

Where it goes: the journal or committee decides the output format (Word or PDF), the citation style, and often the length and the number of figures. Read their instructions for authors first.
The claims and their evidence: for each claim in the results, which figure or table supports it. A figure no sentence refers to is a figure the reader does not need.
What you cite, and why: each citation supports a specific sentence. You must have read, at least, the part you cite it for.
Where references come from: a reference file you built from the publishers’ own records (see “Citations”), never from the AI’s memory.

title: 02-4: Articles with Quarto
section: Numbered figures, tables and equations
text:
Numbered figures, tables and equations
Figures, tables and equations all follow the same pattern: give the item a label with the right prefix and a caption, then refer to the label in the text.

The patternA figureA tableAn equationWhen it goes wrong












Item
Label must start with
Caption
In the text, write
The reader sees




Figure from a chunk
fig-
#| fig-cap: "..."
@fig-yield
Figure 1


Table from a chunk
tbl-
#| tbl-cap: "..."
@tbl-summary
Table 1


Equation
eq-
none
@eq-trend
Equation 1



Numbers are given in order of appearance and change by themselves when items are added or moved. The word “Figure” is added for you: write @fig-yield, not Figure @fig-yield, which gives “Figure Figure 1”.


```{r}
#| label: fig-harvest
#| fig-cap: "Yield on the farm, 2015 to 2024. Drought years in orange."
ggplot(harvest, aes(x = year, y = yield, colour = drought)) + ...
```

Yields rose over the decade, except in drought years (@fig-harvest).
Rendered:








Figure 1: Yield on the farm, 2015 to 2024. Drought years in orange.





Yields rose over the decade, except in drought years (Figure 1).


```{r}
#| label: tbl-drought
#| tbl-cap: "Average yield in drought and other years."
harvest |> group_by(drought) |> summarise(years = n(), yield = mean(yield))
```

Drought years averaged far less than other years (@tbl-drought).
Rendered:




Table 1: Average yield in drought and other years.






drought
years
average_yield




FALSE
8
192.2


TRUE
2
173.5








Drought years averaged far less than other years (Table 1).


Math is written between dollar signs, in the notation of LaTeX (the typesetting system most journals use): $\beta$ inside a sentence, $$ ... $$ on its own line. A label after the closing $$ numbers it:
$$
y_t = \alpha + \beta t + \varepsilon_t
$$ {#eq-trend}

The trend $\beta$ in @eq-trend is estimated by least squares.
Rendered:
\[
y_t = \alpha + \beta t + \varepsilon_t
\qquad(1)\]
The trend \(\beta\) in Equation 1 is estimated by least squares.


A reference to a label that does not exist, or whose prefix is wrong, does not stop the render. Quarto prints a warning in the render log and puts the label, with a question mark, into the text:
See ?@fig-two for the trend.
This happens when the chunk was labelled plot-two instead of fig-two, when a label contains _ where the text has -, or when the AI renamed a chunk and not the reference. Search every output for ?@ before you send it.

title: 02-4: Articles with Quarto
section: Citations
text:
Citations

The patternAn entryWhere entries come fromRendered


References live in a bibliography file, usually ending in .bib. The header names it, and the text cites entries by their key, the first word of each entry:
---
bibliography: references.bib
csl: american-journal-of-agricultural-economics.csl
---

The figures were made with ggplot2 [@wickham2016].
@wickham2016 describes the system behind them.



You write
The reader sees




[@wickham2016]
(Wickham 2016)


@wickham2016
Wickham (2016), as part of the sentence


[@wickham2016; @rcore2025]
two works in one bracket



The reference list is built from what you cite, in the style the csl file names (a CSL file holds one journal’s citation style; thousands are free at zotero.org/styles). Change that one line, and every citation and the list are restyled. Entries in the .bib file that you never cite are left out.


@book{wickham2016,
  title     = {ggplot2: Elegant Graphics for Data Analysis},
  author    = {Wickham, Hadley},
  publisher = {Springer International Publishing},
  year      = {2016},
  doi       = {10.1007/978-3-319-24277-4}
}







Part
What it is




@book
The kind of work: @article, @book, @manual, …


wickham2016
The key, used in [@...]


doi
The DOI (digital object identifier): a permanent address. https://doi.org/ followed by the DOI opens the work at its publisher.





Get each entry from a record you looked up, never typed by anyone:

The article’s page at the journal: “Cite” or “Export citation”, choose BibTeX
Google Scholar: the quotation-mark icon under the result, then BibTeX:


Google Scholar’s entries usually have no DOI and sometimes have errors; compare them with the publisher’s page.

From a DOI: RStudio’s visual editor (Insert, Citation, then paste the DOI) writes the entry into your .bib file
For R and its packages: citation() and citation("ggplot2") print the entry the authors want you to use



The citation (Wickham 2016) and the in-text form R Core Team (2025) on this slide come from 02-4-example.bib, beside this deck. The reference list is on the last slide.

title: 02-4: Articles with Quarto
section: The reference that does not exist
text:
The reference that does not exist

What happensThe check


Asked to “add references” or “find a citation for this sentence”, an AI often writes a .bib entry from memory. Some of what it writes is a real work. Some is not: a plausible title, real-sounding authors, a real journal, a DOI. It looks exactly like the real ones, and it renders exactly like them.
This entry is in the .bib file beside this deck:
@article{miller2019,
  title   = {Irrigation Scheduling and Corn Yield Stability in the Great Plains},
  author  = {Miller, Jonathan and Park, Soo-Jin},
  journal = {American Journal of Agricultural Economics},
  volume  = {101},
  number  = {4},
  pages   = {1102--1121},
  year    = {2019},
  doi     = {10.1093/ajae/aaz999}
}
Cited, it renders without a warning: Miller and Park (2019). It is invented for this slide. The article does not exist, and https://doi.org/10.1093/ajae/aaz999 returns “DOI not found”.


For every entry in the reference list, before anything is sent:

Open https://doi.org/ followed by its DOI.
Check that the page that opens has the same title, the same authors and the same year as the entry.
Check that the work says what the sentence citing it claims.

A DOI that does not open is one failure. A DOI that opens a different work is the other, and it is easy to miss if you check only that the link works.
An entry with no DOI (a book, a report, R itself) is checked by finding it at its publisher or in a library catalogue.



Important


A reference you cannot open and check does not go into the article. Citing a work that does not exist is a serious error in a thesis or a journal submission, whoever wrote the entry.

title: 02-4: Articles with Quarto
section: The header of an article
text:
The header of an article

The patternWhich format


---
title: "Drought and the Trend in Corn Yields"
author:
  - name: Your Name
    affiliations:
      - name: University of Nebraska-Lincoln
abstract: |
  Two or three sentences, which may run over several lines
  because of the | above.
bibliography: references.bib
csl: american-journal-of-agricultural-economics.csl
format:
  docx:
    echo: false
  pdf:
    echo: false
  html:
    echo: true
    embed-resources: true
---







Setting
What it does




author: with - name:
A list of authors, each with their own affiliations


abstract: |
The abstract, set apart from the text


bibliography, csl
The reference file and the citation style


format: with several entries
One .qmd, several outputs: Word (docx), PDF, HTML. In RStudio the Render button gets a menu to choose.


echo: false under docx and pdf, echo: true under html
No code in the article; the code shown in the HTML version you use for checking












Format
Choose it when




Word (docx)
The journal or a coauthor asks for Word; coauthors edit in Word with tracked changes


PDF (pdf)
The journal asks for a PDF, or a LaTeX source


HTML
For you and your advisor while writing: fastest to render and read



The journal’s instructions decide. A Word file edited by a coauthor is no longer rendered from your .qmd: their edits must be copied back into the .qmd by hand, or the next render loses them.

title: 02-4: Articles with Quarto
section: The same way of working, for an article
text:
The same way of working, for an article
The way of working with AI from lecture 02-1 applies to every chunk of an article: the AI writes into the .qmd, with one plain-English sentence above each chunk, and you render and judge the output. Two things differ:

With the code hidden, the sentences above the chunks are for you. Ask for each as a comment on the chunk’s first line (a line starting with #). It then shows with the code in the HTML version, where the code is shown for checking, and stays out of the Word or PDF version.
The AI never supplies references. It may format, sort and insert entries you give it. It may suggest what to search for. It does not write a .bib entry from memory.




Note


Every request for code still ends with the closing instructions; the full text is under Recommended requests near the end.

title: 02-4: Articles with Quarto
section: What to put in your request
text:
What to put in your request

The target: journal or committee, output format, citation style (the .csl file)
For each figure or table: what it must show, the claim in the text it supports, the label (fig-..., tbl-...) and the caption
The text that refers to it: by @ label, never “the figure below” (in a PDF, the figure may land on the next page)
Numbers in sentences: as inline R
Citations: only keys that are already in your .bib file, and a list of any sentence that seems to need a citation you have not provided
The checks, and the closing instructions

title: 02-4: Articles with Quarto
section: A weak request and a strong one
text:
A weak request and a strong one

WeakStrong


Write the results section of my paper with a figure and some citations.
The AI decides what the figure shows, writes text you did not decide, and invents the citations, complete with DOIs.


An example for one figure and one sentence:
In my article paper/article.qmd, add a figure of yield by year for the
farm, with drought years in a different colour, labelled fig-harvest,
with the caption "Yield on the farm, 2015 to 2024. Drought years in
orange." It supports the sentence "Yields rose over the decade, except
in drought years", which you add right after it, referring to the
figure with @fig-harvest. Cite only keys already in references.bib;
add no entries to it. If a sentence seems to need a citation I have
not given, list it for me instead. Check the number of years (I expect
10). Write the sentence for each chunk as a comment on the chunk's
first line, starting with #, so it shows with the code in the HTML
version and stays out of the Word version.

Put the code in my Quarto document paper/article.qmd, under the
heading "Results", as R code chunks. Above each chunk, write one
plain-English sentence saying what it does and why. Build every path
with here::here(); no setwd(), no absolute paths. Print each check on
its own line as "name of check: expected X, got Y". Render the document
to HTML.
In an article, the check lines would appear in the text. Render the HTML version to check, then hide them in the version you send (for example with include: false on the check chunk, the one place where hiding a chunk is right: it changes nothing).

title: 02-4: Articles with Quarto
section: The mistakes that render without an error
text:
The mistakes that render without an error

The checksWhat checks 1 and 2 look like












Check
How
Why




1
No unresolved reference
Search the output for ?@, and the render log for “Unable to resolve”
A broken reference renders as text, with no error


2
No unknown citation key
Search the output for ?) and the log for “citation … not found”
A key not in the .bib renders as “(key?)”


3
Every reference exists
Open every DOI; compare title, authors, year
Invented entries render like real ones


4
Every citation supports its sentence
Read what you cite
Only you can say what a work shows


5
Every figure and table is referred to, and says what its sentence claims
Read each sentence next to its figure
A figure no sentence uses, or one that shows something else, misleads the referee


6
Every number in the text is computed
Open the .qmd: inline R, not typed
The article will be revised many times


7
It renders in the required format
Render to Word or PDF, open it, read it
Each format can fail on its own





A chunk labelled plot-two but referred to as @fig-two, and a citation to a key that is not in the .bib file, render as:

See ?@fig-two. As shown by (smith2020?).

with no error. The render log says, among other lines:
WARNING ... Unable to resolve crossref @fig-two
[WARNING] Citeproc: citation smith2020 not found

What you must decide, and what the AI can write







You need to decide or understand
The AI can write




The target journal or committee, its format and style
The header, the .csl line

title: 02-2: Presentations with Quarto
section: What you will and will not learn today
text:
What you will and will not learn today

The planDirections


A Quarto document can be rendered to a slide deck instead of a page. These lecture slides are made that way. An AI assistant can turn your analysis into a deck in a minute: it knows every slide feature and every option. What it cannot do is:

know who is in the room and what they already know
know how long you have
decide the one thing the audience should remember, and which results support it
see whether the slides can be read from the back of the room

Those are your job. So today is about:

The concept: what a talk needs that a written report does not, and the decisions that come before any slide
Reading code: recognising how a deck is written, so you can find and change a slide
Asking AI: what to put in a request for a deck
Checking: how to judge a deck the way the audience will see it

This lecture does not list slide options. When you want one, ask the AI for the effect (“reveal the bullets one at a time”) and check it in the rendered deck.



Lecture 02-1 (Quarto documents and rendering) comes first; this lecture assumes it.
Ask your AI assistant to install the tidyverse and here packages if you have not already.

title: 02-2: Presentations with Quarto
section: What a talk needs that a report does not
text:
What a talk needs that a report does not
A report and a talk can come from the same analysis, but they are read differently:









Report (HTML page)
Talk (slide deck)




Who sets the pace
The reader, who can go back
You; the audience cannot go back


How much per screen
As much as the argument needs
One point per slide


Code
Shown or folded, so the work can be checked
Hidden; the audience sees results


Numbers
As precise as needed
Rounded to what can be said aloud


Detail and caveats
In the text
In what you say, in speaker notes, or on extra slides after the end






Important


A deck made by pasting a report into slides fails all five rows. Asking the AI to “make slides from my report” without saying more tends to produce exactly that.

title: 02-2: Presentations with Quarto
section: The decisions that come before any slide
text:
The decisions that come before any slide

Four decisionsTitles as sentencesWhy the AI cannot do this



The audience: who they are, and what they already know. Farmers at an extension meeting and economists at a seminar need different words and different detail.
The time: as a rough guide, one slide per minute of talking. A 10-minute talk has about 10 slides.
The message: one sentence the audience should remember. Everything in the deck supports it or is left out.
The outline: the sequence of slide titles, each written as a sentence that states what the slide shows.



A title such as “Results” tells the audience nothing. A title that states the point tells them what to look for in the figure under it:



Title as a topic
Title as a sentence




Data
We use yields from one farm, 2015 to 2024


Results
Yields rose by about 2 bushels per acre per year


Weather
The two lowest years were both drought years



Reading the titles alone, in order, should tell the whole story of the talk. That is also the quickest check of a deck (see “Checking the result”).


The AI can suggest a message and an outline, and it will, if you do not give one. But its suggestion is a guess about your audience and your purpose, built from the results it can see. Decide the message and the outline yourself, then let the AI build the slides from them.

title: 02-2: Presentations with Quarto
section: The pattern
text:
The pattern
A deck is a .qmd file like any other. Two things change: the format, and what the headings do.

The patternA real deckThings you will seeA trap


---
title: "Talk title"
format: revealjs
execute:
  echo: false
---

# Section title

## Slide title, written as a sentence

What goes on the slide.

```{r}
#| label: fig-something
code that draws a figure
```







Part
What it does




format: revealjs
Render to a slide deck (revealjs is the name of the slide format)


execute: echo: false
Hide the code of every chunk: the audience sees results only


# ...
A section slide, with the title alone in the middle


## ...
A new slide, with this title at the top. Everything below it, up to the next heading, is on that slide





---
title: "Yields on the home farm"
author: "Your Name"
format:
  revealjs:
    embed-resources: true
execute:
  echo: false
---

## Yields rose by about 2 bushels per acre per year

```{r}
#| label: fig-trend
ggplot(harvest, aes(x = year, y = yield)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Yield (bushels per acre)")
```

::: {.notes}
The line is a straight-line fit. Mention 2021, the drought year.
:::
The {.notes} block holds speaker notes: text you see while presenting, and the audience does not.


The AI will add features to decks. Recognise them, and ask for them by their effect:







You will see
What it does




::: {.incremental} around a list
Bullets appear one at a time


:::: {.columns} with ::: {.column width="50%"} inside
Side-by-side columns


::: {.notes}
Speaker notes


## Title {.smaller}
Smaller text on that slide


## Title {.scrollable}
The slide scrolls if it is too long


::: {.panel-tabset}
Tabs on one slide, as on these slides


#| code-line-numbers: "1|2-3"
Highlights lines of shown code one step at a time


theme:, logo:, footer: under revealjs:
The look of every slide





Anything between the YAML header and the first heading becomes a slide of its own, without a title. A stray sentence, or a comment the AI left there, gives you an empty-looking first slide. Press o in the rendered deck to see all slides at once and spot it.

title: 02-2: Presentations with Quarto
section: Figures on a slide
text:
Figures on a slide

Two different sizesThe same figure, two canvasesWhat to ask for


A figure has two sizes, set by different chunk options:







Option
What it sets




fig-width, fig-height
The size, in inches, of the canvas R draws on. Text is drawn at a fixed size on that canvas.


out-width
How much of the slide the finished picture takes up, for example 50%. Everything in it, text included, is scaled together.



So the size of the axis text on the slide depends on both: a smaller canvas makes the text larger relative to the plot.


Both are shown at the same width on the slide. Only the canvas differs:


fig-width: 10










fig-width: 5










The text on the right is twice as large, because the canvas is half as wide and then scaled up to the same width.


If the axis text is too small to read, the fix is a smaller canvas, not a larger out-width. Ask for the effect and the reason:
The axis text in the figure on the slide "<slide title>" is too small
to read from the back of the room. Make it larger by drawing the figure
on a smaller canvas (fig-width and fig-height), not by changing
out-width.

title: 02-2: Presentations with Quarto
section: Presenting
text:
Presenting
Open the rendered .html in a web browser. While presenting:







Key
What it does




right arrow, space
next slide or next step


left arrow
back


f
full screen


o or Esc
overview of all slides; click one to go to it


s
speaker view: your notes, the next slide and a timer, in a second window (allow pop-ups if nothing appears)


?
the list of every key







A PDF copy


To make a PDF of the slides, open the deck in Chrome, press e to switch to print view, and print to PDF. Bullets that appear one at a time are all shown at once.

title: 02-2: Presentations with Quarto
section: The same way of working, for a deck
text:
The same way of working, for a deck
The way of working with AI from lecture 02-1 applies to decks unchanged: the AI writes into a .qmd (now with format: revealjs), with one plain-English sentence above each chunk, and you render it and judge the rendered deck, not the chat. Three things differ:

The sentences above the chunks are for you, not the audience. With the code hidden, the audience never sees them; they are still how you check what each chunk does. Ask for them as speaker notes or as comments in the .qmd, so they do not fill the slides.
The checks do not belong on the slides you present. Ask for them on a last slide titled “Checks”, after the final slide of the talk. You read it; you do not show it.
The deck is judged by looking at it, slide by slide, as the audience will.




Note


Every request for code still ends with the closing instructions; the full text is under Recommended requests near the end.

title: 02-2: Presentations with Quarto
section: What to put in your request
text:
What to put in your request
The AI knows every slide feature. Your request supplies what it cannot know:

The analysis: which .qmd or which results the deck is built from
The audience and the time: who, what they know, how many minutes
The message: the one sentence they should remember
The outline: the slide titles, as sentences, in order, and what each slide shows
What stays out of view: code hidden, details in speaker notes, checks on a last slide
That it must work when sent: embed-resources: true
The closing instructions

title: 02-2: Presentations with Quarto
section: A weak request and a strong one
text:
A weak request and a strong one

WeakStrongWhat came back


Make slides from my report.
The AI has to guess everything in the last slide. A typical result: one slide per section of the report, titles copied from its headings (“Data”, “Results”), code shown on every slide, and a dozen bullets where a figure should be.


An example for a short talk on one farm’s yields:
Make a revealjs deck at talks/farm-talk.qmd from the analysis in
analysis/report.qmd. The audience is farmers at an extension meeting,
who know yields in bushels per acre but no statistics. I have 5
minutes. The message: yields on this farm rose by about 2 bushels per
acre per year, but drought years still fall far below the trend.

Slides, in order, with these titles:
1. "We looked at ten years of yields on one farm": what the data is
2. "Yields rose by about 2 bushels per acre per year": figure of yield
   by year with a straight-line fit
3. "Drought years still fall far below the trend": the same figure with
   the drought years marked
4. "What this means for planning": three bullets, which I will write

Hide all code. The sentence above each chunk that the last paragraph
asks for goes in the speaker notes of that slide, not on the slide.
Numbers on slides rounded to whole bushels, written as inline R. Add a
last slide titled "Checks", after slide 4, with the checks: number of
years (I expect 10). Use embed-resources: true.

Put the code in my Quarto document talks/farm-talk.qmd, under the
heading "We looked at ten years of yields on one farm", as R code
chunks. Above each chunk, write one plain-English sentence saying what
it does and why. Build every path with here::here(); no setwd(), no
absolute paths. Print each check on its own line as "name of check:
expected X, got Y". Render the document to HTML.


Slide 2 as the AI wrote it in the .qmd. The sentence for the chunk is in the speaker notes; the audience sees the title and the figure.
## Yields rose by about 2 bushels per acre per year

```{r}
#| label: fig-trend
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4
ggplot(harvest, aes(x = year, y = yield)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Yield (bushels per acre)")
```

::: {.notes}
Plot each year's yield with a straight-line fit, to show the rise.
:::
Check it against the request: the title is the outline’s, the code is hidden by echo: false in the header, the sentence is in the notes. Then check the claim in the title against the data: the slope of the line is what “about 2 bushels per acre per year” says.


Code the AI wrote
slope <- coef(lm(yield ~ year, data = harvest))[["year"]]
cat("yield change per year: expected about 2, got", round(slope, 1), "\n")


yield change per year: expected about 2, got 1.8

title: 02-2: Presentations with Quarto
section: Judging a deck as the audience will see it
text:
Judging a deck as the audience will see it

The checksCheck 8, what it looks like


Render the deck, open it, and go through it as a member of the audience would:










Check
How
Why




1
The titles alone tell the story
Press o; read only the titles, in order
If they do not, the audience will not get the message either


2
Each slide shows evidence for its title
Look at each slide
A title not supported by its slide is a claim with nothing behind it


3
Every claim in a title is true
Compare with the results in your analysis, and the Checks slide
The AI wrote the titles from your outline; the data may say otherwise


4
Nothing runs off the bottom of a slide
Step through every slide
The audience cannot scroll


5
The text in figures can be read
Stand back from the screen, or shrink the browser window to half
Axis text is the most common thing that cannot be read


6
No code on the slides
Step through
Code is for you, not the audience


7
The number of slides fits the time
Count them; rehearse with the timer in speaker view
About one minute per slide


8
It works when sent
Copy only the .html to another folder and open it there
Without embedded resources, the copy has no styling and every slide runs into one page





A deck rendered without embed-resources: true, copied to another folder without its _files folder, opens as plain text: titles and bullets one after another on a single white page, no slides. The same deck rendered with embed-resources: true opens as slides wherever it is copied.
Check it before you email a deck or put it on a USB stick for a conference computer.

title: 02-2: Presentations with Quarto
section: Your turn: judge a slide
text:
Your turn: judge a slide
An AI made this slide for a 10-minute talk to an extension audience:
## Results

```{r}
#| label: results
#| echo: true
#| out-width: 30%
model <- lm(yield ~ year, data = harvest)
summary(model)
ggplot(harvest, aes(x = year, y = yield)) + geom_point()
```

+ We estimated a linear model of yield on year
+ The coefficient on year is positive
+ It is statistically significant at the 5% level
+ The R squared is shown in the output above
+ The figure shows the data
+ Drought years are lower
+ This matters for planning

QuestionsAnswers


A. Which checks from the last slide does it fail?
B. What would the slide’s title be, written as a sentence?
C. Write the request you would send to fix it.


A. Check 1 and 2: “Results” says nothing, and the slide holds three points (the trend, drought years, planning). Check 4: a full regression summary plus a figure plus seven bullets cannot fit. On each, show only the figure, without code; move the regression summary to the speaker notes, and round the slope to a whole number in the title, written as inline R. title: 02-0: Getting a Repository onto Your Computer
section: What you will and will not learn today
text:
What you will and will not learn today

The planWhat this lecture leaves outDirections


Much of what you will use in this course, and in research, is shared on GitHub: datasets, example projects, other people’s code. This short lecture is about one thing: getting a copy of such a project onto your computer, and knowing where it went.
An AI assistant can run the command that makes the copy. What it cannot do is:

know which project you need
know where on your computer you want it, and where you will look for it later
tell whether the copy is complete

So today is about:

The concept: what a repository is, and what cloning one does
Reading code: recognising the one command that clones
Asking AI: what to tell an agent so it clones to the right place
Checking: how to tell that the copy is there and complete



GitHub is built on git, a program that records the history of a project. Recording your own changes, sending them back to GitHub and working with others on the same project are taught in Chapter 6 (lecture 06-2). You do not need any of that today: here, files only come down from GitHub to you.



Install Sublime Merge, a free-to-try program that can clone with three clicks. RStudio can also clone (File, New Project, Version Control, Git, then paste the URL), if git is installed on your computer; so can any other git program you already know.
Sublime Merge may be evaluated without a time limit, but asks now and then for a license. That window does not mean anything has expired; everything in this course works during the evaluation.

title: 02-0: Getting a Repository onto Your Computer
section: Repositories and cloning
text:
Repositories and cloning

RepositoryCloneClone or download?


A repository is a project folder kept by git: the files, plus a record of every change made to them. GitHub is a website that stores repositories online.

A public repository can be seen and copied by anyone.
A private one only by its owner and the people they invite.

Every repository has an address, its URL, for example https://github.com/tmieno2/data-science-course-supplementary-datasets, which holds the datasets used in Chapter 3.


Cloning makes a copy of a repository on your computer: a new folder with all the files in it, named after the repository by default.
The copy remembers where it came from. When the owner changes the files on GitHub, you can bring the changes into your copy instead of copying everything again (called pulling; Chapter 6).


GitHub also offers Download ZIP, which gives you the files once.









Clone
Download ZIP




You get the files
yes
yes


The copy knows where it came from
yes (a hidden .git folder inside it)
no


You can bring in later changes
yes

Needs a git program
yes

For a course whose files are updated during the term, clone. For a file you need once, a download is fine.

title: 02-0: Getting a Repository onto Your Computer
section: What has to be true for a clone to work
text:
What has to be true for a clone to work

The URL is right. It is the address of the repository, not of a single file in it.
You can see the repository. Public: anyone can. Private: you must be invited and signed in.
The destination is free. The new folder’s name is not already taken in the folder you clone into.
You know where the copy went. Otherwise you cannot find it again, and you may end up with several copies.




Important


Conditions 1 to 3 fail with an error message. Condition 4 fails silently: the clone works, and the folder sits somewhere you never look. That is the mistake to guard against.

title: A-1: Reading and Checking data.table Code
section: What you will and will not learn today
text:
What you will and will not learn today

The planDirections


The 03-2 lecture did data wrangling with dplyr: keep some rows, keep some columns, add a column, summarise by group. data.table is another R package that does the same jobs, written differently and much faster on large tables. When your data is large, you may ask an AI to use it, or the AI may choose it without being asked.
You will not learn to write data.table code. You will learn:

The concept: what data.table is, and when it is worth asking for
Reading code: the one pattern every line of data.table code follows, and which dplyr step each line matches
The surprise: data.table can change a table in place, so a table you thought was a separate copy changes too
Asking AI and checking: what to put in your request, and how to confirm the data.table result by comparing it with a dplyr result on the same data




Ask your AI assistant to install the data.table, dplyr and nycflights13 packages if you have not already.
The examples use the table flights from the nycflights13 package: one row per flight that left a New York City airport in 2013, 336,776 rows. It comes with the package, so this deck reads no data files.

title: A-1: Reading and Checking data.table Code
section: What data.table is, and when to ask for it
text:
What data.table is, and when to ask for it

What it isWhen it is worth itWhen it is not


data.table is a package with its own kind of table, also called a data.table. A data.table is still a table in the sense of 03-1 and 03-2: rows, named columns, one type per column. Functions that work on any table, such as nrow() or ggplot(), work on it too.
What differs is how you ask for an operation. dplyr uses one function per step (filter(), mutate(), summarise()) joined with |>. data.table puts the steps inside square brackets after the table’s name: flights_dt[month == 1, .N, by = carrier]. The next slide shows how to read that.
A table becomes a data.table in one of three ways you will see in AI-written code:

fread("file.csv"): data.table’s own csv reader returns one
as.data.table(table): makes a data.table copy of an existing table
setDT(table): turns the existing table itself into a data.table, without a copy



Speed. Here are the same 10 million rows (each row has a group number from 1 to 100,000 and a random value), averaged by group with each package:


Code the AI wrote
set.seed(1)
big <- data.table(group = sample(1e5, 1e7, replace = TRUE), value = runif(1e7))
big_tibble <- as_tibble(big)

time_dt <- system.time(big[, .(mean_value = mean(value)), by = group])["elapsed"]
time_dplyr <- system.time(
  big_tibble |> group_by(group) |> summarise(mean_value = mean(value))
)["elapsed"]

cat("data.table:", time_dt, "seconds\ndplyr:", time_dplyr, "seconds\n")


data.table: 0.112 seconds
dplyr: 0.628 seconds


On the computer that built these slides, data.table was about 6 times faster. The exact ratio changes from computer to computer and run to run; the direction does not. Part of the gain comes from data.table splitting the work across several processor threads (parts of the computer’s processor that can each work on a share of the job at the same time; this computer gave it 8), so the gap is smaller on a computer with fewer. fread() is often several times faster than read_csv() on a large csv.
Notice that dplyr also finished 10 million rows in under a second. Row count alone is not the reason; time is. Ask for data.table when:

a step you run often takes many seconds or minutes with dplyr
a csv file is so large that reading it is slow
matching each row to the nearest earlier date in another table (a rolling join)



For the tables in this course and in most thesis projects (thousands to a few hundred thousand rows), dplyr finishes in well under a second. The speed gain is then invisible, and the cost is real: two styles in one project make the code harder for you, your advisor and coauthors to read.
If the data is large but you want to keep reading dplyr code, the dtplyr package lets the AI write dplyr steps that data.table carries out. Ask the AI which fits your case.

title: A-1: Reading and Checking data.table Code
section: How data.table code is written
text:
How data.table code is written
Whatever the operation, data.table code follows one pattern.

The patternEvery dplyr step fits the patternSteps outside the bracketOne example, part by partThe same in dplyrVariations you will see



table_name[rows, columns or computation, by = groups]









Part
What it is
Required?




table_name
The data.table to work on
Yes


rows
Which rows to use: a condition such as month == 1, or order(...) to sort
No; left empty, all rows


columns or computation
What to return or do: pick columns, compute a summary, or add a column with :=
No; left empty, all columns


by = groups
Do the computation separately for each group defined by these columns
No; left out, the whole table is one group



Read it left to right as a sentence: from this table, take these rows, do this, separately for each of these groups. An empty part is still marked by its comma: table_name[, mean(x)] uses all rows.
The help pages call the three parts i, j and by, so AI explanations often say “in i” or “in j”.


Each step from 03-2 is one bracket. (flights_dt is the flights table made into a data.table.)








What you want
dplyr (03-2)
data.table




keep some rows
filter(flights, month == 1)
flights_dt[month == 1]


keep some columns
select(flights, carrier, month)
flights_dt[, .(carrier, month)]


add a column
mutate(flights, speed = distance / air_time)
flights_dt[, speed := distance / air_time]


one summary
summarise(flights, m = mean(dep_delay, na.rm = TRUE))
flights_dt[, .(m = mean(dep_delay, na.rm = TRUE))]


summary per group
group_by(carrier), then summarise(m = ...)
flights_dt[, .(m = ...), by = carrier]


group value on every row
group_by(carrier), then mutate(m = ...)
flights_dt[, m := ..., by = carrier]


count rows per group
count(flights, carrier)
flights_dt[, .N, by = carrier]


sort
arrange(flights, carrier, desc(dep_delay))
flights_dt[order(carrier, -dep_delay)]



The two := rows are not exact matches: mutate() returns a new table, while := changes flights_dt itself (see “The behaviour that surprises”).


Steps outside the bracket, as functions:








What you want
dplyr or tidyverse
data.table




read or write a csv (03-1)
read_csv(), write_csv()
fread(), fwrite()


rename a column
rename(table, new = old)
setnames(table, "old", "new")


join two tables (03-3)
left_join(x, y, by = "id")
merge(x, y, by = "id", all.x = TRUE), or y[x, on = "id"]


reshape (03-3)
pivot_wider(), pivot_longer()
dcast(), melt()



y[x, on = "id"] reads as “for every row of x, find the matching row of y”: all rows of x are kept, as in left_join(x, y), but the columns come out in a different order. If both tables have a column with the same name, say value, then value holds y’s values and x’s become i.value. merge() sorts the rows by the join column, so its row order can differ from x’s.


Count American Airlines (AA) flights from each airport in each month:

flights_dt <- as.data.table(flights)
aa_dt <- flights_dt[carrier == "AA", .N, by = .(origin, month)]
head(aa_dt, 4)

   origin month     N
   <char> <int> <int>
1:    JFK     1  1236
2:    LGA     1  1260
3:    EWR     1   298
4:    JFK    10  1089










Part
Here
dplyr step it matches




rows
carrier == "AA"
filter(carrier == "AA")


computation
.N, the number of rows (in each group)
summarise(N = n())


by =
.(origin, month): one group per airport and month
group_by(origin, month)





The same in dplyr, for comparison:

aa_dplyr <- flights |>
  filter(carrier == "AA") |>
  group_by(origin, month) |>
  summarise(N = n(), .groups = "drop")
head(aa_dplyr, 4)

# A tibble: 4 × 3
  origin month     N
  <chr>  <int> <int>
1 EWR        1   298
2 EWR        2   268
3 EWR        3   295
4 EWR        4   288


The counts agree, but the rows come out in a different order: dplyr sorts by the groups, data.table keeps the groups in the order they first appear in the table. That matters when you compare the two (see “Checking the result”).



.() is short for list(). flights_dt[, .(m = mean(arr_delay, na.rm = TRUE))] returns a table; without .(), flights_dt[, mean(arr_delay, na.rm = TRUE)] returns a single number.
.N is the number of rows, counted per group when there is a by =.
.SD (subset of data) is “all columns of the current group”. flights_dt[, lapply(.SD, mean, na.rm = TRUE), by = carrier, .SDcols = c("dep_delay", "arr_delay")] averages several columns at once, like summarise(across(...)) in dplyr.
Brackets one after another, flights_dt[...][...], do one step and then the next, like |>.
keyby = instead of by = does the same and sorts the result by the groups.
Inside the brackets, a bare name such as month means the column month, as inside dplyr functions.

title: A-1: Reading and Checking data.table Code
section: The behaviour that surprises: changing a table in place
text:
The behaviour that surprises: changing a table in place

What happensWhy the “copy” changedHow to keep the original


:= (the data.table way to add or change a column) does not make a new table. It changes the table it is applied to, in place. Here a student keeps a second name for a small table, intending it as a backup, and then adds a column:

small <- flights_dt[1:3, .(carrier, distance, air_time)]
backup <- small
small[, speed := distance / air_time]
names(backup)

[1] "carrier"  "distance" "air_time" "speed"   


backup has the new column speed too, although no line touched backup. The same steps in dplyr leave the backup as it was:

small_tb <- select(flights[1:3, ], carrier, distance, air_time)
backup_tb <- small_tb
small_tb <- mutate(small_tb, speed = distance / air_time)
names(backup_tb)

[1] "carrier"  "distance" "air_time"




backup <- small does not copy the table. It gives the same table a second name. In dplyr this never shows, because no dplyr function changes a table; mutate() builds a new table, and <- stores it under the name. With := there is only one table, it is changed, and both names show the change.
The same happens in three other places you will see in AI-written code:

A function that uses := on a table it was given changes the caller’s table, not a copy.
Functions whose names start with set (setDT(), setnames(), setorder(), setkey()) change the table itself and are written without <- in front.
flights_dt[month == 1, dep_delay := 0] changes dep_delay in the January rows of flights_dt itself. It does not return a smaller table.

No error and no warning in any of these. The next step that uses the “original” table quietly uses the changed one.


copy() makes a real, separate copy:

small <- flights_dt[1:3, .(carrier, distance, air_time)]
backup <- copy(small)
small[, speed := distance / air_time]
names(backup)

[1] "carrier"  "distance" "air_time"


as.data.table() also makes a copy, which is why flights itself was not changed by anything on these slides. setDT() does not.
So when you ask the AI for data.table code, say which tables must stay unchanged, and ask it to check that they did (see “Checking the result”).

title: A-1: Reading and Checking data.table Code
section: Working with AI on your own research
text:
Working with AI on your own research
The same way of working as in every other lecture (lecture 02-1, “Working with AI on your own research”, explains why it matters for research):

You ask. Your request says what you want, what you know about the data, and which checks to print.
The AI writes into a Quarto document (.qmd), with one plain-English sentence above each code chunk.
You render the .qmd to HTML.
You read the HTML and decide whether the work is right.

For data.table code, the sentence above each chunk matters more than usual: it is your translation of a dense bracket into words. Check that the bracket does what the sentence says, using the pattern from “How data.table code is written”.

title: A-1: Reading and Checking data.table Code
section: What to put in your request
text:
What to put in your request
The AI knows data.table. What it cannot know:

Why you want data.table: how many rows, which step is slow, or that you have none of these problems and want dplyr
What the result is: what one row of the result should be, for example one carrier in one month
Which tables must not change: otherwise := may change a table you use later
A way to confirm the result: ask for the same result with dplyr, on the full data or a sample of it, and a comparison
The closing instructions, as in every request for code (full text under Recommended requests)

title: A-1: Reading and Checking data.table Code
section: A weak request and a strong one
text:
A weak request and a strong one

WeakStrongWhat came back


Use data.table to get average delays by airline and month.
The AI does not know which table, which delay, whether the original table may change, or how you will know the result is right. It will write something that runs, and you will have nothing to compare it with.


An example for a large flights table, tested first on one year of it:
My data.table flights_dt has one row per flight. The full data has tens
of millions of rows, so I want data.table for speed. I am testing on
2013 only, which has 336,776 rows.

For each carrier and month, compute the average arrival delay
(arr_delay) and the number of flights, leaving out flights with no
arrival delay recorded. One row of the result is one carrier in one
month. Do not change flights_dt; I use it later.

To confirm the result, compute the same with dplyr and compare the two
after sorting both by carrier and month. Also check that the flight
counts add up to the number of flights with an arrival delay, and that
flights_dt is identical to a copy saved before your code runs.

Put the code in my Quarto document analysis/delays.qmd, under the
heading "Average delays", as R code chunks. Above each chunk, write
one plain-English sentence saying what it does and why. Build every path
with here::here(); no setwd(), no absolute paths. Print each check on
its own line as "name of check: expected X, got Y". Render the document
to HTML.


What the AI’s answer looks like in the rendered HTML.
Save a separate copy of flights_dt, so we can check at the end that nothing changed it.

flights_dt_before <- copy(flights_dt)

Average arrival delay and number of flights for each carrier and month, using only flights with an arrival delay recorded.

delays_dt <- flights_dt[!is.na(arr_delay),
                        .(mean_delay = mean(arr_delay), n_flights = .N),
                        by = .(carrier, month)]

The same result with dplyr, to compare against.

delays_dplyr <- flights_dt |>
  filter(!is.na(arr_delay)) |>
  group_by(carrier, month) |>
  summarise(mean_delay = mean(arr_delay), n_flights = n(), .groups = "drop")

Compare the two after sorting both by carrier and month, check the counts, and check that flights_dt is unchanged.


Code the AI wrote
same <- all.equal(
  as.data.frame(delays_dt[order(carrier, month)]),
  as.data.frame(delays_dplyr)
)
cat(
  paste("data.table and dplyr agree: expected TRUE, got", isTRUE(same)),
  paste0("flights counted: expected 327346, got ", sum(delays_dt$n_flights)),
  paste("flights_dt unchanged: expected TRUE, got", identical(flights_dt, flights_dt_before)),
  sep = "\n"
)


data.table and dplyr agree: expected TRUE, got TRUE
flights counted: expected 327346, got 327346
flights_dt unchanged: expected TRUE, got TRUE


All three checks pass. Map each bracket onto the request: rows !is.na(arr_delay) is “leaving out flights with no arrival delay”, the computation is the two columns asked for, and by = .(carrier, month) makes one row per carrier and month.

title: A-1: Reading and Checking data.table Code
section: Checking: what to ask for, and why
text:
Checking: what to ask for, and why

The checksWhy sort before comparingWhen the comparison is too slow


The AI can write the checking code. It cannot know which tables you need unchanged or what the right answer is. Ask for these whenever the AI writes data.table code:










Ask the AI to print
Why
What only you can supply




1
whether the data.table result equals a dplyr result on the same data, after sorting both the same way
Two different ways of computing the same thing rarely make the same mistake
which columns identify one row of the result


2
whether the counts add up to the rows that should be included
A wrong condition in the rows part drops or keeps rows with no error
which rows should be included


3
whether each input table is identical to a copy saved (with copy()) before the data.table code runs
:= changes a table in place, with no error, and may change values without changing the columns
which tables must stay unchanged





Compare the data.table and dplyr results from “What came back” without sorting:


Code the AI wrote
unsorted <- all.equal(as.data.frame(delays_dt), as.data.frame(delays_dplyr))
cat("agree without sorting: expected TRUE, got", isTRUE(unsorted), "\n")


agree without sorting: expected TRUE, got FALSE 


The check fails although both are right: dplyr sorts the groups, data.table keeps them in the order they first appear. Same rows, different order. That is why the request says “after sorting both by carrier and month”.
A failed comparison therefore has two possible causes: the order differs, or the numbers differ. Ask the AI which one, and if it is the numbers, ask it to show the groups that differ.


The dplyr version may be too slow on the full data, which is the reason you wanted data.table. Then run both on a sample, compare there, and run only the data.table version on the full data. The data.table code is the same on the sample and the full data, so agreement on the sample tells you the translation is right.

title: A-1: Reading and Checking data.table Code
section: Your turn: read the AI’s code
text:
Your turn: read the AI’s code
A student asked an AI for “the average corn yield in tonnes per hectare, by state, from 2010 on, with data.table”, and got this. In the file, yield is recorded in bushels per acre.

yields <- fread(here::here("data", "county_yields.csv"))
yields_metric <- yields
yields_metric[, yield_t := yield * 0.0628]
yields_metric[year >= 2010, .(avg_yield = mean(yield_t)), by = state]


QuestionsAnswers


A. Say what each of the four lines does, using the dplyr step it matches where there is one.
B. After these lines run, which columns does yields have?
C. Which rows of the data go into the averages?
D. Name two checks to ask for, and what you would expect each to print.


A. Reads the csv into a data.table (like read_csv()); gives the same table a second name; adds a column of yields in tonnes per hectare (like mutate()); keeps rows from 2010 on (filter()), then averages per state (group_by() and summarise()).
B. Its original columns and yield_t. Line 2 made a second name, not a copy, so line 3 changed yields too. If yields must stay as read, line 2 needs copy(yields).
C. Rows with year 2010 or later. Missing yields are not dropped, so a state with a missing value gets NA as its average.
D. For example: the same averages computed with dplyr and compared after sorting by state (expected: they agree); whether yields is identical to a copy saved right after reading (expected: TRUE; here it would print FALSE). The number of rows in the result should equal the number of states with data from 2010 on.

title: A-1: Reading and Checking data.table Code
section: Requests you can copy
text:
Requests you can copy
Copy one, then replace every <...> with what you know about your data. Every request for code ends with the closing instructions.

Closing instructionsDo it with data.tableExplain data.table codeShould I use data.table?


The lines that end every request for code. Replace the two blanks; leave “expected X, got Y” as it is, because it tells the AI how to print each check:
