to HTML.
A chat assistant cannot render: paste its chunks into your .qmd and render it yourself. An agent in your editor or terminal can do every step.


My table <table name> has one row per <what one row is> and about
<number> rows, so I want data.table for speed. I want <what to compute>.
One row of the result is <what one row of the result is>. Do not change
<tables that must stay unchanged>.

To confirm the result, compute the same with dplyr on <the full data, or
which sample> and compare the two after sorting both by <the columns that
identify a row of the result>. Also check that <a count you know>, and
that <tables that must stay unchanged> are identical to copies saved
before your code runs.

Put the code in my Quarto document <path to your .qmd>, under the
heading "<heading>", as R code chunks. Above each chunk, write one
plain-English sentence saying what it does and why. Build every path
with here::here(); no setwd(), no absolute paths. Print each check on
its own line as "name of check: expected X, got Y". Render the document
to HTML.


For data.table code you were given, or that the AI wrote without being asked:
Explain this data.table code to me. For each line, write one
plain-English sentence, and name the dplyr step it matches, if any.
Then list every line that changes a table in place (:=, or a function
whose name starts with set), and which table it changes.

<paste the code here>


My table <table name> has about <number> rows and <number> columns.
The step <the step that is slow> takes about <how long>. Would
data.table, dtplyr or something else make it faster, by roughly how
much, and what would I give up? Do not write code yet.

title: A-1: Reading and Checking data.table Code
section: What you must understand, and what the AI can write
text:
What you must understand, and what the AI can write







You need to understand
The AI can write




When data.table is worth it: steps that take many seconds or minutes, large csv files, rolling joins
The data.table code


The pattern table[rows, columns or computation, by = groups], and which dplyr step each part matches
Any particular bracket, .N, .SD and the rest


That := and set functions change a table in place, so a second name is not a copy
copy() where it is needed, once you say which tables must not change


That two correct results can differ in row order
The comparison with dplyr, sorted



Every time the AI writes data.table code: say which tables must stay unchanged, and ask for the same result with dplyr and a comparison. Render, and judge the HTML: the comparison, the counts, and whether the tables you wanted kept are identical to the copies saved before the code ran.

title: Ex-9-6: Vector Meets Raster, with an AI Assistant
text: This is an in-class exercise. Before class, work through the lecture 09-6: Vector Meets Raster: Cropping, Masking and Extracting Values. In class, you work through the worksheet with an AI assistant writing the code. Your job is everything the AI cannot do: knowing what the raster holds and whether it covers your area, asking for the right checks, and judging whether the result is right.

title: Ex-9-6: Vector Meets Raster, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 1: Look at the drone image and the field
text:
Task 1: Look at the drone image and the field






What you should find





A. No. The raster is in WGS 84 (longitude and latitude); the plots and points are in WGS 84 / UTM zone 15N (metres). Transform the vector layers to the raster’s CRS: transforming a raster recomputes every cell and loses detail, transforming points and polygons does not.
B. A cell is about 1.8 m by 1.8 m (the cell size is printed in degrees; the AI can convert it). A plot is roughly 24 m across if it were square (the plots are long strips, so their real widths differ). So a plot covers a few hundred cells.
C. Yes: all 25 plots (25 inside the raster’s rectangle) and all 3,830 yield points (3,830).

title: Ex-9-6: Vector Meets Raster, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 2: NDRE at each yield point
text:
Task 2: NDRE at each yield point






What you should find





3,830 rows, one per point; 0 points with a missing value; values from 0.51 to 0.64, inside the raster’s own range of -0.14 to 0.7.
The blanks, filled in: EPSG 4326 (WGS 84 longitude and latitude), 3830, 0 (Task 1C showed every point inside the raster), and the raster’s range from Task 1.
If the AI did not transform the points first, the HTML shows the warning [extract] transforming vector data to the CRS of the raster, and the values are still right. Asking for the transformation keeps the code saying what it does.

title: Ex-9-6: Vector Meets Raster, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 3: Average NDRE in each plot
text:
Task 3: Average NDRE in each plot






What you should find





25 rows, no plot without a value, every plot inside the raster, and the smallest plot covers 204 cells. With so many small cells per plot, the cell-counting rule barely matters: the default rule (cell centre inside) and the weighted rule differ by at most 0.001 in any plot.
Mean of the plot averages by nitrogen rate:

Whatever relation there is between nitrogen and greenness here is small next to the variation across the field, which is worth knowing before reading anything into the order of the five numbers.

title: Ex-9-6: Vector Meets Raster, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 4: Rain in Colorado’s counties
text:
Task 4: Rain in Colorado’s counties






What you should find





64 rows, but the checks fail:

59 counties have no value.
Only 3 of the 64 counties lie entirely inside the raster’s rectangle.
2 more counties have a value but are only partly covered: Weld, Yuma.

The colleague’s file was made for a Nebraska project. It covers latitudes from 39.98 degrees north up to Nebraska’s northern border, and Colorado runs from 37 to 41 degrees north. So the raster covers only a narrow strip along Colorado’s northern border, which the map with the raster’s rectangle shows at once.
Which values to use:

The 3 counties entirely inside the raster: usable.
The 59 counties with no value: nothing to use, and the NA says so.
The 2 partly covered counties: do not use. Their value is the average over their northern edge only, and nothing in the number says so. This is the silent failure of the task.

Next step: download PRISM for Colorado and the same days (lecture 09-7), and extract again. The check “counties not entirely inside the raster’s rectangle” is the one to keep in every extraction request.

title: Ex-9-6: Vector Meets Raster, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 5: Maria’s code
text:
Task 5: Maria’s code






Answers





A. Reads the raster; reads the plots; keeps the five plots of replication 1; extracts their mean NDRE, after transforming them to the raster’s CRS; merges the values onto all plots, treating ID as block_id.
B. ID is the row number within rep1: 1 to 5. The replication-1 plots have block_id 21, 22, 23, 24, 25. So the merge puts the five values on plots 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, which are replication 2, and leaves the five plots she wanted empty.
C. Both pass: 5 plots have a value and 20 have none. The counts are exactly right; the plots are wrong. A count cannot tell one plot from another.
D. A check on which plots got a value: “replication of the plots with a value: expected 1, got 2”, or “block_id of the plots with a value: expected 21, 22, 23, 24, 25”. Line 5 should first turn ID into the plots’ own IDs, block_id = rep1$block_id[ID], and then merge by block_id, as on the lecture’s polygon example.
E. The AI usually explains that ID is a row number when asked how values are matched back. Compare its list with yours.

title: Ex-9-4: Two Vector Layers, with an AI Assistant
text: This is an in-class exercise. Before class, work through the lecture 09-4: Two Vector Layers: Relations, Subsetting, Buffers and Clipping. In class, you work through the worksheet with an AI assistant writing the code. Your job is everything the AI cannot do: deciding which relation and which distance your question means, asking for the right checks, and judging whether the result is right.

title: Ex-9-4: Two Vector Layers, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 1: Look at the two layers
text:
Task 1: Look at the two layers






What you should find





A. 64 counties and 2 aquifer polygons. Both layers are in NAD83 longitude and latitude, EPSG 4269, so the CRSs are the same (TRUE). There are 0 invalid shapes.
B. The eastern plains: the aquifer reaches into Colorado from Nebraska and Kansas, along the eastern edge of the state, and stops well short of the mountains.
C. Any rough count is fine, as long as you wrote it down. Most counties on the eastern plains touch the aquifer, but the aquifer’s western edge cuts through most of them, so few lie entirely over it.

title: Ex-9-4: Two Vector Layers, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 2: Counties over the aquifer, two ways
text:
Task 2: Counties over the aquifer, two ways






What you should find





16 counties have some part over the aquifer; 1 lies entirely over it (Phillips).
The two counts are far apart because the aquifer’s western edge runs through the middle of the eastern counties, not along county lines. “The counties over the aquifer” is not one set of counties until you say which relation you mean. The default, intersects, gives 16; the AI uses it unless told otherwise, and your request named both.

title: Ex-9-4: Two Vector Layers, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 3: How much of each county is over the aquifer?
text:
Task 3: How much of each county is over the aquifer?






What you should find





4 of the 16 counties have less than 5% of their area over the aquifer: Larimer (0.4%), Elbert (0.8%), Bent (2%), Las Animas (2.7%). 7 have more than half.
This is the finding of the exercise: the first count of 16 includes counties whose link to the aquifer is a strip along their edge, and the second count of 1 leaves out counties that are mostly over it. Neither count is a good definition for a study of irrigation from the aquifer. A common choice is a threshold on the share, for example “more than half the county’s area over the aquifer”, which gives 7 counties. Whatever you choose, the share table is what lets you defend it.
A request that does it: “For each county in counties_any, compute the share of its area that lies over the aquifer, in a CRS in metres, and print all of them, smallest first, with the county names and their areas over the aquifer in km²”, followed by the closing instructions.
No count or type check could have shown this. Only the question “how much of each county?”, which came from knowing what the study is for.

title: Ex-9-4: Two Vector Layers, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 4: Counties near the aquifer
text:
Task 4: Counties near the aquifer






What you should find





EPSG 26913 is NAD83 / UTM zone 13N, in metres, so the distance is 20000.
2 counties lie within 20 km of the aquifer with no part over it: Arapahoe and Morgan.
The blanks of the request, filled in: 20 km, 26913, and your estimate from the map.

title: Ex-9-4: Two Vector Layers, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 5: Cut the aquifer at county lines
text:
Task 5: Cut the aquifer at county lines






What you should find





16 pieces, one for each county with some part over the aquifer, and no invalid pieces.
The total to check against is the area of the aquifer inside Colorado, 34,499 km², which the AI can compute by cutting the aquifer at the state’s outline (the counties merged into one). The pieces add up to 34,499 km², so the check passes. The whole aquifer is 452,250 km², which is the wrong total to expect: most of it lies in other states.
The largest piece is in Yuma County, 6,133 km².

title: Ex-9-4: Two Vector Layers, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 6: Maria’s code
text:
Task 6: Maria’s code






Answers





A. Transforms the counties and the aquifer to UTM zone 13N, in metres; cuts the counties to the rectangle around the aquifer; computes each piece’s area in km²; adds them up.
B. Line 3. st_crop() cuts to the aquifer’s bounding box, the rectangle from its westernmost to easternmost and southernmost to northernmost points, not to its outline. The aquifer runs from South Dakota to Texas, so its rectangle covers all of eastern Colorado and more: 42 of the 64 counties keep a piece, many of them whole. The rectangle also depends on the CRS: the aquifer’s bounding box in UTM 13N is not the same rectangle as its bounding box in longitude and latitude, but in either CRS it is a rectangle, not the outline.
C. Much larger: 147,171 km², against 34,499 km² over the aquifer (Task 5), and against 269,603 km² for all of Colorado. Most of the counties’ area east of the rectangle’s western edge was kept, over the aquifer or not. Cutting to the outline needs st_intersection().
D. A total that must be preserved: the pieces should add up to the aquifer’s area inside Colorado. A map of over with the aquifer’s outline on top would show the straight edge at once.
E. The AI usually notices st_crop() when asked whether each line cuts or keeps, because “crop” to a bounding box is in its documentation. Compare its list with yours; treat its answer as something to check, not something to accept.

title: Ex-9-2: Raster Data, with an AI Assistant
text: This is an in-class exercise. Before class, work through the lecture 09-2: Raster Data. In class, you work through the worksheet with an AI assistant writing the code. Your job is everything the AI cannot do: finding out what the cell values mean, asking for the right thing and the right checks, and judging whether the result is right.

title: Ex-9-2: Raster Data, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 1: Look and predict
text:
Task 1: Look and predict






What you should find





A. Daily maximum air temperature, three layers: 1, 2 and 3 June 2023.
B. Tenths of a degree Celsius, stored as whole numbers: 215 means 21.5 °C.
C. -9999, in the cells outside Colorado.
D. NAD83 / Conus Albers, EPSG 5070, in metres. The extent will be in metres, not degrees, so it cannot be compared with longitudes and latitudes directly.
E. Early June daytime highs in Colorado run from cold on the high mountains to hot on the eastern plains. Something like 0 to 35 °C is a believable range; stored in tenths, that is 0 to 350. A prediction in that region is fine; the point is to have one before you look.

Task 2: Look at the raster






What you should find





128 rows, 162 columns, 3 layers named tmax_2023_06_01, tmax_2023_06_02, tmax_2023_06_03. Cells are 4,000 by 4,000 metres. The extent runs from -1,148,294 to -500,294 in x and 1,564,785 to 2,076,785 in y, metres in EPSG 5070.
The values run from -9999 to 304 on the first day, and no cell is missing (0 missing cells). Against the README, both are expected: -9999 has not been declared as no data yet, and the values are still in tenths. Which is why this task only looks: any average computed now would be wrong.

title: Ex-9-2: Raster Data, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 4: A map with the counties
text:
Task 4: A map with the counties






What you should find





The raster is in EPSG 5070 and the counties in EPSG 4269, so the CRS check says they differ.
For a map that does not matter: ggplot2 draws every layer in the CRS of the first one, transforming the others as it draws, so the county lines sit on the raster’s state outline. For any calculation that combines the two, such as the average temperature in each county (lecture 09-6), they must share a CRS first. Transform the counties to the raster’s CRS, not the other way round: projecting the raster recomputes every cell value.
A map like the one below is what to expect:









On the map, the cold cells follow the Rocky Mountains through the middle and west of the state, and the eastern plains are warm on all three days. Without the no-data declaration, the -9999 cells would set the bottom of the colour scale and every real temperature would be drawn in nearly the same colour.

section: Task 5: A check from knowing the place

Task 5: A check from knowing the place

title: Ex-9-2: Raster Data, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 6: Maria’s code
text:
Task 6: Maria’s code






Answers





A. Line 1 reads the raster and divides every value by 10. Line 2 averages each layer, skipping missing cells.
B. The path. C:/Users/maria/Downloads exists only on Maria’s computer.
C. -9999 was never declared as no data. After line 1 it is -999.9, a number, so na.rm = TRUE does not skip it. The averages come out at -157.7, -159.9, -161.7 °C.
D. The smallest value (-999.9 °C is impossible) and the number of missing cells (0, where the cells outside Colorado should be missing). An average below -100 °C is also impossible on its face, but only if you look at it with a believable range in mind.
E. The AI cannot see the README, so it can only find this problem if it asks what the values mean or guesses -9999 from experience. Compare its list with yours.

title: Ex-8-3: Tables in Your Paper, with an AI Assistant
text: This is an in-class exercise. Before class, work through the lecture 08-3: Tables in Your Paper (and 08-1 for the table standard). It is short. In class, you work through the worksheet with an AI assistant writing the code.

title: Ex-8-3: Tables in Your Paper, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 1: Predict
text:
Task 1: Predict






What you should find





A. 43 / 154 = 27.9%, so 28% when rounded to a whole percent.
B. Either works, as long as the format matches:

As a share between 0 and 1 (0.279): fmt_percent() multiplies by 100, which is right.
As a percentage between 0 and 100 (27.9): the format must not multiply again. Use fmt_number() with “%” in the header, or fmt_percent(scale_values = FALSE).

Task 2: The table, in gt






What you should find

The trap. If the share was computed as a percentage (27.9 for Colorado) and then formatted with fmt_percent(), the table shows Colorado as 2,792%. Your check (“expected 28%”) fails, and that is how you would know. If your AI computed a share between 0 and 1 and used fmt_percent(), or a percentage and used fmt_number(), the check passes.
The line to explain is the one starting fmt_percent( or fmt_number( with the share column in it: it changes how the number is shown, and fmt_percent() also multiplies it by 100 unless told scale_values = FALSE.

text:
Task 3: Save it for a paper






What you should find





The read-back check should print a Colorado share of 28%. In the Word file the numbers, headers, the header over several columns, and the notes should all be there; gtsave() puts the title above the table as a Word caption (“Table 1: …”).
What can differ: the width. A table that fits a wide HTML page can be wider than a Word page with margins, and fonts and line spacing follow Word’s defaults. These are things to fix in the code (shorter headers, a narrower table), not by editing the Word file, because the next render replaces the file.

title: Ex-8-1: Communicating with Tables, with an AI Assistant
text: This is an in-class exercise. Before class, work through the lecture 08-1: Communicating with Tables. In class, you work through the worksheet with an AI assistant writing the code. Your job is everything the AI cannot do: deciding what the table should tell the reader, choosing its layout, and judging whether the numbers are right.

title: Ex-8-1: Communicating with Tables, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 1: Look and predict
text:
Task 1: Look and predict






What you should find





A. 1956 data rows, below one line of column names.
B. One county in one year.
C. Many readers would do. For example: farmers and extension agents in the three states, who know what drought does to corn but have not seen the numbers across all counties. Or an advisor, who knows the data source but wants the size of the effect. The reader decides how much the notes must explain: a farmer needs “bushels per acre” spelled out and the drought categories explained; an advisor may not.

title: Ex-8-1: Communicating with Tables, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 2: The message and the layout
text:
Task 2: The message and the layout






What you should find





A. Something like: “In all three states, corn yields were about ___ bushels per acre lower in county-years with extreme drought.”
B. A layout that serves this message:

One row per state.
Columns: the state; the average yield without extreme drought; the average yield with it; the difference; the number of county-years behind each average.
The difference is the comparison the message is about, so it gets its own column, and the reader does not have to subtract.
The rows ordered by the difference, or in a natural order the reader knows. With three rows, either works; say which you chose and why.

Other layouts can work (see Task 5). What matters is that you decided it, not the AI.
C. 1956, the number of rows in the data: every county-year is either with or without extreme drought.

title: Ex-8-1: Communicating with Tables, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 3: Ask badly

title: Ex-8-1: Communicating with Tables, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 4: Ask properly
text:
Task 4: Ask properly






What you should find





Average corn yield (bushels per acre), and the number of county-years behind each average:



State
Without extreme drought
With extreme drought
Difference




Colorado
171.9 (111)
158.9 (43)
-13.0


Kansas
175.6 (399)
165.5 (135)
-10.1


Nebraska
183.9 (985)
174.0 (283)
-9.9



Checks: 3 rows; the counts add up to 1956, which should equal the 1956 rows of the data.
The message, filled in: “In all three states, corn yields were about 10 to 13 bushels per acre lower in county-years with at least one week of extreme drought.”
Rounding. Whole bushels are enough for this message; one decimal is also fine. More than one decimal claims a precision that county yield estimates do not have.
Notes the table needs: the source; what “with extreme drought” means (at least one week from May to September in category D3 or D4); that the numbers are averages over county-years; and the counts, which differ a lot: Colorado’s drought average rests on 43 county-years, Nebraska’s on 283.
What this table does not show. The difference is not the effect of drought alone. Drought years differ from other years in other ways too (yields rose over these 19 years, and the worst droughts came in 2002, 2012 and 2013). A careful note says “lower in”, not “caused by”.

title: Ex-8-1: Communicating with Tables, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 5: Two layouts
text:
Task 5: Two layouts






What you should find





One row per state puts the two averages for each state side by side and, with a difference column, puts the three differences down one column. That serves a message about how large the drop is and whether it is similar across states.
One row per drought status, one column per state puts the three states side by side. That serves a message comparing states, such as “Nebraska has the highest yields, with or without drought”. For the drought message, the reader has to compare up and down within each column, and there is no natural place for the difference.
For the message in Task 2, one row per state is the better choice. If your message was about the states rather than the drought, the second layout may be better. Either answer is right if your reason names the comparison the reader must make.

title: Ex-8-1: Communicating with Tables, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 6: Sam’s code
text:
Task 6: Sam’s code






Answers





A. Mark each county-year as with or without extreme drought; group by state and drought status; average the corn yield in each group; put the two drought statuses side by side as columns; turn the result into a table; rename the headers; round to whole numbers. The first four steps decide the numbers. flextable(), set_header_labels() and colformat_double() only change how it looks.
B. TRUE. drought is TRUE when weeks_extreme is 1 or more.
C. The two drought headers are swapped. FALSE (no extreme drought) is labelled “Extreme drought”, and TRUE is labelled “No extreme drought”. Sam’s table shows:


StateExtreme droughtNo extreme droughtColorado172159Kansas176165Nebraska184174


A reader would conclude that yields were higher in drought, by about 10 to 13 bushels per acre, the opposite of the truth. No error, no warning.
D. Two checks, either of which catches it:

A check from knowing the data. Drought lowers corn yields, so the “Extreme drought” column should be the lower one. It is the higher one in every state. That alone says something is wrong.
One value computed a second way. For example, the average yield of Colorado county-years with weeks_extreme of 1 or more is 158.9, computed with filter() and mean() (or in a spreadsheet). Sam’s table puts 159 under “No extreme drought”.

Also, the table misses items 1 (units) and 10 to 13 (title, notes, counts), and has no difference column.
E. It shows Sam’s table above. The fix is to label FALSE “No extreme drought” and TRUE “Extreme drought”, or better, to give the columns plain names in the display table before flextable(), so the headers do not depend on remembering which of TRUE and FALSE is which.

.Rhistory
keep out
Written by RStudio


.Rproj.user/
keep out
RStudio’s settings for your computer


analysis/01-clean.qmd, 02-summary.qmd
track
The steps


analysis/ex-6-2.qmd
track
Your own work


analysis/01-clean.html, 01-clean_files/
keep out
Rendering 01-clean.qmd rebuilds them


data/raw/corn_yields.csv
track
Raw, small (15 KB) and public. It could not be rebuilt by code.


data/processed/corn_clean.rds
keep out
01-clean.qmd rebuilds it



B. A .gitignore that does it:
# files RStudio writes
.Rhistory
.RData
.Rproj.user/
.DS_Store

# secrets
.Renviron

# rendered output and files the steps rebuild
*.html
*_files/
data/processed/
C. .Renviron holds NASS_API_KEY= and a key (a fake one here). R reads this file when the project opens, so code can use the key without it being written in the code. Committed and pushed, the key would be in the history for anyone who can see the repository, even after you deleted the file in a later commit. The fix would be a new key.

title: Ex-6-2: Version Control, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 2: Start the repository
text:
Task 2: Start the repository






What you should find





With that .gitignore, git status lists 7 files to be committed:
?? .gitignore
?? README.md
?? analysis/01-clean.qmd
?? analysis/02-summary.qmd
?? analysis/ex-6-2.qmd
?? ch6-git.Rproj
?? data/raw/corn_yields.csv
?? means untracked: git has not stored the file yet. .Renviron, .Rhistory, the rendered HTML and data/processed/ are not listed, so they will not be committed.
If analysis/01-clean.html or a file under .Rproj.user/ is listed, a line of the .gitignore is missing or misspelled. If data/processed/corn_clean.rds is listed and you did not mean it to be, add data/processed/. Fix the .gitignore before the first commit: once a file is committed, adding it to .gitignore does not take it out of the history.

title: Ex-6-2: Version Control, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 3: Two changes, two commits
text:
Task 3: Two changes, two commits






What you should find





Two commits, because the two changes are unrelated: one changes the analysis, one documents the data. The worksheet is in neither. For example:
Drop yields of 100 bu/ac or less

In this data, a yield of 100 or less would be a data entry error, not a harvest.
The second commit, for the README:
Say where the data comes from
The second needs no reason: what it does is the reason.
Before the first commit, git diff --staged shows only the cutoff line:
diff --git a/analysis/01-clean.qmd b/analysis/01-clean.qmd
index f43e415..9caffee 100644
--- a/analysis/01-clean.qmd
+++ b/analysis/01-clean.qmd
@@ -14,7 +14,7 @@ corn <- readr::read_csv(
 Drop fields with a yield at or below the cutoff.
 
 ```{r}
-corn <- dplyr::filter(corn, Yield > 0)
+corn <- dplyr::filter(corn, Yield > 100)
 ```
 
 Save the cleaned table for the next step.
git log --oneline then shows 3 commits (your identifiers will differ, because they depend on your name and the time):
29e9698 Say where the data comes from
d2cdb26 Drop yields of 100 bu/ac or less
b068512 Start the project

title: Ex-6-2: Version Control, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 4: Read the history
text:
Task 4: Read the history






What you should find





A. The AI can only report the “why” that you wrote. For “Start the project” and the README commit it can say what changed and little else. For the cutoff commit it should repeat your reason, because the message holds it. A commit whose message was “update” would leave it guessing, and it may guess without saying so.
B. One line, the cutoff:
diff --git a/analysis/01-clean.qmd b/analysis/01-clean.qmd
index f43e415..9caffee 100644
--- a/analysis/01-clean.qmd
+++ b/analysis/01-clean.qmd
@@ -14,7 +14,7 @@ corn <- readr::read_csv(
 Drop fields with a yield at or below the cutoff.
 
 ```{r}
-corn <- dplyr::filter(corn, Yield > 0)
+corn <- dplyr::filter(corn, Yield > 100)
 ```
 
 Save the cleaned table for the next step.

title: Ex-6-2: Version Control, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 5: A branch and a merge conflict
text:
Task 5: A branch and a merge conflict






What you should find





The merge stops, because both branches changed the same line in different ways:
Auto-merging analysis/01-clean.qmd
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in analysis/01-clean.qmd
Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result.
The conflicting lines in the file look like this:
```{r}
<<<<<<< HEAD
corn <- dplyr::filter(corn, Yield > 120)
=======
corn <- dplyr::filter(corn, Yield > 150)
>>>>>>> try-cutoff-150
The line between <<<<<<< HEAD and ======= is on main, the branch you are on (120). The line between ======= and >>>>>>> try-cutoff-150 is on the branch you are merging in (150).
Which to keep is a research decision. In this data, a cutoff of 100 keeps 161 of 161 rows, 120 keeps 158, and 150 keeps 134. The two sides of the conflict are 120 and 150, but you may also write a third version, such as going back to 100. Nothing in the data says any of these yields is an error, and the lowest non-irrigated yield is 103. So the cutoff that drops nothing, 100, is the easiest to defend; any higher cutoff needs a documented reason. Either way, the commit message records the reason.
After you keep one and commit, git log --oneline --graph shows the two lines of work joining. The answers here kept 120, to show the merge; your identifiers, messages and choice may differ:
*   9a9dd0f Keep the 120 bu/ac cutoff
|\  
| * f77fd3e Try a cutoff of 150 bu/ac
* | a9713bb Use a cutoff of 120 bu/ac
|/  
* ebd66e8 Answer Tasks 1 to 4
* 29e9698 Say where the data comes from
* d2cdb26 Drop yields of 100 bu/ac or less
* b068512 Start the project

title: Ex-6-2: Version Control, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 6: Put it on GitHub
text:
Task 6: Put it on GitHub






What you should find





The checks: branch main; no uncommitted changes to tracked files, except this worksheet if you kept typing; git ls-files .Renviron prints nothing; the GitHub page says Private next to the name.
GitHub then holds exactly the files git ls-files listed, 7 of them:
.gitignore
README.md
analysis/01-clean.qmd
analysis/02-summary.qmd
analysis/ex-6-2.qmd
ch6-git.Rproj
data/raw/corn_yields.csv
.Renviron, .Rhistory, the rendered HTML and data/processed/ are not there. If one of them is, it was committed: do not push again until you have asked why. If it is .Renviron, treat the key as public, and replace it.
If you made the repository by hand on github.com, the result is the same once the push succeeds. If the push asks for a password, signing in (Before class, step 6) is not finished.
If the push is refused with a message about “rejected” or “fetch first”, someone (or you, on GitHub’s website) changed the repository on GitHub. Pull, read what came in, then push. Never force it.

title: Ex-6-2: Version Control, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 7: A pull request (if time allows)
text:
Task 7: A pull request (if time allows)






What you should find





A. Files changed shows README.md only, with the new section as green lines starting with +. If any other file is listed, the branch carries a change you did not ask for: ask about it before merging.
B. The pull brings in two commits: the one that added “How to run” (made on your computer, on the branch), and a merge commit whose message starts Merge pull request #1. GitHub made the merge commit when you clicked Merge pull request, which is why it existed on GitHub and not on your computer until you pulled.

title: Ex-6-2: Version Control, with an AI Assistant
section: Wrap-up
text:
Wrap-up






What you should find





B. With no .gitignore, git add . would have taken every file in the folder:
.Renviron
.Rhistory
.Rproj.user/ (RStudio's own files)
analysis/01-clean_files/ (12 files)
analysis/01-clean.html
analysis/01-clean.qmd
analysis/02-summary.qmd
analysis/ex-6-2.qmd
ch6-git.Rproj
data/processed/corn_clean.rds
data/raw/corn_yields.csv
README.md
.Renviron (the key), .Rhistory, the rendered HTML and its _files folder, data/processed/corn_clean.rds, and RStudio’s own .Rproj.user/ files would all be in the first commit, and so in the history for good.

title: Ex-5-1: Functions, Loops and Parallel Processing, with an AI Assistant
text: This is an in-class exercise. Before class, work through the lecture 05-1: Functions, Loops and Parallel Processing. In class, you work through the worksheet with an AI assistant writing the code. Your job is everything the AI cannot do: knowing what the inputs contain, working out a known answer to test against, asking for the right checks, and judging whether the result is right.

title: Ex-5-1: Functions, Loops and Parallel Processing, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 1: Look and predict
text:
Task 1: Look and predict






What you should find





A. 12 files, field_01.csv to field_12.csv.
B. Three columns: plot, n_rate and yield. One row is one plot of the field: the nitrogen rate it received (lb/acre) and the yield it gave (bu/acre).
C. No. Nothing inside a file says which field it is; only the file name does. So the request in Task 3 must ask for a column taken from the file name, or the combined table cannot tell the fields apart.
D. The files differ in length: 24, 30, 36 plots. 360 plots in all, so a correct combined table has 360 rows.

title: Ex-5-1: Functions, Loops and Parallel Processing, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 2: Write and test the function
text:
Task 2: Write and test the function






What you should find





The prediction. The test table follows yield = 120 + 1.2 n - 0.003 n² exactly, so b = 1.2 and c = -0.003. With a corn price of 4 and a nitrogen price of 0.6, the price ratio is 0.15, and the rate is (0.15 - 1.2) / (2 × -0.003) = 175 lb/acre.
In the HTML: “test: expected 175, got 175” (perhaps with a tiny difference in the last decimal places, from rounding inside the regression).
Why this test. The fitted curve passes exactly through a table built from a known curve, so the function’s only job is the formula. If it gives anything else, the formula or the order of the inputs is wrong. A common slip is the order of the prices: the function called with the two prices swapped still runs, and returns a different number.
On field_01 the function gives about 194 lb/acre: inside the tested range of 0 to 250, so believable. There is no known answer for a real field; that is why the test on the made-up table comes first.

title: Ex-5-1: Functions, Loops and Parallel Processing, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 3: Loop over every field
text:
Task 3: Loop over every field






What you should find





The combined table. 360 rows and 4 columns (plot, n_rate, yield, and the field column you asked for), with 12 distinct fields.
The result per field. 12 rows, one per field. For 11 fields, yields run between about 111 and 297 bu/acre and the optimal rate between 158 and 210 lb/acre.
The check that fails. In field_07, yields run from 8,556 to 17,759. No corn field yields that many bushels per acre. These numbers are about 62.77 times a normal corn yield, which is the conversion from bushels per acre to kilograms per hectare: this file was almost certainly recorded in kg/ha.
Notice what did not catch it. The loop ran, the row count and column count passed, and the optimal rate for field_07, 202 lb/acre, looks perfectly believable. Only the per-field yield range showed the problem. If the yields are converted to bu/acre, the optimal rate becomes 179 lb/acre, so the unconverted answer was off by 23 lb/acre with no warning.
What to do. Do not convert it on a guess. Ask whoever produced the file which unit it is in, and leave the field out of any result until you know. A loop assumes every input is the same kind of thing as the one you tested; this check is how you find out whether that is true.

title: Ex-5-1: Functions, Loops and Parallel Processing, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 4: Parallel processing
text:
Task 4: Parallel processing






What you should find





4a. Each repetition (one regression on a few dozen rows) takes a fraction of a millisecond, so the whole loop takes far less than a second. In parallel it is slower, because starting the workers and sending them the data costs more than the work itself. The results are identical either way. The right answer to “should this loop be run in parallel?” is no.
4b. The loop covers the 11 fields that passed Task 3; field_07 stays out until its unit is confirmed. Each repetition now refits the curve 1,000 times, so the sequential loop takes several seconds and the parallel one noticeably less: on a laptop with 4 workers, roughly half to a third of the time. Your numbers depend on your computer.
The comparison. The small case run under plan(sequential) and in parallel must give identical results (“expected TRUE, got TRUE”). That needs future.seed = TRUE, because resampling uses random numbers, and the same set.seed() before each of the two runs: with a different seed, or none, the two runs draw different numbers and the check fails although both are correct. Without future.seed = TRUE, the parallel run warns UNRELIABLE VALUE, and the two runs do not match.
If the AI compared future_lapply() with plain lapply(), the check fails even when both are correct: the two draw their random numbers differently. Compare future_lapply() under plan(sequential) with future_lapply() under plan(multisession).
Why the repetitions are independent. Each field’s resampling uses only that field’s plots, and no field’s result is used by another.

title: Ex-5-1: Functions, Loops and Parallel Processing, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 5: Read someone else’s AI code
text:
Task 5: Read someone else’s AI code






Answers





A. Line 1 lists the files in a folder on Maria’s computer. Line 2 makes an empty result. The loop reads each file in turn, computes its optimal rate and stores it in results. The last line shows results.
B. Line 1, the absolute path: the folder exists only on Maria’s computer. And even on Maria’s computer, list.files() without full.names = TRUE returns bare file names, so read.csv() cannot find them unless R happens to be in that folder.
C. Three silent problems:

results <- optimal_n(...) replaces the result every time round, so only the last field’s rate is left: about 166 lb/acre for field_12, a single number that looks fine.
Even with results[i] <-, nothing records which field each number belongs to.
field_07 is in kg/ha, and nothing in the loop would notice.

D. “Number of results: expected 12” catches 1. “Values of the field column” catches 2. “Smallest and largest yield per field” catches 3.
E. Most AI assistants spot the path and the overwriting. Whether they mention the missing labels varies. A chat assistant cannot spot the kg/ha file, because it sees the code and not the data. An agent that can open the files might, but only if asked to look at the yields. That one is yours to catch.

title: Ex-5-1: Functions, Loops and Parallel Processing, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 6: Does it run anywhere? (if time allows)
text:
Task 6: Does it run anywhere? (if time allows)






What you should find





If it fails after a restart, some chunk depended on something you ran by hand in the Console and the AI never wrote down: a loaded package, an object, or a plan(). The error names the missing thing; ask the AI to add it to the worksheet. If it fails on your neighbour’s computer, look first at paths, and then at the number of workers: a fixed workers = 8 on a laptop with fewer cores than that makes R warn that the computer is overloaded. workers = parallel::detectCores() - 1 adapts to whichever computer runs it.

title: Ex-4-1: Communicating with Figures, with an AI Assistant
text: This is an in-class exercise. Before class, work through the lecture 04-1: Communicating with Figures. In class, you work through the worksheet with an AI assistant writing the code. Your job is everything the AI cannot do: deciding what each figure must say and to whom, choosing among the designs the AI offers, and judging the result in the rendered HTML.

title: Ex-4-1: Communicating with Figures, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 1: Look and predict
text:
Task 1: Look and predict






What you should find





A. 1,957 lines: one line of column names and 1,956 data rows, 6 columns. One row is one county in one year.
B. 3 states (Colorado, Kansas, Nebraska), 154 counties (some county names, such as Lincoln, occur in more than one state, so a county is identified by its state and its name), years 2000 to 2018.
C. corn_yield runs from 0 to 234.3 bushels per acre. The 2 zeros are odd: both are in Colorado (Bent 2003 and Elbert 2002), and the next lowest yield anywhere is 80. A zero could be a crop that failed completely, or a missing value written as 0. The file cannot tell you which. Note it, and keep it in mind for any figure of yields. drought_weeks runs from 0 to 22.
D. The table of counties per state and year shows two things:

Colorado has no rows at all for 2009.
The number of counties falls over time. Kansas has 56 counties in 2000 and 2 in 2008. Colorado has 5 or fewer counties in 7 of its years.

Any average per state and year is therefore an average over a different, sometimes very small, set of counties. Task 7 comes back to this.

title: Ex-4-1: Communicating with Figures, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 2: Write the message
text:
Task 2: Write the message






What a good answer looks like





Average yields in 2000 to 2002 and in 2016 to 2018:



State
2000 to 2002
2016 to 2018




Colorado
152
178


Kansas
159
191


Nebraska
158
205



So yields rose in all three states, most in Nebraska. A good sentence states the direction, the scope and if possible a size: “Corn yields rose in all three states between 2000 and 2018, by about 26 to 47 bushels per acre.” A sentence such as “Yields changed over time” is not a message; nothing in a figure could show it to be wrong.
The reader matters for the wording and the labels: an extension audience knows bushels per acre; a general audience needs it spelled out once.

title: Ex-4-1: Communicating with Figures, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 3: Ask for designs and choose
text:
Task 3: Ask for designs and choose






What a good answer looks like





Designs you may get back include:

One line per state, yearly average. Makes the rise and the comparison between states easy to see. Hides how much counties vary within a year, and each point is an average over a changing set of counties (Task 7).
Small panels per state, every county-year as a point, with a trend line. Shows the rise and the spread, and how few Colorado points there are. Harder to compare the states’ levels at a glance.
Box plots per year. Shows the spread each year, but mixes the states, so it cannot show “in all three states”.

For the sentence in Task 2, one line per state, or panels per state with a trend line, serve the message; box plots per year do not, because the message is about each state. A good written reason names what the message needs (“each state separately, over time”) and what the chosen design makes easy to see.

title: Ex-4-1: Communicating with Figures, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 4: Meet the figure standard
text:
Task 4: Meet the figure standard






What to check in the HTML





Go through the eight items one at a time, in the HTML, not in the code:

Axis titles in words with units: “Corn yield (bushels per acre)”. The years need no axis title. Nothing like corn_yield or state_name anywhere.
Tick labels and axis titles at least as large as the worksheet’s text.
Lines labelled at their ends, or a legend in an empty corner in the order of the lines at the right edge.
Numbers: years printed as 2000, not 2,000 or 2000.0.
No overlapping years along the bottom; every second or fifth year is fine.
Light or no gridlines.
Wider than tall, since this is a change over time.
Colourblind-safe colours, one per state. If you kept colours from earlier figures, the same state has the same colour.

Check every item even though your request listed them all. A request says what you asked for, not what you got.

title: Ex-4-1: Communicating with Figures, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 5: Critique and improve a weak figure
text:
Task 5: Critique and improve a weak figure






What a good answer looks like





The numbers behind the message. County-years with more than 10 weeks of extreme drought, compared with county-years with none:








State
Yield lower by (bushels per acre)
County-years with over 10 weeks




Colorado
22
22


Kansas
17
60


Nebraska
23
69



The message is true for all three states.
The checklist, applied to the weak figure:

Message in a few seconds: no. 1,956 points pile up, and most of them sit in one column at zero weeks.
Colour carries information (the state), but the three states’ points are mixed together in one cloud, and where they overlap, Nebraska’s, drawn last, hide the others. The reader cannot compare the states.
In black and white: no, the states become indistinguishable.
Everything shown is needed, but the comparison the message needs, yields with and without long drought in each state, is not shown.
Figure standard: raw column names, small text, ggplot’s default red and green, a legend to the right.

A good improvement puts the comparison the message needs in front of the reader. Two that work: one small panel per state showing yields per drought range (box plots or averages); or one point per state for “no drought” and one for “over 10 weeks”, joined by a line, so the drop is the length of the line. The first shows the spread too; the second makes the size of the drop easiest to read. Either, with a reason, is a good answer.

title: Ex-4-1: Communicating with Figures, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 6: Is the message true?
text:
Task 6: Is the message true?






What you should find





2012 was a drought year everywhere: on average 12.4 weeks of extreme drought per county in Colorado, 11.5 in Kansas and 9.1 in Nebraska. But the yields did not all fall:



State
2011
2012
2013
Counties in 2012




Colorado
186
160
184
4


Kansas
161
161
175
27


Nebraska
178
186
192
64



Nebraska’s average yield was higher in 2012 than in 2011, and Kansas’s did not change, because 2011 was already a poor year in Kansas (8.4 bushels per acre below its counties’ own averages). The draft message is false for Nebraska, and no design can fix a false message. The data does not say why; it has no information on irrigation, for example.
Because the set of counties changes from year to year, a careful check compares each county with its own average over all years. That gives the same picture: in 2012, Colorado counties were 15.6 bushels per acre below their own average, Kansas counties 12.6 below, and Nebraska counties 2.6 above.
A true message, for example: “In the 2012 drought, yields were below normal in Colorado and Kansas but not in Nebraska.” It is about one year and a difference from normal, so a good design is different from Task 3’s: for example, a bar per state showing 2012’s yield minus normal, coloured on two hues either side of zero, or the Task 3 lines with 2012 marked. Colorado’s 2012 value rests on only 4 counties, which belongs in a note under the figure.

title: Ex-4-1: Communicating with Figures, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 7: Check the figure against its data
text:
Task 7: Check the figure against its data






What you should find





For one line per state, the expected table has 3 states × 19 years = 57 rows. It has 56: Colorado 2009 is missing, and a line drawn from this table joins 2008 straight to 2010 without showing it.
The counties behind each point range from 2 to 82. Colorado’s points rest on 5 or fewer counties in 7 of its years.
What to do about it is your decision, and several answers are good, as long as the figure or its note tells the reader:

break the line at the missing year, so the gap is visible;
show the number of counties, for example as the size of each point, or in a note under the figure;
compare each county with its own average, so a point does not depend on which counties report that year.

Doing nothing and saying nothing is the one answer that is not good.

title: Ex-3-2: The Core Operations of Data Wrangling, with an AI Assistant
text: This is an in-class exercise. Before class, work through the lecture 03-2: The Core Operations of Data Wrangling. In class, you work through the worksheet with an AI assistant writing the code. Your job is everything the AI cannot do: knowing what the data contains, asking for the right thing and the right checks, and judging whether the result is right.

title: Ex-3-2: The Core Operations of Data Wrangling, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 1: Read and look
text:
Task 1: Read and look






What you should find





A. 1956 rows. One row is one county in one year.
B. Colorado (154 rows, 16 counties), Kansas (534 rows, 56 counties), Nebraska (1268 rows, 82 counties). The names are written with a capital first letter and the rest in lower case. Counties do not all have every year: Nebraska’s 82 counties over 19 years would be 1558 rows, not 1268.
C. Only soy_yield: 856 missing values, 44% of the rows. Every other column is complete.

title: Ex-3-2: The Core Operations of Data Wrangling, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 2: Keep rows
text:
Task 2: Keep rows






What you should find





Prediction. At most 82 rows, one per Nebraska county, since one row is one county in one year. Only Nebraska and 2012 in the result.
Result. 64 rows: not every Nebraska county has a 2012 row. Kept plus dropped is 64 + 1892 = 1956, so no row was lost on the way, which is what you expect when the condition’s columns have no missing values.
The blanks, filled in: one row is “one county in one year”, the state is Nebraska (not NEBRASKA or nebraska), and you expect at most 82 rows.

title: Ex-3-2: The Core Operations of Data Wrangling, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 3: Split the rows in two
text:
Task 3: Split the rows in two






What you should find





Prediction. Every row has a soybean yield that is either below 40 or not, so the two tables together should have all 1956 rows.
Result. 26 + 1074 = 1100. The check fails by 856 rows, exactly the number of missing soybean yields from Task 1. A missing value is neither below 40 nor at least 40, so filter() drops those rows from both tables, without a message.
Nothing is wrong with the code. If your prediction was all 1956 rows, the check is what showed it was wrong. In a request that uses soy_yield, say what should happen to the rows where it is missing.

title: Ex-3-2: The Core Operations of Data Wrangling, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 4: Create a column
text:
Task 4: Create a column






What you should find





Prediction. Between 0 (no week in severe drought) and 100 (all 23 weeks). For a row with weeks_severe_drought of 14, the value is 14 / 23 × 100 = 60.9.
Result. From 0 to 100, no missing values. 16 county-years spent the whole season in severe drought or worse.
The blanks, filled in: a column name of your choice, such as pct_severe_drought, equal to “weeks_severe_drought divided by 23, times 100”; range 0 to 100; 0 missing values.
If your hand calculation does not match, check whether the AI divided by 23 or by something else, such as 52 weeks in a year. The range check alone would not catch that: dividing by 52 also gives values between 0 and 100.

title: Ex-3-2: The Core Operations of Data Wrangling, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 5: Summarise by group
text:
Task 5: Summarise by group






What you should find





Prediction. 3 rows, one per state; the numbers of rows add up to 1956. From Task 1, the soybean averages may be a problem, since soy_yield is often missing.
Result.





state_name

The corn averages rest on every row and can be reported as they are.
Colorado has no soybean yields at all: soy_non_missing is 0, and the average shows as NaN (“not a number”, the average of nothing). Without na.rm = TRUE it would show NA. Report no soybean average for Colorado.
Kansas’s soybean average rests on 185 of its 534 rows (35%). The number is a real average, but of a minority of Kansas county-years, likely the counties where soybeans are grown. Report it with that note, or not at all. Nebraska’s rests on 915 of 1268 rows.

This is why the request asked for the number of non-missing values behind each average. Without it, the three soybean averages would look equally trustworthy.
