2002
90
22.0





2 county-years have a corn yield of exactly 0: Bent 2003 and Elbert 2002, both in Colorado. The next lowest is 80. A yield is harvest divided by harvested area, so a county with a harvested area should not have a yield of 0, even in the 2002 drought; a total failure usually means the area was not harvested and no yield is reported. These two values are most likely a code for “no harvest” stored as a number, much like -999 in Ex-3-1.
Before averaging corn yields, decide what these rows mean, ideally by asking whoever produced the data, and say in the .qmd what you did (for example, treat them as missing). Treated as missing, they would move the Colorado corn average in Task 5 from 168.3 to 170.5; in an analysis of how drought affects yield, two values of 0 count for far more than two ordinary rows.
Sorting is the simplest of the five operations, and here it was the one that found a problem: the top of a sorted column is where impossible values show up.

title: Ex-3-2: The Core Operations of Data Wrangling, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 7: Sam’s code
text:
Task 7: Sam’s code






Answers





A. “Take crops, then keep the rows where state_name is nebraska and the year is 2010 or later, then group by county name, then add each county’s average corn yield to each of its rows, then sort from the lowest average up.”
B. A table with no rows. The state is written Nebraska, with a capital letter, so nothing equals "nebraska". Every later step works on an empty table without complaint. A check of the rows after the filter (expected about 82 counties times 9 years) would catch it.
C. mutate(). It keeps every county-year row and writes the county’s average on each. For one row per county, it should be summarise().
D. County names are not unique across states: 15 names appear in more than one state, for example Cheyenne, Greeley, Hamilton. Grouping by county_name alone puts, say, Lincoln County in Colorado and Lincoln County in Nebraska into one group and averages them together. Group by state_name and county_code (and keep county_name for reading). A check of the number of groups against the number of counties from Task 1 (154) would catch it: grouping by name alone gives 137.
E. The AI usually spots the lower-case nebraska if you mention how the state is written; without that, it can only guess, since it has not seen the data. Whether it raises mutate() against summarise() depends on whether it reads “average of each county” as one row per county. Treat its answer as something to check.

title: Ex-2-4: Articles with Quarto, with an AI Assistant
text: This is an in-class exercise. Before class, work through the lecture 02-4: Articles with Quarto. In class, you work through the worksheet with an AI assistant writing the note. Your job is everything the AI cannot do: deciding the claims and what supports each, making sure every reference exists and says what you cite it for, and reading the output for the mistakes that render without an error.

title: Ex-2-4: Articles with Quarto, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 1: Claims and evidence
text:
Task 1: Claims and evidence






What a good answer looks like





A and B. For example:

“Average county yields stayed close to 200 bushels per acre from 2014 to 2017”: a figure of the average yield per year, fig-yield-by-year, caption “Average corn yield of Nebraska counties per year, 2014 to 2018.”
“Fewer counties reported in 2018 than in other years”: a table of the number of counties and the average yield per year, tbl-counties, caption “Counties reporting, and their average yield, per year.”

Any claim the data supports is fine, as long as the figure or table shows exactly that claim and has a label with the right prefix.
C. schlenker2009 (Schlenker and Roberts, 2009), lobell2014 (Lobell and six others, 2014), hansen2017 (Hansen and Ortiz, 2017). From their titles: heat and yields, drought sensitivity in the Midwest, and irrigation and the yield gap in Nebraska. At this point nothing about the file looks wrong.

title: Ex-2-4: Articles with Quarto, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 2: Set up the note
text:
Task 2: Set up the note






What to look for





The header should have bibliography: 2-4-references.bib (the path is from the folder note.qmd is in, so the file name alone), both outputs under format:, and echo: false for the Word version. For example:
format:
  docx:
    echo: false
  html:
    echo: true
    embed-resources: true
bibliography: 2-4-references.bib
If the AI put echo: false under execute: instead, it applies to every format and the HTML hides the code too. Ask for it under docx: only, and echo: true under html:, so you can check the code in the HTML version. Each chunk’s sentence, written as a comment on its first line, then shows with the code in the HTML and stays out of the Word file.

title: Ex-2-4: Articles with Quarto, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 3: A numbered figure and table
text:
Task 3: A numbered figure and table






What you should find





The numbers behind the two example claims:



Year
Counties
Average yield (bushels per acre)




2014
51
198


2015
48
204


2016
50
199


2017
47
205


2018
29
213



The check: 225 rows.
Breaking the label. With the chunk labelled plot-... and the sentence still saying @fig-..., the render does not stop. The sentence shows ?@fig-... where “Figure 1” was, and the figure loses its number and its “Figure 1:” in the caption. The render log has a warning, “Unable to resolve crossref”, which is easy to miss among the other lines. Search the output for ?@ every time.

title: Ex-2-4: Articles with Quarto, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 4: Citations
text:
Task 4: Citations






What you should find





Sentence 1 cites schlenker2009, sentence 2 lobell2014, sentence 3 hansen2017. The HTML shows three citations, such as (Schlenker and Roberts 2009), and a reference list with three entries. No ?), because all three keys are in the file.
Everything renders. Nothing so far says anything is wrong.

title: Ex-2-4: Articles with Quarto, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 5: Does every reference exist?
text:
Task 5: Does every reference exist?






What you should find













Key
DOI
What opens




schlenker2009
10.1073/pnas.0906865106
The same article: same title, authors, year


lobell2014
10.1126/science.1251423
The same article


hansen2017
10.1093/ajae/aaw088
A different article: Horan and Shortle (2017), “Endogenous Risk and Point-Nonpoint Uncertainty Trading Ratios”, in the same journal, volume and pages



The DOI works, the journal is real, the volume and pages are those of a real article; only the title and the authors do not match. There is no article by Hansen and Ortiz with that title. This is what an invented reference looks like: every part that is easy to check is plausible, and checking only that “the link works” would have passed it.
What to do:

In the .bib file: remove hansen2017.
In the note: sentence 3 now has no source. Either find a real study that shows it (search for one, read it, and get its entry from the publisher), or remove the sentence. Do not keep a claim because a reference for it once appeared.
With your coauthor: tell them which entry was invented and how you found it, so they check the rest of their file.

If you asked the AI whether the entries are real: the answer varies. An AI that cannot look the DOI up may say all three look correct, because they are formatted correctly. An agent that can open web pages may find the mismatch. Either way, its answer is one more thing to check, not the check itself.

title: Ex-2-4: Articles with Quarto, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 6: The Word version
text:
Task 6: The Word version






What you should find





The .docx has numbered captions (“Figure 1:”, “Table 1:”), the sentences refer to them by number, there is no code, and the reference list is at the end. If you see code, echo: false is missing for the docx output. If you see ?@, a label was not fixed in Task 3. If the check lines appear in the Word file, hide the check chunk with include: false now that you have read them in the HTML (lecture 02-4, the strong request).
A Word file is an output, like the HTML. If your coauthor edits it, copy their edits back into note.qmd; the next render rebuilds the Word file from the .qmd and their edits would be lost.

title: Ex-2-4: Articles with Quarto, with an AI Assistant
section: Wrap-up
text:
Wrap-up






What a good answer looks like





A. None of today’s problems stopped a render. A broken label and an unknown key give warnings in the render log and visible marks (?@, ?)) in the output; an invented reference gives nothing at all. Only reading the output, and opening every DOI, finds them.
B. Get every entry from a record you looked up (the journal’s “Export citation”, the DOI, or Google Scholar’s BibTeX, whose entries usually have no DOI and sometimes have errors, so compare them with the publisher’s page), never from the AI’s memory; and open every DOI before sending the file to anyone.

title: Ex-2-2: Presentations with Quarto, with an AI Assistant
text: This is an in-class exercise. Before class, work through the lecture 02-2: Presentations with Quarto. In class, you work through the worksheet with an AI assistant building the slides. Your job is everything the AI cannot do: deciding who the talk is for, what it says and in what order, and judging the deck as the audience will see it.

title: Ex-2-2: Presentations with Quarto, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 1: Audience, time and message
text:
Task 1: Audience, time and message






What a good answer looks like





A. About 5, at one per minute, plus a title slide and the Checks slide after the end.
B. The table:



Year
Counties
Average yield (bushels per acre)




2014
51
198


2015
48
204


2016
50
199


2017
47
205


2018
29
213



A good message is one sentence a farmer could repeat, with a number they can say aloud, for example: “Average county corn yields in Nebraska stayed close to 200 bushels per acre from 2014 to 2017, and 2018 was higher.” A message such as “Yields varied over time” says nothing that could be wrong, so it says nothing.
C. Yes. 2018 has only 29 counties, against 47 to 51 in the other years. Its average is over a different, smaller set of counties. Of those 29 counties, the 21 that also reported in 2017 averaged 208 that year, against 205 for all counties: they tend to be higher-yielding counties. So part of the rise in 2018 comes from which counties reported, not from the weather or the farmers. A claim such as “a record year” needs that caveat, on the slide or in what you say.

title: Ex-2-2: Presentations with Quarto, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 2: The outline
text:
Task 2: The outline






What a good answer looks like





For example:

“We looked at corn yields in Nebraska counties, 2014 to 2018”: what the data is, in one figure or two bullets
“Yields stayed close to 200 bushels per acre”: a figure of the average yield per year
“2018 was higher, but fewer counties reported”: the same figure with the number of counties marked, or a second figure
“What this means for you”: two or three bullets you write yourself

Each title is a sentence that a reader of the overview alone would understand, and the four together tell the message. “Data”, “Results” and “Conclusion” fail this test.

title: Ex-2-2: Presentations with Quarto, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 3: Ask the AI for the deck
text:
Task 3: Ask the AI for the deck






What to look for





Your filled-in request should name the audience (“farmers at a county extension meeting, who know yields in bushels per acre but no statistics”), the time (5 minutes), your message, and your outline. The checks: 225 rows, years 2014 to 2018.
On the Checks slide, both lines should match: “number of rows: expected 225, got 225”, and the years.

title: Ex-2-2: Presentations with Quarto, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 4: Judge the deck
text:
Task 4: Judge the deck






What is often found





What the AI produces varies, so your list will differ from your neighbour’s. Failures that are common in decks made by AI:

Titles changed. The AI shortened your sentences into topics, or added slides of its own (an “Introduction”, a “Questions?” slide). Check 1.
A claim stronger than the data. “Record yields in 2018” with no word about the 29 counties. Check 3.
Figure text too small, especially when two figures are placed side by side. Check 5.
Too much on one slide, often a table of every year plus bullets plus a figure. Check 4.
Messages from loading packages on the first slide, when the setup chunk was not hidden. Check 6.

A deck that passes all of them on the first try is possible. Check every item anyway: a request says what you asked for, not what you got.

title: Ex-2-2: Presentations with Quarto, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 5: Fix what failed
text:
Task 5: Fix what failed






What to look for





A good fix request names the slide by its title, describes the problem as it looks in the rendered deck (“the axis text cannot be read when the window is half its width”), and says what it should look like instead, not how to code it. For small figure text, the right fix is a smaller canvas (fig-width, fig-height), not a larger out-width.
“Do not change any other slide” matters: step through the whole deck again after the fix, because an AI asked to change one slide sometimes rewrites others.

title: Ex-2-2: Presentations with Quarto, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 6: Present it
text:
Task 6: Present it






What to look for





A 5-slide talk usually takes longer than people expect: most first attempts run over. If your neighbour remembered something other than your message, look at which slide they remembered it from: that slide may say more, or more loudly, than the one that carries the message.

title: Ex-2-2: Presentations with Quarto, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 7: Send it
text:
Task 7: Send it






What you should find





With embed-resources: true in the header, the copy opens as slides, with its figures. Without it, the copy opens as a plain white page with every title and bullet one after another, and no figures: the styling, the slide machinery and the figures are all in the talk_files/ folder that was left behind. Since your request asked for embed-resources: true, the copy fails only if the AI left it out.
The setting goes under revealjs::
format:
  revealjs:
    embed-resources: true

title: Ex-2-2: Presentations with Quarto, with an AI Assistant
section: Wrap-up
text:
Wrap-up






What a good answer looks like





A. The audience and the time (only you know who will be in the room), the message (a choice about what matters, which the data does not make for you), and whether the 2018 caveat belongs on a slide or in what you say.
B. Usually check 5 (figure text) or check 4 (a slide too full): both are about how the slide looks at the size it is shown, which the .qmd does not show.

title: Ex-2-0: Setup Checklist, Clone the Course Datasets
text:
This is a setup checklist, not an exercise: lecture 02-0: Getting a Repository onto Your Computer has only one task, and this page is it. Do it before the class on Chapter 3, which uses these files. It takes about ten minutes.

1. Decide where course material lives
Choose one folder on your computer for everything in this course, for example a folder courses in your Documents folder. Write its full path here, or in a note you keep:

My course folder:



2. Clone the datasets repository
The repository is https://github.com/tmieno2/data-science-course-supplementary-datasets. Clone it into your course folder, in one of three ways:

Sublime Merge: File, Clone Repository; paste the URL into Source URL; set Destination Path to your course folder; Clone.
RStudio, if git is installed: File, New Project, Version Control, Git; paste the URL; choose your course folder as the place for the new project.
An AI agent that can run commands, with this request (fill in the blank):

Clone the repository
https://github.com/tmieno2/data-science-course-supplementary-datasets
into the folder <full path of your course folder>. Do not change any
file in it. When done, tell me the full path of the new folder and list
the files at its top level.


3. Check it






It worked if




Your course folder now contains a folder named data-science-course-supplementary-datasets.
Inside it are the same files as on the GitHub page: corn_yields.csv, corn_yields.dta, corn_yields.rds, corn_yields.xls, two corn_yields_exp files, corn_yields_exp_rownames.csv and readme.md. If you cloned with RStudio, it has also added a .Rproj file of its own, and possibly a .gitignore file.
With hidden files shown (Mac Finder: Cmd + Shift + period; Windows: View, Show, Hidden items), there is also a .git folder inside it. That is what makes it a clone and not a download.









If it did not work






Repository not found: check the URL; copy it from the GitHub page rather than typing it.
destination path ... already exists: you cloned it before. Use that copy.
A message that git is not found or not recognized, or a window offering to install command line tools (Mac): git is not installed. Use Sublime Merge, or ask the AI how to install git on your system.
You cannot find the folder: in Sublime Merge, with the repository open, choose Repository, Open Containing Folder.






4. Leave it alone
Do not move, rename or edit anything inside the cloned folder. Chapter 3 copies files out of it into your own projects. Keeping the clone unchanged means you can bring in updates later (Chapter 6 explains how).

title: Ex-1-1: Reading R Code, with an AI Assistant
text: This is an in-class exercise. Before class, work through the lecture 01-1: Introduction to R. In class, you work through the worksheet, with an AI assistant for some of the tasks. Today’s job is reading code: predicting what a line does, reading help pages and error messages, and taking apart code an AI wrote.

title: Ex-1-1: Reading R Code, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 1: Predict, then run
text:
Task 1: Predict, then run






What R prints





A. 7. The second line stores x + 2, worked out from the old x, back under the same name, replacing it.
B. 20 40 60. Arithmetic on a vector works element by element.
C. "3" "4" "5". One value in quotation marks makes every value text. No error.
D. NA. One value is missing, so the average is unknown.
E. 3, the average of the 2 values that are there.
F. 3.3.
G. 2 6 10. From 2, in steps of 4, not past 10.
H. 20. Positions count from 1.
The ones most people get wrong are C and D. Both are cases where R gives no error and the result is still not what you wanted.

title: Ex-1-1: Reading R Code, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 2: Read a help page
text:
Task 2: Read a help page






What the help pages say





A. One day of air quality readings in New York.
B. 153 rows (“observations”) and 6 columns (“variables”).
C. May to September 1973 (May 1 to September 30).
D. Mean ozone in parts per billion, from 1 pm to 3 pm, at Roosevelt Island.
E. times repeats the whole vector, each repeats each value before moving to the next:

rep(c(1, 2), times = 3) prints 1 2 1 2 1 2
rep(c(1, 2), each = 3) prints 1 1 1 2 2 2

The same six values, in a different order. The help page is how you find out which input does which, without guessing.

title: Ex-1-1: Reading R Code, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 3: Read the errors
text:
Task 3: Read the errors






What each error means





A and B:

object 'Airquality' not found: no object has that name. R treats capital and small letters as different, and the table is airquality. Fix: mean(airquality$Ozone). That line then runs and prints NA, because Ozone has missing values; add na.rm = TRUE if you want the average of the rest.
could not find function "nrows": no such function. It is nrow(). Fix: n_rows <- nrow(airquality), which stores 153.
non-numeric argument to binary operator: "153" is in quotation marks, so it is text, and + cannot add text. Fix: day_count <- 153. (as.numeric(day_count) + 1 also works.)

C. The AI usually explains all three correctly, because the messages are clear and the code is in front of it. What it cannot know, unless you say so, is what you meant: that you wanted the average of the values that are there, or a count of rows. That is why the request asks you to say what you expected.

title: Ex-1-1: Reading R Code, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 4: Installing versus loading
text:
Task 4: Installing versus loading






What you should find





A. could not find function "glimpse". Rendering runs the document in a fresh R session, which knows nothing about what you did in the Console. In the Console you had loaded dplyr; the document had not.
B. library(dplyr), above glimpse(airquality), in the same chunk or an earlier one. In your own documents, the library() lines go in the first chunk, so every later chunk can use the packages.
C. Installing is a one-time step per computer. In the document, it would download and install the package again at every render, which is slow and needs an internet connection.
This is also the check that a document is complete: if it renders, it does not depend on anything typed into the Console and forgotten.

title: Ex-1-1: Reading R Code, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 5: Take apart code an AI wrote
text:
Task 5: Take apart code an AI wrote






Answers





A. hot_days, a table (the rows of airquality with Temp above 90); n_hot, a single number (how many rows hot_days has); avg_ozone, a single number (the average ozone on those days, rounded).
B. library(), nrow(), mean() and round() are built into R. filter() comes from dplyr.
C. Take the Ozone column of hot_days; average it, leaving out missing values; round the average to 1 decimal place; store it as avg_ozone.
D. How many hot days had no ozone reading. You would want the number of hot days, the number with Ozone missing, and the number the average actually uses.
E. The AI usually explains each line correctly and often points at na.rm = TRUE. It cannot say how many values it removes, because it has not seen the data, only the code.

title: Ex-1-1: Reading R Code, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 6: Ask for code, with checks
text:
Task 6: Ask for code, with checks






What you should find





The prediction. June has 30 days, and the table has one row per day, so 30 rows. Whether any Ozone values are missing you cannot know in advance; the help page does not say.
The result. 30 days in June. Ozone is missing on 21 of them, so the average, 29.4 parts per billion, uses only 9 days.
The day count matches and the code is right. The finding is about the data: more than two thirds of June has no ozone reading. For comparison, July is missing 5 of 31. A June average from 9 days may not represent the month, and anyone reading it should be told how many days it rests on.
This is what na.rm = TRUE hides: the code ran, the number looks reasonable, and only the check “days the average uses” showed how little it rests on. Without that check, nothing would have told you.
The blank of the request, filled in: I expect 30 days in June. The missing-value count and the average are printed as “got Y” only, because you could not know them in advance.

title: Ex-2-1: Quarto Documents and Rendering, with an AI Assistant
text: This is an in-class exercise. Before class, work through the lecture 02-1: Quarto Documents and Rendering. In class, you work through the worksheet with an AI assistant writing the code. Your job is everything the AI cannot do: knowing what the data contains, deciding what the reader must see, and judging the result in the rendered HTML.

title: Ex-2-1: Quarto Documents and Rendering, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 1: Look at the data
text:
Task 1: Look at the data






What you should find





A. 226 lines: one line of column names and 225 data rows.
B. 2014 to 2018, 5 years.
C. One county in one year. There are 69 counties, but not every county has a row in every year: 2014: 51, 2015: 48, 2016: 50, 2017: 47, 2018: 29.
D. No. county_code is written with leading zeros (001, 003), so it is a code, not a quantity. read_csv() keeps it as text here, but read.csv(), which AI assistants often write, would turn 001 into 1. Nothing in this exercise uses that column; Lecture 03-1 is about exactly this.

title: Ex-2-1: Quarto Documents and Rendering, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 2: Read the AI’s report before rendering it
text:
Task 2: Read the AI’s report before rendering it






What you should find











Chunk
Runs?
Code shown?
Result shown?




read-yields
yes
yes
nothing to show


drop-year
yes
no
no (include: false)


by-year
yes
yes
yes


overall
yes
yes
yes



B. Only 2014 to 2017. The hidden chunk drop-year removes 2018 before the table is made.
C. No. The sentence’s 198.6 is typed, not computed, so nothing ties it to the number printed above it.

title: Ex-2-1: Quarto Documents and Rendering, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 3: Render and judge the report
text:
Task 3: Render and judge the report






What you should find





Three problems:

A step is hidden. The table shows 4 years, but the file has 5. A reader who looked at the data, as you did in Task 1, can see from the HTML that a year is missing; the HTML does not say why. Only the .qmd shows the drop-year chunk, which has no sentence above it, only an R comment.
The sentence disagrees with the result above it. overall prints 201.5; the sentence says 198.6. A careful reader of the HTML can see this one.
The sentence says “2014 to 2018”, while the average covers 2014 to 2017. A reader can see this only by comparing it with the table.

Whether the sentence was typed or computed cannot be seen in the HTML at all: the two look identical. You need the .qmd.
The decision about the data. Dropping 2018 is a choice, not a mistake: that year has only 29 counties, against about 50 in the others. There can be good reasons to drop it or to keep it. It is your choice, as the person responsible for the analysis, not the AI’s, and whichever you choose, it must be visible in the HTML with a sentence saying why.

title: Ex-2-1: Quarto Documents and Rendering, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 4: Ask the AI to fix the report
text:
Task 4: Ask the AI to fix the report






What you should find





If you kept every year: yields has 225 rows, years 2014 to 2018, and the last sentence reads 203.0 bushels per acre.
If you kept the step that drops 2018: 196 rows, years 2014 to 2017, the step now visible with a sentence, and the last sentence reads 201.5 and says “2014 to 2017”.
Either way, in the .qmd the number in the last sentence should now be written as inline R, for example `r round(mean(yields$corn_yield), 1)`. In the HTML it looks exactly as a typed number would, which is why the check means opening the .qmd.
The blanks of the request, filled in for the first choice:
Remove the chunk that drops 2018.
...
Check the number of rows in yields (I expect 225) and the years it covers
(I expect 2014 to 2018).

title: Ex-2-1: Quarto Documents and Rendering, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 5: Works at the Console, fails on render
text:
Task 5: Works at the Console, fails on render






What you should find





Step 3 printed a number, because the green button runs the chunk at your Console, where yield_goal exists. Step 4 stopped with:
Error:
! object 'yield_goal' not found
Quitting from ex-2-1.qmd:...-... [task-5]
(the line numbers depend on your file). Rendering starts a new R session, which has never seen yield_goal.
The fix is a line yield_goal <- 200 in a chunk inside the document, above task-5 or in it. After rendering, the count is 145 county-years if you kept every year in Task 4, or 120 if you kept the step that drops 2018.
If the AI’s fix was to tell you to type something at the Console again, it did not fix the document. The test is the render: it starts from nothing, so it shows whether the document works without your Console.

title: Ex-2-1: Quarto Documents and Rendering, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 6: Send the HTML
text:
Task 6: Send the HTML






What you should find





The first copy, on its own, is missing the figure, and it also opens without its styling. Rendering wrote the figure into a folder ex-2-1_files/ next to the HTML, and the HTML only points at it. Copied away from that folder, it has nothing to point at.
With embed-resources: true, written under html: like this:
format:
  html:
    embed-resources: true
the figure and the styling are packed into the HTML file itself. The second copy shows everything. This is the version to send to an advisor or a coauthor, or to submit.
Note that format: html on one line has to become the three lines above: html turns from a value into a group with a setting under it.

title: Ex-2-1: Quarto Documents and Rendering, with an AI Assistant
section: Wrap-up
text:
Wrap-up






What a good answer looks like





A. That the number in the last sentence was typed, or what the hidden drop-year chunk did and why. The HTML showed that a year was missing, but not which step removed it or why.
B. The green button runs the chunk at your Console, where anything you typed earlier still exists. The render starts from nothing. Only a render tests the document. To find a missing step before rendering: Session, Restart R, then Run, Run All, which runs every chunk at your Console as a render would.
C. For example: which years the data covers, so a missing year can be noticed; whether dropping a year is acceptable for your question; that the goal is 200 bushels per acre; who will read the HTML and whether it will be sent on its own.

title: Ex-2-3: Websites with Quarto, with an AI Assistant
text: This is an in-class exercise. Before class, work through the lecture 02-3: Websites with Quarto. In class, you work through the worksheet with an AI assistant writing the configuration and the pages. Your job is everything the AI cannot do: deciding who the site is for and what it holds, keeping out what does not belong, and judging the site by using it.

title: Ex-2-3: Websites with Quarto, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 1: The site map
text:
Task 1: The site map






What a good answer looks like





A. For example:

Home, index.qmd (at the top of the project folder): two sentences on what the project is, and links to the other pages
Data, data.qmd: reads the data and prints its checks
Yields by year, yields.qmd: the average yield per year, as a table and a figure, each with its sentence

index.qmd is required: it becomes the home page.
B. Everything that was there before: the worksheets (analysis/ex-2-1.qmd, analysis/ex-2-2.qmd, analysis/ex-2-3.qmd) and the deck from Ex-2-2 (analysis/talk.qmd). They are class work, not results for your advisor; the worksheets contain the planted mistakes of Ex-2-1, which could be read as your results.

title: Ex-2-3: Websites with Quarto, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 2: Predict
text:
Task 2: Predict






What you should find





Every .qmd in the project becomes a page: the three new ones and the four that were already there, seven in all. Only the three new ones are in the menu. The other four are built into the output folder, where anyone with the folder can open them, but no visitor finds them by clicking.
There is a second effect: once the folder is a website, clicking Render on a worksheet that is part of the site writes its HTML into the output folder, not next to the worksheet.

title: Ex-2-3: Websites with Quarto, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 3: Ask the AI for the site
text:
Task 3: Ask the AI for the site






What to look for





The blanks, filled in:
1. Home (index.qmd): two sentences on what the project is, and links
   to the other pages
2. Data (data.qmd): reads the data and prints its checks
3. Yields by year (yields.qmd): the average yield per year, as a table
   and a figure
Leave out every file in analysis/.
...
check the number of rows (I expect 225) and the years covered (I expect
2014 to 2018).
The usual way the AI leaves files out is a render: list in _quarto.yml, naming only the pages to build:
project:
  type: website
  render:
    - index.qmd
    - data.qmd
    - yields.qmd
Files not on the list are not built into the site. Each can still be rendered on its own with its Render button, and its HTML then appears next to it, as before.

title: Ex-2-3: Websites with Quarto, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 4: Judge the site
text:
Task 4: Judge the site






What you should find





A. If the render stopped, the error names the file. A common cause: a worksheet that is still part of the site and does not render, for example ex-2-1.qmd with the task-5 chunk still broken. One failing page stops the whole website.
B. Three menu entries, in your order, each reachable by clicking.
C. With the worksheets left out: index.html, data.html, yields.html, plus support files (site_libs/, search.json). If you did not ask for them to be left out, you will also find analysis/ex-2-1.html, analysis/ex-2-2.html, analysis/ex-2-3.html and analysis/talk.html. Ask the AI to leave them out, render again, and look again: a full render removes pages that are no longer built.
D. “number of rows: expected 225, got 225”, and the years 2014 to 2018.

title: Ex-2-3: Websites with Quarto, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 5: Add a page
text:
Task 5: Add a page






What you should find





Counties reporting per year: 2014: 51, 2015: 48, 2016: 50, 2017: 47, 2018: 29.
Check three things in the rendered site, not the chat: the new page is in the menu where you asked; its numbers match the list above; and the other pages are unchanged (an AI asked to add one page sometimes also “tidies” the others). If you used a render: list, the new page must be added to it too, or it is not built: a common reason a new menu entry leads nowhere.

title: Ex-2-3: Websites with Quarto, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 6: Share it
text:
Task 6: Share it






What you should find





Step 2 works: the menu, the links and the styling, because the pages link to each other and to site_libs/ inside the same folder, and the whole folder came along.
Step 3 does not: the page opens without its styling, and its menu links point at pages that are not next to it. A website is the folder, not any one file in it. To share it before it is published, send the whole folder, zipped; to put it online, publish the folder (for example with GitHub Pages), after checking, as in Task 4C, that everything in it may be public.

title: Ex-2-3: Websites with Quarto, with an AI Assistant
section: Wrap-up
text:
Wrap-up






What a good answer looks like





A. The three worksheets and the deck. Your advisor would not find them through the menu, but anyone with the folder, or with the site once published, could open them by name.
B. A report is one HTML file, made self-contained with embed-resources: true, and can be sent on its own. A site is a folder of pages that link to each other, and is shared as the whole folder or published.

title: Ex-3-1: Getting Data In and Out, with an AI Assistant
text: This is an in-class exercise. Before class, work through the lecture 03-1: Getting Data In and Out of R. In class, you work through the worksheet with an AI assistant writing the code. Your job is everything the AI cannot do: knowing what the files contain, asking for the right thing and the right checks, and judging whether the result is right.

title: Ex-3-1: Getting Data In and Out, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 1: Look and predict
text:
Task 1: Look and predict






What you should find





A. 162 lines: one line of column names and 161 data rows.
B. 9 columns: Year, State, FIPS, County_name, State_name, Commodity, Data item, Irrigated, Yield. County_name, State_name, Commodity and Data item are text; the rest are numbers. Data item has a space in its name.
C. One county, one year, and one irrigation status (Irrigated is 0 or 1), so most counties appear twice.
D. Two sheets, corn_yields_08 and corn_yields_09.

title: Ex-3-1: Getting Data In and Out, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 2: Read the csv
text:
Task 2: Read the csv






What you should find





161 rows and 9 columns, no missing values, and yields from 103 to 204 bushels per acre.
The checks, and why. The five from the lecture, each tied to a way this import could go wrong:

Rows and columns: a title line read as data, or the reader stopping early, changes the count from the 161 you counted.
Type of every column: Yield read as text would make every later calculation fail or mislead.
Missing values per column: a column that failed to read shows up as all missing.
Range of Yield: a code such as -999, or a number in the wrong units, shows up as an impossible value.
The first row: shifted columns show up when compared with the first data line of the file.

The blanks of the recommended request, filled in:
- above the column names there is nothing
- there are 161 data rows and 9 columns
- one row is one county, one year, and one irrigation status
- missing values are written as: none expected
- ID columns that must stay text: FIPS
- a believable range for Yield is 100 to 250
In the HTML, every “expected, got” line should match.

title: Ex-3-1: Getting Data In and Out, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 3: Both sheets of the Excel file
text:
Task 3: Both sheets of the Excel file






What you should find





161 + 161 = 322 rows. Year is 2008 in one sheet and 2009 in the other.
The check from knowing the data. Yields change from year to year, because the weather does, so each county’s yield should differ between the two years. Asking “is each county’s yield the same in both years?” gives TRUE: every county has exactly the same yield.
That cannot be real data. The code is fine; the file is wrong, and no change to the code fixes it. The right move is to stop and ask whoever produced the file, and not to analyse year-to-year changes until you have an answer.
This is the point of the task: the row count and the types all passed. Only a check you thought of, because you know something about corn, caught the problem.

title: Ex-3-1: Getting Data In and Out, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 4: A messy file
text:
Task 4: A messy file






What you should find





4a, the short request. Plain read_csv() treats the first description line as the column names, so you get 94 rows and only 3 columns with sentence fragments for names, plus a warning about parsing problems. Base R’s read.csv() stops with an error instead. Either way the problem is visible, which is the good case.
4b, the file. Two lines of description sit above the column names. Missing yields are written two ways, -999 and ., and the second description line says so. county_fips holds 5-digit county codes, and the 5 Colorado codes start with 08. There are 95 lines, so 92 data rows.
4c, a correct result. 92 rows, 5 columns, county_fips is text with the leading zeros kept, yield is a number, 5 yields are missing, and the rest run from 102 to 199. Average yield: 157.7.
The checks, and the problem each one catches in this file:

Rows: the description lines read as data.
Type of county_fips: the leading 0 of the Colorado codes lost.
Type of the yield column: text instead of a number, because of the . entries.
Number of missing yields: should be 5. Fewer means a missing-value code was kept as a value.
Range of yields: a minimum of -999 means the -999 code was not recognised.

The silent trap. If your request mentioned . but not -999, the yield column is a number, nothing errors, and the average comes out at 119.2. Checks 4 and 5 both catch it.

title: Ex-3-1: Getting Data In and Out, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 5: Maria’s code
text:
Task 5: Maria’s code






Answers





A. Read the file, skipping the two description lines and treating . as missing; rename the fifth column to yield; average the yields, ignoring missing ones.
B. The path. C:/Users/maria/Downloads exists only on Maria’s computer.
C. First, -999 is not treated as missing, so the average is 119.2 instead of 157.7. Second, read.csv() reads county_fips as a number, so 08125 becomes 8125. Nothing uses that column here, but the first time Maria joins this table to another one by county code, the Colorado counties will quietly fail to match.
D. “Print the smallest and largest yield”: a minimum of -999 is impossible. “Print the type of every column”: county_fips should be text, because it is an ID, not a quantity.
E. The AI usually spots the path and often the -999. It can only spot the -999 because the code itself is visible to it; it has not seen the file. Whether it notices the lost leading zero varies. Either way, compare its list with yours, and treat its answer like any other: something to check, not something to accept.

title: Ex-3-1: Getting Data In and Out, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 6: Save and read back
text:
Task 6: Save and read back






What you should find





The rds file comes back identical. The csv file comes back with state_name as plain text rather than a factor, because a csv stores only text and the reader has to guess types again. This is why the lecture recommends rds for results you will read back into R.
If the AI compares with all.equal(), the csv comparison prints several lines starting with Attributes: before the one that matters, Component "state_name": 'current' is not a factor. The Attributes lines are about hidden bookkeeping that read_csv() attaches to every table it reads, not about your data. Ask the AI which lines are about the data itself if this is unclear.

title: Ex-3-1: Getting Data In and Out, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 7: Does it run anywhere?
text:
Task 7: Does it run anywhere?






What you should find





If it fails on your neighbour’s computer, the error names the line that depended on your machine, almost always a path. Ask the AI to fix that line, explaining what failed, and try again. A worksheet that renders on someone else’s computer unchanged is the final check that every path in it is relative to the project.

title: Ex-3-3: Reshaping and Merging, with an AI Assistant
text: This is an in-class exercise. Before class, work through the lecture 03-3: Reshaping and Merging. In class, you work through the worksheet with an AI assistant writing the code. Your job is everything the AI cannot do: knowing what the files contain, asking for the right thing and the right checks, and judging whether the result is right.

title: Ex-3-3: Reshaping and Merging, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 1: Read and look
text:
Task 1: Read and look






What you should find





A. One row is one county. The year is in the column names: yield_2014, yield_2015, yield_2016, yield_2017, yield_2018. yield_wide has 116 rows and 8 columns.
B. One row should be one county in one year, identified by fips and year. drought has 331 rows.
C. yield_wide uses two columns, state_name and a 3-digit county_code. drought uses one, fips: 5 digits, the 2-digit state code followed by the same 3-digit county code. So Baca County, Colorado is Colorado and 009 in one table and 08009 in the other. The keys have to be made the same before merging; the AI cannot know that unless you tell it how they relate.
D. 264 of the 580 yield cells are missing. Those county-years are absent from the source: county yields are not published for every county in every year (for example, when too few farms report). In the wide layout, every county gets a cell for every year, so an absent county-year shows up as a missing value.

title: Ex-3-3: Reshaping and Merging, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 2: Wide to long
text:
Task 2: Wide to long






What you should find





Prediction. Keeping missing yields: 116 counties × 5 years = 580 rows. Dropping them: 580 − 264 = 316 rows. The total of all yields is 63,094.9 before and after.
Result. 316 rows, no missing values, year a whole number, and the totals match.
The blanks, filled in: one row is “one county”, the columns are yield_2014, yield_2015, yield_2016, yield_2017, yield_2018, and one row of the result is “one county in one year”.
If year came back as text such as "yield_2014", the request’s “Turn year into a whole number” was not followed; the type check shows it. A text year would also make the merge in Task 4 stop with an error, since year is a number in drought.

title: Ex-3-3: Reshaping and Merging, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 3: Look at the keys
text:
Task 3: Look at the keys






What you should find





Prediction. None in either table: each should have one row per county and year.
Result. yield_long has none. drought has 331 rows but only 316 distinct fips-year pairs: 15 pairs appear twice.
A. Every repeated row is from state code 20 (Kansas) in 2016: every Kansas county in that year appears twice. A whole state and year repeated together suggests how the file was put together, for example from two downloads that overlapped by one year.
B. They are exact copies: the same weeks in both rows. Exact copies can be reduced to one row each without losing anything. If the values had differed, you could not pick one without knowing which is right; that would be a question for whoever produced the file, not something to settle in code.
C. 331 rows instead of 316. Each of the 15 Kansas counties with a 2016 yield would appear twice, so any average over county-years would count Kansas 2016 twice. No warning: dplyr warns only when rows repeat on both sides of the match.

title: Ex-3-3: Reshaping and Merging, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 4: Merge
text:
Task 4: Merge






What you should find





Prediction. 316 rows, the same as yield_long. After the copies are removed, drought has 316 county-years, the same number as yield_long, so if the keys are built correctly every row of each should match: 0 unmatched rows on both sides.
Result. 316 rows; no repeated keys after the copies are removed; 0 unmatched rows of yield_long and 0 of drought.
The middle blank, filled in, reads something like: “In yield_long, build a fips column by putting the state code (Colorado 08, Kansas 20, Nebraska 31) in front of county_code, as text. In drought, the rows for Kansas in 2016 appear twice as exact copies; keep one of each.”
The sentence above the key-building chunk. If the AI looked up state codes itself, check them against the three you gave it. A wrong code, or a county_code that had lost its leading zeros (9 instead of 009), makes whole states fail to match; the unmatched-rows check shows it as a number far above 0.
The relationship option did its job only because you dealt with the copies first. Run the merge on the original drought and the code stops with an error, which is the point of asking for it.

title: Ex-3-3: Reshaping and Merging, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 5: Long to wide, for a report (if time allows)
text:
Task 5: Long to wide, for a report (if time allows)






What you should find





Prediction. 3 rows (one per state) and 6 columns (the state and 5 years). No missing cells: each state has at least one county with a yield in every year.
Result.

The averages are not equally trustworthy. The smallest number of counties behind an average is 2, for Colorado 2014 and Colorado 2017, while Nebraska’s averages rest on dozens. Which counties report a yield also changes from year to year, so a change in a state’s average can come from a change in which counties are included, not from a change in yields. A note under the table should give the number of counties behind each average, or the table should include report_n.

title: Ex-3-3: Reshaping and Merging, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 6: Kim’s code
text:
Task 6: Kim’s code






Answers





A. Reads the drought file; keeps the rows of yield_long whose fips appears in drought, adding the drought columns.
B. read.csv() reads fips as a number, so 08009 becomes 8009. The join then stops with an error, because fips is text in yield_long and a number in drought. If the AI “fixes” that by turning the number back into text, Colorado’s codes are "8009" and so on, which match nothing, and inner_join() drops all 18 Colorado rows without a message.
C. year. Each county-year row of yield_long matches every year of that county in drought, so a county with 5 years in each becomes 25 rows. Because fips repeats in both tables, dplyr prints a warning about a “many-to-many relationship”.
D. Rows before and after (both problems), repeated keys (C: with fips alone as the key, almost every key repeats), unmatched rows (B: all Colorado rows unmatched), and the type of fips in each table (B).

title: Ex-4-2: Showing More in One Figure, with an AI Assistant
text: This is an in-class exercise. Before class, work through the lecture 04-2: Showing More in One Figure. In class, you work through the worksheet with an AI assistant writing the code. Your job is everything the AI cannot do: knowing which columns belong together and in what order, deciding which comparison the figure is for, and checking that each line and bar stands for one thing.

title: Ex-4-2: Showing More in One Figure, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 1: Look and predict
text:
Task 1: Look and predict






What you should find





A. Two groups. corn_yield and soy_yield are both yields in bushels per acre, one column per crop. The five weeks_ columns are all numbers of weeks, one column per drought category.
B. 23: the categories do not overlap, and the season has 23 weeks. A county that spent part of the season in no drought at all adds up to less.
C. 1,956 rows × 5 columns = 9,780 rows. Each county-year becomes five rows, one per category.
D. By severity, in either direction, as long as the colours follow the same order (light for mild, dark for severe). For example: Exceptional (D4), Extreme (D3), Severe (D2), Moderate (D1), Abnormally dry (D0). Alphabetical order is wrong here: it would put “exceptional” right after “abnormally dry”.

title: Ex-4-2: Showing More in One Figure, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 2: Reshape and check
text:
Task 2: Reshape and check






What you should find






rows: expected 9,780, got 9,780.
the order: passes only if the AI made the category column follow your order. If the check prints the categories in alphabetical order, the order was not set; ask for it.
the largest total: expected at most 23, got 23.1. This check fails, for 39 county-years.

Look at the failing rows before deciding. Each value in the file was rounded to one decimal, so five rounded values can add up to a little more than the true total: at most 5 × 0.05 = 0.25 more. All the failures are within that. The data is fine; the check was too strict. A good fix is to check “at most 23.25”, and to write down why.
A check that fails is information, not an error to make disappear. Here it taught you that the file is rounded.

title: Ex-4-2: Showing More in One Figure, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 3: Which state had the worst drought in 2012?
text:
Task 3: Which state had the worst drought in 2012?






What you should find





B and C. The answer depends on what you count:










What you count
Colorado
Kansas
Nebraska

So “Colorado had the worst drought in 2012” is true if you count the two worst categories together, and “Kansas had the worst drought” is true if you count exceptional drought alone. A good message names what it counts, for example: “In 2012, Kansas counties spent the most weeks in exceptional drought, 6.2 of 23.” Hold on to the last row of the table; Task 6 comes back to it.
D. Which design serves depends on your message:

Points or bars per state, one panel per category, shared axis: puts the states side by side within each category. Serves a message that compares states in one category.
One stacked bar per state: shows each state’s total weeks in drought. The bottom category can be compared across states; the others start at different heights, so they cannot.
Points per category with the state as colour: shows every number, but the reader has to match three colours across five positions.

Choose the one that puts your comparison on a shared axis, and say so.

title: Ex-4-2: Showing More in One Figure, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 4: Rows and a summary
text:
Task 4: Rows and a summary






What you should find





A. Nebraska’s soybean average comes from 68 counties in 2000 and only 9 in 2018. From 2014 on, it rests on fewer than 30.
The average rose from 47 to 64 bushels per acre. In 2000 the counties differed by up to 26 bushels per acre.
B. A rise in an average of a shrinking set of counties may come partly from which counties are left. A check: the 9 counties still in the data in 2018 averaged 47 bushels per acre in 2000 (9 of them have a 2000 value) and 64 in 2018, about the same rise as the state average. So here the change in which counties report does not explain the rise, and a message can state its size. That is something you know only because you checked.
The reader of the figure should be told, in the caption or the subtitle, that the number of counties falls from 68 to 9. Alternatively, ask for a second panel, or a label at each point, showing the number of counties per year.

title: Ex-4-2: Showing More in One Figure, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 5: Critique and improve a weak figure
text:
Task 5: Critique and improve a weak figure






What a good answer looks like





A. One line is one category, and it passes through every county in every year: 44 to 153 values per year, joined in a vertical run up and down before the line moves to the next year. So the “lines” are columns of zigzags, and no line is an average or a county.

No. The zigzags hide any pattern over time.
Each colour is a category, so it carries information, but five default hues that are not chosen for colour-blind readers, and in alphabetical order, are hard to match to the legend.
No: five hues of similar lightness turn into five similar greys.
No. Four categories are context at most; the message is about exceptional drought.
Fails items 1 (column names weeks, category, weeks_exceptional), 2 (small text), 3 (a legend at the side when the lines could be labelled), 6 (the grey background) and 8.
No: one line joins hundreds of counties.
No: alphabetical.

The essential fix comes first: average the weeks per year and category (one row per year and category, 19 × 5 rows), then draw. Then show exceptional drought in a strong colour and the other categories in grey, or exceptional drought alone; label it directly; give the axis a plain title with units.
C. If the AI’s new figure still draws one line through every county, it did not fix the first problem, whatever else it changed. Check its table: one row per year and category.

title: Ex-4-2: Showing More in One Figure, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 6: Check the figure against its data
text:
Task 6: Check the figure against its data






What you should find





For one value per state and category: 3 × 5 = 15. The smallest number of counties behind any value: expected 4 (Colorado), got the same if the figure is right.
Colorado’s 2012 values rest on 4 counties, against 27 for Kansas and 64 for Nebraska. “Colorado had the worst drought” describes 4 counties that happen to be in this data, not the state. A message that does not mislead says so: “Among the counties in this data, …” or “Colorado (4 counties) …”, and the figure shows the number of counties next to each state’s name.

title: Ex-4-2: Showing More in One Figure, with an AI Assistant
section: Wrap-up
text:
Wrap-up






What a good answer looks like





A. Your answer should name the comparison in your message sentence (for example “states, within exceptional drought”) and say that it was put on a shared axis because that is the comparison readers judge most accurately.
B. For example: the total of the five columns in Task 2 (the file is rounded), or the number of counties behind Colorado’s values in Task 6. Neither shows in a figure.
C. For example: the order of the drought categories, that the categories do not overlap, or that one county-year in the file is one county in one season.

title: Ex-6-1: Organising a Research Project, with an AI Assistant
text: This is an in-class exercise. Before class, work through the lecture 06-1: Organising a Research Project. In class, you work through the worksheet with an AI assistant writing the code. Your job is everything the AI cannot do: knowing what each file is, deciding where it belongs, asking for the right steps and checks, and judging whether the project rebuilds.

title: Ex-6-1: Organising a Research Project, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 1: Look and sort
text:
Task 1: Look and sort






What you should find





A. One reasonable reading:








File
What it is
Why




corn_yields.csv
data as received, probably
notes.txt says the data came from NASS; nothing in the folder writes this file


corn_yields_fixed.csv
cannot tell
Nothing in the folder writes it, so it was made by hand or by code that is gone. notes.txt says only “fixed the data”.


corn_clean.csv
data made by code
analysis_final.R writes it


yield_by_irrigation.png
a result
analysis_final.R saves it


analysis_final.R
code



analysis_final_v2.R
code



notes.txt
a note




B. corn_yields.csv has 162 lines (161 data rows); corn_yields_fixed.csv has 155 (154 data rows).
C. corn_yields.csv, because it has the most rows and no code makes it. To be sure, you would need to know where it was downloaded and that nobody edited it since; in a real project, you would download it again and compare.

title: Ex-6-1: Organising a Research Project, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 2: What is the difference between the two data files?
text:
Task 2: What is the difference between the two data files?






What you should find





161 rows against 154. 7 rows are in corn_yields.csv and missing from the fixed file, and 0 rows are in the fixed file only.
A. All 7 missing rows are non-irrigated fields (Irrigated is 0), and they are the 7 lowest non-irrigated yields in the file: from 103 to 131 bushels per acre. No irrigated row was touched.
B. The irrigated average is 181.6 in both files. The non-irrigated average rises from 158.2 to 161.7. So the gap between irrigated and non-irrigated yields shrinks from 23.4 to 19.9 bushels per acre, which is the number the analysis is about.
C. Nothing records it. “Fixed the data” does not say which rows, or why. The rows may have been real errors, or they may have been real low yields from a dry county, which is exactly the variation an irrigation study needs. You cannot tell from the data.
So corn_yields.csv is the raw data. Ask Jan which rows were removed and why. If there is a good reason, the removal becomes a line in the cleaning step, with a sentence above it giving the reason, where anyone can see it and undo it. Until then, it does not happen.
This is the point of the task: a file edited by hand looks exactly like a raw file. Only the original, kept untouched, let you see what was done.

text:
Task 3: Lay out the project

The check prints TRUE and then corn_yields.csv, alone.

title: Ex-6-1: Organising a Research Project, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 4: Rewrite Jan’s analysis as steps
text:
Task 4: Rewrite Jan’s analysis as steps






What you should find





4a. 161 rows and 4 columns, with FIPS as text. A good check: the number of rows equals the number of data rows you counted in Task 1. Jan’s corn_clean.csv had 154, because it was made from the edited file.
4b. Average yield 181.6 for irrigated and 158.2 for non-irrigated fields: the same as the raw file’s averages in Task 2. A good check: there are 2 groups, and the averages match Task 2.
Jan’s figure does not match your new one: it was drawn from the edited file, so its non-irrigated box is missing the 7 lowest yields. Your figure is now the one you can explain.

title: Ex-6-1: Organising a Research Project, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 5: The test
text:
Task 5: The test






What you should find





Three files come back: data/processed/corn_clean.rds, results/mean-yield-by-irrigation.csv and results/yield_by_irrigation.png. The fingerprint of data/raw/corn_yields.csv is the same before and after.
If a step fails, the error names it. The usual causes: a path not built with here::here(), or a step that uses an object it never read (the summary step must read corn_clean.rds itself).
If run-all.R also tries to render ex-6-1.qmd, its pattern lists every .qmd in analysis/ instead of only names starting with two digits. Rendering the worksheet from inside the worksheet would start the test again from inside itself, over and over.

title: Ex-6-1: Organising a Research Project, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 6: Read Jan’s other script
text:
Task 6: Read Jan’s other script






Answers





A. Changes the working directory; loads the tidyverse; keeps rows with a yield above 120; fits a regression of yield on irrigation; prints its summary; saves the filtered table as corn_yields.csv.
B. Line 1. The folder C:/Users/jan/Desktop/corn exists only on Jan’s computer.
C. corn, in the filter() line. Nothing in this script reads or makes it. It works only if something else made corn earlier in the same R session (or R restored it from .RData). In a fresh session, such as a render, it fails with “object ‘corn’ not found”.
D. The last line. It saves the table over corn_yields.csv, the raw data, without asking. Whatever corn held, the original raw file is gone.
E. analysis_final.R made corn from corn_yields_fixed.csv, keeping 4 columns. So the regression used the edited file: 154 of its 154 rows have a yield above 120, so the filter dropped 0 rows, because the hand edit had already removed every low yield. And after the last line, corn_yields.csv itself would hold those 154 rows and 4 columns: the 7 rows you found in Task 2 would be gone from the raw file too, and nobody could find the edit again.
F. The AI usually spots the path and the overwrite, and often the missing corn. It cannot answer E: that depends on what Jan ran before, which only the folder (and notes.txt) can tell you.

title: Ex-6-1: Organising a Research Project, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 7: Does it rebuild anywhere?
text:
Task 7: Does it rebuild anywhere?






What you should find





If it fails on your neighbour’s computer, the error names the step and usually the line: almost always a path, or a package they have not installed. Fix the step, not their computer. A project that rebuilds on someone else’s computer, from the raw data, with no help from you, has passed the test from the lecture.

title: Ex-7-1: Dates and Text, with an AI Assistant
text: This is an in-class exercise. Before class, work through the lecture 07-1: Dates and Text. In class, you work through the worksheet with an AI assistant writing the code. Your job is everything the AI cannot do: knowing how the dates and names in the file are written, asking for the right thing and the right checks, and judging whether the result is right.

title: Ex-7-1: Dates and Text, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 1: Look and predict
text:
Task 1: Look and predict






What you should find





A. 421 lines: one line of column names and 420 data rows, one per truckload.
B. The first rows are written like 09/01/2025: a two-digit number, a slash, another, a slash, a four-digit year. Since the log starts on 1 September, that looks like month first. But line 6, a South row, says 01/09/2025, right after rows of 09/01/2025: the same day written the other way round. If you looked further, you may have seen a value such as 13/09/2025 (line 72), where the first number is above 12. Hold on to that; Task 3 is about it.
C. Within the first lines or a little further down, the crop column has Corn and corn, Soybeans and Soy beans, and popcorn. The farm column has ORTIZ AG beside Ortiz Ag, miller farms beside Miller Farms, and Schmidt Bros. beside Schmidt Bros.

title: Ex-7-1: Dates and Text, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 2: Dates as text
text:
Task 2: Dates as text






What you should find





The smallest and largest values of the text column are 01/09/2025 and 31/10/2025. Read month first, as the first rows suggest, the first is 9 January and the second is impossible (there is no month 31). They are the smallest and largest only because text is compared character by character from the left.
If you sorted by date as text, the first rows mix days from different months, all starting with 01/. The point: until the column is converted, a sort, a minimum, a maximum or a “group by month” on it is meaningless, and none of them gives an error.

title: Ex-7-1: Dates and Text, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 3: Convert the dates
text:
Task 3: Convert the dates






What you should find





3a. If you told the AI the dates are month first, as the first lines suggest:

dates that failed to parse: expected 0, got 98
first and last date: expected 1 September to 30 November 2025, got 9 January 2025 to 11 December 2025
months with rows: expected 3, got 12

Three checks fail. 52 further rows got a date that is wrong but looks like a date: they did not fail, they just landed in the wrong month.
3b. All 98 failures, and all 52 dates outside the season, come from the South site (165 rows); none of the 255 North rows is affected. The South site writes dates day first: its first row says 01/09/2025, which is 1 September. Day first, a value such as 23/09/2025 has no month 23, so it failed; a value such as 05/10/2025 (5 October) was read as 10 May, so it landed outside the season with no warning at all.
The text-beside-date rows show it too, if one of them is from South.
A further 9 South rows are read wrong but stay inside the season: 10/09/2025, for example, is 10 September 2025 but was read as 9 October 2025. No check catches those. Only knowing how the South site writes dates fixes them, which is why 3c converts each site in its own order rather than just dropping the rows that failed.
3c. Parsed by site (North with mdy(), South with dmy()), every check passes: 0 failures, dates from 1 September 2025 to 30 November 2025, rows in September, October and November only.
If the AI used parse_date_time() with both orders instead, nothing fails to parse (0 failures), but 103 North rows are read day first, and the dates run from 9 January 2025 to 11 December 2025. The range and month checks show it; the failure count does not.
The checks, and why. Each one tied to a way this conversion could go wrong:

Failures to parse: text in another format or order becomes NA with only a warning.
First and last date: swapped day and month push dates outside the season.
Rows in each month: swapped day and month put rows in months when no harvest happens.
Text beside date: shows directly which way a value such as 05/10/2025 was read.

Only the first check catches the 98 failures; only checks 2 and 3 catch the 52 silent ones.

title: Ex-7-1: Dates and Text, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 4: Bushels per month
text:
Task 4: Bushels per month






What you should find





September: 137,609; October: 137,320; November: 118,872 bushels. The three months add up to 393,801, the same as the total of the bushels column, 393,801, so no row was lost.
With the dates from 3a instead, there would be twelve months, and the 98 rows with a missing date would either show up as a month called NA or vanish from the table, depending on the code.

title: Ex-7-1: Dates and Text, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 5: Crop names
text:
Task 5: Crop names






What you should find





5a. 9 distinct spellings before cleaning. The manager says there are three crops. After lower case and removing extra spaces: 4 values, corn, popcorn, soy beans, soybeans. The check “distinct crops: expected 3” fails, because soy beans has a space that soybeans does not. No change of case finds that; you have to see it in the list and say which spelling it should become. After that: corn, popcorn, soybeans.
5b. The search pattern "corn" matches corn and popcorn. Popcorn contains the letters corn. With that search pattern, corn deliveries add up to 244,333 bushels; the right answer, crop_clean == "corn" (or the search pattern "^corn$"), is 215,221. The difference, 29,112 bushels, is all the popcorn.
Only the check “distinct values the search pattern matched” shows this. The row count of the result looks fine, the total looks believable, and nothing warns you.

title: Ex-7-1: Dates and Text, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 6: Farm names (if you have time)
text:
Task 6: Farm names (if you have time)






What you should find





13 distinct spellings before. After lower case and squishing spaces, 9, not the 8 farms the manager listed: schmidt bros and schmidt bros. are still two values (24 and 31 rows). A full stop is a character like any other.
If the AI fixed this by removing every . with the search pattern "." and not fixed(".") or "\\.", every farm name became empty text, which the distinct count (1 instead of 8) would show at once.

title: Ex-7-1: Dates and Text, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 7: Sam’s code
text:
Task 7: Sam’s code






Answers





A. Reads the csv; converts date from text to dates, month first; keeps the rows whose crop, in lower case, contains corn; adds up bushels within each month name.
B. The path "data/7-1-grain-deliveries.csv" is relative to the folder R is in. At the Console of the project that is ch7-practice, so it works; inside a .qmd saved in analysis/ it is analysis, where there is no data folder, so rendering fails. here::here("data", "7-1-grain-deliveries.csv") works in both.
C. Three problems give wrong results without an error:

Every South date is read month first: 54 corn rows get no date, and others land in the wrong month.
tapply() silently leaves out rows whose month is missing, so the monthly totals add up to 193,842, not the 244,333 bushels of all the rows it selected.
The search pattern "corn" also keeps popcorn.

(The months also come out in alphabetical order, April first, which is untidy rather than wrong.)
D. Failures to parse (expected 0); first and last date, or the number of months (expected September to November); the distinct crop values matched (expected only corn); the sum of the monthly totals against the total of the rows (expected equal).

section: Task 1: Look

Task 1: Look






What you should find

B. Only soy_yield, written as NA. Every Colorado row has NA there: the data has no soybean yields for Colorado at all. Kansas and Nebraska rows have them in some county-years and not in others.

Task 2: Count before you predict






What you should find





soy_yield is missing on 856 of the 1956 rows: all 154 Colorado rows, 349 of 534 in Kansas and 353 of 1268 in Nebraska. No other column has missing values.
Prediction. lm() leaves out every row with a missing value in a variable the model uses:

Checklist answers that are often “no” in the AI’s first table: no note saying which standard errors; headers (1) and (2) that do not say which crop each model explains; raw names such as weeks_extreme; no note that column (2) has fewer observations, and why.
A message from this table: “Each additional week of extreme drought goes with corn yields 1.1 bushels per acre lower, and soybean yields 0.16 bushels per acre lower.” Corn yields are larger to begin with (on average 178 against 55), so you might also compare in percent of the average: -0.6% against -0.3%. Hold on to this message until Task 4.

section: Task 4: The same counties?
text:
Task 4: The same counties?






What you should find





A. Column (1) has every county-year; column (2) only those with a soybean yield. So column (1) also includes all of Colorado, and 349 Kansas and 353 Nebraska county-years that column (2) does not. Colorado is missing from column (2) entirely.
B. Without regression. Average corn yield in county-years with extreme drought, minus the average in county-years without:

C. The regression confirms it. The third column, corn on only the 1100 rows with a soybean yield (Kansas and Nebraska only):
