So the message from Task 3 does not hold as written: comparing column (1) with column (2) compares different counties as much as different crops. On the same county-years, the corn estimate is about 0.1 times its size in column (1), roughly a tenth. The data cannot tell us which crop is hurt more.
A side note on the standard errors, if you have met them in a statistics course: on the same county-years, neither estimate is as large as twice its standard error, so neither is clearly different from zero.
This table cannot say why the corn result depends so much on which rows are used; that would be a question for further work, not something to guess.
D. Show the table with column (3), or with columns (2) and (3) only if the comparison of the crops is the message. The notes say: which standard errors; what the drought categories are; and that column (3) uses only county-years with a soybean yield, with the number of observations shown for every column.

title: Ex-8-2: Regression Tables, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 5: Alex’s code
text:
Task 5: Alex’s code






Answers





A. Read the data and remove every row with a missing value in any column; estimate corn yield on the two drought columns; estimate soybean yield on the same; put both in a table with robust standard errors, showing only the weeks of extreme drought row, labelled.
B. 1100. na.omit() removed every row without a soybean yield, so the corn model lost all of Colorado and many Kansas and Nebraska years, although none of its own variables has a missing value. Alex would expect 1956. The corn estimate is -0.11, the same as column (3) in Task 4, not -1.08.
C. coef_map lists only weeks_extreme, so the severe drought rows and the constants are dropped, with nothing saying so. Against the table standard: the bottom rows keep AIC, BIC and other statistics the message does not need, the label has no units, and there is no title and no note saying which standard errors are shown.
D. Using only the rows with both yields is the right choice when the message is a comparison of the two crops on the same county-years, as in Task 4. What was wrong is that nobody decided it: it happened as a side effect of a cleaning step, and the table does not say so. If it is the choice, the note must say “Both models use only the 1100 county-years with a soybean yield (Kansas and Nebraska).”
E. The number of observations of each model against the number expected (catches na.omit()), and every coefficient of each model against the rows of the table (catches coef_map).

title: Ex-9-1: Vector Layers and Their CRS, with an AI Assistant
text: This is an in-class exercise. Before class, work through the lecture 09-1: Spatial Data and Vector Layers. In class, you work through the worksheet with an AI assistant writing the code. Your job is everything the AI cannot do: finding out what the coordinates mean, asking for the right thing and the right checks, and judging whether the result is right.

title: Ex-9-1: Vector Layers and Their CRS, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 1: Look and predict
text:
Task 1: Look and predict






What you should find





A. The counties: longitude and latitude in NAD83, EPSG 4269. The stations: metres in NAD83 / UTM zone 13N, EPSG 26913.
B. The .prj file is missing, and the README says so. That file holds the CRS, so the layer will be read with no CRS at all.
C. 40 stations. easting holds x and northing holds y. Values such as 462,689 and 4,505,656 are metres, not degrees, which agrees with the README.
D. Colorado runs from about -109 to -102 longitude and 37 to 41 latitude, and its area is about 270,000 square kilometres (104,000 square miles). Any map site or encyclopedia gives these.

title: Ex-9-1: Vector Layers and Their CRS, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 2: Read the counties
text:
Task 2: Read the counties






What you should find





64 features of type MULTIPOLYGON, and a bounding box from -109.1 to -102 in x and 37 to 41 in y, which is where Colorado is. The quick map looks like Colorado.
The CRS check fails: expected EPSG 4269, got NA (no CRS). Everything else passes, which is the point: the layer looks right on a map and has the right numbers in it. Only the CRS check says that R does not know what those numbers mean.
The blanks of the request, filled in:
In my R project, data/9-1-co-counties.shp is a shapefile (.shp) file with one
row per county. Its documentation says the CRS is NAD83, EPSG 4269.
...
the number of features (I expect 64), the geometry type (I expect
MULTIPOLYGON), and the bounding box (I expect longitude between -109
and -102 and latitude between 37 and 41).

title: Ex-9-1: Vector Layers and Their CRS, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 3: Fix the CRS, then compute areas
text:
Task 3: Fix the CRS, then compute areas






What you should find





Prediction without the fix. With no CRS, st_area() treats the numbers as plain x and y and returns square degrees: the counties add up to 28, with no units and no warning.
After labelling the layer with EPSG 4269 (st_set_crs(), not st_transform(), because the numbers are already right and only the label is missing): the CRS check passes and the bounding box is unchanged.
Areas. The counties add up to 269,378 square kilometres, against about 270,000 from the encyclopedia: the check passes. The largest county is Las Animas (12,360 km²) and the smallest is Broomfield (87 km²).
If the AI used st_transform() instead of st_set_crs(), it stops with an error, because a layer with no CRS cannot be transformed: there is nothing to transform from. That error is the good case.

title: Ex-9-1: Vector Layers and Their CRS, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 4: The stations
text:
Task 4: The stations






What you should find





40 features, CRS EPSG 26913. The bounding box in the layer’s own CRS runs from 164,159 to 759,041 metres in x: you cannot compare that with a map. Transformed to EPSG 4269, it runs from -108.9 to -102.1 longitude and 37 to 40.7 latitude, inside Colorado.
The check from knowing the place: 40 of 40 stations fall inside a Colorado county. The counting needs both layers in one CRS: the AI should transform the stations to the counties’ CRS (or the other way) first. If it does not, sf stops with the error st_crs(x) == st_crs(y) is not TRUE.
On the map, every point should sit inside the state outline. If the points form a tiny cluster far from Colorado, or the map’s axes run into the hundreds of thousands, one layer was given the wrong CRS.

title: Ex-9-1: Vector Layers and Their CRS, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 5: Maria’s code
text:
Task 5: Maria’s code






Answers





A. Line 1 reads the county shapefile. Line 2 reads the stations csv and makes it a layer of points, with northing as x, easting as y, labelled as longitude and latitude in NAD83. Line 3 adds each county’s area, divided by a million.
B. The paths. C:/Users/maria/Downloads exists only on Maria’s computer.
C. Three problems, none of which gives an error:

Line 2 swaps x and y.
Line 2 labels metres as degrees (EPSG 4269 instead of 26913). The layer’s bounding box runs from 4,096,496 to 4,505,656 in x, numbers no longitude can have.
The counties have no CRS (no .prj), so line 3 computes square degrees and divides them by a million. The largest “area” is 0.0000013.

D. The bounding box catches problems 1 and 2. The CRS check catches the missing CRS behind problem 3, and the total area against Colorado’s known area catches the result.
E. The AI usually spots the paths and often the swapped coordinates, since northing as x is visible in the code. It cannot know that the counties file has no .prj or that the stations are in metres, because it has not seen the files. Compare its list with yours.

title: Ex-9-1: Vector Layers and Their CRS, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 6: Save and read back
text:
Task 6: Save and read back






What you should find





The GeoPackage comes back with EPSG 4269, 64 features and the same columns: the check passes. A .gpkg is one file that keeps its CRS, so the problem you met in Task 2, a shapefile that lost its .prj, cannot happen to it.

title: Ex-9-3: Communicating with Maps, with an AI Assistant
text: This is an in-class exercise. Before class, work through the lecture 09-3: Communicating with Maps (and lecture 04-1 on figures, whose figure standard you will need). In class, you work through the worksheet with an AI assistant drawing the maps. Your job is everything the AI cannot do: deciding the message and the reader, choosing among designs, and checking that the map shows every place it should.

title: Ex-9-3: Communicating with Maps, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 1: Look and predict
text:
Task 1: Look and predict






What you should find





A. One county in one year: county code, county name, year, corn yield in bushels per acre. 568 rows, years 2000 to 2006.
B. The county codes have leading zeros (001), so they must stay text to match countyfp in the county layer. (Here read_csv() keeps them as text, type character; read.csv() would not.)
C. Nebraska has 93 counties, so 7 years of every county would be 651 rows. There are 568, so some counties or years are missing. Only 82 different county codes appear at all.
D. A drought year should show yields below each county’s usual level. A raw 2002 yield cannot show that on its own: irrigated eastern and central counties have higher yields every year.

title: Ex-9-3: Communicating with Maps, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 2: Build the table the map is drawn from
text:
Task 2: Build the table the map is drawn from






What you should find








Check
Expected
Got




places drawn
93
93


places drawn more than once
0
0


places with a value
your prediction
81


places without one (No data)
your prediction
12



The discovery. 12 counties have no 2002 yield: Cass, Dakota, Grant, Hooker, Johnson, Lancaster, Nemaha, Otoe, Pawnee, Richardson, Sarpy, Thomas. Most of them sit together in the south-east corner of the state, around Lincoln and Omaha. A map drawn from the yield table alone would show a state with its south-east corner cut off, and a reader could take that for something about the drought.
Of the 81 counties with a value, 76 were below their own average over the other years, 2000, 2001 and 2003 to 2006. The differences run from -22.7% to 2.5%.
Which side of the join comes first matters. Starting from the county layer, left_join(counties, yield_2002), keeps all 93 counties and gives the 12 without a value NA. Starting from the yield table, left_join(yield_2002, counties), keeps only the 81 counties in the table, and the result is an ordinary table rather than a layer: geom_sf() then stops with “stat_sf() requires the following missing aesthetics: geometry”.

title: Ex-9-3: Communicating with Maps, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 3: Message, designs, choice
text:
Task 3: Message, designs, choice






What a good answer looks like





A message the data supports: “In 2002, corn yields fell below normal in almost every county, and furthest in the west.” Counties whose centre lies west of 100°W averaged -11.3% against -6.5% in the east. Your sentence may differ; it must be something the table supports and be about where.
The designs, and what each makes easy to see:

Raw 2002 yield, one hue light to dark. Shows where yields are high (120 to 187 bushels per acre), which mostly reflects irrigation and soil, not the drought. It does not serve this message.
Percent difference from normal, one hue light to dark. Shows where yields fell most. Good for “furthest in the west”, but a reader cannot tell which counties were above normal.
Percent difference from normal, two hues diverging from 0. Shows above and below normal, with white at no change. Almost every county is on the “below” side, which is itself the first half of the message. Usually the best fit.

A choice of 2 or 3, justified in terms of the message, is a good answer. A choice of 1 needs a different message.
Design 3, with the counties without data named, looks like this:









The classes are not symmetric around zero, because almost every county fell and none rose by more than 3%: symmetric classes would leave the “rose” colours almost unused and squeeze every fall into two shades. The middle is still “Within 1%”, in white, the browns and the blue-green come from the two ends of one diverging palette, and the no-data counties are a darker grey so they cannot be read as “no change”.
Whatever the design, every county without data should be in a grey the scale does not use (a darker grey on a diverging scale) and labelled “No data”. If the AI left them out, the map standard was not followed.

title: Ex-9-3: Communicating with Maps, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 4: Critique and improve a map
text:
Task 4: Critique and improve a map






What you should find





What is wrong, by the checklist and the standards:

It maps the raw yield, which does not show the drought (the message).
inner_join() keeps only counties with a 2002 yield, so 12 counties are missing and the south-east corner is cut off (map standard item 4).
A rainbow scale for an amount: no order a reader can see, and hard for colour-blind readers (map standard item 3).
Longitude and latitude axes and a grey background (map standard item 5).
The legend is titled corn_yield, a column name (figure standard item 1).
Dark default borders compete with the fill (map standard item 6).
No title stating the finding.

The improved map should start from all 93 counties with left_join() (or a join from the county layer), show the percent difference with a diverging scale centred at 0, name the “No data” counties, and have no axes. A version with all of these, side by side with the original, is what the request asks for.

title: Ex-9-3: Communicating with Maps, with an AI Assistant

Task 5: Check the map against its data






What you should find





The counts are those of Task 2: 93 drawn, 0 drawn more than once, 81 with a value, 12 without.
Lowest five (furthest below normal): Red Willow (-22.7%), Scotts Bluff (-21.2%), Frontier (-21.1%), Blaine (-19.8%), Garfield (-19.7%). On the map they should be the darkest “below normal” colour; three of them are in the west.
Highest five: Nuckolls (2.5%), Hamilton (1.2%), Wayne (1.1%), Washington (0.6%), Clay (0.2%). 5 counties are above 0. On a diverging map none of them should be brown: the ones above 1% are on the “rose” side, the rest in the white middle.
If a county named here has a colour that does not match its value, the join went wrong: check that countyfp and county_code are both text with their leading zeros.

title: Ex-9-5: Spatial Joins, with an AI Assistant
text: This is an in-class exercise. Before class, work through the lecture 09-5: Spatial Joins: Matching Rows by Location. In class, you work through the worksheet with an AI assistant writing the code. Your job is everything the AI cannot do: deciding what one row of the result is, knowing how many matches to expect, asking for the right checks, and judging whether the result is right.

title: Ex-9-5: Spatial Joins, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 1: Look at the corn field
text:
Task 1: Look at the corn field






What you should find





A. 3,830 yield points and 25 plots, both in WGS 84 / UTM zone 15N (same CRS: TRUE).
B. No. The plots cover only part of the field; the map shows many yield points between and around them. (The share is the answer to Task 2.)
C. No. The plots do not overlap, so a point can lie in at most one. A point exactly on a shared boundary would match both, which is why the check for “more than one plot” is still worth asking for.

title: Ex-9-5: Spatial Joins, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 2: Give each yield point its plot
text:
Task 2: Give each yield point its plot






What you should find





3,830 rows, one per yield point, as expected. 2,961 points have no plot; only 869 (23%) lie inside one. 0 points match more than one plot.
This is the main finding of the task. The plots cover 13,917 m² of a field of about 60,420 m², so most of the combine’s points are outside the trial: in the gaps between plots and around them. The files record no nitrogen rate for those points, so they have no target_rate and should not be in an analysis of the trial.
The join kept them, with NA, because a spatial join keeps every target row. Nothing went wrong in the code; the check for points with no plot is what tells you how much of your data the analysis is really about.

section: Task 3: Average yield by nitrogen rate

Task 3: Average yield by nitrogen rate

title: Ex-9-5: Spatial Joins, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 4 (if time allows): Where is the soybean field?
text:
Task 4 (if time allows): Where is the soybean field?






What you should find





Both files record WGS 84 / UTM zone 28N, in metres (same CRS: TRUE). Transformed to longitude and latitude, the field’s centre is at longitude -16.7, latitude 39.1: in the Atlantic Ocean, west of Portugal. UTM zone 28N covers longitudes 18 to 12 degrees west, nowhere near the US.
So the CRS recorded in the files is wrong. The numbers are metres, as the README says, but they do not belong to zone 28N, and the files do not say which CRS they do belong to. Whoever produced the files has to be asked.
What you can still do:

Yes. Matching within 10 m uses distances computed from the numbers themselves, in two layers that carry the same label. The numbers are metres (README), so distances inside the field are right even though the label is wrong.
No. Joining to counties needs the field’s true location. With the recorded CRS, it matches no county.
No, for the same reason: PRISM covers the US, and the field, as recorded, is in the ocean. The extraction would return NA for every point.

This is why the four checks of lecture 09-1 include the bounding box and a map: a CRS label that is wrong gives no error until you combine the layer with one whose location is right.

title: Ex-9-5: Spatial Joins, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 5: Match each soybean yield point to nearby seed-rate points
text:
Task 5: Match each soybean yield point to nearby seed-rate points






What you should find





The CRS is in metres, so the distance is 10.
1,683 yield points before; 2,076 rows after the join, because 355 yield points have more than one seed-rate point within 10 m (up to 4), and each match is a row. After the summary, 1,683 rows again.
341 yield points have no seed-rate point within 10 m, so their mean seed rate is NA. They should be left out of any analysis of seed rate and yield, and the number left out reported. A larger distance would match more of them, but with seed-rate points farther away that may not describe what was planted at that spot; the distance is a decision about the planter and the combine, not about the code.

Task 6: Maria’s code






Answers





A. The join keeps one row per plot and yield point inside it (869 rows here), plus one row with NA for each plot with no point. The summary computes each row’s plot area, drops the shapes, and adds up the areas and counts the rows for each rate.
B. Five plots of roughly 557 m² each, so about 2,786 m² per rate. Maria gets about 35 times that, because each plot’s area is added once per yield point in it:

text:
Task 2: Kansas county boundaries






What you should find





105 features, in NAD83 longitude and latitude, all in Kansas. The map shows the rectangle of Kansas with its north-eastern corner cut by the Missouri River.
On the second render, the file exists, so the download step is skipped and the file is read. If it downloaded again, the code is missing the “only if the file does not exist” condition; ask the AI to add it.

title: Ex-9-7: Getting Spatial Data from Online Sources, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 3 (if time allows): A map of the contiguous states
text:
Task 3 (if time allows): A map of the contiguous states






What you should find





56 features, not 48 or 50. Besides the 50 states, the file holds 6 more: District of Columbia, American Samoa, Puerto Rico, United States Virgin Islands, Guam, Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands. These are the District of Columbia and the US territories, which the Census Bureau publishes with the states. With Alaska and Hawaii, 8 features are not contiguous states.
Nothing failed: the function returned what the Census Bureau calls “states and equivalent entities”. Only the count check, and the list of names, showed that it was not what you meant. Drawn on a map, the territories and Alaska also stretch the map across the Pacific, which is often how people first notice.
A request that keeps what you need:
From the states layer, keep only the 48 contiguous states: drop Alaska,
Hawaii, the District of Columbia and the territories. Then check: the
number of features (I expect 48), and draw a map.
48 features remain. Whether to keep the District of Columbia is a decision about your map; say which in the request.

title: Ex-9-7: Getting Spatial Data from Online Sources, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 4: Daily rain from PRISM
text:
Task 4: Daily rain from PRISM






What you should find





5 layers, with the dates 20230710, 20230711, 20230712, 20230713, 20230714 in their names, in NAD83 longitude and latitude, with cells of 0.0417 degrees (about 4 km). Daily values over Kansas range from 0 to 123.4 mm, the largest on 20230713.
The units are not in the raster. They are in PRISM’s documentation, and in the .info.txt file the download saved beside each .bil. That file is where “mm” in your checks comes from.
The blanks, filled in: ppt, 2023-07-10, 2023-07-14, 5, and a range such as 0 to 150 (a single day’s rain above about 150 mm anywhere in Kansas would be extraordinary).

title: Ex-9-7: Getting Spatial Data from Online Sources, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 5: Rain in each county
text:
Task 5: Rain in each county






What you should find





105 rows and 0 counties with no value, but one check fails: counties not entirely inside the raster’s rectangle: expected 0, got 1 (Wyandotte).
You cropped the raster to the counties, so how can a county stick out? crop() cuts along cell edges, and by default it rounds the counties’ rectangle to the nearest cell edge. Where the nearest edge lies inside the counties’ rectangle, a sliver of the edge county is cut off: here about 1.4 km of Wyandotte County’s eastern tip, on the Missouri River. Its average comes from the rest of the county, with no NA and no warning.
The fix is to round outward: crop(ppt, counties, snap = "out") keeps every cell any county touches. With it, the same check gives 0. A sliver this small barely moves one county’s average, but the same rounding on a coarser raster cuts off whole cells.
County averages of the five-day total range from 0 mm (Shawnee) to 58 mm (Crawford). Summer rain in Kansas comes from storms, so neighbouring counties can differ a great deal over a few days; compare the county map with the daily maps of Task 4, where the same pattern should be visible.
The checks from lecture 09-6 caught a problem created by your own code, in a step that looked too simple to need checking.

title: Ex-9-7: Getting Spatial Data from Online Sources, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 6: Statistics from USDA-NASS
text:
Task 6: Statistics from USDA-NASS






What you should find





The search returns 10 items. The one for all soybeans is SOYBEANS - ACRES HARVESTED; the others are parts of it (irrigated, non-irrigated, double cropped, organic, and so on). Choosing among them is your decision, not the AI’s. At most 105 counties times 3 years, 315 rows, can arrive.
These answers cannot list your exact numbers, because the download needs your own key, and they were written without one: the rnassqs code was not run for this page. The list of items above comes from the tidyUSDA package’s saved list of NASS items. What to look for in your HTML:

Fewer rows than counties times years. NASS does not publish a county when too few farms report, and western Kansas grows few soybeans. Count the counties per year and compare with 105.
Rows that are not counties. Rows named OTHER (COMBINED) COUNTIES, county code 998, combine the unpublished counties of one district. They are not counties, and must not be mapped or averaged with them.
Units and type. unit_desc should say ACRES. Value is acres harvested in the county, not a share, and may arrive as text with commas (12,300) and (D) for withheld values; converting it to a number turns (D) into NA, so ask how many became missing.

If any year is missing entirely, NASS may not have published the survey for that year yet. That is a check on “which years arrived”, which you asked for.

title: Data Science with R for Environmental, Agricultural, and Social Scientists
text: Course materials for Data Science with R (AECN 896-05) at UNL, redesigned for working alongside AI. The lectures teach what each step of a data project is, what has to be true for it to succeed, what to ask an AI assistant to do, and how to check what comes back.

title: 01-1: Introduction to R
section: What you will and will not learn today
text:
What you will and will not learn today

The planDirections


An AI assistant can write R code. What it cannot do is tell you whether that code did what you needed. To judge that, you have to be able to read R code: say what each line does, even if you could not have written it yourself.
This first lecture gives you the foundation for reading code. Every line of R you will see in this course is built from three things:

Objects: named things that hold values, created with <-
Functions: commands that take inputs and give back a result
Packages: collections of functions written by other people, which you install and then load

You will not learn to write these from memory. You will learn to recognise them, so that when an AI hands you code, you can follow it line by line.



Install R, then RStudio (see “Installing them” under “R and RStudio” below)
Install the packages tidyverse, rmarkdown and here, at the Console: install.packages(c("tidyverse", "rmarkdown", "here")). Do this before class; it can take several minutes. What packages are, and why installing happens once, is on the slide “Packages: installing and loading”
Have an AI assistant available: a chat assistant in your browser, or an agent such as Claude Code in your editor or terminal
To move around these slides: click the three stacked horizontal lines in the bottom-left corner for the table of contents, or press the o key to see every slide at once

The code on these slides was run when the slides were made, and its output is shown under it. To try it yourself, copy it into RStudio.

title: 01-1: Introduction to R
section: Why the course works this way
text:
Why the course works this way

R does exactly what the code saysYour job, and the AI’sWhat the course is for


R runs each line exactly as written. Given a line it cannot make sense of, it stops and prints an error. Given a line it can run, it follows its own rules, even when the result is not what you meant.
An AI assistant is the opposite. Given a request with gaps, it fills them in with guesses: where your files are, what your data holds, what you wanted the result for. It writes code that runs, and the guesses are inside it.
So the risk has moved. Code that does not run is easy to spot. Code that runs and does the wrong thing is not, and that is what you have to catch.









The AI does
You do




Knows every function and every input
Understand the step: what it is for, and what has to be true for it to work (the concept)


Writes the code
Recognise what each line does (reading code)


Fills gaps with guesses
Tell it what it cannot know: your files, your data, your purpose (asking)


Reports that the code ran
Decide whether the result is right, using checks whose answer you know in advance (checking)



Every lecture in this course is organised around those four parts.


By the end, you should be able to carry out your own research in R with an AI assistant writing the code: get data in, reshape it, make figures and tables, report the results, and work with maps.
The AI will write that code into a Quarto document (a .qmd file: plain text with R code in it). Rendering the document runs its code from the top and makes a web page showing the code and its results. Chapter 2 teaches Quarto.

title: 01-1: Introduction to R
section: R and RStudio
text:
R and RStudio

What they areInstalling themThe four panesRunning code


R is a programming language for statistics and data, and the program that runs code written in it.

Free and open source, and widely used in universities and in industry
Started as software for statistics, designed by statisticians
Grows through its users: new statistical methods often appear first as R packages written by the people who developed the method, and R also handles maps and large datasets

RStudio is a separate program that you work in. It sends your code to R and shows you the results, your files, your figures and the help pages in one window. R’s own window is very basic, so almost everyone uses R through RStudio.


Install both, R first, then RStudio, because RStudio looks for an existing R installation when it starts.

R
RStudio

It worked if RStudio opens and the lower-left pane shows a line starting with R version followed by a >.










Where
Pane
What it is for




Upper left
Script or document
Code you want to keep, saved in a file


Lower left
Console
Where R runs code. Type a line after > and press Enter


Upper right
Environment
Lists the objects R is currently holding


Lower right
Files, Plots, Packages, Help
Your folders, figures, installed packages and help pages



Appearance and pane layout can be changed under Tools, Global Options.



At the Console: type a line and press Enter. R prints the result.
In a file: put the cursor on a line, or select several lines, and press Command + Enter (Mac) or Ctrl + Enter (Windows). RStudio sends them to the Console.

Anything after # on a line is a comment: R ignores it. Comments explain the code to people.

# this whole line is a comment
2 + 3 # a comment can follow code on the same line

[1] 5


The [1] at the start of the output is not part of the result. It says the line of output starts with the first value.

title: 01-1: Introduction to R
section: The three building blocks in one line
text:
The three building blocks in one line
Here is a typical line of R, of the kind an AI writes all the time:

average_yield <- mean(yields, na.rm = TRUE)









Piece
What it is
Slide




average_yield
The name of a new object, which will hold the result
Objects and <-


<-
Stores the result of the right-hand side under that name
Objects and <-


mean
A function: it computes an average
Functions and their inputs


yields
An existing object, the first input to the function
Functions and their inputs


na.rm = TRUE
A named input: an option that changes what the function does
Functions and their inputs



mean() is built into R. Many functions are not: they come from a package, which has to be installed and loaded first (slide “Packages”).
The rest of this section takes the pieces one at a time. By the end of it, you should be able to read the line above out loud: “compute the average of yields, leaving out missing values, and store it as average_yield”.

title: 01-1: Introduction to R
section: Objects and <-
text:
Objects and <-

The patternPrinting an objectOverwriting<- versus =


An object is a named thing R holds in memory: a number, some text, a table of data, a fitted model. Every object is made by the same pattern:

name <- value








Part
What it is




name
The name you will use to refer to the object later


<-
“Store the right-hand side under this name”. Read it as “gets”: a gets 1


value
Anything that produces a result: a number, text, or a whole calculation



R works out the right-hand side first, then stores the result. So d <- 1 == 2 stores FALSE, the answer to “is 1 equal to 2?”, not the question.

a <- 1
b <- "R rocks"
d <- 1 == 2

These three objects now appear in RStudio’s Environment pane.


Running an object’s name on its own prints what it holds. This is the simplest check there is: did the object get the value you expected?

a

[1] 1

b

[1] "R rocks"

d

[1] FALSE




Storing under a name that already exists replaces the old object, without a warning:

a <- 3
a <- 1
a

[1] 1




Outside a function, name = value does the same as name <- value. You will see both in AI-written code; this course uses <-.
Inside a function’s parentheses, = means something different: it sets one of the function’s inputs. In mean(yields, na.rm = TRUE), na.rm = TRUE does not create an object called na.rm. It tells mean() to leave out missing values (slide “Functions and their inputs”).

title: 01-1: Introduction to R
section: Values and their types
text:
Values and their types

The typesOperatorsMissing values: NA


Every value has a type. The type decides what R can do with it.








Type
Examples
What it is




numeric
1, 1.3, -999
A number, whole or with decimals


character
"Nebraska", "31001"
Text, always written inside quotation marks


logical
TRUE, FALSE
The answer to a yes-or-no question



You will also see integer (a whole number written with an L, such as 3L); it behaves like numeric.
Quotation marks matter: "31001" is text, 31001 is a number. You cannot do arithmetic on text:

"5" + 1

Error in "5" + 1: non-numeric argument to binary operator




Arithmetic and comparisons follow the usual signs, with a few that may be new:









Operator
Meaning
Example
Result




+ - * /
add, subtract, multiply, divide
6 / 4
1.5


^
to the power of
2^3
8


==, !=
is equal to, is not equal to
5 == 4
FALSE


>, <, >=, <=
greater than, less than, and so on
5 > 4
TRUE



A comparison gives back a logical value. == (two equals signs) asks a question; a single = sets a value. Comparisons are how rows are kept or dropped from a table later in the course.


NA means “this value is missing”. It is not zero, and it is not the text "NA".

yields

[1] 150 162  NA 171

is.na(yields)

[1] FALSE FALSE  TRUE FALSE


is.na() asks of each value “is it missing?”. The third one is.
Most calculations that include a missing value give NA, because the true answer is unknown:

mean(yields)

[1] NA


How to get the average of the values that are there is on the slide “Functions and their inputs”, tab “Defaults”.

title: 01-1: Introduction to R
section: Vectors and tables
text:
Vectors and tables

VectorsOne type per vectorTablesOther objects you will seeWhat kind of object is it?


A vector is a sequence of values, all of the same type. c() (short for “combine”) makes one:

v <- c(4, 3, 5, 9, 1)
v

[1] 4 3 5 9 1


Arithmetic on vectors works element by element: the first value with the first, the second with the second, and so on.

v * 2

[1]  8  6 10 18  2

v + c(10, 20, 30, 40, 50)

[1] 14 23 35 49 51


R code rarely needs a loop to do the same thing to every value; this is why.


A vector can hold only one type. Mix types, and R converts everything to the type that can hold all of them, without an error:

mixed <- c(4, 3, "5", 9, 1)
mixed

[1] "4" "3" "5" "9" "1"


Every value is now text (note the quotation marks). One text value turned the whole vector into text. When a column of numbers arrives in your analysis as text, this is usually why, and arithmetic on it will then fail or give NA.


A table holds data in rows and columns. Each column is a vector, so each column has one type, but different columns can have different types. All columns have the same length. R calls a table a data frame; this course says table.

yield_data <- data.frame(
  nitrogen = c(200, 180, 300),
  yield = c(240, 220, 230),
  state = c("Kansas", "Nebraska", "Iowa")
)
yield_data

  nitrogen yield    state
1      200   240   Kansas
2      180   220 Nebraska
3      300   230     Iowa


Inside data.frame(), each name = c(...) makes one column. Values in the same position make one row.
You will also see tibble and data.table. They are tables too, with some extra conveniences; read them as tables.



list: holds any mix of objects, each of any type and length. Results of a statistical model usually come back as a list.
matrix: values of one type in rows and columns, used for linear algebra. You will rarely meet one in this course.


a_list <- list(numbers = c(10, 20), state = "Iowa", data = yield_data)
names(a_list)

[1] "numbers" "state"   "data"   




Many surprises in R come from an object not being what you thought: a column of text instead of numbers, a vector instead of a table. Three functions tell you:

class(yield_data)

[1] "data.frame"

class(mixed)

[1] "character"

str(yield_data)

'data.frame':   3 obs. of  3 variables:
 $ nitrogen: num  200 180 300
 $ yield   : num  240 220 230
 $ state   : chr  "Kansas" "Nebraska" "Iowa"


class() gives the kind of object; for a vector, the type of its values. str() (structure) gives the size and the type of every column: here 3 rows (“obs.”) and 3 columns (“variables”), with num for numeric and chr for character. In RStudio, View(yield_data) opens a table in a spreadsheet-style viewer.

title: 01-1: Introduction to R
section: Pulling parts out of an object
text:
Pulling parts out of an object
AI-written code constantly takes one column, some rows or one value out of an object. Whatever the object, it is done with brackets or $, in one of these patterns:









Pattern
Gives
Example
Result




vector[position]
values at those positions
v[2]
3


table$column
one column, as a vector
yield_data$yield
240 220 230


table[condition, ]
the rows where the condition is TRUE; the empty place after the comma means “all columns”
yield_data[yield_data$yield > 225, ]
the 2 rows with yield above 225


list[[position]] or list$name
one element of a list
a_list$state
Iowa



Positions count from 1, not 0. table$column is the one you will see most often: mean(yield_data$yield) reads “the average of the yield column of yield_data”.

mean(yield_data$yield)

[1] 230


The condition is itself a comparison that gives one TRUE or FALSE per row, and the rows marked TRUE are kept:

yield_data$yield > 225

[1]  TRUE FALSE  TRUE

yield_data[yield_data$yield > 225, ]

  nitrogen yield  state
1      200   240 Kansas
3      300   230   Iowa

title: 01-1: Introduction to R
section: Functions and their inputs
text:
Functions and their inputs

The patternFunctions you will seeDefaultsVariations you will see


A function takes inputs, does something with them, and gives back a result. Every function call follows the same pattern:

result <- function_name(first_input, name = value, ...)









Part
What it is
Required?




result <-
Stores what the function gives back
No; without it, the result is printed and then gone


function_name
What to do
Yes


( )
Holds the inputs, separated by commas. R calls the inputs arguments
Yes, even if empty


first_input
Usually the data to work on, matched by its position
Usually


name = value
An option, matched by its name
No; each has a default



A real call:

round(3.14159, digits = 2)

[1] 3.14


The first input, 3.14159, is the number to round. digits = 2 is an option. Leave it out and round() uses its default, 0 digits: round(3.14159) gives 3.


All of these follow the pattern. You do not need to remember them; you need to recognise the pattern when you see them.









Function
What it gives back
Example
Result




mean(), sum(), min(), max()
one number summarising a vector
sum(v)
22


length()
how many values a vector has
length(v)
5


nrow(), ncol()
rows or columns of a table
nrow(yield_data)
3


round()
rounded numbers
round(2.567, digits = 1)
2.6


seq()
a sequence of numbers
seq(0, 10, by = 5)
0 5 10


rep()
repeated values
rep(10, times = 3)
10 10 10


is.na()
TRUE where a value is missing
is.na(c(1, NA))
FALSE TRUE


class(), str()
what kind of object something is
class(v)
numeric





Every option has a default: the value it takes when you do not set it, chosen by whoever wrote the function. mean() has an option na.rm (remove NAs) whose default is FALSE. That is why the average above came back NA:

mean(yields)

[1] NA

mean(yields, na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 161


With na.rm = TRUE, the average is of the 3 values that are there: (150 + 162 + 171) / 3 = 161.



Important


AI-written code often adds na.rm = TRUE as a matter of routine. It removes missing values without saying how many. An average of 3 values out of 4 is fine; an average of 3 out of 300 is not. When you see na.rm = TRUE, ask how many values were left out.





AI-written code often arranges the same pattern differently. These change how the code looks, not what it does:

One call inside another: round(mean(yields, na.rm = TRUE), digits = 1). Read from the inside out: first the average, then round it.
Spread over several lines: a long call, like data.frame(...) above, is split after commas. It is still one call; the closing ) ends it.
Inputs without names: round(3.14159, 2) is the same as round(3.14159, digits = 2), because digits is the second input. Named inputs are easier to read.
The pipe, |>: yields |> mean(na.rm = TRUE) means mean(yields, na.rm = TRUE). The object on the left becomes the first input of the function on the right. You will see it in nearly every chapter from Chapter 3 on.


yields |> mean(na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 161

title: 01-1: Introduction to R
section: Reading a help page
text:
Reading a help page
Every function has a help page. Put ? in front of its name, at the Console, and the page opens in the Help pane: ?seq. Three sections tell you most of what you need.

DescriptionUsageArguments, Examples, or ask


At the top, one or two sentences on what the function does. For seq(): “Generate regular sequences.” If that is not what you wanted, you are on the wrong page.


The function’s inputs, in order, each with its default. The real ?seq page also covers some related functions (seq_len(), seq_along() and others), so its Usage section lists several lines. The one for seq() itself is under ## Default S3 method:, a technical label you can ignore:
seq(from = 1, to = 1, by = ((to - from)/(length.out - 1)),
    length.out = NULL, along.with = NULL, ...)

Each name = value is an input and its default. Leave out from, and it is 1.
Inputs without names are matched by position: seq(0, 10) means from = 0, to = 10.
NULL means “not set”. ... means further inputs can be passed on; you can ignore it.

You only supply the inputs whose defaults you want to change. That is why seq(0, 10) works although seq() lists five inputs.


Arguments says what each input means. For seq(), by is the step between values and length.out is how many values you want, so the same sequence can be described two ways:

seq(0, 1, by = 0.25)

[1] 0.00 0.25 0.50 0.75 1.00

seq(0, 1, length.out = 5)

[1] 0.00 0.25 0.50 0.75 1.00


Examples, at the very bottom, is code you can copy and run. Running an example and then looking back at Usage is often the fastest way to understand a function.
You can also paste a line into an AI assistant and ask what each input does (see “Recommended requests”, tab “Explain code”). The help page is the reference to check its answer against: it describes the version of the function installed on your computer, which the AI cannot see.

title: 01-1: Introduction to R
section: Packages: installing and loading
text:
Packages: installing and loading

What are packages?Installing versus loadingWhen it goes wrongWhich package is a function from?


A package is a drawer in your workspace (the R environment) holding specialized tools (functions) for a particular set of tasks. Packages are written by R’s users and shared for free; most of the functions in this course come from them.
Example packages:

dplyr (data wrangling)
data.table (data wrangling)
ggplot2 (data visualization)
sf (spatial vector data handling)
terra (spatial raster data handling)
stars (spatiotemporal data handling)

tidyverse is a package that installs and loads a set of others at once, including dplyr, ggplot2 and readr.


Two separate steps:

Install: before you can use the tools (functions) in a drawer (package), you have to obtain the drawer. Installing downloads the package onto your computer. The name goes in quotation marks:


install.packages("ggplot2")


Load: you then bring the drawer into your workspace with library(). The name goes without quotation marks:


library(ggplot2)

You can now use the tools (functions) that drawer contains.




Install once, load every time


You install a package once per computer, at the Console. You load it with library() in every new R session (R from the moment it starts until it is closed or restarted), and that includes every time a Quarto document is rendered, because rendering starts a fresh R session. So library() lines belong at the top of your document, and install.packages() lines do not belong in it at all: they would download the package again at every render.






The two steps fail with two different errors, and the error tells you which step is missing:

library(notapkg)

Error in library(notapkg): there is no package called 'notapkg'


“There is no package called …”: the package is not installed (or the name is misspelled).

tidy_table <- as_tibble(yield_data)

Error in as_tibble(yield_data): could not find function "as_tibble"


“Could not find function …”: the package that has the function is not loaded (here, as_tibble() comes from the tibble package, which also comes with dplyr and tidyverse), or the function name is misspelled.


A line does not say which package its function comes from, unless it is written as package::function():

dplyr::filter(yield_data, yield > 225)

dplyr::filter means “the filter() function from dplyr”. It uses the function without loading the whole package, and it tells the reader where the function comes from. When you cannot tell, ask the AI, or run ?filter after the package is loaded: if several packages have a function of that name, the help pane lists them all, each with the package it comes from. Each help page also names its package at the top left, as in filter {dplyr}.

title: 01-1: Introduction to R
section: Errors, and failures without one
text:
Errors, and failures without one

Reading an errorErrors you will seeNo error is not the same as right


When R cannot run a line, it stops and prints an error. Read it before anything else: it usually names the function that failed and what it objected to.

sum("a")

Error in sum("a"): invalid 'type' (character) of argument


“invalid ‘type’ (character) of argument”: sum() ran, but its input was text, and text cannot be added up.


Four errors you will see often:








The error says
What it means
Usual cause




object 'x' not found
No object has that name
A typo (R treats Yield and yield as different names), or the line that creates it was never run, or it was made in the Console but not in the document


could not find function "f"
No loaded function has that name
The package was not loaded, or a typo


there is no package called 'p'
The package is not installed
Not installed on this computer, or a typo


non-numeric argument to binary operator
Arithmetic on something that is not a number
A number stored as text



When you ask an AI about an error, send the whole error message, the code that produced it, and what you expected. The AI cannot see your screen.


An error is the good case: you know something went wrong. Worse are lines that run and give a wrong answer. Two you have already met:

One text value in c(...) turned every value to text, with no error.
na.rm = TRUE leaves out missing values without saying how many.

And one more. Text that looks like numbers is sorted as text, character by character:

sort(c("9", "10", "100"))

[1] "10"  "100" "9"  


“10” comes before “9” because “1” comes before “9”. No error, wrong order. Checking the type of a value (class(), str()) would catch it.



Important


Code that runs is not the same as code that is right. Deciding whether it is right is the part that stays your job.

title: 01-1: Introduction to R
section: What the AI cannot know
text:
What the AI cannot know
The AI knows R. It does not know your session or your intentions. Each of these has to be in your request:

The code: paste the exact lines, not a description of them
What came out: the whole error message or output, copied, not retyped from memory
What you expected: the result you thought you would get, and why
What is around it: which objects already exist and what they hold, which packages you loaded. Running str() on an object and pasting the output is a quick way to describe it
What you want back: an explanation, a corrected line, or both





Using an agent in your editor or terminal?


An agent such as Claude Code can run the code and see the error itself. Still say what you expected before it runs, so you have something to compare its answer with.

title: 01-1: Introduction to R
section: A weak request and a strong one
text:
A weak request and a strong one

WeakStrongWhat came back


My R code doesn't work, please fix it.
The AI does not see the code, the error or what you wanted. It will guess, and a typical reply is a list of five common R mistakes, none of which may be yours.


I ran these two lines:

yields <- c(150, 162, NA, 171)
average_yield <- mean(yields)

average_yield prints NA. I expected the average of the three yields
that are not missing, 161. Explain in one plain-English sentence why I
got NA, then correct the code. Also print how many values the average
used.

Put the code in my Quarto document analysis/yields.qmd, under the
heading "Average yield", as R code chunks. Above each chunk, write one
plain-English sentence saying what it does and why. Build every path
with here::here(); no setwd(), no absolute paths. Print each check on
its own line as "name of check: expected X, got Y". Render the document
to HTML.
The last paragraph is the closing instructions: the same lines end every request that asks for code. They make the AI put its code into a Quarto document, with a sentence above each piece of code, so that the result is a web page you can read and keep. Chapter 2 teaches Quarto; the full text is under “Recommended requests”.
here::here() builds a file’s path from the top folder of your project, so the path works on any computer. Chapter 3 explains it.


What the AI’s answer looks like in the rendered page: a sentence, then the code it describes. Read each sentence, and check that the code under it does what the sentence says.
mean() gives NA when any value is missing, unless told to leave missing values out with na.rm = TRUE.

average_yield <- mean(yields, na.rm = TRUE)

Print the checks: how many values there are, how many are missing, and the average of the rest.

cat(
  paste("values: expected 4, got", length(yields)),
  paste("missing values: expected 1, got", sum(is.na(yields))),
  paste("values used: expected 3, got", sum(!is.na(yields))),
  paste("average yield: expected 161, got", average_yield),
  sep = "\n"
)

values: expected 4, got 4
missing values: expected 1, got 1
values used: expected 3, got 3
average yield: expected 161, got 161


Every check matches, and each line says what it is checking. Two functions that may be new: cat() prints text, and paste() joins pieces of text into one. sum(!is.na(yields)) counts the values that are not missing (! means “not”).

title: 01-1: Introduction to R
section: Checking: what to ask for, and why
text:
Checking: what to ask for, and why

Checks you can know in advanceAsking for themA check that fails


A check is only useful if you know the right answer before you see the result. The AI can write the checking code; only you can supply the answer. Sources of answers you know in advance:









Ask the AI to print
You know the answer from




1
how many values, rows or columns there are
counting, or the description of the data (a help page, a codebook)


2
the type of each key value or column
knowing what it measures: a yield is a number, a state name is text


3
how many values are missing
the data’s description, or counting them yourself on a small case


4
the smallest and largest value
what is believable: a corn yield is not negative


5
the result on a small case
working it out by hand, as for the average of 150, 162 and 171





Say what you expect, and ask for each check in one form, so the rendered page says which passed:
I expect <number> values, <number> of them missing, and an average of
<number>. Print each check on its own line as "name of check: expected
X, got Y".
If you cannot fill in a blank, that is a sign to look at the data, or its description, before asking.


A student expected the values to be numbers. The AI’s code, and what it printed:


Code the AI wrote
cat("type of mixed: expected numeric, got", class(mixed), "\n")


type of mixed: expected numeric, got character 


The check fails: mixed holds text. Nothing errored, and any average of it would be wrong or NA. The right move is to find out where the text came from (here, the "5" written in quotation marks) before going on.

title: 01-1: Introduction to R
section: Your turn: read the AI’s code
text:
Your turn: read the AI’s code
A student asked an AI to “average my yields”, and got this:

library(dplyr)
my_yields <- c(150, 162, "171", 140)
avg = mean(my_yields)
avg


QuestionsAnswers


A. What does each of the four lines do?
B. What will avg print, and why? Is there an error?
C. Which check from the previous slide would have caught the problem, and what would it have printed?
D. Is line 1 needed?


A. Loads the dplyr package; stores four yields under the name my_yields; computes their average and stores it as avg (= does the same as <- here); prints avg.
B. NA. Because "171" is in quotation marks, the whole vector is text, and the average of text is NA. There is no error, only a warning (“argument is not numeric or logical: returning NA”), which is easy to miss.
C. Check 2, the type: “type of my_yields: expected numeric, got character”.
D. No. None of the functions used (c(), mean()) comes from dplyr; both are built into R. It does no harm, but a line you cannot explain is worth asking about.

title: 01-1: Introduction to R
section: Requests you can copy
text:
Requests you can copy
Copy one, then replace every <...> with what you know. The blanks are the part the AI cannot fill in for you. Every request for code ends with the closing instructions.

Closing instructionsExplain codeExplain an errorInstall packagesCompute something, with checks


The lines that end every request for code. Replace the two blanks; leave “expected X, got Y” as it is, because it tells the AI how to print each check:
Put the code in my Quarto document <path to your .qmd>, under the
heading "<heading>", as R code chunks. Above each chunk, write one
plain-English sentence saying what it does and why. Build every path
with here::here(); no setwd(), no absolute paths. Print each check on
its own line as "name of check: expected X, got Y". Render the document
to HTML.
A chat assistant cannot render: paste its chunks into your .qmd and render it yourself. An agent in your editor or terminal can do every step.


For code you did not write, or code you are not sure about:
Explain this R code to me. For each line, write one plain-English
sentence. Then list:
1. any line that would only work on the computer it was written on
2. any line that could give a wrong result without an error, and what
   check would reveal it

<paste the code here>


I ran this R code:

<paste the code here>

and got this message:

<paste the whole error or warning here>

I expected <what you expected to get>. The objects it uses hold
<what they hold, or the output of str() on each>, and I loaded the
packages <package names>. Explain in plain English what the message
means and which line caused it, then correct the code.

Put the code in my Quarto document <path to your .qmd>, under the
heading "<heading>", as R code chunks. Above each chunk, write one
plain-English sentence saying what it does and why. Build every path
with here::here(); no setwd(), no absolute paths. Print each check on
its own line as "name of check: expected X, got Y". Render the document
to HTML.


Installing happens once, at the Console, so this request asks the AI to act rather than to write code into your document:
Install the R packages <package names> on my computer, at the R
Console, not in any document. Then load each one with library() and
tell me whether it loaded, and its version.
A chat assistant cannot run anything: it will give you an install.packages() line to paste into the Console yourself.


In my Quarto document <path to your .qmd>, the object <object name> is
created earlier and holds <what it holds>. Compute <what you want>.
I expect <number> values, <number> of them missing, and a result of
about <number>.

Put the code in my Quarto document <path to your .qmd>, under the
heading "<heading>", as R code chunks. Above each chunk, write one
plain-English sentence saying what it does and why. Build every path
with here::here(); no setwd(), no absolute paths. Print each check on
its own line as "name of check: expected X, got Y". Render the document
to HTML.

title: 01-1: Introduction to R
section: What you must understand, and what the AI can write
text:
What you must understand, and what the AI can write







You need to understand
The AI can write




What an object is, and that <- stores a result under a name, replacing any old one
The names and the assignments


That table$column takes one column out of a table
The extraction code


The types of values, and that mixing them converts everything to text without an error
The conversions between types


The pattern of a function call: name, inputs by position, options by name, defaults
Which function to use and which options to set


What a default does, especially na.rm = TRUE
The options themselves


That a help page lists each input and its default
Which inputs to set


Installing (once, at the Console) versus loading (every session, at the top of the document)
The install.packages() and library() lines


What the four common errors mean
The fix, once you have told it the code, the error and what you expected


What a correct result looks like
The checking code



Every time AI hands you code: read it line by line, and name the objects, functions, inputs and packages in it. If you cannot say what a line does, ask before you keep it. Then judge the result by checks whose answer you knew beforehand.

title: 02-1: Quarto Documents and Rendering
section: What you will and will not learn today
text:
What you will and will not learn today

The planDirections


In this course, and in your own research, an AI assistant writes most of the R code. Where that code lives, and how you judge it, is what this lecture is about: the code goes into a Quarto document (a file ending in .qmd), and you judge the work by reading the HTML page that the document produces.
The AI can write a Quarto document. What it cannot do is:

decide what your reader should see and what can stay out of view
know whether the document still works outside the AI’s own session
tell whether the sentences in the document match the results under them

Those three are your job. So today is about:

The concept: what a .qmd file is, and what rendering does to it
Reading code: recognising the parts of a .qmd file (header, chunks, chunk options, numbers written into sentences) without memorising them
Asking AI: what to put in a request so the AI’s work arrives as a document you can judge
Checking: what to look at in the HTML, and what the HTML can hide




Open RStudio. It comes with Quarto, so there is nothing else to install. If RStudio asks to install the rmarkdown or knitr packages the first time you render, say yes.
Ask your AI assistant to install the tidyverse and here packages if you have not already (see the packages slide in Chapter 1).
To follow along, make a new document: File, New File, Quarto Document, then click Create.

title: 02-1: Quarto Documents and Rendering
section: Why research is written in a Quarto document
text:
Why research is written in a Quarto document

The problemWhat Quarto does


The usual way of reporting an analysis is to run code in one place and copy the results into another: a Word file, an email, a chat window. Three things go wrong:

Numbers drift. The data changes, the code is rerun, and the number typed into the report is not updated.
Nobody can see how a number was made. The report shows the result, not the steps that led to it.
The steps get lost. Code typed at the Console and never saved cannot be run again, by you or anyone else.



A Quarto document is one plain-text file that holds both the sentences and the code. Rendering it (clicking the Render button in RStudio) runs the code and writes an HTML page in which each piece of code sits next to its result and the sentence that explains it.

The .qmd file is the source: you, or the AI, edit it.
The .html file is the output: you read it, and you send it to whoever needs to see the work.

These slides are themselves a Quarto document, rendered to a slide format instead of a page.



Note


Quarto can also render to slides, websites, Word files and PDF articles. Lectures 02-2 to 02-4 cover those. This lecture uses HTML pages throughout.

title: 02-1: Quarto Documents and Rendering
section: How a .qmd file is written
text:
How a .qmd file is written
Every .qmd file, short or long, written by you or by an AI, follows the same pattern.

The patternThe text partA real fileWhat the HTML shows


---
title: "Report title"
format: html
---

Text written in Markdown, with a `r expression` inside a sentence.

```{r}
#| option: value
R code
```








Part
What it is
Required?




The YAML header, between the two --- lines
Settings for the whole document: title, output format, and so on
Yes, at the very top


Text
Ordinary sentences and headings, written in Markdown (plain text with a few marks for formatting, next tab)
No, but a report without it explains nothing


Code chunks, from ```{r} to ```
R code that runs when the document is rendered
No


#| lines at the top of a chunk
Chunk options: settings for that one chunk
No; each has a default


`r ` inside a sentence
Inline R: a short piece of R whose result is written into the sentence
No





The text is written in Markdown. You only need to recognise a few marks:



What you type
What you get




# Heading
a first-level heading


## Smaller heading
a second-level heading


+ item or - item
a bullet list item


1. item
a numbered list item


**text**
bold


*text*
italic


`text`
code style, inside a sentence


[UNL](https://www.unl.edu)
a link: UNL



The headings matter beyond looks: they are how you tell the AI where to put its code (“under the heading …”).


A short report that follows the pattern. The next tab shows what rendering makes of it.
---
title: "Field yields"
format: html
---

## Average yield

Make a table of four fields, written straight into the code.

```{r}
#| label: make-fields
fields <- data.frame(
  field = c("North", "South", "East", "West"),
  acres = c(40, 80, 35, 120),
  yield = c(182, 201, 175, 196)
)
```

Compute the average yield across the four fields.

```{r}
#| label: average-yield
mean(fields$yield)
```

The average yield is `r mean(fields$yield)` bushels per acre.


Below the title and the heading “Average yield”, the reader sees each sentence, then the code under it, then its result:
Compute the average yield across the four fields.

mean(fields$yield)

[1] 188.5


The average yield is 188.5 bushels per acre.
The first chunk made a table and printed nothing, so the reader sees only its code (not repeated on this slide). In the last sentence, the number was computed when the document was rendered, not typed.

title: 02-1: Quarto Documents and Rendering
section: What rendering does
text:
What rendering does

The four stepsOnly what is in the document existsOrder mattersThe folder


When you click Render, Quarto:

Starts a new R session (a fresh, empty R, separate from the one at your RStudio Console)
Runs every chunk, in order, from the top, with the folder that holds the .qmd as the working directory (the folder R treats as “here”)
Puts the text, the code and the results together
Writes the HTML file next to the .qmd, and opens it

If any chunk stops with an error, the render stops there and no new HTML is written. The HTML from the last successful render stays where it was, so after a failed render the page you open is out of date. Check the render’s message before reading the page.


The new R session in step 1 knows nothing about your Console. A table you made by typing at the Console, or a package you loaded there, does not exist for the render.
Suppose you typed farms <- read_csv("farms.csv") at the Console, and the document has a chunk labelled count-farms with nrow(farms) in it. Clicking the chunk’s green run button works, because that button runs the chunk at your Console. Rendering stops with:
Error:
! object 'farms' not found
Quitting from report.qmd:6-9 [count-farms]
The fix is never to type more at the Console. It is to put the line that makes farms into a chunk above count-farms.


Step 2 runs the chunks once, from top to bottom. A chunk can use only what the chunks above it made.
While you work, you can run chunks by hand in any order, so a document can seem to work when it does not: a chunk near the top that uses a table made further down works if you happened to run the lower chunk first. The render does not; it stops at the first chunk that needs something not yet made.


During the render, R’s working directory is the folder the .qmd is saved in, not necessarily your project folder (the folder RStudio opens as an R Project, marked by a .Rproj file; lecture 03-1). A path such as "data/farms.csv" is looked up starting from that folder.
So a path that works at the Console can fail inside a .qmd saved in a subfolder. The fix is here::here(), which builds a path starting from the project folder wherever the .qmd is. Lecture 03-1 explains paths in full; for now, recognise here::here("data", "farms.csv") as “the file farms.csv in the data folder of this project”.

title: 02-1: Quarto Documents and Rendering
section: Why a document that renders is reproducible
text:
Why a document that renders is reproducible
Reproducible means that someone else, or you a year from now, can run the same steps on the same data and get the same results.
Rendering tests that every time: it starts from nothing and builds every result from the document alone. So if a document renders:

every step is written down in it, in the order it runs
nothing depends on something typed at the Console and forgotten
every number computed in it comes from the data, through the code you can read





What rendering does not tell you


A document that renders is complete, not necessarily right. The code can run and still do the wrong thing, a sentence can describe something the code does not do, and a chunk option can keep a step out of view. That is why you read the HTML (see “Checking the result”).
If a chunk has cache: true, a render reuses its result from an earlier render even when the data has changed. Before the final render, delete the folder ending in _cache next to the .qmd.








A habit before you render


Session, Restart R, then Run, Run All (the menu of the Run button above the editor). This runs every chunk at your Console as a render would, so you find a missing step before rendering.

title: 02-1: Quarto Documents and Rendering
section: How the YAML header is written
text:
How the YAML header is written

The patternSettings you will seeWhen the indentation is wrong


Every line of the header is a setting, written as a name, a colon and a value:
---
name: value
group:
  name: value
---







Part
What it is




name: value
One setting. Text values with spaces or colons go in quotes: title: "Yield: a first look"


A name with nothing after the colon
A group. The settings that belong to it are on the lines below, indented further


Indentation
Spaces, never tabs. How far a line is indented says which group it belongs to





---
title: "Field yields"
author: "Your Name"
date: today
format:
  html:
    toc: true
    embed-resources: true
    code-fold: true
execute:
  warning: false
---







Setting
What it does




title, author
Printed at the top of the page


date: today
Prints the date of the render


format: html
Produce an HTML page. Settings for that format go in the group under html:


toc: true
Add a table of contents built from the headings


embed-resources: true
Pack figures and styling into the one HTML file, so it can be sent on its own (see “Checking the result”)


code-fold: true
Hide each chunk’s code behind a “Code” button the reader can click


execute:
Chunk options that apply to every chunk; here, hide warnings everywhere





toc belongs to html, so it must be indented further than html:. Here it is not:
---
title: "Field yields"
format:
  html:
  toc: true
---
Quarto refuses to render, names the line, and prints Render failed due to invalid YAML. When the AI changes a header and the render then fails at once, the header is the first place to look.

title: 02-1: Quarto Documents and Rendering
section: How a code chunk is written
text:
How a code chunk is written

The patternOptions you will seeWhat the reader seesVariations you will see


```{r}
#| label: name-of-chunk
#| option: value
R code
```








Part
What it is
Required?




```{r} and ```
The start and end of the chunk; r says the code is R
Yes


#| label: ...
A name for the chunk: unique in the document, no spaces
No, but an error message then names the chunk by its label


#| option: value
One chunk option per line, right below the first line, with no blank line in between
No; each has a default


R code
Runs when the document is rendered
Yes













Option
What it controls
Default




echo
Whether the code is shown in the HTML
true


eval
Whether the code is run at all
true


include: false
Runs the code but shows nothing: no code, no result
shows everything


message, warning
Whether messages and warnings from the code are shown
true


code-fold: true
Hides the code behind a button the reader can click
not folded


fig-cap
A caption under a figure
none


error: true
Lets the render continue past an error, printing the error in the page
false: stop



The same options can be set for every chunk at once under execute: in the YAML header. An option written in a chunk overrides the one in the header.


The options that matter most for judging a document are the ones that decide what the reader can see:



Chunk options
Code runs?
Code shown?
Result shown?

yes
behind a button

yes
