The rows marked no are the ones to notice. A chunk with include: false can still change the data; the reader of the HTML sees no trace of it.



#| echo: false and {r, echo = FALSE} (options inside the braces): the second is an older way of writing the same thing. Both work.
#| label: fig-yield with #| fig-cap: "...": a label that starts with fig- makes a numbered figure that the text can refer to (lecture 02-4).
A chunk with only library(...) lines and include: false at the top of the document: a setup chunk. It loads packages without filling the page with them.

title: 02-1: Quarto Documents and Rendering
section: How inline R is written
text:
How inline R is written

The patternWhy it mattersVariations you will see


Inside a sentence, a backtick, the letter r, a space, an R expression and a closing backtick:
The average yield is `r mean(fields$yield)` bushels per acre.
When the document is rendered, the expression is run and its result replaces it. The reader of the HTML sees only the number:

The average yield is 188.5 bushels per acre.

It runs in the same R session as the chunks, so it can use anything made by a chunk above it.


A number typed into a sentence is a copy, made once. A number written with inline R is computed at every render, so it always matches the data and the code.
If someone adds a fifth field to fields and renders again, the sentence changes by itself:

fields_5 <- rbind(fields, data.frame(field = "Creek", acres = 25, yield = 150))
mean(fields_5$yield)

[1] 180.8


A typed “188.5 bushels per acre” would now be wrong, and nothing would say so.



`r round(mean(fields$yield), 1)`: rounded inside the sentence
A value computed in a chunk, given a name, and only the name used inline: `r avg_yield`. Long calculations belong in a chunk, not in a sentence.
`{r} mean(fields$yield)`: a newer way of writing the same thing. Both work.

title: 02-1: Quarto Documents and Rendering
section: When a render fails
text:
When a render fails

Read the messageErrors you will meetWhat to send the AI


Quarto prints the error in the Background Jobs tab of RStudio. Read the last lines first:
Error:
! object 'farms' not found
Quitting from report.qmd:6-9 [count-farms]

The line starting with ! is R’s own error.
Quitting from names the file, the lines, and the chunk’s label in square brackets.










The error says
What it usually means




object '...' not found
The table or value is made at your Console or further down the document, not in a chunk above this one


could not find function "..."
The package is loaded at your Console but not in the document, or the name is misspelled


cannot open file '...' or does not exist
The path is wrong from the .qmd’s folder (Lecture 03-1)


Render failed due to invalid YAML
A mistake in the header: usually indentation, or a missing colon





The AI did not see your render. Send it:

the error lines, copied exactly
the chunk the error names
the folder the .qmd is in, if the error is about a file

Then render again yourself. “Fixed” means the document renders, not that the AI says it is fixed.

title: 02-1: Quarto Documents and Rendering
section: Working with AI on your own research
text:
Working with AI on your own research
This is the way of working with AI that you should take into your own research. Every exercise in this course uses it, so that it is a habit by the time your thesis needs it.

You ask. Your request says what you want, what you know about the data, and which checks to print.
The AI writes into a Quarto document (.qmd). Code goes into code chunks, with one plain-English sentence above each chunk saying what it does and why.
You render the .qmd to HTML.
You read the HTML and decide whether the work is right: the sentences, the code, and the check results side by side.

Why this matters for research, and why you judge the HTML rather than the chat window:

Rendering runs every chunk from the top in a fresh R session. If the HTML is right, the analysis is reproducible; nothing depends on something typed into the Console and forgotten.
The HTML is a record of what was done to the data and why, with each explanation next to its code and its result. You can reread it months later, and your advisor or a coauthor can review your analysis by reading it, without running anything.
The chat disappears; the .qmd and its HTML stay with your project.




Note


Every request that asks for code ends with the same few lines telling the AI to work this way. This deck calls them the closing instructions; the full text is under Recommended requests near the end.

title: 02-1: Quarto Documents and Rendering
section: What to put in your request
text:
What to put in your request
The AI can write any chunk and any header. What it cannot know is how your document is organised and who reads it. Your request supplies:

Where the code goes: which .qmd, and under which heading
What the reader should see: code shown, code folded behind a button, or only the result. Only setup chunks (loading packages) should be hidden completely.
Which numbers go into sentences: ask for them as inline R, never typed
The checks: what to print so the HTML shows whether the step worked
The closing instructions: which .qmd and heading, a sentence above each chunk, paths built with here::here(), checks printed as expected and got, and render to HTML





Chat assistant or agent?


A chat assistant cannot open or render your files: paste its chunks into your .qmd under the right heading and render yourself. An agent in your editor or terminal, such as Claude Code, can edit and render the file itself. Either way, you read the HTML.

title: 02-1: Quarto Documents and Rendering
section: A weak request and a strong one
text:
A weak request and a strong one

WeakStrongWhat came back


What is the average yield of my fields?
A typical reply is a number in the chat window, or a chunk of code you run at the Console. Either way, the number is not in your document, no one can see how it was made, and the next time the data changes, nothing updates it.


My table fields has one row per field, with columns field, acres and
yield (bushels per acre). Compute the average yield across all fields,
and write one sentence reporting it, with the number written as inline
R rounded to one decimal, not typed. Show the code; do not hide any
chunk. Check the number of fields (I expect 4).

Put the code in my Quarto document analysis/report.qmd, under the
heading "Average yield", as R code chunks. Above each chunk, write one
plain-English sentence saying what it does and why. Build every path
with here::here(); no setwd(), no absolute paths. Print each check on
its own line as "name of check: expected X, got Y". Render the document
to HTML.


What the AI’s answer looks like in the rendered HTML: a sentence, then the chunk it describes, then the sentence with the number.
Check that the table has the four fields expected, then compute the average yield.

cat("number of fields: expected 4, got", nrow(fields), "\n")

number of fields: expected 4, got 4 

avg_yield <- round(mean(fields$yield), 1)

The average yield across the fields is 188.5 bushels per acre.
In the .qmd, that last sentence reads `r avg_yield`, not a typed number. Opening the .qmd to confirm it is part of checking: the HTML looks the same either way.

title: 02-1: Quarto Documents and Rendering
section: What to check in the HTML, and why
text:
What to check in the HTML, and why

The checksWhat the HTML can hideSending the HTML


The AI cannot see the rendered page the way your reader does. Check these every time:










Check
Why
What only you can supply




1
It renders
A render starts from nothing, so it proves nothing depends on your Console
Doing it, and reading the render’s message


2
Every chunk has a sentence above it, and the code does what the sentence says
The sentence is what a reader trusts; a wrong one misleads
Reading both


3
Every “expected X, got Y” line matches
The checks are where a silent mistake shows up
The expected values, from knowing your data


4
No step that changes the data is hidden
A hidden chunk changes the results without a trace in the HTML
Opening the .qmd and looking at the chunk options


5
Every number in a sentence agrees with the result above it, and is inline R in the .qmd
A typed number goes stale without warning
Comparing them





The HTML shows what the chunk options let it show. Here, a chunk with include: false dropped the smallest field before the average was computed. The reader sees only this:
Compute the average yield across the fields.

mean(fields_shown$yield)

[1] 193


Nothing on the page says that a field was dropped. Only the .qmd does, or a check of the number of fields printed in the HTML (expected 4, got 3). This is why check 4 means opening the .qmd, and why every chunk except the setup chunk should be shown or folded, never hidden (an article may also hide a chunk that only prints checks, lecture 02-4).


By default, rendering report.qmd writes report.html and a folder report_files/ holding its figures and styling. The HTML only points at that folder.

Send report.html on its own, and the reader sees it without its figures and styling.
With embed-resources: true under html: in the header, everything is packed into the one HTML file.

To check: move only the .html file to another folder, open it there, and confirm the figures are still in it.

title: 02-1: Quarto Documents and Rendering
section: Your turn: read a .qmd before rendering it
text:
Your turn: read a .qmd before rendering it
An AI added this to a student’s report:
```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(dplyr)
```

```{r}
#| label: clean
#| echo: false
fields <- filter(fields, yield > 0)
```

Compute the total acres.

```{r}
#| label: total-acres
#| eval: false
sum(fields$acres)
```

The fields cover 275 acres in total.

QuestionsAnswers


A. For each of the three chunks: does it run, is its code shown, is its result shown?
B. What happens to the data that the reader of the HTML cannot see?
C. Is “275 acres” computed? How would you tell from the HTML alone, and from the .qmd?
D. What would you ask the AI to change?


A. setup: runs, nothing shown. clean: runs, code hidden (it prints nothing, so the reader sees nothing). total-acres: code shown, but not run, so no total is printed.
B. The clean chunk drops every field with a yield of 0 or less, with no sentence and no code on the page.
C. No. It is typed, and the chunk that would compute it never ran. From the HTML you cannot tell a typed number from a computed one; from the .qmd you can: no `r ` in the sentence.
D. Show the clean chunk with a sentence saying why fields are dropped, and print how many were dropped; remove eval: false; write the total as inline R.

title: 02-1: Quarto Documents and Rendering
section: What you must understand, and what the AI can write
text:
What you must understand, and what the AI can write







You need to understand
The AI can write




What rendering does: a new R session, every chunk from the top, in the .qmd’s folder
The chunks


Why a document that renders is reproducible, and why that does not make it right
The YAML header


What the reader sees under each chunk option, and which steps must stay visible
The chunk options


Which numbers belong in sentences, and that they must be computed
The inline R


How to read a render error and what to send back
The fix



Every document: ask for the code to go into your .qmd, with a sentence above each chunk and checks printed as expected and got. Render, and judge the HTML: the sentences, the code, the checks, and the numbers in the text. Open the .qmd to see what the HTML does not show.

title: 02-3: Websites with Quarto
section: What you will and will not learn today
text:
What you will and will not learn today

The planDirections


A single .qmd renders to one page. When a project has several documents (the data, several analyses, notes for your advisor), Quarto can render them all together into a website: a set of pages joined by a menu. The course website you are reading these slides on is one.
An AI assistant can set up a website and write every configuration line. What it cannot do is:

know who will visit the site and what they come for
decide which pages exist, what is on each, and in what order they appear in the menu
know what must not be made public

So today is about:

The concept: what a website project is, what rendering it does, and what it is for in research
Reading code: recognising the files that make up a website, and the one file that ties them together
Asking AI: what to put in a request for a site
Checking: how to judge a site the way a visitor will use it




Lecture 02-1 (Quarto documents and rendering) comes first; this lecture assumes it.
In RStudio, a new website starts from File, New Project, New Directory, Quarto Website. You will not need to remember that: the AI can create it, or tell you.

title: 02-3: Websites with Quarto
section: What a website is for in research
text:
What a website is for in research

UsesPage or site?










Use
Who visits
What they look for




A project site shared with an advisor or coauthors
People who know the project
The latest results, each with its code and checks, in one place


A lab notebook
You, months later
What was done, when, and why


A course or workshop site
Students
Material in a fixed order


A personal site
Anyone
Who you are, your papers



The first two follow the way of working from lecture 02-1: every analysis is a .qmd that renders to a page with its sentences, code and checks. A website puts those pages under one menu, so a reader can find them without being sent a dozen HTML files.











One .qmd (lecture 02-1)
A website




What you send
One HTML file (with embed-resources: true)
A folder of HTML files, or a web address once it is published


How pages connect
They do not
A menu on every page


Shared settings
Each file has its own header
One file sets the look and the menu for all pages



A website is a folder, not a file. That decides how it is shared (see “Checking the result”).

title: 02-3: Websites with Quarto
section: What rendering a website does
text:
What rendering a website does
When you render the whole website (RStudio: Build tab, Render Website), Quarto:

Renders every .qmd in the project folder, one by one. Each page is rendered in its own new R session, with its own folder as the working directory, exactly as in lecture 02-1.
Adds the menu and the shared look to every page.
Writes the pages into one output folder, _site/ by default, and opens the home page.

What follows from this:

Pages do not share anything. A table made on one page does not exist on another. A page that needs the data reads it itself. (Rendered on its own, a page that uses a table made only on another page stops with object '...' not found.)
Every .qmd becomes a page, whether or not the menu links to it. Files and folders whose names start with _ are left out.
One page that fails stops the render. The error names the file and the chunk, as for a single document.
The _site/ folder is output. Edit the .qmd files, never the HTML in _site/: the next render overwrites it.

title: 02-3: Websites with Quarto
section: The pattern
text:
The pattern

The files_quarto.ymlA pageVariations you will see


Every Quarto website has the same parts:
my-project/
├── _quarto.yml        the settings for the whole site, and the menu
├── index.qmd          the home page
├── data.qmd           one .qmd per page
├── analysis.qmd
├── about.qmd
├── data/              files the pages read
└── _site/             the rendered website (output; never edit)








Part
What it is
Required?




_quarto.yml
Makes the folder a website, and sets the menu and look for every page
Yes


index.qmd
The home page; it becomes index.html, which a browser opens first
Yes


Other .qmd files
One per page
No


_site/
Written by rendering
Made for you





_quarto.yml is written in YAML, like a document’s header (lecture 02-1), but on its own in a file:
project:
  type: website

website:
  title: "Corn yield project"
  navbar:
    left:
      - href: index.qmd
        text: Home
      - href: data.qmd
        text: Data
      - href: analysis.qmd
        text: Analysis
      - about.qmd

format:
  html:
    toc: true







Part
What it does




project: type: website
Makes the folder a website


website: title:
The site name, at the left of the menu


navbar: left:
The menu along the top, in this order. Each - href: is one entry: the file, and text: the word shown. A file alone (- about.qmd) shows the page’s own title.


format: html:
Settings that apply to every page, so pages do not repeat them in their own headers





A page is an ordinary .qmd. Its header can be short, because the shared settings come from _quarto.yml:
---
title: "Analysis"
---

Read the county yield data.

```{r}
#| label: read-yields
yields <- readr::read_csv(here::here("data", "yields.csv"))
```
here::here() works on every page, wherever its .qmd sits in the project, because it builds paths from the project folder (lecture 03-1).



output-dir: docs under project:: write the site into docs/ instead of _site/. Used when the site is published from GitHub.
execute: freeze: auto: rerun a page’s code only when that page’s .qmd has changed. With many slow pages, this saves time; the results of unchanged pages come from the last time they ran, kept in a _freeze/ folder.
sidebar: instead of, or with, navbar:: a menu down the side.
A listing: in a page’s header: the page lists other pages automatically, as the course’s lecture index does.
render: under project:: a list saying which files to render, so others are left out.

title: 02-3: Websites with Quarto
section: The same way of working, for a website
text:
The same way of working, for a website
The way of working with AI from lecture 02-1 applies to every page: the AI writes into a .qmd, with one plain-English sentence above each chunk, and you render and judge the rendered pages, not the chat. Two things are added for a site:

The structure is a decision, made before any code. Which pages, what is on each, in what order in the menu. Write it down as a list, the site map, and give it to the AI.
You judge the site by using it: starting from the home page and clicking, as a visitor would.




Note


Every request for code still ends with the closing instructions; the full text is under Recommended requests near the end. For a site, the .qmd they name is the page the code goes on.

title: 02-3: Websites with Quarto
section: What to put in your request
text:
What to put in your request

Who visits, and what for: an advisor checking results, a coauthor, the public
The site map: each page, its file name, what it shows, and the order in the menu
Where the data is, and which pages read it
What must stay out: data you may not share, passwords and keys, drafts
The checks, on the page where the data is read
The closing instructions





Public means public


A website that is published can be read by anyone, and so can any file inside the published folder. Data under a licence, personal information, and keys to online services (for example a key to a data service written in a chunk) must not be in it. The AI does not know what your data agreement allows; you must tell it.

title: 02-3: Websites with Quarto
section: A weak request and a strong one
text:
A weak request and a strong one

WeakStrongWhat came back


Make a website for my project.
A typical result: the template’s two pages, “Home” and “About”, with placeholder text, and nothing from your project. Or, if the AI can see your files, one page for each .qmd it finds, in alphabetical order, including drafts and notes you never meant to show.


An example for a project shared with an advisor:
Turn my project folder into a Quarto website. The visitor is my
advisor, who wants to see the latest results with their code and
checks. Pages, in this order in the menu at the top:
1. Home (index.qmd): two sentences on what the project is, and links
   to the other pages
2. Data (data.qmd): reads data/yields.csv and shows its checks
3. Analysis (analysis.qmd): the analysis now in analysis/report.qmd
Move the analysis out of analysis/report.qmd into analysis.qmd, and
leave out the folders notes/ and analysis/. Every page reads the data it
needs itself. On the Data page, check the number of rows (I expect 400).

Put the code in my Quarto document data.qmd, under the heading "Read
the data", as R code chunks. Above each chunk, write one plain-English
sentence saying what it does and why. Build every path with
here::here(); no setwd(), no absolute paths. Print each check on its
own line as "name of check: expected X, got Y". Render the document to
HTML.


The menu part of the _quarto.yml the AI wrote:
website:
  title: "Corn yield project"
  navbar:
    left:
      - href: index.qmd
        text: Home
      - href: data.qmd
        text: Data
      - href: analysis.qmd
        text: Analysis
Check it against the site map: three entries, in the order asked. Then check what is not in the menu: if notes/ or analysis/ holds .qmd files, they are still rendered into pages unless they are excluded (for example with render: under project:, or by a folder name starting with _). Ask the AI which of the two it did, and look in _site/ to confirm.

title: 02-3: Websites with Quarto
section: Judging a site as a visitor will use it
text:
Judging a site as a visitor will use it

The checksSharing a site












Check
How
Why




1
The whole site renders
Render Website, and read its message
Proves every page builds from its own .qmd


2
Every page in the site map is in the menu, in order
Open the home page; read the menu
A page not in the menu exists, but no visitor will find it


3
Every page can be reached by clicking, starting from the home page
Click through every menu entry and every link
Typing an address is not how visitors arrive


4
Nothing is on the site that should not be
Look at every file in _site/, not only the pages in the menu
Every .qmd becomes a page, and published files can be read by anyone


5
Each page passes the checks from lecture 02-1
Sentences, checks printed as expected and got, no hidden steps
A page of a site is a document like any other





A website is the whole output folder: pages link to each other and to the shared files in site_libs/ inside it. So:

Sending one page’s HTML file does not send the site: its menu points at pages the recipient does not have.
To share it before it is published, send the whole _site/ folder, zipped. Opened from the folder, index.html works, and so do the links between pages.
To put it online, the folder is published, for example with GitHub Pages or Quarto Pub. Ask the AI for the steps when you need them, and decide first, with check 4, what may be public.

title: 02-3: Websites with Quarto
section: Your turn: read a _quarto.yml
text:
Your turn: read a _quarto.yml
A student’s project folder holds index.qmd, cleaning.qmd, results.qmd, old-results.qmd and _quarto.yml:
project:
  type: website

website:
  title: "Thesis"
  navbar:
    left:
      - href: index.qmd
        text: Home
      - href: results.qmd
        text: Results

QuestionsAnswers


A. Which pages will be in _site/ after rendering the website?
B. Which can a visitor reach by clicking from the home page?
C. The student’s advisor asks how the data was cleaned. What is wrong, and what would you ask the AI to change?


A. Four: index.html, cleaning.html, results.html, old-results.html. Every .qmd is rendered.
B. Home and Results only (unless the text of a page links to the others).
C. The cleaning page exists but is not in the menu, so the advisor cannot find it; and the old results are built and sit in the site, where they could be mistaken for current ones if anyone found them. Ask the AI to add the cleaning page to the menu before Results, and to leave old-results.qmd out of the render (or move it into a folder whose name starts with _). Then render and check _site/ again.

title: 02-3: Websites with Quarto

Requests you can copy

Closing instructionsMake a siteAdd a pageExplain a site

title: 03-1: Getting Data In and Out of R
section: What you will and will not learn today
text:
What you will and will not learn today

The planDirections


An AI assistant can write the code that reads a file into R. It knows every function and every argument. What it cannot do is:

see the files on your computer
know what is inside them
know what the data is for
tell whether the result is right

Those four are your job. So today is about:

The concept: what importing and exporting are, and what has to be true for them to work
Reading code: recognising what a line of import code does, without memorising it
Asking AI: what to put in your request
Checking: how to tell whether the code the AI wrote did the right thing




Clone this repository, which holds the datasets used here
Ask your AI assistant to install the tidyverse, haven and here packages if you have not already. Installing is a one-time step per computer (see the packages slide in Chapter 1).

title: 03-1: Getting Data In and Out of R
section: How reading code is written
text:
How reading code is written
A data file is a table saved on disk in some format. Reading it means a function opens the file and builds a table inside R (R calls it a data frame; this deck says table) that you give a name to. Whatever the format, and whichever function the AI picks, the code follows the same pattern.

The patternEvery reader follows the patternOptionsVariations you will see



table_name <- reader_function("path/to/file", option = value, ...)









Part
What it is
Required?




table_name <-
The name the table will have inside R. <- stores the result under that name.
Needed to keep the result


reader_function
The function that understands the file’s format
Yes


"path/to/file"
Where the file is, always the first input
Yes, the only required input


option = value
Extra instructions about the layout and types
No; each has a default



A real line that follows the pattern:

corn <- read_csv("corn_yields.csv")

On these slides the data files sit in the same folder as the slides, so a path is just the file name. In your own project, paths are built with here::here() (see Condition 1).


Readers differ in name and package, not in pattern. The shortest call to each is the path and nothing else:








Format
Shortest call
Package




csv
read_csv("corn.csv")
readr (tidyverse)


csv
read.csv("corn.csv")
built into R


Excel
read_excel("corn.xlsx"), or read_xls(), read_xlsx()
readxl


STATA
read_dta("corn.dta")
haven


R’s own
readRDS("corn.rds")
built into R



The help pages call the first input file for some readers and path for others. The name differs; its position, first, does not.


Everything after the path is optional and written as name = value. Each option you leave out takes its default, a value chosen by whoever wrote the function. Options you will see, grouped by what they tell the reader:

Which part of the file: sheet = "corn_yields_08" (Excel), skip = 2 (ignore lines above the column names)
What marks a missing value: na = c("", ".", "-999") (for read.csv(), na.strings =)
What type each column is: col_types = ..., for example to keep an ID column as text




Important


A default is a guess about your file. When the guess is wrong, R gives no error, and that is where the silent failures later in this deck come from. Knowing what your file looks like is how you know which options the AI must set.





AI-written code often wraps the same pattern in extra pieces. They change how the line looks, not what it does:

readr::read_csv(...): the package name, then ::, then the function. Uses the function without loading the whole package.
read_csv(here::here("data", "corn.csv")): the path is built by another function instead of typed out (see Condition 1).
path <- here::here("data", "corn.csv") on one line, then read_csv(path) on the next: the path is stored first and used later.
read_csv(...) |> some_other_step(): the table is passed straight on to a next step (|>) before it is stored.

title: 03-1: Getting Data In and Out of R
section: What has to be true for an import to work
text:
What has to be true for an import to work

The four conditionsFailures with and without an error



R can find the file. The path points at a file that exists.
The reader matches the format. A csv reader for a csv file, an Excel reader for an Excel file.
The reader understands the layout. Where the column names are, which sheet to read, what marks a missing value.
Each column gets the right type. Numbers as numbers, text as text, IDs kept exactly as written.




If condition 1 or 2 fails, R stops with an error. Annoying, but you know something is wrong.
If condition 3 or 4 fails, R gives you a table with no error, and the table is wrong. This deck calls these silent failures.




Important


The silent failures are why checking matters. Code that runs is not the same as code that is right.

title: 03-1: Getting Data In and Out of R
section: Condition 1: R can find the file
text:
Condition 1: R can find the file

PathsThe project root and here()Why AI gets this wrong


A path is the address of a file. There are two kinds:

Absolute path: starts at the top of the disk, for example "/Users/taro/Documents/class/corn_yields.csv". It works only on the computer it was written on, because nobody else has those folders.
Relative path: starts from the folder R is currently in (the working directory), for example "data/corn_yields.csv". It works only if R is in the folder you expected, and that folder changes:
At the Console: your project folder (if you opened an R Project, explained in the next tab)
Inside a .qmd file: the folder the .qmd is saved in

So "data/corn_yields.csv" can work at the Console and fail when a .qmd in analysis/ is rendered.


An R Project is a folder that RStudio marks with a .Rproj file; you open the project by opening that file. The top of that folder is the project root.
The safest path is one measured from the project root, whatever folder R is in. The here package does that: it finds the project root by looking for the .Rproj file. Recognise it when you see it:

corn <- read_csv(here::here("data", "corn_yields.csv"))

This reads data/corn_yields.csv inside your project, whichever subfolder your code is in and whoever’s computer it runs on. To check it is set up, run here::here() on its own at the Console: it should print your project folder.


The AI cannot see your folders, so it guesses the path. Its guesses tend to be one of these:

just the file name, assuming the file is in the working directory
an absolute path copied from an example, such as "C:/Users/yourname/..."
setwd(...) to change the working directory first

All three break as soon as the code runs somewhere else. Tell it where the file is (see “Asking AI” below).
If R says the file does not exist, send the AI the exact error message, the folder your .qmd is in, and where the file is inside your project.

title: 03-1: Getting Data In and Out of R
section: Condition 2: the reader matches the format
text:
Condition 2: the reader matches the format
The file extension (the part after the last dot) tells you the format. Tell the AI the extension and it will pick a reader from the list under “How reading code is written”. What you need to know is what each format keeps, because that decides what can go wrong:








Extension
Format
What the file keeps




.csv
plain text, any software opens it
Only text. Types are guessed on reading.


.xls, .xlsx
Excel workbook
Several sheets per file; a reader takes the first unless told otherwise


.dta
STATA
Types, and a description stored with each column


.rds
R’s own format
The exact R object, nothing guessed






Note


A csv file stores everything as text, so the reader has to guess each column’s type. That guessing is where conditions 3 and 4 go wrong.

title: 03-1: Getting Data In and Out of R
section: Conditions 3 and 4: the silent failures
text:
Conditions 3 and 4: the silent failures

Lost leading zerosCodes for missing valuesThe wrong sheet


County codes (FIPS) for Alabama start with 0. Here is a tiny csv, written straight into the code, and what the reader makes of it:

small_csv <- "fips,county,yield
01001,Autauga,150
01003,Baldwin,-999
31019,Buffalo,173"

small <- read_csv(I(small_csv), show_col_types = FALSE)
small$fips

[1] "01001" "01003" "31019"

read.csv(text = small_csv)$fips

[1]  1001  1003 31019


The two readers guessed differently about the same file. read_csv() kept 01001 as text. read.csv(), the built-in reader that AI assistants often write, decided the column was a number and turned 01001 into 1001. No error either way. Later, joining that table to another one by fips would quietly fail to match these counties.


The same file uses -999 to mean “no data”, a common convention. The reader does not know that:

mean(small$yield)

[1] -225.3333


An average yield of -225.3 bushels per acre, which is impossible. Again no error. The reader has to be told that -999 means missing.


corn_yields.xls has two sheets:

readxl::excel_sheets("corn_yields.xls")

[1] "corn_yields_08" "corn_yields_09"


A reader told nothing about sheets reads the first one only. If you wanted both years, you now have half the data, with no error.

title: 03-1: Getting Data In and Out of R
section: Working with AI on your own research
text:
Working with AI on your own research
Importing follows the way of working with AI from lecture 02-1 (“Working with AI on your own research”), which is also how to work on your own research:

You ask. Your request says what you want, what you know about the data, and which checks to print.
The AI writes into a Quarto document (.qmd), with one plain-English sentence above each chunk saying what it does and why.
You render the .qmd to HTML.
You read the HTML and decide whether the work is right: the sentences, the code, and the check results side by side.




Note


Every request that asks for code ends with the same few lines telling the AI to work this way. This deck calls them the closing instructions; the full text is under Recommended requests near the end.

title: 03-1: Getting Data In and Out of R
section: Look at the file before you ask
text:
Look at the file before you ask

WhyRaw first lines of a csvCounting lines


You cannot describe a file you have not looked at, and you cannot check an import without knowing what the file holds. Two ways to look:

Open it: a csv in a text editor, an Excel file in Excel
Ask R to show the raw first lines, before any reader has guessed anything




readLines("corn_yields.csv", n = 3)

[1] "Year,State,FIPS,County_name,State_name,Commodity,Data item,Irrigated,Yield"                         
[2] "2008,31,31019,BUFFALO,NEBRASKA,CORN,\"CORN, GRAIN - YIELD, MEASURED IN BU / ACRE\",0,173"           
[3] "2008,31,31019,BUFFALO,NEBRASKA,CORN,\"CORN, GRAIN, IRRIGATED - YIELD, MEASURED IN BU / ACRE\",1,182"


From this you learn: the first line is column names, values are separated by commas, FIPS is a 5-digit code, one column name (Data item) has a space in it.



length(readLines("corn_yields.csv"))

[1] 162


162 lines, one of which is the column names. So a correct import has 161 rows. Write that number down before you import.

title: 03-1: Getting Data In and Out of R
section: What to put in your request
text:
What to put in your request
The AI already knows the functions. Your request supplies what it cannot know, most of it from looking at the file:

The file: its name, its format, and where it sits inside your project
What is inside: the first few lines, the sheet names, and anything unusual (IDs with leading zeros, codes for missing values)
What you want back: the name of the table, what one row is, and which type each key column should be
Your project’s rules, if you have any beyond the closing instructions: for example, use the tidyverse
Ask for checks: have it print the numbers you will check against (next section)
The closing instructions: which .qmd and heading the code goes under, a sentence above each chunk, paths built with here::here(), checks printed as expected and got, and render to HTML





Using an agent in your editor or terminal?


An agent such as Claude Code can open the file and look for itself. Still write down what you expect (number of rows, types of key columns) before it runs, so you have something to compare against.

title: 03-1: Getting Data In and Out of R
section: A weak request and a strong one
text:
A weak request and a strong one

WeakStrongWhat came back


Read my corn data into R.
The AI has to guess the file name, its location, its format, its layout and what you want. A typical reply:

setwd("C:/Users/yourname/Documents")
corn <- read.csv("corn.csv")

It runs on nobody’s computer as written, and if you fix the path, it still guesses every type.


An example for a workbook with one sheet per year:
In my R project, the file data/corn_yields.xls is an Excel workbook with
two sheets, corn_yields_08 and corn_yields_09 (one per year). Each row is
one county, one year, and one irrigation status. I want both sheets
stacked into one table called corn, using the tidyverse, with FIPS kept
as text so leading zeros survive.

Then check the number of rows from each sheet (I expect 161 each), the
number of rows in corn (322), the type of every column, and the number
of missing values in each column (I expect none).

Put the code in my Quarto document analysis/import.qmd, under the
heading "Read the corn data", as R code chunks. Above each chunk, write
one plain-English sentence saying what it does and why. Build every path
with here::here(); no setwd(), no absolute paths. Print each check on
its own line as "name of check: expected X, got Y". Render the document
to HTML.


What the AI’s answer looks like in the rendered HTML: a sentence, then the chunk it describes. Read each sentence and check that the code under it does what the sentence says.
Read both sheets, keeping every column as text so that FIPS keeps its leading zeros.

library(readxl)
library(dplyr)

path <- here::here("data", "corn_yields.xls")
corn_08 <- read_excel(path, sheet = "corn_yields_08", col_types = "text")
corn_09 <- read_excel(path, sheet = "corn_yields_09", col_types = "text")

Stack the two sheets into one table, then turn Year and Yield back into numbers, since they were read as text.

corn <- bind_rows(corn_08, corn_09) |>
  mutate(Year = as.integer(Year), Yield = as.numeric(Yield))

Print the checks: rows per sheet and in total, the type of every column, and missing values per column.

cat("rows in 2008 sheet: expected 161, got", nrow(corn_08), "\n")
cat("rows in 2009 sheet: expected 161, got", nrow(corn_09), "\n")
cat("rows in corn: expected 322, got", nrow(corn), "\n")
sapply(corn, class)
cat("missing values: expected 0, got", sum(is.na(corn)), "\n")

Two things to notice. library() loads a package so its functions can be used, and bind_rows() stacks one table on top of another (you will meet it properly later in this chapter). And the type check would show that State and Irrigated are still text, because only Year and Yield were turned back into numbers. That is the type check doing its job: you would ask the AI to make those two numbers as well.

title: 03-1: Getting Data In and Out of R
section: Checking: what to ask for, and why
text:
Checking: what to ask for, and why

The five checksAsking for themReading the HTML


The AI can write the checking code. It cannot decide which checks your file needs, and it cannot know the right answers. Ask for these after every import:










Ask the AI to print
Why
What only you can supply




1
the number of rows and columns
Rows go missing or appear when the wrong sheet is read or a title line is read as data
the row count from looking at the file


2
the type of every column
A wrong guess (an ID read as a number, a number read as text) gives no error
which type each key column should be


3
the number of missing values in each column
A missing-value code the reader was not told about, such as -999, is kept as a real value
how the file marks missing values


4
the smallest and largest value of each numeric column
Impossible values expose those codes, and unit mistakes
what range is believable


5
the first row
Shifted or merged columns show up at once
the same row in the raw file





One sentence at the end of your request does it:
After reading the file, print: the number of rows and columns, the type of
every column, the number of missing values in each column, the smallest and
largest value of each numeric column, and the first row.
Better still, tell it what you expect, so the HTML says which checks passed:
I expect <number> rows, <number> columns, <ID columns> as text, <how many>
missing values, and <column> between <lowest> and <highest>. Print each
check on its own line as "name of check: expected X, got Y".
The second version only works if you looked at the file first. That part only you can do.


For corn_yields.csv, the student expected 161 rows (from counting lines), 9 columns, FIPS as text, no missing values, and yields between 100 and 250. The AI wrote the code; in the rendered HTML, you read each line:


Code the AI wrote
cat(
  paste("rows: expected 161, got", nrow(corn)),
  paste("columns: expected 9, got", ncol(corn)),
  paste("type of FIPS: expected character, got", class(corn$FIPS)),
  paste("missing values: expected 0, got", sum(is.na(corn))),
  paste("Yield range: expected 100 to 250, got", min(corn$Yield), "to", max(corn$Yield)),
  paste("first row:", paste(unlist(corn[1, ]), collapse = ", ")),
  sep = "\n"
)


rows: expected 161, got 161
columns: expected 9, got 9
type of FIPS: expected character, got numeric
missing values: expected 0, got 0
Yield range: expected 100 to 250, got 103 to 204
first row: 2008, 31, 31019, BUFFALO, NEBRASKA, CORN, CORN, GRAIN - YIELD, MEASURED IN BU / ACRE, 0, 173



Rows, columns, missing values and the yield range match.
The first row matches the second line of the file (shown under “Look at the file before you ask”).
FIPS came back as a number, not the text you expected. In this file every code starts with 31, so nothing was lost, but the check fails, and you would ask the AI to read FIPS as text.

title: 03-1: Getting Data In and Out of R
section: Checks that come from knowing the data
text:
Checks that come from knowing the data
The five checks apply to any file. The most useful checks come from what you know about this data, and no AI will think of them for you.
In corn_yields.csv, most counties have two rows: one for irrigated corn and one for non-irrigated corn. Irrigated corn gets water that rain-fed corn does not, so in each county the irrigated yield should be the higher one. So ask:
Using the table corn, for each county with one irrigated and one
non-irrigated row, check whether the irrigated yield is higher. Print
how many counties pass and how many fail.

Put the code in my Quarto document analysis/import.qmd, under the
heading "Read the corn data", as R code chunks. Above each chunk, write
one plain-English sentence saying what it does and why. Build every path
with here::here(); no setwd(), no absolute paths. Print each check on
its own line as "name of check: expected X, got Y". Render the document
to HTML.
The AI’s code, and what it printed:


Code the AI wrote
corn |>
  group_by(FIPS) |>
  filter(n() == 2, n_distinct(Irrigated) == 2) |>
  summarise(irrigated_higher = Yield[Irrigated == 1] > Yield[Irrigated == 0]) |>
  count(irrigated_higher)


# A tibble: 1 × 2
  irrigated_higher     n
  <lgl>            <int>
1 TRUE                70


All 70 counties pass. A row count or a type check could never have tested this; only what you know about corn could.
When a check like this fails, the code is usually not the problem: the file is. Stop, and ask whoever produced the file before you analyse it.

title: 03-1: Getting Data In and Out of R
section: Your turn: read the AI’s code
text:
Your turn: read the AI’s code
A student asked an AI to “load corn_yields.xls and compute the average yield”, and got this:

setwd("C:/Users/jsmith/Desktop/class")
library(readxl)
corn <- read_excel("corn_yields.xls")
mean(corn$Yield)


QuestionsAnswers


A. What does each of the four lines do?
B. Which line will fail on your computer, and why?
C. Which problem would give a wrong answer without an error?
D. Rewrite the request so the AI could not make these mistakes.


A. Changes the working directory; loads readxl; reads the workbook into corn; averages the Yield column.
B. Line 1. The folder C:/Users/jsmith/... exists only on jsmith’s computer.
C. Line 3 reads only the first sheet, so corn holds 2008 only, and nothing says so. The average leaves out 2009.
D. Name both sheets, say whether you want both years or one, ask for here::here() and no setwd(), and ask it to print the row count per sheet.

title: 03-1: Getting Data In and Out of R
section: How writing code is written
text:
How writing code is written
Writing (exporting) is reading in reverse: a function takes a table from R and saves it as a file. Again, every writer follows the same pattern.

The patternEvery writer follows the patternA default that surprisesChoosing a format



writer_function(table_name, "path/to/file", option = value, ...)









Part
What it is
Required?




writer_function
The function that writes this format
Yes


table_name
The table to save, always the first input
Yes


"path/to/file"
Where to save it, always the second input
Yes


option = value
Extra instructions, such as how to write missing values
No; each has a default



Two differences from reading:

There is no table_name <- in front. The result is a file on disk, not a new table in R.
If a file already exists at that path, it is replaced without asking. Writing to the same path as your raw data destroys the raw data.






Format
Shortest call
Package




csv
write_csv(corn, "corn.csv")
readr (tidyverse)


csv
write.csv(corn, "corn.csv")
built into R


Excel
write_xlsx(corn, "corn.xlsx")
writexl


STATA
write_dta(corn, "corn.dta")
haven


R’s own
saveRDS(corn, "corn.rds")
built into R



The same variations as for reading appear here too: readr::write_csv(...), and the path built with here::here(...).


Defaults matter when writing too. The built-in write.csv() adds a column of row numbers by default. Read the file back, and that column returns as an extra column:

tmp <- file.path(tempdir(), "corn_base.csv")
write.csv(corn, tmp)
names(read.csv(tmp))

 [1] "X"           "Year"        "State"       "FIPS"        "County_name"
 [6] "State_name"  "Commodity"   "Data.item"   "Irrigated"   "Yield"      


The extra first column, X, holds 1, 2, 3, and so on. Adding row.names = FALSE prevents it; write_csv() never adds it. When the AI writes write.csv(), check for that option.
Notice also that Data item came back as Data.item. That one is a default of the reader: read.csv() replaces spaces in column names with dots, and read_csv() does not.


The decision that is yours is the format, and it depends on who reads the file next and what has to survive:








Format
Choose it when
What is lost




csv
anyone, in any software, must be able to read it
every type: dates, factors (columns of categories) and text IDs come back as guesses


rds
you, in R, will read it in the next step of the project
nothing, but only R can open it


dta
a collaborator uses STATA
some R-only types







A reasonable default


Keep raw data as you received it. Save intermediate results as rds, so types survive from one script to the next.

title: 03-1: Getting Data In and Out of R
section: Checking an export: the round trip
text:
Checking an export: the round trip
Why: a file can quietly keep less than you saved. The only way to know what it kept is to read it back.
What to ask: “Save the table, read it back, and compare it with the original.” Here Irrigated was first made a factor, then saved as csv and as rds:


Code the AI wrote
corn_f <- mutate(corn, Irrigated = factor(Irrigated, labels = c("no", "yes")))

csv_file <- file.path(tempdir(), "corn.csv")
rds_file <- file.path(tempdir(), "corn.rds")
write_csv(corn_f, csv_file)
saveRDS(corn_f, rds_file)

c(
  from_csv = class(read_csv(csv_file, show_col_types = FALSE)$Irrigated),
  from_rds = class(readRDS(rds_file)$Irrigated)
)


   from_csv    from_rds 
"character"    "factor" 


The csv gave back text: the factor was lost. The rds gave back the factor.
The request is under Recommended requests, tab “Save and read back”.

title: 03-1: Getting Data In and Out of R
section: Requests you can copy
text:
Requests you can copy
Copy one, then replace every <...> with what you found by looking at the file. The blanks are the part the AI cannot fill in for you. Every request for code ends with the closing instructions.

What you must understand, and what the AI can write







You need to understand
The AI can write

The here::here() call

Which reader to use and its arguments

col_types, na, sheet and so on

title: 03-3: Reshaping and Merging
section: What you will and will not learn today
text:
What you will and will not learn today

The planDirections


Two operations change how your data is spread over rows, columns and tables:

Reshaping rearranges one table, so that one row means something else
Merging combines two tables, by matching their rows

An AI assistant writes the code for both in a line or two. What it cannot do is:

know what one row of each of your tables is
know which columns identify a row, and whether they really do
know whether the same county, year or person is written the same way in both tables
tell whether the result has the rows it should

Those four are your job. So today is about:

The concept: what long and wide are, what a merge is, and what has to be true for each to work
Reading code: the pattern reshaping and merging code follows
Asking AI: what to put in your request
Checking: the row counts, unmatched rows and repeated keys that tell you whether it worked




You need the tidyverse package, installed in 03-1. It includes tidyr (reshaping) and dplyr (merging).
The examples use corn_yields.csv from 03-1: corn yields for Nebraska counties in 2008, one row per county and irrigation status. On these slides the file sits in the same folder as the slides, so the code uses just its name. FIPS, the county code, is read as text, as 03-1 recommended.

title: 03-3: Reshaping and Merging
section: Long and wide
text:
Long and wide
The same numbers can be laid out in two ways. Three counties from corn_yields.csv:

LongWideWhich one you need




# A tibble: 6 × 4
  FIPS  County_name Irrigated Yield
  <chr> <chr>           <dbl> <dbl>
1 31019 BUFFALO             0   173
2 31019 BUFFALO             1   182
3 31041 CUSTER              0   163
4 31041 CUSTER              1   182
5 31047 DAWSON              0   177
6 31047 DAWSON              1   180


One row is one county and one irrigation status. Each yield has its own row; the column Irrigated says which kind of yield it is.




# A tibble: 3 × 4
  FIPS  County_name yield_0 yield_1
  <chr> <chr>         <dbl>   <dbl>
1 31019 BUFFALO         173     182
2 31041 CUSTER          163     182
3 31047 DAWSON          177     180


One row is one county. The irrigation status has moved into the column names: yield_0 holds non-irrigated yields and yield_1 irrigated ones. Nothing in the data says that; you have to know it.


Neither layout is right in general. The one you need depends on the next step:

Wide when the next step compares values side by side within a row: “irrigated minus non-irrigated yield, for each county” is one mutate() on the wide table.
Long when the next step works on one column of values: “the average yield by irrigation status” is group_by() and summarise() on the long table, and most figures (Chapter 4) want long data.

So “reshape this table” is not a request. “Make one row per county, with one yield column per irrigation status” is.

title: 03-3: Reshaping and Merging
section: How reshaping code is written
text:
How reshaping code is written
Reshaping goes in one of two directions, and the code for each follows its own pattern.

Long to wideWide to longVariations you will see



wide_table <- long_table |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = column_with_new_names, values_from = column_with_values)









Part
What it is
Required?




long_table
The table to reshape
Yes


names_from =
The column whose values become the new column names (here Irrigated)
Yes


values_from =
The column whose values fill the new columns (here Yield)
Yes


every other column
Used to decide which rows belong together in one wide row (here FIPS and County_name)
Not written; all the remaining columns are used


names_prefix = and others
Extra instructions, such as text put in front of the new names
No



The last row is where most problems come from: the columns you did not mention decide what one row of the result is.



long_table <- wide_table |>
  pivot_longer(columns_to_stack, names_to = "new_name_column", values_to = "new_value_column")









Part
What it is
Required?




wide_table
The table to reshape
Yes


columns_to_stack
The columns whose values go into one column, for example starts_with("yield_")
Yes


names_to =
The name of the new column that will hold the old column names
No; the default is "name"


values_to =
The name of the new column that will hold the values
No; the default is "value"



A real example, the three-county table back to long:

three_wide |>
  pivot_longer(starts_with("yield_"), names_to = "Irrigated", values_to = "Yield")

# A tibble: 6 × 4
  FIPS  County_name Irrigated Yield
  <chr> <chr>       <chr>     <dbl>
1 31019 BUFFALO     yield_0     173
2 31019 BUFFALO     yield_1     182
3 31041 CUSTER      yield_0     163
4 31041 CUSTER      yield_1     182
5 31047 DAWSON      yield_0     177
6 31047 DAWSON      yield_1     180


The old column names are now values, and they are text: "yield_0", not the number 0. Turning them back into numbers is a separate step.


The same two operations have other names, from older packages and other styles:








Long to wide
Wide to long
Where from




pivot_wider()
pivot_longer()
tidyr (tidyverse), current


spread()
gather()
tidyr, older versions


dcast()
melt()
data.table and reshape2


reshape(direction = "wide")
reshape(direction = "long")
built into R



Whatever the name, look for the same three things: which columns become names, which hold values, and which identify a row.

title: 03-3: Reshaping and Merging
section: What has to be true for a reshape to work
text:
What has to be true for a reshape to work

The conditionsA column that differsA combination that repeats


For long to wide:

You know which columns identify one row of the result (here, FIPS and County_name for one row per county).
No other column differs within that row. Every column that is neither the identifier, nor the names column, nor the values column must have the same value on all the rows that are combined, or be dropped first.
Each identifier and name appears only once. One county must not have two non-irrigated yields.

For wide to long, the main condition is that the stacked columns hold the same kind of value (all yields, in the same units).
Breaking condition 2 gives a wrong table with no error. Breaking condition 3 gives a warning. The next two tabs show both with corn_yields.csv.


Data item describes the row, and the description is different for irrigated and non-irrigated corn. Leave it in, and it becomes part of the identifier:

corn_wide <- corn |>
  filter(FIPS != "31000") |>
  select(FIPS, County_name, `Data item`, Irrigated, Yield) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = Irrigated, values_from = Yield, names_prefix = "yield_")
nrow(corn_wide)

[1] 155

n_distinct(corn_wide$FIPS)

[1] 85


155 rows for 85 counties. The rows were never combined: each county with both kinds of yield still has two rows, one with yield_1 missing and one with yield_0 missing. No error, no warning. (FIPS 31000 is left out here; the next tab explains why.)
Without Data item:

corn_wide <- corn |>
  filter(FIPS != "31000") |>
  select(FIPS, County_name, Irrigated, Yield) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = Irrigated, values_from = Yield, names_prefix = "yield_")
nrow(corn_wide)

[1] 85

colSums(is.na(corn_wide))

       FIPS County_name     yield_0     yield_1 
          0           0           0          15 


One row per county. The 15 missing irrigated yields are real: those counties have no irrigated row in the file.



corn_wide_all <- corn |>
  select(FIPS, County_name, Irrigated, Yield) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = Irrigated, values_from = Yield, names_prefix = "yield_")

Warning: Values from `Yield` are not uniquely identified; output will contain list-cols.
• Use `values_fn = list` to suppress this warning.
• Use `values_fn = {summary_fun}` to summarise duplicates.
• Use the following dplyr code to identify duplicates.
  {data} |>
  dplyr::summarise(n = dplyr::n(), .by = c(FIPS, County_name, Irrigated)) |>
  dplyr::filter(n > 1L)


The warning says some values “are not uniquely identified”. The cause is one code:

count(corn, FIPS, County_name, Irrigated) |>
  filter(n > 1)

# A tibble: 2 × 4
  FIPS  County_name               Irrigated     n
  <chr> <chr>                         <dbl> <int>
1 31000 OTHER (COMBINED) COUNTIES         0     2
2 31000 OTHER (COMBINED) COUNTIES         1     4


FIPS 31000 is OTHER (COMBINED) COUNTIES: the yields of several small counties, reported together under one code. It has 4 irrigated and 2 non-irrigated rows, so there is no single value to put in its cell. Here R warns. R still returns a table, with several values stored in the cell for 31000. The warning suggests values_fn =, and an AI asked to get rid of the warning may add values_fn = mean, which averages the rows and hides the problem. Read the repeated rows first (see “Checks that come from knowing the data”). What to do (drop these rows, or find out which counties each one covers) is a decision about the data, not the code.

title: 03-3: Reshaping and Merging
section: Checking a reshape
text:
Checking a reshape
Why: a reshape changes the number of rows in a way you can work out before running it. If the count is wrong, the identifier was wrong.








Direction
Expected rows
Expected missing values




Long to wide
the number of distinct identifiers (for one row per county: the number of counties)
the identifier and name combinations that are not in the long table


Wide to long
wide rows × the number of stacked columns
the missing values in the stacked columns, unless the request says to drop them



For the table above: 85 counties after leaving out 31000, so 85 rows wide, and back to long 85 × 2 = 170 rows, of which 15 have a missing yield.
A third check needs no arithmetic: the total of the values does not change. The sum of all yields before and after a reshape must be the same, apart from missing values.


Code the AI wrote
before <- corn |> filter(FIPS != "31000")
back_long <- corn_wide |>
  pivot_longer(starts_with("yield_"), names_to = "Irrigated", values_to = "Yield")
cat(
  paste("wide rows: expected", n_distinct(before$FIPS), "got", nrow(corn_wide)),
  paste("long rows: expected", 2 * nrow(corn_wide), "got", nrow(back_long)),
  paste("missing yields after: expected", sum(is.na(corn_wide$yield_1)), "got", sum(is.na(back_long$Yield))),
  paste("total yield: expected", sum(before$Yield), "got", sum(back_long$Yield, na.rm = TRUE)),
  sep = "\n"
)


wide rows: expected 85 got 85
long rows: expected 170 got 170
missing yields after: expected 15 got 15
total yield: expected 26231 got 26231

title: 03-3: Reshaping and Merging
section: What a merge is
text:
What a merge is

Matching rows by keyMerging and stacking


A merge (also called a join) adds columns from a second table to a first one, by matching rows that refer to the same thing: the same county, the same county and year, the same person.
The columns used to match are the key. A key has to identify each row: in a table with one row per county and year, the key is the county code and the year together.
The yields:


# A tibble: 3 × 3
  fips   year yield
  <chr> <dbl> <dbl>
1 31019  2008   173
2 31041  2008   163
3 31047  2008   177


The rainfall:


# A tibble: 3 × 3
  fips   year rain_mm
  <chr> <dbl>   <dbl>
1 31019  2008     510
2 31041  2008     480
3 31047  2008     530


Matching on fips and year puts each county’s rainfall next to its yield. (These rainfall numbers are made up for this example.)


# A tibble: 3 × 4
  fips   year yield rain_mm
  <chr> <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl>
1 31019  2008   173     510
2 31041  2008   163     480
3 31047  2008   177     530




There are two ways to combine tables, and they answer different needs:









Merging
Stacking




What it adds
columns, from another table about the same things
rows, from another table with the same columns


Example
yields and rainfall, both by county and year
the 2008 sheet and the 2009 sheet of corn_yields.xls


What has to match
the values in the key columns
the column names and types



Stacking has its own slide after the merging slides.

title: 03-3: Reshaping and Merging
section: How merging code is written
text:
How merging code is written

The patternEvery join follows the patternVariations you will see



merged_table <- join_function(first_table, second_table, by = c("key_column_1", "key_column_2"))









Part
What it is
Required?




join_function
Which rows to keep (next tab)
Yes


first_table
The table you start from; with a left join, every one of its rows is kept
Yes


second_table
The table whose columns are added
Yes


by =
The key columns, which must exist in both tables
Without it, every column with the same name in both is used, and a message says which


relationship =, unmatched =
Instructions to stop with an error if the tables are not as expected: a row matching more than one row, or a row that would be dropped
No, but worth asking for (see “Checking a merge”)





The joins differ only in which rows they keep:








Join
Keeps
Rows of the first table with no match




left_join()
every row of the first table
kept, with the new columns missing (NA)


inner_join()
only rows that match in both
dropped


full_join()
every row of both tables
kept, with missing values on whichever side has no match


anti_join()
rows of the first table that have no match; adds no columns
(this is the check for unmatched rows)



left_join() is the usual choice: it keeps the table you started with and adds to it.



by = join_by(fips, year): the same keys, written without quotes.
by = c("fips" = "county_code"): the key has a different name in each table; the first name is in the first table.
first_table |> left_join(second_table, by = ...): the first table piped in.
Base R: merge(first_table, second_table, by = c("fips", "year"), all.x = TRUE), where all.x = TRUE makes it a left join.
data.table: second_table[first_table, on = .(fips, year)].

title: 03-3: Reshaping and Merging
section: What has to be true for a merge to work
text:
What has to be true for a merge to work

The key is complete and identifies each row: every column needed (county and year), in every table where you assume one row per key. If the second table is meant to have one row per county, each county code must appear in it once.
The key has the same values in both tables. The same county must be written the same way: "01001" in one table and 1001 in the other are different values.
The key has the same type in both tables. Text in one and a number in the other gives an error in dplyr. In base R’s merge() it gives no error: the codes that lost their zeros simply fail to match.
You know which rows should match. Every county in the first table, or only some?

Condition 3 is the only one that gives an error, and only in dplyr. If 1, 2 or 4 fails, R gives you a merged table with no error, and the table is wrong. These are the silent failures of merging; the next slide shows each with corn_yields.csv.

title: 03-3: Reshaping and Merging
section: What goes wrong without an error
text:
What goes wrong without an error
The task for all three tabs: start from a list of the counties in corn_yields.csv, one row per county, and add each county’s irrigated yield.

counties  <- corn |> distinct(FIPS, County_name)
irrigated <- corn |> filter(Irrigated == 1) |> select(FIPS, irrigated_yield = Yield)
c(counties = nrow(counties), irrigated = nrow(irrigated))

 counties irrigated 
       86        74 



A repeated key adds rowsA key with no matchLeading zeros lost



merged <- left_join(counties, irrigated, by = "FIPS")
nrow(merged)

[1] 89


The list had 86 counties; the result has 89 rows. A left join should keep the rows of the first table, so where did 3 rows come from?

count(irrigated, FIPS) |> filter(n > 1)

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  FIPS      n
  <chr> <int>
1 31000     4


FIPS 31000 (OTHER (COMBINED) COUNTIES, several small counties reported together) has 4 irrigated rows. A row of the first table that matches 4 rows becomes 4 rows. No warning: dplyr warns only when rows repeat on both sides of the match. Any later sum or average over counties now counts 31000 four times.



sum(is.na(merged$irrigated_yield))

[1] 15

nrow(anti_join(counties, irrigated, by = "FIPS"))

[1] 15


15 counties have no irrigated yield in the file, so they get NA. That is correct here: those counties have no irrigated row. But the same NA appears when a match should exist and the key is written differently, and the table looks the same either way. Count the unmatched rows, and decide whether the number is believable.
With inner_join() instead, the same 15 counties disappear from the result, again with no message.


A second table read with read.csv(), which, as in 03-1, turns 01001 into a number:

yields <- tibble(fips = c("01001", "01003", "31019"), yield = c(150, 162, 173))
drought <- read.csv(text = "fips,weeks
01001,3
01003,0
31019,1")
drought$fips

[1]  1001  1003 31019


Joining now stops with an error, because one key is text and the other a number (condition 3). The usual fix an AI suggests is to turn the number into text:

drought$fips <- as.character(drought$fips)
left_join(yields, drought, by = "fips")

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  fips  yield weeks
  <chr> <dbl> <int>
1 01001   150    NA
2 01003   162    NA
3 31019   173     1


The error is gone, and so are the two Alabama matches: "1001" is not "01001". No error, no warning, just missing values. The right fix is to read the key as text in the first place, or to put the zeros back.

title: 03-3: Reshaping and Merging
section: Checking a merge
text:
Checking a merge

The checksMaking the code stopReading the HTML


The AI can write the checking code. It cannot know the right answers. Ask for these with every merge:










Ask the AI to print
What it catches
What only you can supply




1
the rows of each table, and of the result
a repeated key (more rows), an inner join dropping rows (fewer)
the number of rows the result should have


2
the keys that appear more than once, in each table
the cause of extra rows
which table should have one row per key


3
the number of rows of each table with no match in the other
keys written differently; rows you did not expect to match
how many should fail to match, and why


4
the number of missing values in the added columns
unmatched rows, seen from the result
the same


5
the type of the key in each table, and a few of its values
lost leading zeros, text against numbers
how the key should look





Two options make a join stop with an error instead of continuing silently. Ask for them when you know what to expect:

relationship = "many-to-one": stop if a row of the first table matches more than one row of the second
unmatched = "error": stop if a row would be dropped. In left_join() that means a row of the second table that matches nothing, since every row of the first table is kept anyway. To stop when a row of the first table has no match, ask for inner_join(..., unmatched = "error"), or for a check that stops when the number of unmatched rows is not 0.


left_join(counties, irrigated, by = "FIPS", relationship = "many-to-one")

Error in `left_join()`:
! Each row in `x` must match at most 1 row in `y`.
ℹ Row 18 of `x` matches multiple rows in `y`.


Here the code stops at 31000 instead of quietly adding rows.


For the county list, the student expected 86 rows after the join (one per county), one row per county in irrigated, and, having counted 71 distinct county codes among the irrigated rows, 86 − 71 = 15 counties without an irrigated yield. The AI wrote the code; in the rendered HTML, you read each line:


Code the AI wrote
cat(
  paste("rows after join: expected", nrow(counties), "got", nrow(merged)),
  paste("repeated FIPS in irrigated: expected 0, got", sum(duplicated(irrigated$FIPS))),
  paste("counties with no irrigated row: expected 15, got", nrow(anti_join(counties, irrigated, by = "FIPS"))),
  paste("irrigated rows with no county: expected 0, got", nrow(anti_join(irrigated, counties, by = "FIPS"))),
  sep = "\n"
)


rows after join: expected 86 got 89
repeated FIPS in irrigated: expected 0, got 3
counties with no irrigated row: expected 15, got 15
irrigated rows with no county: expected 0, got 0



Two checks fail, and they point at the same thing: FIPS 31000 appears 4 times in irrigated, which adds 3 rows. duplicated() marks each row that repeats an earlier one, so its sum counts the repeats: 4 copies of 31000 are 3 repeats.
The two unmatched counts are as expected.

title: 03-3: Reshaping and Merging
section: Stacking tables
text:
Stacking tables
Stacking puts one table under another. It is the step that combined the two sheets of corn_yields.xls in 03-1. It needs the two tables to have the same column names and types. When a name differs, R does not refuse:

sheet_08 <- readxl::read_excel("corn_yields.xls", sheet = "corn_yields_08")
sheet_09 <- readxl::read_excel("corn_yields.xls", sheet = "corn_yields_09") |>
  rename(yield = Yield)
stacked <- bind_rows(sheet_08, sheet_09)
dim(stacked)

[1] 322  10


Here the 2009 sheet’s Yield column was renamed yield, the kind of difference two files from different sources often have. bind_rows() keeps both as separate columns, so the result has 10 columns, and each of the two yield columns is missing in half the rows. The row count, 322, looks right.
Checks for stacking: the rows add up (161 + 161); the number of columns is the same as in each table (9); no column is missing in exactly the rows of one table.

title: 03-3: Reshaping and Merging
section: Working with AI on your own research
text:
Working with AI on your own research
The same way of working as on the slide of this name in lecture 02-1: you ask, the AI writes into your .qmd with one plain-English sentence above each chunk, you render, and you judge the HTML. For reshaping and merging, judging the HTML is mostly reading row counts, which you can do only if you wrote down the numbers you expected before asking. Every request for code ends with the closing instructions, under Recommended requests.

title: 03-3: Reshaping and Merging
section: Look at both tables before you ask
text:
Look at both tables before you ask
For a merge, look at each table and answer four questions in writing:

What is one row? One county? One county and year?
Which columns identify a row, and do they really? Count the rows per key value; any count above 1 is a repeat.
How is the key written? Its type, its length, whether codes have leading zeros, and whether the two tables identify a row with the same columns at all. One table may use a county name where the other uses a county code, or a date where the other uses a year.
Which rows should match? The same counties and years in both, or only some?

The answer to question 2 for the irrigated yields:

count(irrigated, FIPS) |>
  count(n, name = "number_of_codes")

# A tibble: 2 × 2
      n number_of_codes
  <int>           <int>
1     1              70
2     4               1


70 county codes appear once and one appears 4 times. That one row of output, read before asking, predicts the extra rows of the merge.
For a reshape, questions 1 and 2 are the whole job: what one row is now, what it should be after, and which columns identify it.

title: 03-3: Reshaping and Merging
section: What to put in your request
text:
What to put in your request
The AI already knows the functions. Your request supplies what it cannot know:

Each table: its name and what one row of it is
The key: which columns identify a row in each table, how they are written, and whether they need to be built or converted before they can match
What you want back: what one row of the result is, and which rows to keep (all rows of the first table, or only matches)
What you expect: the number of rows of the result, and how many rows should fail to match
Ask for checks: row counts, repeated keys and unmatched rows (see “Checking a merge”)
The closing instructions: which .qmd and heading the code goes under, a sentence above each chunk, paths built with here::here(), checks printed as expected and got, and render to HTML

title: 03-3: Reshaping and Merging
section: A weak request and a strong one
text:
A weak request and a strong one

WeakStrongWhat came back


Merge my yield data and my rainfall data.
The AI has to guess the key. It may pick by columns by matching names, or join on the county name, which repeats across states. It will not check for repeated keys or count unmatched rows, so a result with extra or missing rows looks finished.


An example for a yield table and a rainfall table:
In my R project I have two tables. In yields, one row is one county
and year; the county is identified by fips, a 5-digit code stored as
text with leading zeros, and year. In rain, one row should also be one
county and year, with the same two columns. Add the rainfall to yields,
keeping every row of yields, using the tidyverse. Stop with an error if
a row of yields matches more than one row of rain.

Then check the number of rows of yields, rain and the result (I expect
the result to have as many rows as yields), the number of repeated
fips-year pairs in each table (I expect 0), and the number of rows of
yields with no rainfall (I expect 0).

Put the code in my Quarto document analysis/merge.qmd, under the
heading "Add rainfall to yields", as R code chunks. Above each chunk,
write one plain-English sentence saying what it does and why. Build
every path with here::here(); no setwd(), no absolute paths. Print each
check on its own line as "name of check: expected X, got Y". Render the
document to HTML.


What the AI’s answer looks like in the rendered HTML, using the small yields and rain tables from “What a merge is”:
Add each county’s rainfall to its yield, matching on county code and year, and stop if a county-year of yields matches more than one rainfall row.

yields_rain <- left_join(yields, rain, by = c("fips", "year"), relationship = "many-to-one")

Check the row counts, repeated keys and unmatched rows.

cat("rows of result: expected", nrow(yields), "got", nrow(yields_rain), "\n")

rows of result: expected 3 got 3 

cat("repeated fips-year in yields: expected 0, got", sum(duplicated(yields[c("fips", "year")])), "\n")

repeated fips-year in yields: expected 0, got 0 

cat("repeated fips-year in rain: expected 0, got", sum(duplicated(rain[c("fips", "year")])), "\n")

repeated fips-year in rain: expected 0, got 0 

cat("yields rows with no rainfall: expected 0, got", sum(is.na(yields_rain$rain_mm)), "\n")

yields rows with no rainfall: expected 0, got 0 


Every check passes.

title: 03-3: Reshaping and Merging
section: Checks that come from knowing the data
text:
Checks that come from knowing the data
The checks on “Checking a merge” found that FIPS 31000 repeats. They cannot say what to do about it. Knowing the data can.
The name, OTHER (COMBINED) COUNTIES, says this code is not a county. The US Department of Agriculture reports counties with few farms together, one combined row for each of its crop reporting districts (groups of neighbouring counties). So the six rows belong to several districts, and the file has no column saying which. So:

In a table meant to have one row per county, these rows do not belong. Leave them out, and say so in the sentence above the chunk.
If you need them, you need the district, which means going back to the source, not changing the code.

Any time a key repeats, look at the repeated rows before deciding. They may be exact copies (keep one), corrections (keep the latest, if you can tell), or different things sharing a code, as here (no code change fixes it).


Code the AI wrote
corn |>
  filter(FIPS == "31000") |>
  select(County_name, Irrigated, Yield)


# A tibble: 6 × 3
  County_name               Irrigated Yield
  <chr>                         <dbl> <dbl>
1 OTHER (COMBINED) COUNTIES         1   156
2 OTHER (COMBINED) COUNTIES         0   167
3 OTHER (COMBINED) COUNTIES         1   186
4 OTHER (COMBINED) COUNTIES         1   193
5 OTHER (COMBINED) COUNTIES         0   114
6 OTHER (COMBINED) COUNTIES         1   157


Six rows, six different yields: not copies.
In 03-2, one row of this file was described as one county, in one year, with one irrigation status. These six rows show that description was not quite true, and only the check on the key found it.

title: 03-3: Reshaping and Merging
section: Your turn: read the AI’s code
text:
Your turn: read the AI’s code
A student asked an AI to “add drought data to my yields table and give me the average yield”. Both tables have one row per county and year, for counties in Colorado, Kansas and Nebraska, with columns state_name, county_name and year. The student’s .qmd is in the analysis folder of the project, and the data in data. The AI wrote:

yields  <- read_csv("data/yields.csv")
drought <- read_csv("data/drought.csv")
both <- left_join(yields, drought, by = c("county_name", "year"))
mean(both$yield)


QuestionsAnswers


A. What does each line do?
B. The key is incomplete. What is missing, and why does it matter in these three states?
C. What happens to the number of rows, and to the average?
D. Which lines fail when the student renders the .qmd, and why?
E. Which checks would have shown the problems in B and C?


A. Reads the yields; reads the drought data; adds the drought columns to every row of yields, matching on county name and year; averages the yield.
B. state_name. County names are not unique across states: there is a Lincoln County in Colorado, in Kansas and in Nebraska. Without the state, Lincoln County, Nebraska in 2010 matches the drought rows of all three Lincoln counties in 2010.
C. Every row of a repeated name becomes several rows, so the result has more rows than yields, and the average counts those counties several times. Because the key repeats on both sides of the match, dplyr prints a warning about a “many-to-many relationship”; read warnings, do not ignore them. A second clue: state_name is in both tables but not in the key, so the result has two columns, state_name.x and state_name.y, which disagree on the extra rows.
D. The two read_csv() lines. A .qmd is rendered from its own folder, analysis, where there is no data folder (03-1, Condition 1). Paths built with here::here() fix it.
E. Rows of yields and of the result (more rows after a left join), and repeated keys in each table (county_name and year together repeat in both).
