title: 03-3: Reshaping and Merging
section: What you must understand, and what the AI can write
text:
What you must understand, and what the AI can write







You need to understand
The AI can write




What one row is, before and after a reshape
pivot_wider(), pivot_longer() and their options


Which columns identify a row, and whether they really do
The code that counts repeated keys


Whether the key is written the same way, with the same type, in both tables
The code that fixes a key once you say what is wrong


Which rows should match, and which join keeps the rows you want
The join and its by =


How many rows the result should have
The checking code



Every reshape or merge: write down what one row is and how many rows you expect, before asking. Ask the AI to write the code and the checks (rows, repeated keys, unmatched rows) into your .qmd. Render it, and judge the HTML against what you wrote down.

title: 04-2: Showing More in One Figure
section: What you will and will not learn today
text:
What you will and will not learn today

The planDirections


In 04-1 a figure showed two things: a value and what it depends on, sometimes with one more column as colour. Real messages often involve more: yields by state and year and crop. Every extra column needs its own visual property (colour, shape, panel), and each one costs the reader effort.
What the AI cannot know is which comparison your message is about, so it cannot know which column should get the clearest visual property. Today:

The concept: which visual property to give each column, so the comparison the message is about is the easiest one to make
Reading code: recognising which column sets what, and which table each layer of a figure is drawn from
Asking AI: what to tell it about how the table is laid out and which comparison matters
Checking: that each line, bar or panel stands for exactly one thing, and that nothing is missing without a mark




The figures on these slides are drawn from one table. It has the same 1,956 county-years as the table in 04-1, plus the soybean yield and the number of weeks from May to September (23 in all) each county spent in each of five drought categories, from D0 (abnormally dry) to D4 (exceptional drought).
The rules from 04-1 still hold: start from the message and the reader, judge the figure in the HTML, and append the figure standard to every figure request.

title: 04-2: Showing More in One Figure
section: Readers compare some properties better than others
text:
Readers compare some properties better than others

What you needThe same three numbers, three ways


Give the comparison your message is about to position on a shared axis. Give the other columns the remaining properties, in this order:








Visual property
Readers can tell
Suits




Position on a shared axis
how much larger, accurately
the comparison the message is about


Length (bars from zero)
how much larger, fairly accurately
amounts


Separate panels
which group, and the pattern within it
a column with a few groups


Colour hue
which group, not how much
a few categories


Shape of points
which group, not how much
a few categories, also in black and white


Shade from light to dark, size
more or less, roughly
amounts, when position is already used



The order comes from experiments in which people judged values shown each way (Cleveland and McGill, 1984).
How to tell it is done: the comparison in your message sentence can be read off one axis.


The average number of weeks in extreme or exceptional drought in 2012, per state. Which state had the most, and by how much more than Nebraska?









The values are Colorado 12.4, Kansas 11.5, Nebraska 9.1. In A the gap can be read as a distance. In B the three circles look almost the same. In C the gap looks far larger than it is, because the scale gives its lightest shade to the smallest value and its darkest to the largest, however close they are.

title: 04-2: Showing More in One Figure
section: A third column: colour or shape
text:
A third column: colour or shape
Message: “Nebraska had the highest average corn yield of the three states in 10 of the 19 years.”

Colour only, printed in greyColour and shape, printed in greyHow many


A figure that will be printed, or read on a black-and-white screen, loses its hues. Here is the figure with colour alone telling the states apart, converted to grey (with the colorspace package):









The three states are now three greys that are hard to tell apart, so the reader cannot find Nebraska.


The same figure, with the state shown by colour and by the shape of the points:









Giving the same column two properties (here colour and shape) is the one case where repeating information helps: each property works when the other fails.


Shapes and hues tell groups apart only while there are few of them. ggplot’s default set of shapes stops at six: give it a seventh group and it draws no points for that group, and warns that “The shape palette can deal with a maximum of 6 discrete values”. The warning appears in the rendered HTML unless the chunk hides warnings.
With more groups than that, use panels, or highlight the group the message is about and grey out the rest (04-1).

title: 04-2: Showing More in One Figure
section: Shared or separate axes
text:
Shared or separate axes
Panels repeat the same figure for each group. Whether the panels share one vertical axis decides which comparison the reader can make.

What you needShared: soybean looks flatSeparate: both rises visibleThe code



Shared axes (the default) when the message compares levels across panels: “Nebraska yields more than Kansas.”
Separate axes only when the message is about the pattern within each panel and the panels measure things on different scales, and then the reader must be told, because the same height means different values in different panels.

How to tell it is done: read the message sentence, then cover all panels but one. If the sentence compares numbers across panels, the axes must be shared.


Message: “In Nebraska, soybean yields rose about as fast as corn yields: by 34% against 30%, from 2000 to 2002 to 2016 to 2018.”









Soybean yields are about a third of corn yields, so on a shared axis their rise is a small slope, and the message is lost.











scales = "free_y" gives each panel its own vertical axis. The message is about each crop’s rise, so this serves it. The title tells the reader the axes differ. The same option would mislead for “Nebraska yields more than Kansas”, because a higher line in one panel would no longer mean a higher yield.


The part of the code that makes panels, and the option that frees the axes:

ggplot(ne_crops, aes(year, yield)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ crop, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Average yield,\nNebraska (bushels per acre)",
       title = "Each panel has its own vertical axis")

facet_wrap(~ crop) reads “one panel per value of the column crop”. The column must exist in the table; the next section is about when it does not.

title: 04-2: Showing More in One Figure
section: Wide and long tables
text:
Wide and long tables

What you needThe wide fileThe long tableThe figure


Every visual property is set by one column: one column for colour, one for panels. If the thing you want to show as colour is spread across several columns, the table has to be reshaped first.

Wide: one column per category. The table on these slides has five drought columns, one per category.
Long: one column saying which category, one column holding the value. Each county-year then takes five rows.

How to tell it is done: the long table has (rows of the wide table) × (number of columns stacked) rows: 1,956 × 5 = 9,780.




# A tibble: 3 × 7
  county_name  year weeks_abnormally_dry weeks_moderate weeks_severe
  <chr>       <dbl>                <dbl>          <dbl>        <dbl>
1 Baca         2000                  9.1            0.8            0
2 Baca         2001                  2.6            0              0
3 Baca         2002                  0              0.3            4
# ℹ 2 more variables: weeks_extreme <dbl>, weeks_exceptional <dbl>


Message: “In 2012, counties spent on average 9.9 of the 23 weeks in extreme or exceptional drought, more than in any other year.” The figure needs the drought category as a colour, and there is no single column that holds it.


The code the AI writes for this follows one pattern, whatever the data:

long_table <- pivot_longer(wide_table, columns_to_stack,
                           names_to = "name_column", values_to = "value_column")

A real line that follows the pattern, and what it gives:

long <- pivot_longer(cd, starts_with("weeks_"),
                     names_to = "category", values_to = "weeks")
nrow(long)

[1] 9780


The column names (weeks_extreme and so on) are now values in the column category, and the numbers sit in weeks.











The categories are ordered from worst to mildest, and coloured from dark to light in the same order.

title: 04-2: Showing More in One Figure
section: After reshaping: the order of the categories
text:
After reshaping: the order of the categories

What went wrongThe check


The same figure drawn straight from the reshaped table, as an AI might write it. A deliberately bad example:









No error. But after reshaping, the categories are text, and ggplot puts text in alphabetical order: abnormally_dry, exceptional, extreme, moderate, severe. The shades from dark to light now follow the alphabet, not the severity: “abnormally dry”, the mildest category, gets the darkest red, and “severe” the lightest yellow. The column names appear as labels.


The category order is something only you know. Tell the AI the order, worst first, and the words to show, and check the legend:

expected, top to bottom: Exceptional (D4), Extreme (D3), Severe (D2), Moderate (D1), Abnormally dry (D0)
got: the legend of the rendered figure

The figure on the previous slide passes; this one does not.

title: 04-2: Showing More in One Figure
section: Each layer can have its own table
text:
Each layer can have its own table

What you needThe figureThe codeOthers in grey


Some messages need the individual rows and a summary of them at once: “Nebraska’s average yield rose, but in any year its counties differed by 61 to 100 bushels per acre.” The points come from one table (one row per county and year), the line from another (one row per year).
How to tell it is done: for every layer you can name the table it is drawn from, and what one row of that table is.














ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = ne, aes(year, corn_yield),
             colour = "grey60", position = position_jitter(width = 0.2, seed = 1)) +
  geom_line(data = ne_avg, aes(year, corn), colour = state_colours["Nebraska"], linewidth = 1.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2000, 2018, 2)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Corn yield, Nebraska\n(bushels per acre)",
       title = "County yields (grey) and the state average (green)")

ggplot() names no table. Each layer names its own with data =: the points come from ne (one row per county and year), the line from ne_avg (one row per year). A layer with no data = uses the table named in ggplot(), and if there is none there, R stops with an error.
position_jitter() moves each point sideways by a small random amount, so points of the same year do not hide each other.


The same idea gives panels in which each state is highlighted and the other two are drawn in grey behind it, so a reader can compare without leaving the panel:









The grey layer’s table has no state_name column (it is renamed), so facet_wrap(~ state_name) cannot split it, and it is drawn whole in every panel.

title: 04-2: Showing More in One Figure
section: One line, bar or panel per what?
text:
One line, bar or panel per what?

Two counties, one lineA state with no line


One line per county, grouped by the county’s name. A deliberately bad example, drawn for the counties called Lincoln only:









There is a Lincoln County in Colorado and in Nebraska, and 15 county names occur in more than one state. Grouped by name alone, the two counties become one line that jumps between them in every year both have data. No error.
The check: print the number of rows behind each line. Expected: at most 19, one per year. Got for Lincoln: 31. The fix is to group by state and county together.











Colorado is in the legend but has no line: the data holds 0 soybean yields for Colorado. Kansas’s line has gaps in the years with no Kansas soybean yields in the data. A reader cannot tell “no data” from “a line hidden behind another”.
The check: print the number of counties behind each value next to the figure, and say in the figure or its caption which states and years have no data.

title: 04-2: Showing More in One Figure
section: The checklist, for figures that show more
text:
The checklist, for figures that show more
The six questions from 04-1 still apply. Figures with three or more columns add four:

Is the comparison the message is about shown by position on a shared axis?
Can every colour and shape be told apart, and matched to its label, also in black and white?
If there are panels: are the axes shared, or, if not, does the figure say so and does the message only compare within panels?
Does the table printed next to the figure show one row per line, bar or point, with categories in the order you intended and every missing group stated?

title: 04-2: Showing More in One Figure
section: What to add to a figure request
text:
What to add to a figure request
Everything from 04-1 (the data, the message, the reader, the group that matters, alternatives, the figure standard, the closing instructions), plus what only you know about a figure with more columns:

The comparison the message is about, so that it gets position on a shared axis
What one line, bar or panel stands for, and which columns together identify it (here, state and county name)
The order of categories, and the words to show for them
Whether the data must be reshaped first: which columns hold the same kind of value
What is missing: groups or years with no data, and how the figure should say so





Using an agent in your editor or terminal?


An agent can open the file and find the missing groups itself. Ask it to print what it found before it draws, and compare that with what you expected.

title: 04-2: Showing More in One Figure
section: Requests you can copy
text:
Requests you can copy
Copy one, then replace every <...> with what you know. Every figure request ends with the figure standard and then the closing instructions.

Closing instructionsThe figure standardReshape before drawingDesigns for a third columnRows and a summaryCheck against the dataExplain code


The lines that end every request for code. Replace the two blanks; leave “expected X, got Y” as it is, because it tells the AI how to print each check:
Put the code in my Quarto document <path to your .qmd>, under the
heading "<heading>", as R code chunks. Above each chunk, write one
plain-English sentence saying what it does and why. Build every path
with here::here(); no setwd(), no absolute paths. Print each check on
its own line as "name of check: expected X, got Y". Render the document
to HTML.
A chat assistant cannot render: paste its chunks into your .qmd and render it yourself. An agent in your editor or terminal can do every step.


Paste this into every figure request, just before the closing instructions:
Every figure must meet this standard:
1. Axis titles, legend titles and category labels in plain words with
   units, such as "Corn yield (bushels per acre)", never a column name;
   categories in words, such as "Irrigated", never a code such as 1.
2. Tick labels, axis titles and legend text no smaller than the
   document's body text, at the size the figure appears in the HTML.
3. No legend when lines or points can be labelled directly or there is
   only one group. Otherwise, the legend inside an empty corner of the
   plot, or above or below a wide figure, in the same order as the lines
   or bars it describes.
4. Numbers formatted for reading: thousands separators, no more decimals
   than the message needs, percentages shown as percentages.
5. No overlapping tick labels; for long category names, put the
   categories on the vertical axis rather than rotating the text.
6. Light or no gridlines and no heavy borders, so the data is the
   darkest thing in the figure.
7. A shape that suits the content: wide for a change over time, close
   to square for a relationship between two variables.
8. Colours readable by colour-blind readers (such as the Okabe-Ito
   palette), and no more colours than the message needs.
Keep your own copy of this block, and add to it each time you find something the AI keeps getting wrong.


In my R project, <path to the file> has one row per <what one row
is>. The columns <columns> all hold <the same kind of value, with
units>, one column per <what each column stands for>.

title: 06-1: Organising a Research Project
section: What you will and will not learn today
text:
What you will and will not learn today

The planDirections


A research project runs for months or years and has many pieces: data files, code, figures, tables, the paper. An AI assistant can write any single piece of code in it. What it cannot do is:

see how your project folder is laid out
know which files you received and which your code made
know which step a piece of code belongs to, or what has to run before it
tell whether the whole project still rebuilds from the start

Those four are your job. So today is about:

The concept: what a reproducible project is, and what has to be true of its folder and its code
Reading code: recognising how a step of a project reads and writes files, without memorising it
Asking AI: what to tell the AI about your project
Checking: how to tell whether your project still rebuilds, and whether the AI broke a rule of it




Ask your AI assistant to install the here and quarto packages if you have not already.
Lecture 03-1 introduced paths and here::here() for reading one file. This lecture builds on its slide “Condition 1: R can find the file”.
The examples on these slides use a small project that is built in a temporary folder each time the slides are made, from corn_yields.csv (the corn data from 03-1). Every output shown is real. In the code that runs these examples, paths start from proj, the temporary project’s folder, instead of here::here(), and render_step() is a small function written for these slides that renders one .qmd in its own R session, as quarto render in a terminal does, and reports whether it worked.

title: 06-1: Organising a Research Project
section: What a project has to do
text:
What a project has to do

ReproducibleThe testWho it is for


A research project is reproducible if anyone, including you a year from now, can produce exactly the same results from the same data by following what the project records.
The minimum requirement: every action taken on the data is recorded, so nobody has to guess a step. An action you took and did not record (deleting rows in Excel, renaming a column by hand, running a line at the Console and not saving it) is called a hidden action on these slides. A project with a hidden action is not reproducible, however tidy it looks.



Note


Reproducible is not the same as replicable (another team reaches the same conclusion with different data). This lecture is about reproducible only.





A project passes one test, and you can run it yourself:

Delete every file your code made.
Start a fresh R session.
Run the code, in order, from the raw data.
Everything comes back, and the numbers are the same.

If a step fails, it depended on something that was never recorded: a file made by hand, an object left in R’s memory, a step you ran once and forgot. Each of those is invisible until you delete the outputs and try.



You, later. You will need to rerun the analysis with one change, months after you last opened it, for a revision or a referee.
Your advisor and coauthors. They can check a result by following the project, without asking you how it was made.
Readers of the paper. Many journals now ask for the code and data, and check that they run.

title: 06-1: Organising a Research Project
section: How a project folder is laid out
text:
How a project folder is laid out
Most research projects need the same few places. Folder names vary; what each one holds does not.

The patternVariations you will seeThe smallest versionMaking the projectThe New Project window


my-project/
  my-project.Rproj    marks the project root
  README.md           what the project is, and what to run in what order
  data/
    raw/              files exactly as you received them
    processed/        files your code made from them
  analysis/
    01-clean.qmd      one step per document, numbered in run order
    02-merge.qmd
    03-regression.qmd
  results/            figures and tables your code saved
  writing/            the paper or report








Part
What it holds
Required?




.Rproj file
Marks the top of the project (the project root). here::here() builds every path from it.
Yes


data/raw/
Data as you received it. Your code reads it and never writes to it.
Yes, if you have data


data/processed/
Tables your code made. Can be deleted and rebuilt at any time.
Yes, once any step saves a table


analysis/
The code, one .qmd per step
Yes


results/
Figures and tables for the paper. Can be deleted and rebuilt.
Once you save any


README.md
A short text file saying what the project is and how to rerun it
Strongly recommended


writing/
The paper, if you write it in the project
No





AI assistants and other people’s projects use other names for the same places. They change how the folder looks, not what it does:

Code/, R/, scripts/ or src/ for analysis/
Data/Raw/ and Data/Processed/, data-raw/ and data/, or input/ and output/ for the two kinds of data
output/, figures/ or tables/ for results/
steps written as .R scripts instead of .qmd documents

What to look for in any of them: one place for data you received, a separate place for data the code made, and code whose names tell you the order.


Lecture 03-1 used the smallest version of this pattern: a project with data/ and analysis/. That is enough while your code only reads files.
Split data/ into raw/ and processed/ as soon as any step saves a table. From then on, a file’s folder tells you whether you can delete it.


An R Project is a folder with a .Rproj file in it. In RStudio: File, New Project, New Directory, New Project. RStudio writes the .Rproj file and opens a fresh R session in that folder.



Important


here recognises a .Rproj file only if its first line starts with Version:. Every .Rproj that RStudio creates has that line. An empty file named something.Rproj, made any other way, does not count, and here::here() then points at the wrong folder.

title: 06-1: Organising a Research Project
section: What has to be true for a project to rebuild
text:
What has to be true for a project to rebuild

The four conditionsFailures with and without an error



Every path starts from the project root. No path depends on whose computer it is or which folder R happens to be in.
Raw data is never changed. Every change to the data is code that reads from data/raw/ and writes somewhere else.
Each step reads files and writes files. No step depends on objects that another step, or the Console, left in R’s memory.
The order is written down. Anyone can tell which step runs first.




If condition 1 fails, the project stops with an error on the next computer: the file is not found.
If condition 2, 3 or 4 fails, the project usually still runs today, on your computer, with no error. It fails later: when someone else runs it, when you restart R, or never visibly, because the raw file you would compare against has been overwritten.




Important


Like the silent failures in 03-1, these are why checking matters. A project that runs is not the same as a project that rebuilds.

title: 06-1: Organising a Research Project
section: Condition 1: every path starts from the project root
text:
Condition 1: every path starts from the project root

The ruleWhy it matters more in a projectWhat else breaks it


In 03-1, Condition 1 was about one file. In a project, every step reads from one folder and writes to another, so every path in every step is built the same way:

here::here("folder", "subfolder", "file name")








Part
What it is




here::here(
Finds the project root by looking for the .Rproj file, starting from wherever R is


"folder", "subfolder"
The folders below the root, one piece each, in order


"file name"
The file, last



The result is the full path, correct on any computer that has the project.


A .qmd file runs with its own folder as the working directory (the folder R is in, see 03-1). Every step lives in analysis/, so a typed path such as "data/raw/corn_yields.csv" is looked for in analysis/data/raw/, which does not exist.








Written as
At the Console of the project
When analysis/01-clean.qmd is rendered




"data/raw/corn_yields.csv"
works
fails: no such file


"../data/raw/corn_yields.csv"
fails
works


here::here("data", "raw", "corn_yields.csv")
works
works



.. means “the folder above”. It works in one place and not the other, which is why here::here() is the one to use.



setwd("C:/Users/yourname/..."): changes the working directory to a folder that exists only on one computer.
An absolute path such as "/Users/yourname/Desktop/corn.csv": the same problem, without setwd().
A file kept outside the project folder, such as in Downloads: no path from the root reaches it. Copy it into data/raw/.

title: 06-1: Organising a Research Project
section: Condition 2: raw data is never changed
text:
Condition 2: raw data is never changed

Raw and processedWhy it mattersHow a step keeps it


Raw data is a file as you received it: downloaded, sent by a coauthor, typed in from a paper form. Processed data is a file your code made. The test for which is which:

If you deleted it, could you get it back by rerunning your code?

Yes: processed, and it goes in data/processed/. No: raw, and it goes in data/raw/, untouched.







File
Which




A csv downloaded from USDA
raw


A table your cleaning step saved as .rds
processed


A figure saved by your code
a result, in results/


A survey you typed in from paper forms
raw, with a note in the README saying where it came from


The USDA csv after you converted a column to metric by hand in Excel
neither: a hidden action. Keep the original as raw, and do the conversion in a step






A raw file is the only part of the project your code cannot rebuild. Everything else can be deleted and made again.
A writer function replaces an existing file without asking (03-1, “How writing code is written”). A step that saves to the path it read from destroys the raw file, and with it the only thing you could have compared against.
A correction made to a raw file by hand cannot be seen, checked or undone by anyone else. Written as code in a step, with a sentence above it saying why, the same correction can be.



Every step that changes data reads from data/raw/ (or data/processed/) and writes to data/processed/. The example project’s cleaning step does that. The check below compares a fingerprint of the raw file (a short code computed from its contents, which changes when the contents change) before and after the step runs:


Code that ran the check
raw_file <- file.path(proj, "data", "raw", "corn_yields.csv")
before <- tools::md5sum(raw_file)
step <- render_step(file.path(proj, "analysis", "01-clean.qmd"))
after <- tools::md5sum(raw_file)
cat(
  paste("step 01 rendered: expected TRUE, got", step$ok),
  paste("raw file unchanged: expected TRUE, got", unname(before == after)),
  sep = "\n"
)


step 01 rendered: expected TRUE, got TRUE
raw file unchanged: expected TRUE, got TRUE

title: 06-1: Organising a Research Project
section: Condition 3: each step reads files and writes files
text:
Condition 3: each step reads files and writes files
A step is one document that does one job: it reads its inputs from files, does the job, saves its outputs to files, and checks them. Whatever the job, a step follows the same pattern.

The patternSteps in a typical projectWhy not objects in memoryR’s memory between sessions



input  <- reader_function(here::here("<folder>", "<subfolder>", "input file"))
output <- ...one job done to input...
writer_function(output, here::here("<folder>", "<subfolder>", "output file"))
cat("name of check: expected X, got", ..., "\n")









Part
What it is
Required?




read
Every input comes from a file, by a path built with here::here(): data/raw/ or data/processed/
Yes


one job
Clean, merge, estimate, draw: one thing you can name in a few words
Yes


write
Every output another step needs is saved to a file, in data/processed/ or results/
Yes, if a later step uses it


check
Prints what you expected and what you got
Strongly recommended













Step
Reads
Writes




01-clean.qmd
data/raw/
data/processed/


02-merge.qmd
data/processed/ (two or more tables)
data/processed/


03-regression.qmd
data/processed/
results/ (a table of estimates)


04-figures.qmd
data/processed/, results/
results/ (figures)



The files are how one step hands its work to the next. A reader of the project can see every hand-over by looking at the folders.


Rendering a .qmd runs it from the top in a fresh R session (02-1, “Working with AI on your own research”). So a step that uses an object it never read or made fails at render, even if the same code works at the Console because the object happens to be there.
Here the example project’s summary step is changed so that it uses irrigated without reading it, as if the cleaning step had left it in memory:


Code that renders the changed step
broken <- sub("^irrigated <- readRDS.*$", "# (line that read the file removed)", step_summary)
broken_file <- file.path(proj, "analysis", "02-broken.qmd")
writeLines(broken, broken_file)
res <- render_step(broken_file)
unlink(broken_file)
cat("step rendered:", res$ok, "\n")


step rendered: FALSE 


Code that renders the changed step
cat("error message:", grep("not found", res$output, value = TRUE)[1], "\n")


error message: ! object 'irrigated' not found 


The render fails with an error naming the missing object. That is the good outcome: it shows the step was not reproducible, today, instead of a year from now.


By default RStudio saves the objects in your Environment pane to a file called .RData when you quit, and loads them back when R starts. Objects that come back were made by code you may since have changed, so code can appear to work only because an object it needs is still there.
Turn it off once: Tools, Global Options, General. Untick Restore .RData into workspace at startup, and set Save workspace to .RData on exit to Never.

title: 06-1: Organising a Research Project
section: Condition 4: the order is written down
text:
Condition 4: the order is written down

Numbered namesA script that runs every stepPackage versions


Number each step’s file name in the order it runs: 01-clean.qmd, 02-merge.qmd. Then listing the folder in alphabetical order lists the steps in run order, and nobody has to ask.
Use two digits from the start. File names are sorted as text, character by character, so without the leading zero, step 10 comes before step 2:

sort(c("1-clean.qmd", "2-merge.qmd", "10-figures.qmd"))

[1] "1-clean.qmd"    "10-figures.qmd" "2-merge.qmd"   

sort(c("01-clean.qmd", "02-merge.qmd", "10-figures.qmd"))

[1] "01-clean.qmd"   "02-merge.qmd"   "10-figures.qmd"




A run-all script is one file at the project root that renders every step in order. It turns “the order is written down” into “the order runs”. Whichever function the AI uses, it follows this pattern:

steps <- list.files(here::here("analysis"), pattern = "\\.qmd$", full.names = TRUE)
for (step in steps) quarto::quarto_render(step)








Part
What it does




list.files(..., pattern = "\\.qmd$")
Lists every .qmd in analysis/, in alphabetical order, which the numbers make the run order


for (step in steps)
Repeats the next line once for each file


quarto::quarto_render(step)
Renders one step in its own fresh R session, and stops everything with an error if that step fails



If analysis/ also holds documents that are not steps (notes, a worksheet), the pattern must exclude them, for example by listing only names that start with two digits: pattern = "^[0-9]{2}-.*\\.qmd$".


Packages change. An update can change a default or remove a function, so the same code can give a different number a year later. The renv package records the version of every package the project uses in a file called renv.lock at the project root.

renv::init(): start recording, once per project
renv::snapshot(): write the versions you use now into renv.lock; run it after installing or updating a package
renv::restore(): install exactly the versions in renv.lock; what someone rebuilding your project runs first

title: 06-1: Organising a Research Project
section: The test, run on the example project
text:
The test, run on the example project
Everything in data/processed/ and results/ was made by code, so all of it can be deleted. The run-all pattern then renders both steps from the raw data, and the check compares what came back with what was there before:


Code that ran the test
invisible(render_step(file.path(proj, "analysis", "02-summary.qmd")))
made_before <- list_outputs()
mean_file <- file.path(proj, "results", "mean-yield.csv")
mean_before <- round(read.csv(mean_file)$mean_yield, 1)

unlink(file.path(proj, "data", "processed", "*"))
unlink(file.path(proj, "results", "*"))
cat("files left after deleting:", length(list_outputs()), "\n")


files left after deleting: 0 


Code that ran the test
steps <- list.files(file.path(proj, "analysis"), pattern = "^[0-9]{2}-.*\\.qmd$", full.names = TRUE)
for (step in steps) render_step(step)

cat(
  paste("files rebuilt: expected", paste(made_before, collapse = ", "),
        "got", paste(list_outputs(), collapse = ", ")),
  paste("average irrigated yield: expected", mean_before,
        "got", round(read.csv(mean_file)$mean_yield, 1)),
  sep = "\n"
)


files rebuilt: expected irrigated.rds, mean-yield.csv got irrigated.rds, mean-yield.csv
average irrigated yield: expected 181.6 got 181.6


Both files came back, with the same number in them. Run this test once in the middle of a project, not only at the end, when a failure is still easy to trace.

title: 06-1: Organising a Research Project
section: Working with AI on your own research
text:
Working with AI on your own research
The way of working from lecture 02-1 (“Working with AI on your own research”) fits a project laid out like this one: you ask for one step, naming what it reads, what it writes and which checks to print; the AI writes into that step’s .qmd, with one plain-English sentence above each chunk; you render the step and read the HTML.
What the layout adds:

Each step’s .qmd and its HTML are a record of one job, small enough to read in a few minutes.
Rendering each step in a fresh session is the Condition 3 check, done every time, for free.
The run-all script and the README turn the separate records into a project anyone can rebuild.




Note


Every request that asks for code ends with the same few lines, the closing instructions from 03-1. The full text is under Recommended requests near the end.

title: 06-1: Organising a Research Project
section: What the AI cannot know about your project
text:
What the AI cannot know about your project

What to put in your requestWrite it down once


The AI sees only what you show it. For a project, it needs:

The layout: the folders, and which one holds raw data. Pasting the folder tree is the quickest way.
The step: which .qmd the code goes into, and the one job it does.
The inputs and outputs: which files the step reads, and which files it saves, with their paths from the project root.
The project’s rules: raw data is never written to; outputs go to data/processed/ or results/; no setwd().
The checks: what you expect, so the HTML says whether the step did it.
The closing instructions.



Most of the layout and rules are the same in every request. Write them once, in a short file at the project root that the AI can read:
# About this project
Corn yield response to irrigation, Nebraska counties, 2008.

# Layout
data/raw/        data as received. Read only: no code writes here.
data/processed/  tables made by the steps; can be deleted and rebuilt.
analysis/        one .qmd per step, numbered in run order.
results/         figures and tables for the paper.

# Rules
Build every path with here::here(). No setwd(), no absolute paths.
Every step reads files and writes files.

A chat assistant reads it if you paste it at the start of a conversation.
An agent in your editor or terminal can read it from the project. Claude Code reads a file named CLAUDE.md at the project root automatically at the start of every session; other agents have their own file name for the same purpose.

Keep it short and current: an out-of-date rule in it gets followed.

title: 06-1: Organising a Research Project
section: A weak request and a strong one
text:
A weak request and a strong one

WeakStrongWhat came back


Clean my corn data and work out the average irrigated yield.
The AI does not know the layout, so it guesses. A typical reply puts everything in one script, sets the working directory, and saves over the file it read:

setwd("C:/Users/yourname/Documents")
corn <- read_csv("corn_yields.csv")
corn <- filter(corn, Irrigated == 1)
write_csv(corn, "corn_yields.csv")
mean(corn$Yield)

The fourth line replaces the raw file with the cleaned one. The next run reads the cleaned file as if it were raw, and nothing says so.


An example for a project laid out as on these slides:
My project has data/raw/ (read only), data/processed/, analysis/ and
results/. Write one step, the cleaning step. It reads
data/raw/corn_yields.csv, keeps only the irrigated rows (Irrigated is
1), and saves the result as data/processed/irrigated.rds. It must not
write anything to data/raw/. Check the number of rows (I expect 74,
from counting the irrigated rows in the raw file).

Put the code in my Quarto document analysis/01-clean.qmd, under the
heading "Clean", as R code chunks. Above each chunk, write one
plain-English sentence saying what it does and why. Build every path
with here::here(); no setwd(), no absolute paths. Print each check on
its own line as "name of check: expected X, got Y". Render the document
to HTML.


The rendered HTML of analysis/01-clean.qmd in the example project. Read each sentence, then check that the chunk under it does what it says and follows the project’s rules.

Clean

Read the raw yields and keep only the irrigated fields, since the analysis is about irrigated corn.
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
corn <- read_csv(here::here("data", "raw", "corn_yields.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
irrigated <- filter(corn, Irrigated == 1)
Save the cleaned table for the next step.
saveRDS(irrigated, here::here("data", "processed", "irrigated.rds"))
Check the number of rows against the count of irrigated rows in the raw file.
cat("irrigated rows: expected 74, got", nrow(irrigated), "\n")
Rendered, it printed:


irrigated rows: expected 74, got 74 


The step reads from data/raw/, writes only to data/processed/, builds both paths with here::here(), and the check matches.

title: 06-1: Organising a Research Project
section: Checking: what to ask for, and why
text:
Checking: what to ask for, and why

The five checksAsking for themReading the HTML


Each check tests one condition. You know the right answer to each before you run it:










Check
Condition
What you expect




1
Search the project’s code for setwd(, C:/, /Users/ and ~/
1
none found


2
Fingerprint of every file in data/raw/, before and after running a step
2
unchanged


3
Restart R, then render each step on its own
3
every step renders


4
Delete data/processed/ and results/, run the run-all script
3 and 4
every file comes back


5
For every file in data/processed/ and results/, the step that writes it
2 and 4
one step for each file



Check 5 finds files made by hand: a file that no step writes is a hidden action.


Check my project. Search every .qmd and .R file for setwd(), and for
paths starting with C:/, /Users/ or ~/. Then, for every file in
data/processed/ and results/, name the step that writes it.

Put the code in my Quarto document <path to your .qmd>, under the
heading "<heading>", as R code chunks. Above each chunk, write one
plain-English sentence saying what it does and why. Build every path
with here::here(); no setwd(), no absolute paths. Print each check on
its own line as "name of check: expected X, got Y". Render the document
to HTML.


The example project, with one more step added the way the weak request on the previous slide would have written it:


Code that ran the check
writeLines(
  c("```{r}", "setwd(\"C:/Users/yourname/Documents\")", "```"),
  file.path(proj, "analysis", "03-extra.qmd")
)
code_files <- list.files(proj, pattern = "\\.(qmd|R)$", recursive = TRUE, full.names = TRUE)
pattern <- "setwd\\(|\"C:/|\"/Users/|\"~/"
hits <- unlist(lapply(code_files, function(f) {
  lines <- readLines(f)
  if (any(grepl(pattern, lines))) basename(f)
}))
cat("files with setwd() or an absolute path: expected 0, got", length(hits), "\n")


files with setwd() or an absolute path: expected 0, got 1 


Code that ran the check
hits


[1] "03-extra.qmd"


The check fails, and names the file to fix. Passing it would not prove that the project rebuilds; failing it proves that it does not, on any other computer.

title: 06-1: Organising a Research Project
section: Your turn: read the AI’s code
text:
Your turn: read the AI’s code
A student asked an AI to “add the regression to my project”, and got this in analysis/03-regression.qmd:

setwd("/Users/jsmith/thesis")
corn <- read_csv("data/raw/corn_yields.csv")
corn <- filter(corn, Yield > 0)
write_csv(corn, "data/raw/corn_yields.csv")
model <- lm(Yield ~ Irrigated + rainfall, data = corn_weather)


QuestionsAnswers


A. What does each of the five lines do?
B. Which line will fail on your computer, and why?
C. Which line destroys something the project cannot get back?
D. Which line works at the student’s Console but fails when the document is rendered? Why?
E. Rewrite the request so the AI could not make these mistakes.


A. Changes the working directory; reads the raw yields; drops rows with a yield of 0 or less; saves the table over the raw file; fits a regression of yield on irrigation and rainfall using a table called corn_weather.
B. Line 1. The folder /Users/jsmith/thesis exists only on jsmith’s computer.
C. Line 4. It replaces the raw file with the filtered one. The dropped rows are gone, and nothing records that they existed.
D. Line 5. corn_weather is not read or made anywhere in this document. It exists at the Console only because another step, or the Console, left it in memory. Rendering starts a fresh session, so the object is not found.
E. Name the step and its one job, the files it reads (data/processed/ for the merged table) and writes (results/), say that data/raw/ is read only, and end with the closing instructions.

What you must understand, and what the AI can write







You need to understand
The AI can write

Which of your files are raw, and that nothing writes to them

title: 07-1: Dates and Text
section: What you will and will not learn today
text:
What you will and will not learn today

The planDirections


Two kinds of column cause more quiet mistakes than any other: dates and text. An AI assistant can write the code that converts a date or cleans a text column. It knows every function. What it cannot do is:

see how the dates in your file are written
know whether 03/04/2025 means 4 March or 3 April
see every spelling of a name that occurs in your data
tell whether the result is right

Those are your job. So today is about:

The concept: what a date is to R, and what pattern matching on text is, and what has to be true for each to work
Reading code: recognising what a line of date or text code does, without memorising it
Asking AI: what to put in your request
Checking: how to tell whether the code the AI wrote did the right thing




Ask your AI assistant to install the tidyverse, here and gt packages if you have not already. The tidyverse includes lubridate (dates) and stringr (text).
The examples use pizzaplace, a table that comes with the gt package: a year of orders from a pizza shop, one row per pizza sold, 49,574 rows. Its columns include date (the day of the order), name (the pizza, such as thai_ckn) and price. On these slides the table is called pizza.

title: 07-1: Dates and Text
section: A date stored as text, and a date stored as a date
text:
A date stored as text, and a date stored as a date
A file stores a date as characters, such as 2015-01-01. When it is read into R, the column is still text (R says character): a row of characters that happens to look like a date. Only after it is converted is it a date (R says Date): a value that R knows is a day in the calendar. The two print almost the same. They do not behave the same.

What R seesSortingSubtractingGrouping by month



class(pizza$date)

[1] "character"

class(ymd(pizza$date))

[1] "Date"


ymd() converts text written year, month, day into a date. Converting is called parsing in R’s help pages and on these slides.


Three dates written month/day/year, sorted as text and as dates:

as_text <- c("12/15/2014", "01/03/2015", "06/20/2015")
sort(as_text)

[1] "01/03/2015" "06/20/2015" "12/15/2014"

sort(mdy(as_text))

[1] "2014-12-15" "2015-01-03" "2015-06-20"


Text is sorted character by character, from the left, so 01/... comes first whatever the year. The December 2014 date ends up last. No error. Only the dates sort in calendar order.


How many days from the first order to the last?

max(pizza$date) - min(pizza$date)

Error in max(pizza$date) - min(pizza$date): non-numeric argument to binary operator


Text cannot be subtracted, and R says so. As dates:

max(ymd(pizza$date)) - min(ymd(pizza$date))

Time difference of 364 days




To count orders per month from text, you would take the characters that hold the month. Characters 6 and 7 of 2015-01-15 are the month, 01. Characters 6 and 7 of the same day written 01/15/2015 are /2. It depends on how the text was written, and nothing warns you when it is wrong.
From a date, month() gives the month whatever the text looked like:

pizza |>
  mutate(date = ymd(date)) |>
  count(month = month(date)) |>
  head(4)

# A tibble: 4 × 2
  month     n
  <dbl> <int>
1     1  4232
2     2  3961
3     3  4261
4     4  4151

title: 07-1: Dates and Text
section: How date code is written
text:
How date code is written
Date code comes in two kinds: code that parses text into dates, and code that uses dates once they exist. Each follows one pattern.

Parsing: the patternEvery parser follows the patternUsing dates: the patternVariations you will see



table_name <- table_name |> mutate(date_column = parser(text_column))









Part
What it is
Required?




mutate(...)
Adds a column to the table, or replaces one with the same name
Needed to keep the result in the table


date_column =
The name of the new date column. Often the same name as the text column, which replaces it.
Yes


parser
The function that reads the text. In lubridate, its name gives the order of the pieces: ymd is year, month, day.
Yes


text_column
The text to parse
Yes, the only required input



A real line that follows the pattern:

pizza_dated <- pizza |> mutate(date = ymd(date))






Text looks like
Parser
Package




2015-03-04
ymd(x)
lubridate (tidyverse)


03/04/2015 (month first)
mdy(x)
lubridate


04/03/2015 (day first)
dmy(x)
lubridate


2015-03-04 11:38:36
ymd_hms(x)
lubridate


03/04/2015
as.Date(x, format = "%m/%d/%Y")
built into R



lubridate’s parsers do not care about the separators: mdy() reads 03/04/2015, 03-04-2015 and March 4, 2015 alike. What they need is the order.
as.Date() instead takes a format, written with codes: %Y four-digit year, %y two-digit year, %m month as a number, %b or %B month as a word, %d day.


Once a column is a date, two kinds of line are common: taking a part of each date, and arithmetic with dates.







Code
What it gives




year(date), month(date), mday(date)
the year, the month (1 to 12), the day of the month


wday(date, label = TRUE)
the day of the week, as Sun, Mon, …


yday(date)
the day of the year, 1 to 366


floor_date(date, "month")
the first day of the date’s month, still a date, so months of different years stay apart


date2 - date1
the number of days between them


date + days(7)
the date a week later


date %m+% months(1)
the same day one month later (see “Adding a month” under “Dates: the silent failures”)


date >= ymd("2015-05-01"), filter(table, date >= ymd("2015-05-01"))
TRUE or FALSE for each date, in calendar order; inside filter(), the rows on or after that day


seq(first_date, last_date, by = "day")
every date from the first to the last


format(date, "%d %B %Y")
the date turned back into text, written as you choose (for example 15 December 2010), for labels in tables and figures; it is text again, so do this last






lubridate::ymd(...): the package name, then ::, then the function.
as.Date(x, "%m/%d/%Y"): base R; the format is the second input, named or not.
parse_date_time(x, orders = c("mdy", "dmy")): tries more than one order. It decides which order to use from the values themselves; the order you list them in decides only when the values do not. A value that fits both orders, such as 03/04/2025, can be read either way with no warning, and since nothing fails to parse, the count of failures stays at 0. Only the range of the dates and the rows per month reveal it. Ask why the AI used it.
mutate(across(c(start, end), mdy)): the same parser applied to several columns at once.

title: 07-1: Dates and Text
section: Date formats, and what 03/04/2025 means
text:
Date formats, and what 03/04/2025 means

Many ways to write one day03/04/2025Two-digit years


All of these are 15 December 2010:

2010-12-15 (the international standard, year first)
12/15/2010 (the usual US order, month first)
15/12/2010 (most of the rest of the world, day first)
Dec 15 10
15 December 2010

The parser has to match the way your file writes them, and only looking at the file tells you which that is.


Month first, it is 4 March. Day first, it is 3 April. Both parsers accept it without complaint:

mdy("03/04/2025")

[1] "2025-03-04"

dmy("03/04/2025")

[1] "2025-04-03"


The text alone cannot tell you which is right. Two things can:

Who wrote it: US software and people usually write month first; most other countries write day first.
The other values in the column: a first number above 12 can only be a day. If a column holds 25/03/2025, it is written day first.



A two-digit year has lost its century, so the parser guesses one:

mdy("01/01/68")

[1] "2068-01-01"

mdy("01/01/69")

[1] "1969-01-01"


68 became 2068 and 69 became 1969. A birth year or a weather record from 1968 would land 100 years in the future. And a format that expects two digits reads only two of a four-digit year:

as.Date("03/04/2025", format = "%m/%d/%y")

[1] "2020-03-04"


The year 2025 was read as 20, so 2020. No error.

title: 07-1: Dates and Text
section: Dates: the silent failures
text:
Dates: the silent failures
As with reading files (lecture 03-1), some failures stop with an error and some give a wrong result with no error. This deck calls the second kind silent failures. These are the common ones for dates.

Text that does not fit becomes missingThe wrong orderAdding a month


A value the parser cannot read becomes NA (missing). R gives a warning, not an error, so the code carries on:

ymd(c("2015-01-05", "Jan 5 2015", "2015-13-01"))

Warning: 2 failed to parse.


[1] "2015-01-05" NA           NA          


The second value is written in another format; the third has a month 13. In a rendered document the warning is one short line that is easy to scroll past, and in a column of thousands you would not see the NAs at all. The check: count the missing values before and after parsing. Any increase is text that failed to parse.


If a column written day first is parsed month first, two things happen at once, and only one of them is visible:

day_first <- c("25/03/2025", "05/03/2025")
mdy(day_first)

Warning: 1 failed to parse.


[1] NA           "2025-05-03"


25/03/2025 has no month 25, so it becomes NA (the warning is visible). 05/03/2025 is accepted as 3 May instead of 5 March, a wrong date with no warning. The check: the range of the dates, and the number of rows in each month. Dates outside the period the data should cover, or months that should be empty, reveal it.


Adding a month to 31 January asks for 31 February, which does not exist:

ymd("2015-01-31") + months(1)

[1] NA

ymd("2015-01-31") %m+% months(1)

[1] "2015-02-28"


Plain + gives NA, without a warning. %m+% moves to the last day of the target month. If the AI builds dates by adding months, look at which operator it used, and count the missing values afterwards.

title: 07-1: Dates and Text
section: What pattern matching is
text:
What pattern matching is

Exact comparisonPattern matchingRegular expressions


R compares text character by character. To R, these are four different values:

counties <- c("Lancaster", "LANCASTER", "Lancaster  County", "lancaster")
counties == "Lancaster"

[1]  TRUE FALSE FALSE FALSE


Only the first equals "Lancaster": case differs in two, and the third has more characters (including two spaces). So counting, grouping or joining on this column treats one county as four.


Pattern matching asks a different question: does the text contain a given sequence of characters, anywhere? The sequence is called the search pattern (in code, the input named pattern).

str_detect(counties, "Lancaster")

[1]  TRUE FALSE  TRUE FALSE


The third value now matches too, because it contains Lancaster. Pattern matching is how code finds rows by part of their text, replaces part of a value, or takes a value apart. For example, pizzas with chicken have ckn in their name:

unique(pizza$name[str_detect(pizza$name, "ckn")])

[1] "thai_ckn"    "bbq_ckn"     "southw_ckn"  "cali_ckn"    "ckn_pesto"  
[6] "ckn_alfredo"




A regular expression is a search pattern written in a small language in which some characters have a special meaning. "ckn" is a regular expression with no special characters, so it means just those three letters. With special characters, one search pattern can say more:

"^ckn": ckn at the start of the text
"ckn$": ckn at the end
"ckn|chicken": either one


unique(pizza$name[str_detect(pizza$name, "^ckn")])

[1] "ckn_pesto"   "ckn_alfredo"


The table of special characters is on the slide “Regular expressions”. You do not need to write regular expressions; you need to recognise that a search pattern is one, and to check what it matched.

title: 07-1: Dates and Text
section: How text code is written
text:
How text code is written
Almost every function in stringr, the tidyverse package for text, starts with str_ and follows one pattern.

The patternEvery function follows the patternVariations you will see



str_function(text, pattern, replacement)









Part
What it is
Required?




str_function
What to do with the matches: detect, replace, extract, count, split
Yes


text
The text to work on, usually a column, always the first input
Yes


pattern
The search pattern, a regular expression saying what to look for, the second input
Yes, for functions that look for something


replacement
What a match becomes
Only for str_replace() and str_replace_all()



A real line that follows the pattern, making pizza names readable:

str_replace_all("thai_ckn", "_", " ")

[1] "thai ckn"











Code
What it gives




str_detect(text, pattern)
TRUE or FALSE for each value: does it contain the search pattern?


str_count(text, pattern)
how many times each value contains it


str_replace(text, pattern, replacement)
the first match in each value replaced


str_replace_all(text, pattern, replacement)
every match replaced


str_remove_all(text, pattern)
every match deleted


str_extract(text, pattern)
the part of each value that matched


str_split(text, pattern)
each value cut into pieces where the search pattern occurs



Some take no search pattern, only the text: str_to_lower() and str_to_upper() (change case), str_trim() (remove spaces at the start and end), str_squish() (also turn runs of spaces inside into one), str_pad() (add characters until a set width, such as leading zeros), and str_c() (join pieces into one text).



filter(table, str_detect(name, "ckn")): keep the rows that match; mutate(name = str_to_lower(name)): change a column.
grepl("ckn", x), sub(), gsub("_", " ", x): the base R versions. Note the order: in base R the search pattern comes first and the text later.
str_detect(x, regex("corn", ignore_case = TRUE)): the search pattern ignores upper and lower case.
str_detect(x, fixed(".")): the search pattern is taken literally, with no special characters.

title: 07-1: Dates and Text
section: Regular expressions: characters with a special meaning
text:
Regular expressions: characters with a special meaning

The tableA special character used by mistake





In a search pattern
Means
Example
Matches




.
any one character
"c.n"
can, con, c5n


^
the start of the text
"^ckn"
ckn_pesto, not thai_ckn


$
the end of the text
"ckn$"
thai_ckn, not ckn_pesto


[0-9] or \\d
one digit
"[0-9]"
any value with a digit


+
one or more of the previous
"[0-9]+"
7, 2015


\\s
a space (or tab)
"\\s+"
one or more spaces


\\.
a real dot
"\\."
. only



And | means or: "veg|garden" matches text containing either word.
The two backslashes are how R writes one backslash inside quotes. They turn a special character back into an ordinary one.


Removing the dot from 3.5:

str_replace_all("3.5", ".", "")

[1] ""

str_replace_all("3.5", fixed("."), "")

[1] "35"


. means any character, so every character was removed, leaving empty text. No error. fixed(".") (or "\\.") means the dot itself. Text with ., (, +, $ or ? in it, such as Bros. or ($), needs this care.

title: 07-1: Dates and Text
section: Text: the silent failures
text:
Text: the silent failures

A search pattern that matches more than intendedA search pattern that matches less than intendedOnly the first match


You want the pepperoni pizzas, and the AI uses the search pattern "pep":

unique(pizza$name[str_detect(pizza$name, "pep")])

[1] "pepperoni"    "peppr_salami" "pep_msh_pep" 


peppr_salami is a pepper salami pizza. It contains pep too, so it is counted as pepperoni. No error, and a count or a total that is too large. The check: list the distinct values the search pattern matched, and read them.


Text that means the same thing but is written differently does not match:

crops <- c("Wheat", "wheat", "WHEAT", "Winter  wheat", "Barley")
sum(str_detect(crops, "wheat"))

[1] 2


Wheat and WHEAT were missed, because upper and lower case are different characters. The usual fix makes the text consistent first:

cleaned <- str_squish(str_to_lower(crops))
cleaned

[1] "wheat"        "wheat"        "wheat"        "winter wheat" "barley"      


The check: the distinct values, with a count of each, before and after cleaning. Here 5 distinct values became 3. Whether that is right depends on what you know: is winter wheat its own crop, or wheat?


str_replace() changes the first match in each value; str_replace_all() changes every one:

str_replace("pep_msh_pep", "_", " ")

[1] "pep msh_pep"

str_replace_all("pep_msh_pep", "_", " ")

[1] "pep msh pep"


On a column where most values have one _, the first version looks right on every row you happen to look at. The check: a few rows before and after, including one with more than one match.

title: 07-1: Dates and Text
section: Working with AI on your own research
text:
Working with AI on your own research
Dates and text follow the same way of working as everything else (lecture 02-1, “Working with AI on your own research”): you ask, the AI writes into a Quarto document with one plain-English sentence above each chunk, you render, and you judge the HTML.
For dates and text, the HTML matters because the failures are silent. A warning that some values failed to parse is one line in the chat that scrolls away; in the HTML it sits under the chunk that caused it, next to the check that counts the missing values.
Every request that asks for code ends with the closing instructions, the same lines as in 03-1. The full text is under Recommended requests.

title: 07-1: Dates and Text
section: Look at the column before you ask
text:
Look at the column before you ask

WhyDistinct values of a text columnRaw values of a date column


You cannot tell the AI how dates are written, or which spellings mean the same thing, without looking. Two things to look at:

Dates: a handful of raw values, from different parts of the file. Do they put the year, the month or the day first? Is any first or second number above 12? Is the year written with two digits or four?
Text: every distinct value, with how often it occurs. That is the only way to see every spelling.




pizza |> count(size)

# A tibble: 5 × 2
  size      n
  <chr> <int>
1 L     18956
2 M     15635
3 S     14403
4 XL      552
5 XXL      28


5 sizes, each spelled one way, so this column needs no cleaning. On a column typed by people, this list is where you find Corn, corn and CORN.



pizza$date[c(1, 20000, 40000)]

[1] "2015-01-01" "2015-05-24" "2015-10-21"


Year first, four digits, then month, then day: ymd(). Looking at rows from different parts of the file matters: the first few rows may not represent the rest.

title: 07-1: Dates and Text
section: What to put in your request
text:
What to put in your request
The AI already knows the functions. Your request supplies what it cannot know, most of it from looking at the data:

The column: which table and column, and what it holds
How it is written: for dates, the order of year, month and day, with an example value; for text, the spellings you found
What you want back: a date column; or the one spelling each group should have, such as all lower case
What you expect: the first and last date the data should cover, how many values fail to parse (usually 0), how many distinct values there should be after cleaning
Ask for checks: missing values before and after, the range of dates, distinct values before and after, a few rows before and after (see “Checking the result”)
The closing instructions





Using an agent in your editor or terminal?


An agent such as Claude Code can look at the column itself. Still write down how the dates are written and what range you expect before it runs, so you have something to compare against.

title: 07-1: Dates and Text
section: A weak request and a strong one
text:
A weak request and a strong one

WeakStrongWhat came backOrders per month


Convert the date column and count the orders in each month.
The AI has to guess how the dates are written, and nothing in its answer will tell you whether any failed to parse or landed in the wrong month.


An example for the pizza orders:
The table pizza has a text column date, written year-month-day with a
four-digit year, for example 2015-01-01. The data should cover every day
of 2015. Convert date into a date column, using the tidyverse, then
count the orders in each month.

Check: the number of dates that failed to parse (I expect 0), the first
and last date (2015-01-01 and 2015-12-31), the number of distinct dates
(365), and three rows showing the text beside the parsed date.

Put the code in my Quarto document analysis/dates.qmd, under the
heading "Orders per month", as R code chunks. Above each chunk, write

The four checksReading the HTML

Why

A student asked for readable pizza names (underscores as spaces, each word capitalised) and expected the 32 distinct names to stay 32. In the HTML:


Code the AI wrote

  mutate(name_nice = str_to_title(str_replace(name, "_", " ")))

cat(
  paste("distinct names: expected 32, got", n_distinct(named$name_nice)),
  paste("rows: expected 49574, got", nrow(named)),
  sep = "\n"
)


distinct names: expected 32, got 32
rows: expected 49574, got 49574

  distinct(name, name_nice) |>
  filter(name %in% c("thai_ckn", "five_cheese", "pep_msh_pep"))

Checks that come from knowing the data
The checks above apply to any date or text column. The most useful checks come from what you know about this data.

to HTML.
The AI’s code and what it printed. It makes every day of 2015 with seq() (a sequence of dates, one day apart), then keeps the days that do not occur in orders:


Code the AI wrote

no_orders <- every_day[!every_day %in% orders$date]
data.frame(date = no_orders, weekday = wday(no_orders, label = TRUE))

Christmas Day, four Mondays in a row in October, and two days in September. Believable closures, not a parsing problem. But a daily average over “every day of the year” must know these days are missing.


Every pizza with ckn in its name should have the type chicken, and no other pizza should:


Code the AI wrote
pizza |> count(has_ckn = str_detect(name, "ckn"), type)


# A tibble: 4 × 3

1 FALSE   classic 14888

3 FALSE   veggie  11649
4 TRUE    chicken 11050


They agree: all 11,050 rows whose name contains ckn are chicken, and no other row is. A check like this tests the search pattern against a second column you trust.

title: 07-1: Dates and Text
section: Your turn: read the AI’s code
text:
Your turn: read the AI’s code
A student asked an AI to “add up the sales of vegetable items” from a file of shop sales whose dates look like 03/04/2025, and got this:

sales <- read.csv("C:/Users/kim/Desktop/sales.csv")
sales$day <- as.Date(sales$day, "%m/%d/%y")
veg <- sales[grepl("veg", sales$item), ]
sum(veg$amount)


QuestionsAnswers


A. What does each of the four lines do?
B. Which line will fail on your computer, and why?
C. Which two problems give a wrong result without an error?
D. Which check would have caught each one?


A. Reads the file; converts day from text to dates, month first; keeps the rows whose item contains veg; adds up amount over those rows.
B. Line 1. The folder C:/Users/kim/... exists only on Kim’s computer.
C. Line 2 uses %y, a two-digit year, for four-digit years, so every date lands in 2020 (it reads 20 of 2025). Line 3 is case sensitive, so it would miss a value such as Veg box, and would also match one such as vegan cookies, if the file has them. (Whether 03/04 is month first is a third question: only the source of the file can tell you.)
D. The first and last date would show 2020. The distinct values of item that matched, and the distinct values that did not, would show both search pattern problems.

title: 08-2: Regression Tables
section: What you will and will not learn today
text:
What you will and will not learn today

The planDirections


An AI assistant can estimate regressions and put them in a table in seconds. What it cannot do is:

know which models you meant to compare, and why
know which estimate your message is about
know how many observations each model should have
tell whether the table shows the models you meant

Those are your job. So today is about:

The concept: what a reader needs from a regression table
Reading code: recognising what a line of regression-table code does
Asking AI: what to put in the request
Checking: that the table shows the models you meant, with the observations you expected

This deck assumes lecture 08-1 (the message, the display table, the table standard). It does not teach regression itself: what an estimate or a standard error means is the subject of your econometrics course.



Ask your AI assistant to install the modelsummary package if you have not already.
The data on these slides is airquality, which comes with R, so there is no file to download.

title: 08-2: Regression Tables
section: The data and the models on these slides
text:
The data and the models on these slides
airquality has one row per day in New York, May to September 1973: 153 rows. The columns used here:







Column
What it is




Ozone
Ozone concentration (parts per billion)


Temp
Maximum temperature (degrees Fahrenheit)


Wind
Average wind speed (miles per hour)


Solar.R
Solar radiation (langleys, a unit of sunlight energy per area)



The message: “Hotter days have more ozone, and the relationship holds after accounting for wind and sunlight.” So three models (regressions), each adding a variable:

m1 <- lm(Ozone ~ Temp, data = air)
m2 <- lm(Ozone ~ Temp + Wind, data = air)
m3 <- lm(Ozone ~ Temp + Wind + Solar.R, data = air)

lm() estimates a linear regression. To the left of ~ is the outcome (what the model explains); to the right, the variables that explain it.

title: 08-2: Regression Tables
section: What the reader needs from a regression table
text:
What the reader needs from a regression table
A reader of a regression table is asking four questions. Each part of the table answers one:







The reader asks
The part of the table that answers




Which models are these? What does each explain, with which variables?
The column headers and title; which coefficient rows are filled in for each column


How large is the estimate the message is about?
The coefficient rows (one per variable), in plain words with units


How precise is it?
The standard error in parentheses below each estimate, and a note saying which kind of standard error


What data is behind each model?
The number of observations at the bottom of each column, and notes on the sample



Anything that does not answer one of these questions is clutter for this reader. The comparison the message is about runs across the columns: here, how the temperature estimate changes as wind and sunlight are added.

title: 08-2: Regression Tables
section: The pattern
text:
The pattern
A regression table function does the work of the display table (lecture 08-1) for you: it takes the estimated models and lays out one column per model. Every call follows the same pattern.

The patternCommon optionsVariations you will see



modelsummary(
  list("header 1" = model_1, "header 2" = model_2, ...),
  option = value, ...
)









Part
What it is
Required?




list(...)
The models, one per column, in the order of the columns
Yes, the only required input


"header 1" =
The header of that column. Leave it out and the header is (1), (2), …
No


option = value
What to show and how: labels, which rows, standard errors, title, notes
No; each has a default



The header is attached to the model by the = inside list(). Nothing checks that the header describes the model: list("Soybeans" = corn_model) gives a column called “Soybeans” with the corn results in it.










Option
What it does
Default if left out




coef_map = c("raw" = "Label")
Renames coefficient rows, sets their order, and drops every coefficient not listed
raw names, in the order the models have them


coef_rename = c("raw" = "Label")
Renames only; keeps every coefficient
raw names


gof_map = ...
Which rows go at the bottom (observations, R squared)
about eight rows


vcov = "HC1"
Which standard errors
the classical ones from lm()


fmt = 2
Number of decimals
3


align = "lrrr"
Alignment, one letter per column: l left, r right
centred numbers


stars = TRUE
Adds significance stars and a note defining them
no stars


title = "...", notes = "..."
Title and notes
none


output = "flextable" or "gt"
Hands back a flextable or gt table, to change further with the steps from 08-1
a table for the document being rendered



msummary() is a shorter name for the same function.



modelsummary::modelsummary(...): the package name, then ::, then the function.
The list of models stored first under a name, models <- list(...), then modelsummary(models, ...).
Models from other functions in the same list, such as fixest::feols() for models with fixed effects (one constant per group, such as per county). The table code is the same.
modelsummary(...) |> some_step(): the table passed on to a styling step from 08-1, after output = "flextable" or "gt".

title: 08-2: Regression Tables
section: One real example
text:
One real example
The “After” table, as you would see it in the HTML: a sentence, then the chunk.
Put the three ozone models side by side, with plain labels and the temperature row first, only observations and R squared at the bottom, robust standard errors, two decimals, a title and notes.


Code the AI wrote
coef_labels <- c(
  "Temp" = "Temperature (°F)",
  "Wind" = "Wind speed (miles per hour)",
  "Solar.R" = "Solar radiation (langleys)",
  "(Intercept)" = "Constant"
)
modelsummary(
  list("(1)" = m1, "(2)" = m2, "(3)" = m3),
  coef_map = coef_labels,
  gof_map = list(
    list(raw = "nobs", clean = "Observations (days)", fmt = 0),
    list(raw = "r.squared", clean = "R squared", fmt = 2)
  ),
  vcov = "HC1",
  fmt = 2,
  align = "lrrr",
  title = "Ozone (parts per billion) and the weather, New York, May to September 1973",
  notes = c(
    "Each column is a linear regression of ozone on the variables listed. Robust standard errors (HC1) in parentheses.",
    "Days with a missing value in any variable a model uses are left out of that model.",
    "Data: airquality, which comes with R."
  )
)


You should be able to point at the part that sets each label, the part that decides which rows appear at the bottom, and the part that chooses the standard errors. The column order comes from the order inside list().

title: 08-2: Regression Tables
section: Which standard errors, and saying so
text:
Which standard errors, and saying so

Same estimates, different standard errorsAn option that does nothing


There are several ways to compute standard errors, and your econometrics course says which one a model needs. In the table, vcov = chooses. It changes the standard errors only, never the estimates:


Code the AI wrote
modelsummary(
  list("Classical" = m2, "Robust (HC1)" = m2),
  vcov = list("classical", "HC1"),
  coef_map = c("Temp" = "Temperature (°F)", "Wind" = "Wind speed (miles per hour)"),
  gof_map = list(list(raw = "nobs", clean = "Observations (days)", fmt = 0)),
  fmt = 2
)

The estimates are identical; the standard errors in parentheses are not. A reader cannot tell which kind they are looking at unless a note says so.


Older code and older tutorials write statistic_override = instead of vcov =. That name no longer exists, and modelsummary() accepts it without an error or a warning, and ignores it:


Code the AI wrote
modelsummary(
  list("Asked for robust" = m2),
  statistic_override = list(sandwich::vcovHC(m2, type = "HC1")),
  coef_map = c("Temp" = "Temperature (°F)", "Wind" = "Wind speed (miles per hour)"),

The standard errors are the classical ones from the previous tab, not the robust ones that were asked for. AI assistants learned from older code too, so they sometimes write this. The same happens with any option name modelsummary() does not know, such as a misspelling (vcovv =).
The check: for one model, print the table with and without the change of standard errors. If nothing moves, the change was not applied.

title: 08-2: Regression Tables
section: Does the table show the models you meant?
text:
Does the table show the models you meant?
The AI can write the checking code. It cannot know which models you meant or how many observations each should have. Ask for these after every regression table:










Ask the AI to print
Why
What only you can supply




1
each column’s header next to its model’s formula
A header is attached by position in list(), and nothing checks it describes the model
which model goes in which column


2
the number of observations of each model
Rows with a missing value are dropped without a word (next slide)
the count you expect, from looking at the data


3
one estimate, straight from the model
Confirms the table shows that model’s numbers
which estimate the message is about


4
every coefficient each model has, against the rows in the table
coef_map drops any coefficient it does not list
which variables each model should have



Checks 2 and 4 catch failures that give no error at all. The next two slides show them.

title: 08-2: Regression Tables
section: Observations: what lm() drops without saying
text:
Observations: what lm() drops without saying

The checkWhyWhat it means for the table


air has 153 rows. A student expects each model to use all of them, and asks the AI to print the check:


Code the AI wrote
models <- list("(1)" = m1, "(2)" = m2, "(3)" = m3)
for (name in names(models)) {
  cat(paste0("observations in model ", name, ": expected ", nrow(air),
             ", got ", nobs(models[[name]])), "\n")
}


observations in model (1): expected 153, got 116 
observations in model (2): expected 153, got 116 
observations in model (3): expected 153, got 111 


All three checks fail.


lm() leaves out every row with a missing value in any variable the model uses, and says nothing. Ozone is missing on 37 days and Solar.R on 7, some of them the same days:


Code the AI wrote
cat(
  paste("days with Ozone and Temp:", sum(complete.cases(air[, c("Ozone", "Temp")]))),
  paste("days with Ozone, Temp, Wind and Solar.R:",
        sum(complete.cases(air[, c("Ozone", "Temp", "Wind", "Solar.R")]))),
  sep = "\n"
)


days with Ozone and Temp: 116
days with Ozone, Temp, Wind and Solar.R: 111


So the expected count is the number of rows with no missing value in any variable the model uses: 116, 116 and 111. Model (3) uses 5 fewer days than model (2).


When the columns use different rows, a change across the columns has two possible causes: the added variable, or the different days. Here the difference is small; in other data it can be large.
What to do, and to decide before you look at the estimates:

Say it in a note: “Days with a missing value in any variable a model uses are left out of that model”, with the number of observations shown for every column.
If the comparison across columns is the message, estimate every model on the same rows, those with no missing value in any variable of the largest model, and say so in a note.

title: 08-2: Regression Tables
section: Coefficients that disappear
text:
Coefficients that disappear
coef_map renames coefficient rows and sets their order, and drops every coefficient it does not list. Here the AI was asked to label temperature and forgot wind:


Code the AI wrote
modelsummary(
  list("(1)" = m1, "(2)" = m2),
  coef_map = c("Temp" = "Temperature (°F)"),
  gof_map = list(list(raw = "nobs", clean = "Observations (days)", fmt = 0)),
  fmt = 2
)

                (2)
