Column (2) is a model with wind in it, but the table shows no wind row and no constant, and nothing says they are missing. Sometimes leaving rows out is what you want (a note then says “also includes …”); it should never happen by accident.
The check: ask the AI to list each model’s coefficients next to the rows of the table, and to say which ones are not shown.

title: 08-2: Regression Tables
section: The table that comes before the regressions
text:
The table that comes before the regressions
Papers usually show a table of the variables before the regressions: how many observations, the average, the spread, the range. The same package makes it, with a pattern of its own.

The patternOne real example



datasummary(rows ~ columns, data = table)









Part
What it is
Required?




rows
The variables, joined with +, one row each
Yes


columns
The statistics, joined with +: N, Mean, SD, Min, Max, Median
Yes


data = table
The data
Yes



Swap the two sides of ~ and the variables become columns. datasummary_skim(table) is a shortcut that summarises every column with its own choice of statistics.




Code the AI wrote
datasummary(
  Heading("Ozone (parts per billion)") * Ozone +
    Heading("Maximum temperature (°F)") * Temp +
    Heading("Wind speed (miles per hour)") * Wind +
    Heading("Solar radiation (langleys)") * Solar.R ~
    Heading("Days") * N + Mean + Heading("Std. dev.") * SD + Min + Max,
  data = air,
  fmt = 1,
  title = "Daily weather and ozone, New York, May to September 1973",
  notes = "Data: airquality, which comes with R."
)

title: 08-2: Regression Tables
section: The checklist
text:
The checklist
Apply it to any regression table, yours or the AI’s, in the rendered HTML. Each question has a yes or no answer.

Can a reader tell, from the headers and title alone, what each model explains and how the models differ?
Is the estimate the message is about easy to find (first row, plain label with units)?
Does a note say which standard errors are shown, and define any stars?
Is the number of observations shown for every model, and does it match what you expected?
Did the printed formulas match the column headers?
Is every coefficient each model has either shown, or mentioned in a note?
Does it meet every item of the table standard?

title: 08-2: Regression Tables
section: Your turn: read the AI’s code
text:
Your turn: read the AI’s code
A student asked an AI to “make a regression table of my ozone models with robust standard errors” and kept this:

modelsummary(
  list("Temperature only" = m1, "Plus sunlight" = m2, "Plus wind" = m3),
  statistic_override = list(sandwich::vcovHC(m1), sandwich::vcovHC(m2), sandwich::vcovHC(m3)),
  coef_map = c("Temp" = "Temperature", "Solar.R" = "Sunlight")
)


QuestionsAnswers


A. What does each part of the call do?
B. Which header is wrong? (Look at how m2 and m3 were defined on “The data and the models on these slides”.)
C. Besides the headers, which two problems give a wrong table without any error?
D. Which checks from “Does the table show the models you meant?” would catch each problem?


A. list(...): the three models, one column each, with their headers. statistic_override =: meant to use robust standard errors. coef_map =: label the temperature and sunlight rows, and show only those.
B. m2 is temperature plus wind, and m3 adds sunlight to that. The headers “Plus sunlight” and “Plus wind” are on the wrong columns.
C. statistic_override is ignored, so the standard errors are the classical ones, not the robust ones asked for. And coef_map drops wind and the constant, so the reader sees a model labelled “Plus wind” with no wind row. (Also missing: units in the labels, a title, a note on the standard errors.)
D. Check 1 (headers against formulas) catches the swapped headers. Check 4 (every coefficient against the table’s rows) catches the missing wind row. Printing the table with and without the change of standard errors catches the ignored statistic_override.

title: 08-2: Regression Tables
section: Working with AI on your own research
text:
Working with AI on your own research
Regression tables follow the same way of working as everything else (lecture 02-1, “Working with AI on your own research”): you ask, the AI writes into a Quarto document (.qmd) with one plain-English sentence above each chunk, you render it to HTML, and you judge the HTML.
For regression tables this matters because:

The models, the table and the checks sit in one document, so a header can be read next to the formula it describes.
When the data changes, rendering again re-estimates every model and rebuilds the table. No number is ever copied by hand.
Your advisor reviews the models by reading the HTML: what was estimated, on which rows, with which standard errors.

title: 08-2: Regression Tables
section: What to put in a regression table request
text:
What to put in a regression table request
The AI already knows modelsummary. Your request supplies what it cannot know:

The data: what one row is, the columns used, their units, and which have missing values
The models: for each column, the outcome and the variables, in the order the columns should appear
The message: which estimate the reader should look at, and the comparison across columns
The standard errors: which kind, from your econometrics course or your advisor
What to show: which coefficient rows, in which order and with which labels; which rows at the bottom
The checks: the number of observations you expect for each model, headers against formulas, every coefficient accounted for
The table standard, then the closing instructions

title: 08-2: Regression Tables
section: A weak request and a strong one
text:
A weak request and a strong one

WeakStrongWhat came back


Run regressions of ozone on the weather and make a nice table.
The AI chooses the models, their order, the standard errors and what to show. Whatever comes back, you have nothing to check it against.


In my R project, the table air has one row per day: Ozone (parts per
billion, missing on some days), Temp (degrees Fahrenheit), Wind (miles
per hour) and Solar.R (langleys, missing on some days).

Estimate three linear regressions of Ozone, one per column, in this
order: (1) on Temp; (2) on Temp and Wind; (3) on Temp, Wind and
Solar.R. The message is about the Temp estimate and how it changes
across the columns. Use robust standard errors (HC1). Show the rows
Temp, Wind, Solar.R and the constant, in that order, and at the bottom
only the number of observations and R squared. Use modelsummary.

Check: each column's header next to its model's formula; the number of
observations of each model (I expect 116, 116 and 111, the days with no
missing value in the model's variables); and every coefficient of each
model against the rows of the table.

<the table standard>

Put the code in my Quarto document analysis/regressions.qmd, under the
heading "Ozone and the weather", as R code chunks. Above each chunk,
write one plain-English sentence saying what it does and why. Build
every path with here::here(); no setwd(), no absolute paths. Print each
check on its own line as "name of check: expected X, got Y". Render the
document to HTML.
Replace <the table standard> with the block from Recommended requests.


The table on “One real example”, followed by the checks:


Code the AI wrote
models <- list("(1)" = m1, "(2)" = m2, "(3)" = m3)
expected_n <- c(116, 116, 111)
shown <- names(coef_labels)
not_shown <- setdiff(unlist(lapply(models, \(m) names(coef(m)))), shown)
lines <- c()
for (i in seq_along(models)) {
  col <- names(models)[i]
  lines <- c(lines,
    paste0("formula of column ", col, ": ", deparse(formula(models[[i]]))),
    paste0("observations in column ", col, ": expected ", expected_n[i],
           ", got ", nobs(models[[i]])))
}
lines <- c(lines, paste("coefficients not shown in the table: expected 0, got",
                        length(not_shown)))
cat(lines, sep = "\n")


formula of column (1): Ozone ~ Temp
observations in column (1): expected 116, got 116
formula of column (2): Ozone ~ Temp + Wind
observations in column (2): expected 116, got 116
formula of column (3): Ozone ~ Temp + Wind + Solar.R
observations in column (3): expected 111, got 111
coefficients not shown in the table: expected 0, got 0


Every line matches. The last check compares each model’s own list of coefficients with the labels the table uses (coef_labels, from the table’s code), so neither list is typed twice. The student could only write “116, 116 and 111” by counting the complete days first, as on “Observations: what lm() drops without saying”.

title: 08-2: Regression Tables
section: Requests you can copy
text:
Requests you can copy
Copy one, then replace every <...> with what you know: the models, the message, the observations you expect. Every table request ends with the table standard and then the closing instructions.

Closing instructionsThe table standardRegression tableSame rows for every modelSummary statistics tableExplain code


The lines that end every request for code. Replace the two blanks; leave “expected X, got Y” as it is, because it tells the AI how to print each check:
Put the code in my Quarto document <path to your .qmd>, under the
heading "<heading>", as R code chunks. Above each chunk, write one
plain-English sentence saying what it does and why. Build every path
with here::here(); no setwd(), no absolute paths. Print each check on
its own line as "name of check: expected X, got Y". Render the document
to HTML.
A chat assistant cannot render: paste its chunks into your .qmd and render it yourself. An agent in your editor or terminal can do every step.


The same block as in lecture 08-1. Paste it into every table request, just before the closing instructions:
Every table must meet this standard:
1. Column headers and row labels in plain words with units, such as
   "Corn yield (bushels per acre)", never a column name such as
   corn_yield.
2. Categories in words, such as "Irrigated", never a code such as 1.
3. Numbers rounded to what the message needs, with the same number of
   decimals down each column.
4. Thousands separators in large numbers, except in years.
5. Percentages shown as percentages.
6. Numbers right-aligned so that the digits line up; text left-aligned.
7. Text no smaller than the document's body text.
8. Fits the page width where it will appear, without scrolling.
9. Rows in an order that serves the message (by value, or in time
   order), not alphabetical unless the reader will search a long table.
10. A title that says what the numbers are.
11. A note giving the source of the data.
12. A note saying how any computed column was computed.
13. The number of observations behind each value, when it varies.
14. Nothing the message does not need: no extra columns, no row
    numbers, no heavy borders, no colours that only decorate.
For regression tables, also:
15. One column per model, with headers or a title saying what each
    model explains.
16. Standard errors in parentheses below each estimate, with their kind
    stated in a note.
17. Significance stars left out, or defined in a note and used the same
    way in every table.
18. The number of observations for every model.


In my R project, <the table or file> has one row per <what one row
is>. The columns used: <each column, what it means, its units, and
whether it has missing values>.

Estimate <the kind of model, such as linear regressions>, one per
column, in this order: <for each column, the outcome and the
variables>. The message is about <the estimate the reader should look
at, and the comparison across columns>. Use <the kind of standard
errors>. Show the rows <the coefficients, in order>, and at the bottom
only <the rows you want, such as the number of observations>. Use
modelsummary.

Check: each column's header next to its model's formula; the number of
observations of each model (I expect <the number for each model>); and
every coefficient of each model against the rows of the table.

<the table standard>

Put the code in my Quarto document <path to your .qmd>, under the
heading "<heading>", as R code chunks. Above each chunk, write one
plain-English sentence saying what it does and why. Build every path
with here::here(); no setwd(), no absolute paths. Print each check on
its own line as "name of check: expected X, got Y". Render the document
to HTML.


When the comparison across columns is the message and the models would otherwise use different rows:
Estimate every model in the table on the same rows: those with no
missing value in any of <the variables of the largest model>. I expect
<number> rows. Add a note to the table saying so, and print the number
of observations of each model as a check.

Put the code in my Quarto document <path to your .qmd>, under the
heading "<heading>", as R code chunks. Above each chunk, write one
plain-English sentence saying what it does and why. Build every path
with here::here(); no setwd(), no absolute paths. Print each check on
its own line as "name of check: expected X, got Y". Render the document
to HTML.


In my R project, <the table or file> has one row per <what one row
is>. Make a table of summary statistics with one row per variable for
<the variables, each with its plain-word label and units>, and the
columns: number of observations, mean, standard deviation, minimum and
maximum. Use modelsummary's datasummary(). Check the number of
observations of each variable against <the counts you expect>.

<the table standard>

Put the code in my Quarto document <path to your .qmd>, under the
heading "<heading>", as R code chunks. Above each chunk, write one
plain-English sentence saying what it does and why. Build every path
with here::here(); no setwd(), no absolute paths. Print each check on
its own line as "name of check: expected X, got Y". Render the document
to HTML.


For code you did not write, or code you are not sure about:
Explain this R code to me. For each line, write one plain-English
sentence. Then list:
1. which model ends up in which column, with its formula
2. any option that is ignored, misspelled, or drops rows or
   coefficients without saying so

<paste the code here>

title: 08-2: Regression Tables
section: What you must understand, and what the AI can write
text:
What you must understand, and what the AI can write







You need to understand
The AI can write




Which models answer your question, and in which order to show them
lm() and the list() of models


Which estimate the message is about
coef_map, labels and order


Which standard errors the models need
vcov =


How many observations each model should have, from the missing values in the data
The check that prints them


What the reader needs: labels with units, observations, notes
gof_map, title, notes



Every regression table: write down the models and the number of observations you expect, then ask for the table with the table standard and the checks, written into your .qmd. Render it, and check that every header matches its formula, every count matches, and every coefficient is accounted for.

title: 09-1: Spatial Data and Vector Layers
section: What you will and will not learn today
text:
What you will and will not learn today

The planDirections


Spatial data is data about where things are: counties, wells, rivers, fields. An AI assistant can write the code that reads it, combines it and measures it. What it cannot do is:

know what the coordinates in your files mean
see where your places are supposed to be
tell whether a map or an area it produced is right

Those are your job. So today is about:

The concept: the two kinds of spatial data, what one row of a spatial table is, and what a coordinate reference system is
Reading code: recognising what a line of spatial code does
Asking AI: what to put in your request
Checking: four checks to print for every spatial layer, and why each one matters




Ask your AI assistant to install the sf, tidyverse and here packages if you have not already. sf is the package for vector data in R.
The data files used on these slides sit in the same folder as the slides, so a path here is just the file name. In your own project, paths are built with here::here() (lecture 03-1).

title: 09-1: Spatial Data and Vector Layers
section: Two kinds of spatial data
text:
Two kinds of spatial data

Vector and rasterWhat they look likeWhich one when



Vector data stores separate things, each with a shape made of coordinates: a point (a well), a line (a railroad), a polygon (a county). Each thing is called a feature, and each feature has its own values, such as a county’s name.
Raster data stores a grid of equal cells covering an area, with one value per cell: precipitation, temperature, elevation, a satellite image. There are no separate things, only cells.

This lecture is about vector data. Lecture 09-2 is about raster data.


Nebraska’s 93 counties (polygons) and 1,000 irrigation wells (points), two vector layers drawn together. A layer is one spatial dataset: one file, one table in R.



















Your data is about
Kind
Examples




Separate things with a boundary or a location
Vector
counties, fields, farms, wells, roads, weather stations


A quantity that varies continuously over an area
Raster
rainfall, temperature, elevation, satellite images

title: 09-1: Spatial Data and Vector Layers
section: One row of a spatial table is one feature
text:
One row of a spatial table is one feature

The tableThe lines above the tableKinds of shape


In R, a vector layer is a table (an sf table, after the package). It looks like any other table, with one extra column, geom or geometry, that holds each feature’s shape:

counties

Bounding box:  xmin: -104.0535 ymin: 40 xmax: -95.30829 ymax: 43.00171

2       003  Antelope MULTIPOLYGON (((-98.3006 42...
3       005    Arthur MULTIPOLYGON (((-101.9856 4...

One row is one county: its code, its name, and its shape. Filtering rows, adding columns, and joining other tables by countyfp, with the layer first (left_join(layer, table)), work as on any table, and the shape stays attached to its row. With the ordinary table first, the result is no longer a layer.









Line
What it tells you




Simple feature collection with 93 features and 2 fields
93 rows (features) and 2 columns besides the shape


Geometry type: MULTIPOLYGON
The kind of shape in every row


Bounding box:
The smallest rectangle that holds every feature: lowest and highest x, lowest and highest y


Geodetic CRS: NAD83
What the coordinates mean (next slide)



These four lines hold three of the four checks this lecture asks you to print for every layer.










Geometry type
What it is
Example




POINT
One location
a well


LINESTRING
A path through several points
a stretch of railroad


POLYGON
An area enclosed by a boundary
a field


MULTI...
Several pieces that belong to one feature
a county with an island, a river with branches



The AI picks the right functions for each type. What you need is to know which type your data should be, so that a layer of farms that comes back as POINT (one location per farm) instead of POLYGON (each farm’s boundary) is caught.

title: 09-1: Spatial Data and Vector Layers
section: A coordinate reference system says what the numbers mean
text:
A coordinate reference system says what the numbers mean

The ideaThe same place, two CRSsWhy layers must share one


A shape is stored as numbers: pairs of x and y. The numbers alone do not say where on Earth the place is. The coordinate reference system (CRS) does: it says what the numbers are measured in and from where. There are two kinds:

Geographic: longitude and latitude, in degrees. Longitude is x, latitude is y.
Projected: the curved Earth drawn onto a flat surface, with x and y in metres (or feet) from a chosen starting point. Each one is accurate for one region, for example UTM zone 14N for central North America.

Each common CRS has a catalogue number, its EPSG code: 4269 is NAD83 longitude and latitude, used by most US government data; 4326 is WGS84 longitude and latitude, used by GPS; 26914 is NAD83 / UTM zone 14N, in metres.


The centre of Lancaster County, Nebraska:



CRS
x
y




NAD83, EPSG 4269 (degrees)
-96.69
40.78


NAD83 / UTM zone 14N, EPSG 26914 (metres)
695,105
4,517,342



Same place, completely different numbers. Moving a layer from one CRS to another (transforming it) recomputes every coordinate.


Combining two layers, for example asking which county each well is in, compares their numbers directly. That only makes sense if both sets of numbers mean the same thing, so two layers must be in the same CRS before they can be combined.
sf checks this for you, as far as it can. If the two CRSs differ, it stops with an error:

st_intersects(wells, st_transform(counties, 26914))

Error in st_geos_binop("intersects", x, y, sparse = sparse, prepared = prepared, : st_crs(x) == st_crs(y) is not TRUE


That is the good case: you know something is wrong. The silent failures come when a layer’s CRS is wrong or missing, because then sf has nothing correct to check against. They are later in this deck.

title: 09-1: Spatial Data and Vector Layers
section: Reading a layer from a file
text:
Reading a layer from a file

The patternFormatsWriting


Vector layers come in several file formats. Whatever the format, reading one follows the same pattern as reading a table in lecture 03-1:

layer <- reader_function("path/to/file")









Part
What it is
Required?




layer <-
The name the layer will have inside R
Needed to keep the result


reader_function
st_read() or read_sf(), both from sf; they differ only in how they print
Yes


"path/to/file"
Where the file is
Yes, the only required input



A real line:

counties <- st_read("ne_counties.gpkg")

Reading layer `ne_counties' from data source 
  `/Users/taromieno/Teaching/Data-Science-with-R-AI/lectures/Chapter-9-Spatial-Data/ne_counties.gpkg' 
  using driver `GPKG'
Simple feature collection with 93 features and 2 fields
Geometry type: MULTIPOLYGON
Dimension:     XY
Bounding box:  xmin: -104.0535 ymin: 40 xmax: -95.30829 ymax: 43.00171
Geodetic CRS:  NAD83


st_read() prints a short report as it reads; the CRS is on its last line.


The same reader opens all of them:








Extension
Format
What to know




.shp
Shapefile, the format of ArcGIS
One layer is several files with the same name: .shp (shapes), .shx (an index), .dbf (the columns), .prj (the CRS). Without the .prj, the layer has no CRS.


.gpkg
GeoPackage
One file, keeps the CRS


.geojson
GeoJSON
One file, always longitude and latitude in WGS84


.rds
R’s own format
One file, the exact R object, only R opens it





Saving a layer follows the writing pattern of lecture 03-1:

st_write(layer, "path/to/file.gpkg")

The extension picks the format. Two things to know:

A csv cannot hold a shape. write_csv() on a layer writes the shapes as long lines of text that nothing reads back as shapes. Save layers as .gpkg (or .rds if only R will read them).
st_write() refuses to replace an existing file unless told to (delete_dsn = TRUE), unlike the writers in lecture 03-1.

title: 09-1: Spatial Data and Vector Layers
section: Turning a table with coordinates into a layer
text:
Turning a table with coordinates into a layer

The patternA real example


Data often arrives as an ordinary table with two coordinate columns, for example a csv of wells. To R it is just a table with two columns of numbers. One function turns it into a layer:

layer <- st_as_sf(table, coords = c("x column", "y column"), crs = code)









Part
What it is
Required?




table
The ordinary table
Yes


coords = c(...)
The two coordinate columns, x first: longitude before latitude, or easting before northing (x and y in metres in a projected CRS)
Yes


crs = code
What the numbers mean, as an EPSG code
Not required by R, but required by you. Left out, the layer has no CRS at all, and nothing warns you.



Only you can supply the CRS. It is not in the numbers; it is in the documentation that came with the data.



wells_table <- read_csv("wells_ne.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
head(wells_table, 3)

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  wellid longdd latdd
   <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>
1  13242  -98.3  40.5
2  26925  -98.4  40.3
3  30542  -99.4  40.4


longdd and latdd are longitude and latitude in decimal degrees. The source of this data documents them as NAD83, EPSG 4269.

wells <- st_as_sf(wells_table, coords = c("longdd", "latdd"), crs = 4269)

title: 09-1: Spatial Data and Vector Layers
section: Doing things with a layer
text:
Doing things with a layer

The patternTable verbs still workVariations you will see


Almost every spatial function in sf starts with st_ and takes the layer first:

result <- st_function(layer, other_inputs)









Function
What it does
What to know




st_crs(layer)
Prints the CRS
The first check


st_transform(layer, code)
Moves the layer into another CRS, recomputing every coordinate
Use it to make two layers share a CRS


st_set_crs(layer, code)
Labels the layer with a CRS, changing no number
Only for a layer whose CRS is missing and known from its documentation. On a layer that has a CRS, it puts the layer in the wrong place.


st_area(layer)
Area of each polygon
Units come with the result, such as [m^2]


st_length(layer)
Length of each line
Same


st_distance(a, b)
Distance between every feature of a and every feature of b
Same


st_buffer(layer, dist)
A zone of width dist around each feature
dist is in metres for a longitude/latitude layer, and in the units of the CRS for a projected one. State the units in your request.


st_centroid(layer)
The centre point of each feature



st_drop_geometry(layer)
Removes the shape, giving an ordinary table






filter(), mutate(), select() and joins by a column work on a layer as on any table, and the shape stays with its row:

counties |>
  filter(name %in% c("Lancaster", "Douglas")) |>
  mutate(area_km2 = as.numeric(st_area(geom)) / 1e6)

Simple feature collection with 2 features and 3 fields
Geometry type: MULTIPOLYGON
Dimension:     XY
Bounding box:  xmin: -96.91393 ymin: 40.52301 xmax: -95.87149 ymax: 41.39331
Geodetic CRS:  NAD83

1      055   Douglas MULTIPOLYGON (((-96.47072 4...  878.490
2      109 Lancaster MULTIPOLYGON (((-96.91393 4... 2189.456


Two variations you will see in AI-written code: sf::st_area(...), with the package name in front, and units::set_units(st_area(geom), km^2), which converts the units instead of dividing by a million. Both do the same thing as above.



layer |> st_transform(26914) |> st_buffer(2000): several steps passed along with |>
st_transform(layer, st_crs(other_layer)): “use the other layer’s CRS”, the usual way to make two layers match
st_transform(layer, "EPSG:26914"): the code written as text; the same as 26914

title: 09-1: Spatial Data and Vector Layers
section: Conditions for spatial data to be right
text:
Conditions for spatial data to be right

The conditionsWith and without an error



Every layer has the right CRS: its label says what its numbers really mean.
Layers share a CRS before they are combined.
x and y are in the right order: longitude (or easting) first.
Distances and areas are computed in known units, metres or feet, never in degrees.
One row is the feature you think it is, and the count of rows matches what you expect.




If condition 2 fails, sf stops with an error (previous section). Annoying, but you know.
If condition 1, 3, 4 or 5 fails, you get a layer, a map or a number with no error, and it is wrong. This deck calls these silent failures, as lecture 03-1 does.




Important


Every one of these silent failures is visible in the printed CRS, the bounding box, or a quick map. That is why those are the checks.

title: 09-1: Spatial Data and Vector Layers
section: Silent failures
text:
Silent failures

Coordinates in the wrong orderThe wrong CRSNo CRS: areas in degrees


People say “lat/long”, so latitude often ends up first:

wells_swapped <- st_as_sf(wells_table, coords = c("latdd", "longdd"), crs = 4269)
st_bbox(wells_swapped)

      xmin       ymin       xmax       ymax 
  40.00194 -103.96276   41.68503  -97.04458 


The bounding box puts the wells at x between 40 and 42 and y between -104 and -97. Nebraska is at longitude -104 to -95 and latitude 40 to 43, so x and y are swapped. A latitude of -104 does not exist, yet the layer was created with no error and no warning, and any map or calculation that follows runs.


The same wells, with their coordinates in UTM zone 14N metres, read with the CRS a quick request would guess, longitude and latitude:

wells_utm_table <- wells |>
  st_transform(26914) |>
  mutate(easting = st_coordinates(geometry)[, 1],
         northing = st_coordinates(geometry)[, 2]) |>
  st_drop_geometry()

wells_mislabelled <- st_as_sf(wells_utm_table, coords = c("easting", "northing"), crs = 4269)
st_bbox(wells_mislabelled)

      xmin       ymin       xmax       ymax 
  84452.06 4429383.06  664818.05 4618751.22 


Asking how many wells lie in a Nebraska county:

sum(lengths(st_intersects(wells_mislabelled, counties)) > 0)

Warning in st_is_longlat(x): bounding box has potentially an invalid value
range for longlat data


[1] 0


Zero of 1000, with no error. The only sign is a warning that the bounding box “has potentially an invalid value range for longlat data”, easy to miss among other output. The two layers carry the same CRS label, so sf combined them, but the numbers in one of them are metres. Only the bounding box (x in the hundreds of thousands cannot be a longitude) shows why.


A shapefile whose .prj file was lost has no CRS. Here the counties are saved as a shapefile, the .prj is deleted, and the rest is read back:

shp <- file.path(tempdir(), "counties.shp")
st_write(counties, shp, delete_dsn = TRUE, quiet = TRUE)
invisible(file.remove(sub("shp$", "prj", shp)))
counties_no_crs <- st_read(shp, quiet = TRUE)
st_crs(counties_no_crs)

Coordinate Reference System: NA


Its areas:

head(st_area(counties_no_crs), 3)

[1] 0.1553024 0.2423037 0.2007834

sum(st_area(counties_no_crs))

[1] 21.61443


Without a CRS, st_area() treats the numbers as plain x and y and returns square degrees, with no units and no warning. All of Nebraska comes to 21.6. With the CRS, it comes to 200,052 square kilometres. A square degree is not a fixed area either: it shrinks toward the poles.
The fix here is st_set_crs(), with the CRS from the data’s documentation, because the numbers are right and only the label is missing.

title: 09-1: Spatial Data and Vector Layers
section: Working with AI on your own research
text:
Working with AI on your own research
The way of working from lecture 02-1, “Working with AI on your own research”, applies unchanged:

You ask. Your request says what you want, what you know about the data, and which checks to print.
The AI writes into a Quarto document (.qmd). Code goes into code chunks, with one plain-English sentence above each chunk saying what it does and why.
You render the .qmd to HTML.
You read the HTML and decide whether the work is right: the sentences, the code, and the check results side by side.

For spatial data the HTML matters even more, because two of the four checks are a printed bounding box and a quick map, and you judge both by eye. The rendered document puts each map next to the code that made it and the numbers that describe it, and it stays with your project after the chat is gone.



Note


Every request that asks for code ends with the same few lines, the closing instructions; the full text is under Recommended requests near the end.

title: 09-1: Spatial Data and Vector Layers
section: Look at the files before you ask
text:
Look at the files before you ask

What to look forThe numbers tell you a little


You cannot tell the AI what the coordinates mean without finding out first. For each file:

Its format, from the extension. For a shapefile, check that the .shx, .dbf and .prj files are there too.
Its CRS. It is in the documentation: a README, a metadata page, the website it came from. For a csv with coordinates, this is the only place it is.
What one row is: a well, a county, a county in one year.
How many rows there should be: 93 counties in Nebraska, 1,000 wells in the file.
Where the place is, roughly, in longitude and latitude. Nebraska is about -104 to -95 longitude and 40 to 43 latitude; any map site will tell you this for any place.



The raw first lines of a csv with coordinates:

readLines("wells_ne.csv", n = 3)

[1] "wellid,longdd,latdd"        "13242,-98.293531,40.506244"
[3] "26925,-98.422662,40.301043"


Numbers between -180 and 180 with several decimals look like longitude and latitude in degrees. Numbers in the hundreds of thousands or millions are metres or feet in a projected CRS. That narrows it down; it does not tell you which CRS. Only the documentation does.

title: 09-1: Spatial Data and Vector Layers
section: What to put in your request
text:
What to put in your request
The AI knows every st_ function. Your request supplies what it cannot know:

The files: names, formats, and where they sit in your project
The CRS of each file, from its documentation, as an EPSG code if you have one, and which columns hold x and y for a csv
What one row is, and how many rows there should be
What you want back: the layers, the CRS to work in, and units for any area or distance
Ask for checks: the CRS of every layer, the number of features, the bounding box, a quick map (next section)
The closing instructions





Using an agent in your editor or terminal?


An agent such as Claude Code can open the files itself. It still cannot read a CRS that is not in the file. Write down the CRS and where the place should be before it runs.

title: 09-1: Spatial Data and Vector Layers
section: A weak request and a strong one
text:
A weak request and a strong one

WeakStrongWhat came back


Load my wells csv and the county map and count the wells in each county.
The AI has to guess the file names, which columns are coordinates, and what they mean. A typical reply:

wells <- read.csv("wells.csv")
wells_sf <- st_as_sf(wells, coords = c("lat", "lon"), crs = 4326)
counties <- st_read("counties.shp")

Latitude first, a CRS guessed, and a shapefile read without checking it has a CRS. Every one of these runs.


An example for wells and counties:
In my R project, data/wells.csv has one row per irrigation well (1,000
wells). Columns longdd and latdd are longitude and latitude in NAD83,
EPSG 4269. data/counties.gpkg has the 93 counties of Nebraska, also in
EPSG 4269. Read both, making the wells a spatial layer.

Then check, for each layer: the CRS (I expect EPSG 4269), the number of
features (1,000 and 93), and the bounding box (I expect longitude
between -104 and -95 and latitude between 40 and 43). Draw a quick map
of each layer on its own.

Put the code in my Quarto document analysis/import.qmd, under the
heading "Read the spatial data", as R code chunks. Above each chunk,
write one plain-English sentence saying what it does and why. Build every
path with here::here(); no setwd(), no absolute paths. Print each check
on its own line as "name of check: expected X, got Y". Render the
document to HTML.


In the rendered HTML, a sentence, then the chunk it describes.
Read the county layer, and make the wells table a spatial layer using its longitude and latitude columns in NAD83.

counties <- st_read(here::here("data", "counties.gpkg"), quiet = TRUE)
wells <- read_csv(here::here("data", "wells.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("longdd", "latdd"), crs = 4269)

Print the CRS, the number of features and the bounding box of each layer, against what was expected.

for (nm in c("counties", "wells")) {
  layer <- get(nm)
  bb <- round(st_bbox(layer), 1)
  cat(nm, "CRS: expected EPSG 4269, got EPSG", st_crs(layer)$epsg, "\n")
  cat(nm, "features: expected", paste0(c(counties = 93, wells = 1000)[[nm]], ","), "got", nrow(layer), "\n")
  cat(nm, "longitude: expected -104 to -95, got", bb["xmin"], "to", bb["xmax"], "\n")
  cat(nm, "latitude: expected 40 to 43, got", bb["ymin"], "to", bb["ymax"], "\n")
}

for (nm in ...) repeats the lines inside the braces once for each layer name, and get(nm) fetches the layer by its name. The output is in the next section.

title: 09-1: Spatial Data and Vector Layers
section: The four checks
text:
The four checks

What to ask for, and whyAsking for themReading the HTML


The AI can write the checking code. It cannot know the right answers. Ask for these for every layer, after reading it and after every step that changes it:










Ask the AI to print
Catches
What only you can supply




1
the CRS
a missing CRS, a guessed one, two layers that do not match
the CRS from the documentation


2
the number of features
rows lost or duplicated, a file cut short
the count you expect


3
the bounding box
x and y swapped, numbers in metres labelled as degrees, a layer in the wrong place
where the place is


4
a quick map of each layer on its own
anything the numbers did not show: a missing piece, points in the sea, the wrong shapes
what the place looks like



For a layer of shapes, also ask for the geometry type, and for any area or distance, ask for the units to be printed with the numbers.


One sentence at the end of your request does it:
For every layer, print the CRS, the number of features and the bounding
box, and draw a quick map of the layer on its own.
Better, say what you expect, so the HTML says which checks passed:
I expect <layer> to be in EPSG <code>, with <number> features, and
longitude between <west> and <east> and latitude between <south> and
<north>. Print each check on its own line as "name of check: expected X,
got Y".
The bounding box is in the units of the layer’s CRS. For a layer in metres, ask for the box after transforming to longitude and latitude, so you can compare it with a map.


What the checking code on the previous slide printed:


counties CRS: expected EPSG 4269, got EPSG 4269 
counties features: expected 93, got 93 
counties longitude: expected -104 to -95, got -104.1 to -95.3 
counties latitude: expected 40 to 43, got 40 to 43 
wells CRS: expected EPSG 4269, got EPSG 4269 
wells features: expected 1000, got 1000 
wells longitude: expected -104 to -95, got -104 to -97 
wells latitude: expected 40 to 43, got 40 to 41.7 


Every line matches. The wells cover only part of the state (their box is smaller than the counties’ box), which is what the quick map on the “Two kinds of spatial data” slide also shows: no wells in the northern part of the state. Whether that is right is a question about the data, for whoever produced it.

title: 09-1: Spatial Data and Vector Layers
section: Checks that come from knowing the place
text:
Checks that come from knowing the place
The four checks apply to any layer. Checks from what you know about this place are stronger, and no AI will think of them for you.

The counties of a state should add up to the state’s area. Nebraska is about 200,000 square kilometres (any encyclopedia).
Every well in a file of Nebraska wells should fall inside a Nebraska county.

Using the layers counties and wells, print the total area of the
counties in square kilometres (I expect about 200,000), and the number
of wells that fall inside a county (I expect all 1,000).

Put the code in my Quarto document analysis/import.qmd, under the
heading "Check against the place", as R code chunks. Above each chunk,
write one plain-English sentence saying what it does and why. Build
every path with here::here(); no setwd(), no absolute paths. Print each
check on its own line as "name of check: expected X, got Y". Render the
document to HTML.
The AI’s code, and what it printed:


Code the AI wrote
total_km2 <- sum(units::set_units(st_area(counties), km^2))
inside <- sum(lengths(st_intersects(wells, counties)) > 0)
cat("total area: expected about 200,000 km2, got", format(round(as.numeric(total_km2)), big.mark = ","), "\n")


total area: expected about 200,000 km2, got 200,052 


Code the AI wrote
cat("wells inside a county: expected 1000, got", inside, "\n")


wells inside a county: expected 1000, got 1000 


Both pass. Run on wells_mislabelled from the “Silent failures” slide, the second check gives 0; run on counties_no_crs, the first gives 21.6. Neither failure can get past these two lines.

title: 09-1: Spatial Data and Vector Layers
section: Your turn: read the AI’s code
text:
Your turn: read the AI’s code
A student asked an AI to “draw a 5 km zone around each well and give me the area of one zone”, and got this:

setwd("C:/Users/jsmith/Desktop/gis")
wells <- st_as_sf(read_csv("wells.csv"), coords = c("longdd", "latdd"), crs = 4269)
zones <- st_buffer(wells, dist = 5)
st_area(zones[1, ])


QuestionsAnswers


A. What does each line do?
B. Which line will fail on your computer?
C. Which problem gives a wrong answer without an error?
D. Which check would catch it, and what is its expected value?


A. Changes the working directory; reads the csv and makes it a layer of points in NAD83 longitude and latitude; draws a zone of width 5 around each well; prints the area of the first zone.
B. Line 1. That folder exists only on jsmith’s computer.
C. Line 3. For a longitude/latitude layer, sf measures dist in metres, so dist = 5 draws a zone of 5 metres, not 5 kilometres. When run, line 4 prints 79 [m^2]. The request said “5 km”, the code says 5, and nothing warns that the units differ.
D. The area of one zone, with its units. A circle of radius 5 km has an area of about 78.5 square kilometres, so the expected value is known before anything runs; 79 square metres is a million times too small. The fix is dist = 5000, or units::set_units(5, km), and a request that states the units.

title: 09-1: Spatial Data and Vector Layers
section: What you must understand, and what the AI can write
text:
What you must understand, and what the AI can write







You need to understand
The AI can write




Vector or raster, and which geometry type your features are
The reader and the geometry functions


What one row of a layer is, and how many there should be
filter(), mutate(), joins on layers


What a CRS is, and which one each of your files is in, from its documentation
st_as_sf(..., crs = ), st_set_crs(), st_transform()


That layers must share a CRS before being combined
Transforming one to match the other


Where your place is, and how big it is
The checking code



Every spatial layer: find its CRS in the documentation and write down how many features it has and where it should be. Ask the AI to write the code and the four checks into your .qmd: CRS, number of features, bounding box, quick map. Render it, and judge the HTML against what you wrote down.

title: 09-3: Communicating with Maps
section: What you will and will not learn today
text:
What you will and will not learn today

The planDirections


A map is a figure in which position means place. Everything in lecture 04-1 about figures applies: a map exists to convey one fact or idea to a reader. An AI assistant can draw any map in seconds. What it cannot know is:

what you want the reader to take away
who the reader is
whether a map is the right figure for that at all
whether the map shows every place it should

So today is about:

The message: when a map is the right figure, and what to map
Reading code: recognising what each line of map code does
Design: the choices that decide whether a map conveys its message, collected in a map standard to add to every map request
Checking: what must be true of the data before a map can be right




Lectures 04-1 (communicating with figures), 09-1 (vector data) and 09-2 (raster data) come first.
Ask your AI assistant to install sf, terra, tidyterra and tidyverse if you have not already.
The data on these slides is about Nebraska: county boundaries, corn harvested acres by county for 2020 to 2023, irrigation wells, and daily precipitation. The files sit in the same folder as the slides.

title: 09-3: Communicating with Maps
section: A map only when the message is about where
text:
A map only when the message is about where

The ruleMessage A, about whereMessage B, a ranking


Before any map, write the one sentence the reader should take away, and who the reader is (lecture 04-1). Then ask: is the sentence about where? A map makes location easy to see and almost everything else hard: comparing two counties’ values on a map means matching two shades of colour against a legend.







The message is about
Best figure




Where something is high or low, or a pattern across space
A map


Which places rank highest, or how two places compare
A sorted bar or dot chart


How a value changes over time
A line chart, or a few maps if the change is about where





“On 2 August 2012, rain fell in two bands, one across the south of Nebraska and one across the north-east, while the west stayed dry.”









The pattern across the state is the message, and only a map shows it.


“Custer County harvested the most corn acres in Nebraska in 2023.”









A ranking. On a map, the reader would have to find ten counties and compare their shades; sorted bars make it a glance.

title: 09-3: Communicating with Maps
section: What to map: totals or rates
text:
What to map: totals or rates

The problemTotal acresShare of land


Places on a map differ in size, and the eye reads area. A large county with a middling value covers more of the page than a small county with a high one. So the choice of what to map is part of the message:

Total, such as acres of corn: the right choice when the message is about where the amount is.
Rate, such as the share of land in corn, or acres per square kilometre: the right choice when the message is about how intensely a place does something.












Custer County, the largest total at 236,500 acres, is also one of the largest counties: corn covers only 14% of its land.











Hamilton County has the highest share, 59%. Same data, a different map, and a different message. Neither is wrong; only the message decides.

title: 09-3: Communicating with Maps
section: The shape every map shares
text:
The shape every map shares
You will not write map code from memory. You need to look at any map code the AI writes and say which layer is drawn, and which column is shown by what. A map in ggplot2 has the same shape as any figure in lecture 04-1, with one difference: each layer usually has its own data.

The patternEvery map layer has this shapeOne real exampleLayers and CRS



ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = layer, aes(fill = column)) +
  geom_sf(data = other_layer) +
  scale_fill_...() +
  labs(...) +
  theme_void()

title: 09-3: Communicating with Maps
section: Colour on a map
text:
Colour on a map

Three kinds of scaleAbove or below a midpointContinuous or classes


The same three kinds of colour scale as in lecture 04-1, with the same rule: the kind of value decides.








The value is
Scale
Example




An amount, from low to high
One hue, light to dark (sequential)
acres, share of land, precipitation


Above or below a meaningful midpoint
Two hues, diverging from a neutral middle at the midpoint
change since 2020, with no change at the middle


A category
Distinct hues
land-cover type, irrigated or not



All scales on these slides are from the viridis and ColorBrewer families, which colour-blind readers can tell apart.


“Between 2020 and 2023, corn acres fell in most counties that report both years.”









Brown for a fall, blue-green for a rise, white for a change within 1%, with the classes symmetric around zero. 23 of the 69 counties with both years rose. The 24 counties without both years are a darker grey, because light grey is too close to the white middle.



A continuous scale (previous tabs) shows every difference, but the reader cannot match a shade to a number closely.
Classes, such as “20 to 30%”, give a few colours the reader can match to the legend exactly, at the cost of hiding differences inside a class.

Use classes when the reader needs to read values off the map; a continuous scale when the overall pattern is the message. Five or six classes are as many as a reader can tell apart. In ggplot2, the legend of a continuous scale has no entry for missing values, which is one more reason the maps on these slides use classes: “No data” can be one of them.

title: 09-3: Communicating with Maps
section: Places with no data
text:
Places with no data

The problemThe fix


In the 2023 data, only 69 of Nebraska’s 93 counties report corn acres. If the map is drawn from the corn table alone, the other 24 are simply not there:









The reader sees a state with pieces missing, or, on a white page, reads the gaps as “no corn”. Neither is what the data says: the data says nothing about those counties.


Start from all the places (the county layer), join the values to it, and give the places without a value a class of their own, “No data”, named in the legend. Every map of corn acres from the “What to map” slide on is drawn this way. The step that keeps every county:

corn_2023 <- counties |>
  left_join(filter(corn_table, year == 2023), by = c("countyfp" = "county_code"))

The layer comes first, so all 93 counties stay, and the 24 without a 2023 value get NA.

On a light-to-dark scale, light grey has no hue, unlike every colour of the scale, so it cannot be read as a low value.
On a diverging scale the middle is nearly white, so light grey can look like “no change”. Use a darker grey there, and name it in the legend.
On a raster, cells outside the area were never measured: draw them transparent, not grey or black.

title: 09-3: Communicating with Maps
section: Other choices that decide whether the message lands
text:
Other choices that decide whether the message lands

Leave out what the message does not needPoints on polygonsSeveral maps



Longitude and latitude axes and gridlines: the reader knows where Nebraska is. theme_void() removes them. Keep them only if the reader needs to read coordinates.
Heavy borders: thin white or light grey lines separate places without competing with the colours.
A scale bar and a north arrow (from the ggspatial package): only when distance or direction matters to the message, or the area is unfamiliar to the reader.



Layers drawn later sit on top, so the layer that carries the message goes last. With many points, small points let the reader see where they crowd together:









The counties are context, so they are light; the wells are the message, so they are the darkest thing on the map.


Several maps of the same variable, such as one per day, must share one colour scale, or the same colour means different values in different maps. facet_wrap() does that by default:









Five days, one scale, no-data cells transparent, and the legend in the empty sixth panel.

title: 09-3: Communicating with Maps
section: The map standard
text:
The map standard
A map is a figure, so it must meet the figure standard from lecture 04-1. On top of that, every map must meet this standard. Each item has a yes or no answer.

If the message is not about where, say so and suggest a chart instead.
Map a rate rather than a total when places differ in size and the message is about intensity; say which you mapped and why.
The colour scale suits the value: one hue from light to dark for amounts; two hues diverging from a neutral middle at the midpoint given in my request for values above or below it; distinct hues for categories. Readable by colour-blind readers.
Start from the full layer of places. Places with no data inside the mapped area drawn in a grey that the colour scale does not use (light grey, or a darker grey on a diverging scale whose middle is nearly white) and labelled “No data” in the legend; never left out, never shown as zero. Raster cells outside the area, which were never measured, are transparent.
No longitude and latitude axes or gridlines, unless the reader needs to read coordinates.
Boundaries thin and light; the layer that carries the message drawn on top.
Several maps of the same variable share one colour scale.
No scale bar or north arrow unless distance or direction matters to the message.
Item 7 of the figure standard does not apply: a map’s shape is the place’s shape.

The copyable version, to add to every map request after the figure standard, is in Recommended requests at the end of this deck.

title: 09-3: Communicating with Maps
section: What must be true of the data
text:
What must be true of the data

The conditionsSeveral rows per placeThe check



One row per place drawn. A table with several rows per place (one per year) draws several shapes on top of each other.
Every place is there: the map starts from the full layer of places, and the values are joined to it.
The layers line up: every layer has the right CRS (lecture 09-1), so the wells sit inside the state.
The colour column has the right type: a county code stored as a number gets a colour gradient, as in lecture 04-1.



The corn file has one row per county and year, 277 rows for four years. Drawn without choosing a year:









No error, and it looks like a finished map. But each county is drawn up to four times, one shape on top of the other, and the one on top is the last row of that county in the file, which is sorted by year: 2023 for 69 counties, 2022 for 11 counties, 2021 for 4 counties, 2020 for 1 county. The map mixes four years and says nothing about it.


Ask the AI to print the table the map is drawn from, next to the map, with the counts that matter:


Code the AI wrote
map_table <- st_drop_geometry(corn_2023)
cat("places drawn: expected 93, got", nrow(map_table), "\n")


places drawn: expected 93, got 93 


Code the AI wrote
cat("places drawn more than once: expected 0, got", sum(duplicated(map_table$countyfp)), "\n")


places drawn more than once: expected 0, got 0 


Code the AI wrote
cat("places with a value plus No data: expected 93, got",
    sum(!is.na(map_table$acre)), "+", sum(is.na(map_table$acre)), "\n")


places with a value plus No data: expected 93, got 69 + 24 


The map table has one row per county and every county in it. The same lines for corn itself would say 277 places drawn and 192 drawn more than once.

title: 09-3: Communicating with Maps
section: The checklist
text:
The checklist
Apply it to any map, yours or the AI’s, by looking at it in the rendered HTML, at the size a reader will see it. Each question has a yes or no answer.

Can someone who has not seen the data state the message within a few seconds?
Is the message about where?
Does the colour scale match the kind of value?
Are places with no data visible and named, and distinguishable from low values?
Does every colour carry information?
Is everything on the map needed for the message?
Does it meet each item of the figure standard and the map standard?
Does the table printed next to the map have one row per place drawn, with every place in it?

A “no” to any question is something to fix or a reason to choose a different design.

title: 09-3: Communicating with Maps
section: Your turn: judge a map
text:
Your turn: judge a map
The message is meant to be: “Irrigation wells are concentrated along the Platte River and in the south of the state.”


QuestionsAnswers


A. What in this map carries information, and what is decoration?
B. Which items of the map standard does it fail?
C. Write the request you would send to fix it.


A. The positions of the wells carry the message. The colour shows wellid, a registration number with no meaning for the message: decoration that the reader will try to interpret. The rainbow scale is also hard for colour-blind readers.
B. Item 5 (longitude and latitude axes and gridlines), item 6 (heavy black borders and dark grey fill compete with the wells; large points hide where they crowd), item 3 (a colour scale for a value that should not be shown at all), and the figure standard’s plain-word legend.
C. Something like: “The message: irrigation wells are concentrated along the Platte River and in the south. The reader: an extension audience. Draw the wells as small points of one colour on light county outlines, with no colour scale and no axes”, followed by the figure standard, the map standard and the closing instructions. A layer of rivers would help a reader who does not know where the Platte runs.

title: 09-3: Communicating with Maps
section: Working with AI on your own research
text:
Working with AI on your own research
Maps follow the same way of working as everything else (lecture 02-1, “Working with AI on your own research”): you ask, the AI writes into a Quarto document, you render, and you judge the HTML.
For maps, the HTML matters even more:

A map’s colours, legend and text only exist at the size it is shown in the document.
The map sits next to the sentence that says what it shows, so you can check that the two agree.
The table the map is drawn from, with its counts of places, can be printed right next to it.

Every map request ends with the figure standard, the map standard, and then the closing instructions. All three are under Recommended requests.

title: 09-3: Communicating with Maps
section: What to put in a map request
text:
What to put in a map request
The AI already knows how to draw any map. Your request supplies what it cannot know:

The data: the files, their CRS (lecture 09-1), what one row is, which column the map shows and its units
The places: the full layer of places, so that none goes missing
The message: the one sentence the reader should take away
The reader: who will see it, and what they already know about the area
Totals or rates, and for a value with a midpoint, what the midpoint is
Alternatives, not one answer: two or three designs to choose from
The figure standard, the map standard, then the closing instructions





Using an agent in your editor or terminal?


An agent such as Claude Code can open the files and look for itself. It still cannot know your message or your reader. Write those down before it runs.

title: 09-5: Spatial Joins: Matching Rows by Location
section: What you will and will not learn today
text:
What you will and will not learn today

The planDirections


You have a layer of wells and a layer of counties, and you want to know which county each well is in. Or you have nitrogen use by county and water quality by watershed, and you need them in one table. Neither layer has a column the other one shares. What they share is location.
An AI assistant can write the code that matches rows by location. What it cannot do is:

know which layer should keep one row per feature in your result
know whether a feature matching several others, or none, is a problem for your question
tell whether the matched table is right

So today is about:

The concept: what a spatial join is, how it differs from the merge by a key column of lecture 03-3, and what decides the number of rows it returns
Reading code: the pattern a join follows, and the summarising step that usually comes after it
Asking AI: what to say so the result has the rows you want
Checking: row counts before and after, features with no match, totals that must not change, and a map




Ask your AI assistant to install the sf, tidyverse and here packages if you have not already.
This lecture assumes lecture 09-1 (vector basics) and lecture 09-4 (spatial relations: intersects, within, within a distance), and the merges of lecture 03-3.
The data files used on these slides sit in the same folder as the slides, so a path here is just the file name. In your own project, paths are built with here::here() (lecture 03-1).

title: 09-5: Spatial Joins: Matching Rows by Location
section: A spatial join matches rows by where they are
text:
A spatial join matches rows by where they are

The ideaCompared with a merge by key columnAn example


A spatial join adds the columns of one layer to the rows of another, matching each row to the features it has a spatial relation with (lecture 09-4), usually “intersects”.

The target layer is the one whose rows you keep: you want a result with one row per target feature, or close to it.
The source layer is the one whose columns are brought in.

For each target feature, the join finds the source features that pass the relation and copies their columns onto the target’s row.


In lecture 03-3, two tables were merged by a key column (a column that identifies each row, such as a county code) that both tables had. A spatial join is the same operation with a different matching rule:









Merge by key column (lecture 03-3)
Spatial join




Rows are matched when
the key values are equal
the shapes pass a spatial relation


What both tables need
the same key column
shapes in the same CRS


Typical function
left_join(a, b, by = "fips")
st_join(a, b)


A row of a with no match
kept, with missing values (NA)
kept, with missing values (NA)


A row of a with several matches
repeated once per match
repeated once per match



The last two rows are the same in both. Everything you learned about unmatched rows and repeated rows in lecture 03-3 applies here. With locations, you count the matches of each target feature with lengths(st_intersects(target, source)) (lecture 09-4), before or after the join. st_join() has no relationship = or unmatched = option and never warns about many matches, so the printed checks are the only guard.


The wells layer has a well ID and the groundwater pumped (gw_extracted, acre-feet), but no county:

head(wells, 3)

Dimension:     XY
Bounding box:  xmin: -99.43785 ymin: 40.30104 xmax: -98.29353 ymax: 40.50624
Geodetic CRS:  NAD83

1  13242     65.95048 POINT (-98.29353 40.50624)
2  26925     74.39934 POINT (-98.42266 40.30104)
3  30542    162.28777 POINT (-99.43785 40.35229)


Joined to the counties, each well gets its county’s code and name:

wells_county <- st_join(wells, counties)
head(wells_county, 3)

Simple feature collection with 3 features and 4 fields

Dimension:     XY
Bounding box:  xmin: -99.43785 ymin: 40.30104 xmax: -98.29353 ymax: 40.50624
Geodetic CRS:  NAD83

1  13242     65.95048      001   Adams POINT (-98.29353 40.50624)
2  26925     74.39934      181 Webster POINT (-98.42266 40.30104)
3  30542    162.28777      137  Phelps POINT (-99.43785 40.35229)


The wells are the target, so the result is still 1000 wells, now with countyfp and name columns.

title: 09-5: Spatial Joins: Matching Rows by Location
section: How many rows come back
text:
How many rows come back
The number of rows a join returns is decided by how many source features each target feature matches:








Each target feature matches
Its rows in the result
Typical case




exactly one source feature
1
a well (point) in counties (polygons) that do not overlap


none
1, with NA in the source’s columns
a point outside every polygon


several
one per match, each a copy of the target row
a county (polygon) containing many wells; a watershed crossing several counties



So the same two layers give very different results depending on which is the target:

c(
  wells_as_target = nrow(st_join(wells, counties)),
  counties_as_target = nrow(st_join(counties, wells))
)

   wells_as_target counties_as_target 
              1000               1052 


1000 wells, each inside one county: 1000 rows. 93 counties as target: 1052 rows, because a county with 50 wells appears 50 times, and the 52 counties with no well appear once each with NA for the well’s columns (1000 + 52 = 1052).



Important


Before any join, decide which layer is the target and what one row of the result should be. “One row per county with the number of wells in it” is not what st_join(counties, wells) returns; it needs a summarising step after the join (next section).

title: 09-5: Spatial Joins: Matching Rows by Location
section: The join
text:
The join

The patternVariations you will seeA real example



joined <- st_join(target, source, join = st_relation, options)









Part
What it is
Required?




joined <-
The result: target rows with source columns added
Needed to keep the result


target
The layer whose rows (and shapes) you keep, always first
Yes


source
The layer whose columns are added, always second
Yes


join =
The spatial relation
No; the default is st_intersects


options
dist = for distance relations; left = FALSE to drop unmatched target rows; largest = TRUE to keep only the source feature with the largest overlap
No



The shapes in the result are the target’s. The source’s shapes are dropped.



st_join(wells, counties, join = st_within): a relation other than the default
st_join(yield_points, seed_points, join = st_is_within_distance, dist = 10): every source feature within 10 units of the CRS (lecture 09-4)
st_join(watersheds, counties, largest = TRUE): one match per target, the one it overlaps most
st_join(wells, select(counties, name)): only some source columns brought in
aggregate(wells["gw_extracted"], counties, FUN = sum): a join and a summary in one call (next slide), with the source first



The example on the previous slide, written out with its checks, as the AI would put it in a .qmd:
Join each well to the county it lies in.

wells_county <- st_join(wells, counties, join = st_intersects)

Check the rows and the matches.

cat(
  paste("rows: expected", nrow(wells), "(one per well), got", nrow(wells_county)),
  paste("wells with no county: expected 0, got", sum(is.na(wells_county$countyfp))),
  paste("wells matched twice: expected 0, got", sum(duplicated(wells_county$wellid))),
  sep = "\n"
)

rows: expected 1000 (one per well), got 1000
wells with no county: expected 0, got 0
wells matched twice: expected 0, got 0

title: 09-5: Spatial Joins: Matching Rows by Location
section: Summarising after a join
text:
Summarising after a join

The patternA real exampleArea-weighted summaries


When the target matches several source features (a county with many wells), the joined table has several rows per target. To get one row per target, summarise by the target’s ID:

summary_table <- joined |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  group_by(target_id) |>
  summarise(new_column = summary_function(source_column))








Step
What it does




st_drop_geometry()
Removes the shapes. Summarising with shapes attached also merges the shapes of each group, which is slow and not needed


group_by(target_id)
One group per target feature, by its ID column


summarise(...)
One row per group: a count, a sum, a mean of the source’s columns



The result is an ordinary table, which goes back onto the target layer with the key-column merge of lecture 03-3: left_join(counties, summary_table, by = "countyfp").


Groundwater pumped per county:

gw_by_county <- st_join(counties, wells) |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  group_by(countyfp, name) |>
  summarise(
    n_wells = sum(!is.na(wellid)),
    gw_total = sum(gw_extracted, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
arrange(gw_by_county, desc(n_wells)) |> head(3)

# A tibble: 3 × 4
  countyfp name    n_wells gw_total
  <chr>    <chr>     <int>    <dbl>
1 121      Merrick      83   10551.
2 047      Dawson       77    9879.
3 079      Hall         76    9413.


n_wells = sum(!is.na(wellid)) counts the rows that matched a well. The slide on silent failures shows why n(), which counts rows, is wrong here.


When target and source are both polygons (a watershed crossing several counties), a plain summary gives every overlapping source feature the same weight, however small the overlap. To weight by area, cut first, then summarise:

pieces <- st_intersection(target, source) |>     # one piece per overlap (lecture 09-4)
  mutate(area = st_area(geometry))
pieces |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  group_by(target_id) |>
  summarise(weighted = sum(source_value * area) / sum(area))

Each piece is the part of one target feature inside one source feature, with the columns of both, so its area is the weight.

title: 09-5: Spatial Joins: Matching Rows by Location
section: Conditions for a spatial join to be right
text:
Conditions for a spatial join to be right

The conditionsWith and without an error



Both layers are in the right CRS, and the same one (lecture 09-1). A layer with a wrong CRS lies somewhere else, and matches nothing.
The right layer is the target. It decides what one row of the result is.
The relation matches the question (lecture 09-4): “in”, “overlapping”, “within 10 m”.
You know how many matches each target should have: exactly one, at most one, or several. That decides whether a summarising step is needed and which checks to print.
For polygons against polygons, you know whether size of overlap matters. If it does, the summary must be weighted by area.




If the two layers have different CRSs, st_join() stops with an error. Good.
Every other failure gives a table with no error: rows quietly multiplied, rows with NA where a match was expected, averages that count a sliver of overlap as much as the whole. The next slide shows each one.

title: 09-5: Spatial Joins: Matching Rows by Location
section: Silent failures
text:
Silent failures

Several matches multiply rowsNo match still makes a rowA wrong CRS matches nothingEvery overlap counts the same


After st_join(counties, wells), each county appears once per well. Anything computed from the county’s own columns is now counted many times. Nebraska’s area, from the counties before and after the join:

area_km2 <- function(x) as.numeric(units::set_units(st_area(x), km^2))
c(before = sum(area_km2(counties)), after_join = sum(area_km2(county_wells)))

    before after_join 
  200052.3  2232722.6 


200,052 km² before, 2,232,723 after: each county’s area added once per well. No error; a total that should not change did.


Counting wells per county with n(), which counts rows:

county_wells |> st_drop_geometry() |> count(name) |> filter(name == "Loup")

  name n
1 Loup 1


Loup County has 0 wells, but it still has one row in the joined table (with NA for the well’s columns), so counting rows says 1. Every county without a well is reported as having one. Counting non-missing well IDs, sum(!is.na(wellid)), gives the right number.


Suppose the wells’ coordinates (longitude and latitude) were labelled with the wrong CRS, here UTM zone 14N, when the layer was made (lecture 09-1). Transformed so the CRSs agree, the join runs without error:

wells_mislabelled <- st_set_crs(st_drop_geometry(wells) |>
  bind_cols(st_coordinates(wells)) |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("X", "Y")), 26914)
joined_wrong <- st_join(st_transform(wells_mislabelled, st_crs(counties)), counties)
sum(is.na(joined_wrong$countyfp))

[1] 1000


All 1000 wells have no county. Read as metres in UTM zone 14N, numbers such as -98 and 40 put every well within a few metres of one spot on the equator, in the Pacific Ocean, far from any Nebraska county. The number of wells with no match is the check that catches it.


Watershed 07060004 (a hydrologic unit, or watershed, in Iowa) overlaps 8 counties. A plain join and mean gives each county the same weight:

round(sort(p_one$area / sum(p_one$area)), 3)

[1] 0.001 0.007 0.030 0.072 0.119 0.141 0.296 0.335


Those are the shares of the watershed in each county: the smallest is 0.1% of the watershed, yet it counts as one of 8 equal parts of the plain average. Plain mean of nitrogen rate: 216.9 lb/acre; weighted by area: 211.2. Here the two are close; with a large difference between a sliver county and the rest, they would not be.

title: 09-5: Spatial Joins: Matching Rows by Location
section: Working with AI on your own research
text:
Working with AI on your own research
The same way of working as on the slide of this name in lecture 02-1: you ask, the AI writes into your .qmd with one plain-English sentence above each chunk, you render, and you judge the HTML. For a join, judging the HTML means reading the row counts and the map, since a join that runs is not yet a join that matched the right rows. Every request for code ends with the closing instructions of lecture 03-1, under Recommended requests.

title: 09-5: Spatial Joins: Matching Rows by Location
section: Before you ask: three numbers to write down
text:
Before you ask: three numbers to write down

WhyFor the wells and counties


A join’s result is right or wrong mostly by its number of rows, and you can only judge that number if you wrote down what it should be before the code ran. Look at both layers (the four checks of lecture 09-1, plus a map of the two together), then write down:

What one row of the result should be: one well, one county, one watershed
How many matches each target should have: exactly one, at most one, or several
How many targets should have no match: often zero, sometimes some, and you should know why




One row should be one well, so the target is the wells, and the result should have 1000 rows.
Each well should lie in exactly one county, since counties do not overlap.
Every well in a Nebraska wells file should be in a Nebraska county, so zero wells without a county.

For “groundwater per county”, one row should be one county: 93 rows after the summarising step, with a count of 0 wells for some counties, and the county totals adding up to the total pumped by all wells.

title: 09-5: Spatial Joins: Matching Rows by Location
section: What to put in your request
text:
What to put in your request
The AI knows st_join(). Your request supplies what it cannot know:

The layers: file names, where they are, their CRSs, and the ID column of each
The target: which layer’s rows you keep, and what one row of the final table is
The relation: “inside”, “overlapping”, “within 10 m”
What to do with several matches: keep all, keep the largest overlap, or summarise (count, sum, mean, area-weighted mean) by the target’s ID
What to do with no match: keep with NA (the default) or drop, and how many you expect
Checks: rows before and after, targets with no match and with several, a total that must not change, a map
The closing instructions

title: 09-5: Spatial Joins: Matching Rows by Location
section: A weak request and a strong one
text:
A weak request and a strong one

WeakStrongWhat came back


Join the wells to the counties and get the number of wells per county.
The AI has to guess the target. With counties first and count() after it, every county without a well reports 1, as on the “Silent failures” slide.


In my R project, data/wells.gpkg (1,000 wells, ID column wellid) and
data/counties.gpkg (93 counties, ID column countyfp) are both in EPSG
4269. I want one row per county, with the number of wells in the county
and the total of gw_extracted, in a table called gw_by_county. Counties
with no well should be kept, with 0 wells and 0 pumped.

Then check: the number of rows (I expect 93), the number of wells with no
county (I expect 0), that the well counts add up to 1,000, that the
county totals add up to the total gw_extracted of all wells, and draw a
map of the counties filled by number of wells.

Put the code in my Quarto document analysis/wells.qmd, under the heading
"Wells per county", as R code chunks. Above each chunk, write one
plain-English sentence saying what it does and why. Build every path
with here::here(); no setwd(), no absolute paths. Print each check on its
own line as "name of check: expected X, got Y". Render the document to
HTML.


In the rendered HTML, a sentence, then the chunk it describes.
Join each well to its county, with the wells as the target so each well is one row.

wells <- st_read(here::here("data", "wells.gpkg"), quiet = TRUE)
counties <- st_read(here::here("data", "counties.gpkg"), quiet = TRUE)
wells_county <- st_join(wells, select(counties, countyfp))

Count wells and add up pumping by county, then put the result back on all 93 counties so those with no well get 0.

by_county <- wells_county |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  group_by(countyfp) |>
  summarise(n_wells = n(), gw_total = sum(gw_extracted))
gw_by_county <- counties |>
  left_join(by_county, by = "countyfp") |>
  mutate(n_wells = coalesce(n_wells, 0L), gw_total = coalesce(gw_total, 0))

Here n() is right, because the wells are the target: every row is a well. The counties with no well enter through the key-column merge, and coalesce() turns their NA into 0.
Print the checks.

cat(
  paste("rows: expected 93, got", nrow(gw_by_county)),
  paste("wells with no county: expected 0, got", sum(is.na(wells_county$countyfp))),
  paste("wells counted: expected 1000, got", sum(gw_by_county$n_wells)),
  paste("total pumped: expected", round(sum(wells$gw_extracted)), "got", round(sum(gw_by_county$gw_total))),
  sep = "\n"
)

rows: expected 93, got 93
wells with no county: expected 0, got 0
wells counted: expected 1000, got 1000
total pumped: expected 125449 got 125449


Every line matches.

The map from the strong request’s code, which the HTML shows under the checks:

  geom_sf(aes(fill = n_wells), colour = "grey60") +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Wells") +

title: 09-5: Spatial Joins: Matching Rows by Location
section: Checks that come from knowing the data

title: 09-5: Spatial Joins: Matching Rows by Location
section: Your turn: read the AI’s code
text:
Your turn: read the AI’s code
A student asked an AI to “get the average nitrogen rate for each watershed”, and got this:

huc_n <- st_join(huc, nitrogen)
avg <- huc_n |>
  group_by(HUC_CODE) |>
  summarise(n_rate = mean(nitrogen_rate))


QuestionsAnswers


A. What does each line do, and what is one row of huc_n? Of avg?
B. Watershed 07060004 overlaps 8 counties. How much does a county covering 0.1% of it count in its average?
C. What is slow about the second line, and how would you fix it?
D. Which watersheds’ averages describe only part of the watershed, and how would you find out?


A. The join gives one row per watershed-and-county overlap (224 rows from 28 watersheds); the summary gives one row per watershed, the plain mean of its counties’ rates.
B. Exactly as much as the county covering most of it: each of the 8 counties counts equally. An area-weighted mean (cut with st_intersection(), weight by area) fixes that.
C. The shapes are still attached, so summarise() also merges the shapes of each group. st_drop_geometry() before group_by() avoids it.
D. Those extending beyond the counties in nitrogen. Print, for each watershed, the share of its area covered by the pieces from st_intersection().
